**Surah Yusuf (Peace be upon him) (12)**

It is Meccan in its entirety according to the accepted view (al-mu'tamad). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that they said: "Except for the first three verses." Some scholars excepted a fourth, which is His (glorified is He) saying: ﴿Certainly there were signs in Joseph and his brothers for those who ask.﴾ All of these reports are extremely weak and should not be relied upon. What we have adopted, like others, is what is authentically related from the Scholar of the Community (al-Habr, i.e. Ibn 'Abbas). An-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from him. The last of them also narrated it from Ibn al-Zubayr. This is what is implied by what al-Hakim narrated and graded authentic from Rifa'ah ibn Rafi' in a lengthy report recounting Rafi''s arrival in Mecca, his acceptance of Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) teaching him this surah and (Read in the name of your Lord). Its number of verses is one hundred and eleven by consensus, as transmitted from al-Dani and others.

The occasion of its revelation, as narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, is that: "The Qur'an was sent down to the Messenger of Allah (upon him be blessings and peace), and he recited it to his companions for a time. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us,' and so it was revealed." It has also been said that it is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding what his people do to him, by comparison with what the brothers of Joseph (peace be upon him) did to him. It has also been said that the Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to tell them about the affair of Ya'qub (Jacob), his sons, and the circumstances of Yusuf and what befell him, and so it was revealed. It has also been said that the Meccan polytheists were instructed by the Jews to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the cause that led the Children of Israel to settle in Egypt, and so they asked him and it was revealed. What weakens the last two opinions, according to what they claim, is what al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Dala'il through the chain of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, that: "A Jewish scholar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him reciting the surah of Yusuf. He said: 'O Muhammad, who taught you this?' He said: 'Allah taught it to me.' The scholar was amazed at what he heard from him, so he returned to the Jews and said to them: 'By Allah, Muhammad recites the Qur'an as it was revealed in the Torah.' So he set off with a group of them until they entered upon him. They recognised him by his description and looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders. They began listening to the recitation of the surah of Yusuf, and they were amazed and embraced Islam at that moment." There is, however, what there is concerning the soundness of this report.

The connection between this surah and the one before it lies in its containing an account of what some of the prophets (peace be upon them) suffered from their relatives, whereas the earlier surah mentioned what they suffered from strangers. Also, what occurred earlier includes ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, and His saying: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾. Here there occurs the state of Ya'qub with his sons and the outcome of their affair, which is the strongest evidence of mercy. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir ibn Zayd that Yunus was revealed, then Hud, then Yusuf. This has been counted as another aspect of the connection.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾**

The discussion concerning this and its like is well known, and what has been given to you earlier of it is sufficiently convincing. The demonstrative in His saying (glorified is He): ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ refers, according to one view, to the Qur'an (the Book), and according to another, to the verses of this surah. It is indicated by the distant demonstrative, although these verses have not yet been mentioned, either because their revelation is anticipated, so they are treated as already preceding, or because their presence in the mind is treated as their external existence. The demonstrative used for the distant is employed in the first case because what is indicated, not being sensible, is treated as distant owing to its remoteness from the sphere of pointing, or because of its grandeur and the loftiness of its rank. In the second case, it is because, having reached the addressee from the sender, it has become like something far away.

Some have claimed that the demonstrative refers to what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), which is remote. More remote than that is the claim that it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, or to the verses mentioned in the surah of Hud. The intended "Book" is either this surah or the Qur'an. You have already been given, in the commentary on Yunus, something that should reassure you, so recall it here. As for *al-mubin* (the Clear), it derives from *abana*, meaning *bana* (to be evident), i.e., it became manifest. It is then intransitive: "the one whose matter is manifest," in that it is from the presence of Allah (exalted is He) and in its inimitability (i'jaz), or "the one whose meanings are clear to the Arabs," such that its realities are not confused for them and its subtleties are not obscure to them. It seems that, on both meanings, the genitive noun was omitted and the noun after it was put in its place, so it took the nominative and became concealed. This is not counted as the forbidden omission of the agent, so there is no need to say that the attribution is metaphorical in order to avoid it. Alternatively, it means *buyyina* (was made clear) in the sense of *azhara* (made manifest), in which case it is transitive and its object is understood: "the one that makes manifest what is in it of guidance and right direction," or "what the Jews asked about," or "what you were commanded to ask about, namely the cause that brought the Children of Israel to Egypt," or "the rulings and laws, the hidden aspects of dominion and sovereignty (al-mulk wa'l-malakut), the secrets of the two creations (the worldly and the otherworldly), and other things of wisdom, knowledge, and narratives."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that it is restricted to the lawful and the unlawful and what is needed in matters of religion. Ibn Jarir narrated from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said concerning this: "Allah (exalted is He) has made clear in it the letters that have dropped from the tongues of non-Arabs, and they are six letters: the *ta'*, *za'*, *sad*, *dad*, *'ayn*, and *ha'*, the unmarked ones (i.e. the emphatic and pharyngeal sounds)." What is stated in the *Farhang* and other books compiled in the Persian language is that the dropped letters are eight. Someone versified this as follows:

*Hashtt harfast ankih andar Farsi nayad hami tay namuzi binashi andarin ma'na mu'af*
*Bashnawa kanun ta kadam ast an huruf wa ya ki bir* ∗∗∗ *tha wa ha wa sad wa dad wa ta' wa za' wa 'ayn wa qaf*

However, the matter is based on what is common and prevalent. Otherwise, some of these letters exist in some of their words, as will not be hidden from one who investigates. It seems that the description according to the first opinions is more praiseworthy than according to the last one. The apparent view is that this is a description of it in terms of its inherent nobility (al-sharaf al-dhati).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is a description of it in terms of its relative nobility (al-sharaf al-idafi). The pronoun of absence refers to the Book mentioned earlier. If the intended referent is the entire Qur'an, as is the apparent meaning that suits the context, then that is the case. If the intended referent is this surah alone, then calling it "Qur'an" is because "Qur'an" is a generic noun (ism jins) that applies to the many and the few alike. Just as it is applied to the whole, it is applied to a part. Yet it has become predominant for the whole when used without qualification, being definite (ma'rifa) because that is what comes to mind first. Has this predominance reached the level of being a proper name ('alamiyya) or not? There is a difference of opinion on this. al-Baydawi, may Allah sanctify his secret, held the first view, and so the definite article (al-) is obligatory for it. Even so, the original meaning has not been abandoned. It occurs in the books of usul al-fiqh that it was at one time coined for the whole specifically, and at another time for what includes it, and the part, namely the speech transmitted in the mushaf by mass transmission (tawatur). This has been criticized on the grounds that predominance (al-ghalaba) does not have a second coinage (wad' thani). Rather, it is a specification (takhsis) of some of the individual instances of what was coined. This is why the definite article or the idafa is required with it. The exception is if one claims that there is an implicit coinage (wad' taqdiri) in it. So it is said. Among those who explicitly stated that determination by predominance is a counterpart (qasim) to determination by coinage is the scholar al-Zarqani and others. However, al-Himsi objected to this, saying: the indication of identification (al-i'lam) by predominance, for determining its referent, is by coinage, even if it is other than the first coinage. So let this be considered.

It is narrated from al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari that the pronoun refers to the story of Yusuf, even though it is not mentioned in the noble text. It is also said that it refers to the sending down (al-inzal) understood from the verb. Its accusative case is as a absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). "Qur'an" is the direct object. Both opinions are weak, as is not hidden. "Qur'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Regardless of what follows it and of its interpretation as a derived noun (mushtaq), it is a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatti'a) for the circumstantial "Arabic". If it is interpreted as a derived noun, meaning "recited", then it is a non-preparatory circumstantial (hal ghayr muwatti'a). "Arabic" is either its adjective according to the view of those who permit describing an adjective, or a circumstantial qualifier of the implicit pronoun in it according to the view of those who hold that a verbal noun (masdar) bears a pronoun when it is interpreted as a passive participle, for example. It is also said that "Qur'an" is an apposition (badal) of the pronoun, and "Arabic" is its adjective. The apparent practice of Abu Hayyan requires his preference for this. The meaning of it being
[Page 172]
"Arabic" is that it is attributed to the Arabs, in that it was sent down in their language, which is an ancient language.

Ibn Asakir reported in his History, from Ibn Abbas, that the language of Adam, peace be upon him, in Paradise was Arabic. When he ate from the tree, it was taken from him, and he spoke in Syriac. When he repented, Allah the Exalted returned it to him. Abd al-Malik ibn Habib said: The first tongue with which Adam, peace be upon him, descended from Paradise was Arabic. Until time passed and the era grew long, it was altered and became Syriac. It is attributed to the land of Suriyya, which is the land of al-Jazira, and where Nuh, peace be upon him, and his people were before the flood. It resembled the Arabic tongue, except that it was altered. It was also the tongue of all who were in the ark, except one man called Jurhum. His tongue remained the first Arabic. When they came out of the ark, Iram ibn Sam married some of his daughters, and the Arabic tongue came to be in his offspring: Ud, father of 'Ad, and 'Abil and Jathir, fathers of Thamud and Jadis. 'Ad was named after Jurhum, because he was their maternal grandfather. The Syriac tongue remained among the descendants of Arfakhshad ibn Sam until it reached Qahtan from his descendants. He was in Yemen, and there the sons of Isma'il, peace be upon him, settled. The sons of Qahtan learned the Arabic tongue from them.

Ibn Dihya said: The Arabs are divided into categories. The first are 'Aariba and 'Arba' (the pure ones, al-khullas). They are nine tribes from the offspring of Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh: they are 'Ad, Thamud, Umaym, 'Abil, Tasm, Jadis, 'Amaliq, Jurhum, and Wibar. From them Isma'il, peace be upon him, learned Arabic. The second are the al-Muta'arriba (the Arabicized), said in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari): They are those who are not pure, and they are the sons of Qahtan. The third are the al-Musta'riba (those who were made Arab), who are also not pure, and they are the sons of Isma'il. They are the offspring of Ma'add ibn 'Adnan ibn Udad. End quote.

Ibn Duraid said in al-Jamhara: The 'Arab al-'Aariba are seven tribes: 'Ad, Thamud, 'Amaliq, Tasm, Jadis, Umaym, and Jasim. Most of them have died out, except for scattered remnants of the tribes. The first whose tongue deviated from Syriac to Arabic was Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. This is what al-Jawhari meant by his statement that he was the first to speak Arabic. Some people used as evidence that he was the first to speak it what Ibn Asakir reported in his History with a chain of narration transmitted from Anas ibn Malik as a mawquf (a report ending at a Companion). I do not think it is sound. It mentions the confusion of tongues at Babel and that he was the first to speak Arabic.

al-Hakim reported in al-Mustadrak and declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, through the route of Sufyan al-Thawri from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with them: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ etc. Then he said: "Isma'il, peace be upon him, was inspired with this Arabic tongue by inspiration." al-Shirazi said in the Book of Titles (Kitab al-Alqab): Ahmad ibn Isma'il al-Mudani informed us, Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Mashi informed us, Muhammad ibn Jabir narrated to us, Abu Yusuf ibn al-Sikkit narrated to us, saying: al-Athram narrated to me from Abu Ubayda; Masma' ibn Abd al-Malik narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his fathers, may Allah be pleased with them all, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The first whose tongue was opened with clear Arabic was Isma'il, peace be upon him, and he was fourteen years old." It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas that Isma'il, peace be upon him, was the first to speak pure Arabic. This was meant, according to what some of the memorizers of hadith (huffaz) said, as the Arabic of the Quraysh in which the Qur'an was revealed. Otherwise, the Arabic language in general existed before Isma'il, peace be upon him, and it was the language of Himyar and Qahtan. Muhammad ibn Sallam said: Yunus informed me, from Abu Amr ibn al-Ala, who said: All the Arabs are the sons of Isma'il except Himyar and the remnants of Jurhum, who lived alongside them and intermarried with them. Ibn Kathir mentioned that among the Arabs are some who are not of his offspring, such as 'Ad, Thamud, Tasm, Jadis, Umaym, Jurhum, the 'Amaliq, and other nations that none knows except Allah the Exalted. They existed before the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, and in his time. The Arabs of the Hijaz were of his offspring. As for the Arabs of Yemen, who are Himyar, the well-known view, as Ibn Makula said, is that they are of Qahtan, whose name was Mihzam, and he is the son of Hud. It is said that he was his brother, and it is said that he was of his offspring. It is said that Qahtan is Hud. Ibn Ishaq and others related that they are of the offspring of Isma'il. The majority hold that the Qahtani Arabs, from the Arabs of Yemen and others, are not of his offspring, peace be upon him. They also hold that the Arabic language in general existed before him. It is one of the languages that Adam, peace be upon him, knew, and he would speak it and other languages as well. It is said that he spoke Syriac most often. Some claimed that it is the first of languages, and that every other language came after it, either by revelation (tawqif) or by convention (istilah). They used as evidence for its priority in existence that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah the Exalted, and it is Arabic, and it contains what it contains. It is also the most excellent of languages. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya reported from Imam Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on him, his disapproval of speaking other languages for one who has good command of Arabic without need. After it in excellence, according to what is said, is Persian, the Dari dialect. It is even narrated from Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, the permissibility of reciting the Qur'an in it, whether in what is praise, such as Surat al-Ikhlas, or otherwise, and whether this is due to inability in Arabic or not. It is narrated from his two companions that it is permissible to recite in prayer in a language other than Arabic for one who does not have good command of it. In al-Nihaya wal-Dirayah it is mentioned that the people of Persia wrote to Salman al-Farisi asking him to write for them al-Fatiha in Persian. He wrote it, and they used to recite what he wrote in prayer until their tongues became fluent.

This was presented to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he did not disapprove of it. Indeed, the sound position is that the Imam retracted from that. In al-Nafha al-Qudsiyya fi Ahkam Qira'at al-Qur'an wa Kitabatihi bil-Farisiyya by al-Shurunbulali, there is a summary of the following: the writing of the Qur'an in Persian is forbidden, unless one writes it in Arabic and writes the explanation and translation of every letter. Touching it by one who is not in a state of purity is forbidden by consensus, as is reciting it. The prayer is not valid if it is opened in Persian, nor is it valid if the recitation in it is praise. Confining oneself to it while able to use Arabic is also invalid. A prayer is not invalidated by what is remembrance (dhikr), but it is invalidated by what is not remembrance, merely by reciting it in Persian. Such a person does not leave the status of an unlettered person (ummi) if he knows only Persian. The prayer is valid without recitation for one who is unable to recite in Arabic, according to the sound view of the Imam and his two companions. He expanded considerably on this. In Mi'raj al-Dirayah: whoever deliberately recites the Qur'an or writes it in Persian is either insane or a heretic (zindiq). The insane is to be treated, and the heretic is to be killed. This was narrated from Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Bukhari. Nevertheless, the excellence of Persian is not denied. In a hadith: "The tongue of the people of Paradise is Arabic, and Persian is the Dari." This is well known. However, al-Dhahabi mentioned in his History, from Sufyan, that he said: We have been told that people will speak Syriac on the Day of Resurrection, and when they enter Paradise, they will speak Arabic.

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi, and others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Love the Arabs for three reasons: because I am an Arab, the Qur'an is Arabic, and the speech of the people of Paradise is Arabic."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayra something that supports it. It is not hidden from one knowledgeable in the excellences of speech that in Arabic speech there are subtle meanings and fine secrets that no other tongue alone can fully convey, and after it in this respect comes Persian speech. If this is the basis of excellence, then no two people should dispute the superiority of Arabic, then Persian, among the languages that have reached us. If it is something else, then it is apparent that it exists in the Arabic in which Allah the Exalted chose to send down the Qur'an, and nothing else. Allah has allotted to our Prophet,
[Page 174]
(ﷺ), from this tongue what He did not allot to any of the eloquent Arabs. Ibn Asakir reported in his History from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is it with you that you are more eloquent than us, and yet you did not grow up among us?" He said: "The language of Isma'il had been effaced. Jibril, peace be upon him, brought it to me and made me memorize it, so I memorized it."

al-Bayhaqi reported through the route of Yunus from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi, from his father, in a lengthy hadith: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, how eloquent you are! We have never seen anyone more clear in Arabic than you. He said: It is right for me, for the Qur'an was revealed to me in a clear Arabic tongue."

Beyond this, he (al-Alusi) permitted that "Arabic" may be ascribed to 'Araba, which is a region of the dwelling of Isma'il, peace be upon him. The poet said:

("'Araba") is a land whose sanctuary none among people may enter except the shrewd, intelligent one.

The intended meaning is the language of the people of this region. A group, among them al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Jarir, Abu Ubayda, and al-Qadi Abu Bakr, used as evidence the description of the Qur'an as being Arabic, to mean that there is no mu'arrab in it (a foreign word that has been Arabicized). Al-Shafi'i strongly denounced whoever claimed that there is any non-Arabic element in it. Likewise Abu Ubayda, for he said: Whoever claims that it contains other than Arabic has greatly erred in speech.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) explained what was reported from Ibn Abbas, and from others, concerning some words in the Qur'an: that they are Persian, or Abyssinian, or Nabataean. He held that this is among the cases where languages coincidentally share words (tawarrud al-lughat). Others said: rather, the Arabs to whose language the Qur'an was revealed had some mixing with the people of other tongues during their journeys. Words from those languages clung to them, and they altered some of them by dropping some of their letters, and used them in their poetry and their speech until they became like pure Arabic and were used for clear expression. It was in this manner that the Qur'an was revealed with them.

Others said: all those words are purely Arabic, but the language of the Arabs is very vast, and it is not unlikely that they were hidden from the great and eminent scholars. Indeed, the meaning of *fatir* and *fatih* was hidden from Ibn Abbas. For this reason al-Shafi'i said in *al-Risala*: "None encompasses the language except a prophet."

A group held that non-Arabic words do occur in the Qur'an. They answered the verse by saying that a few non-Arabic words do not remove it from being Arabic, just as a Persian poem does not cease to be Persian because of one Arabic word.

Another said: the meaning is that it is Arabic in its style (uslub). They argued from the agreement of the grammarians (nuhat) that the diptote form (man' al-sarf) of words like Ibrahim is due to being a proper name and to being non-Arabic (al-'ujma). This was refuted by saying that proper names are not the subject of dispute, and that the disagreement concerns other words. It was answered that if the occurrence of proper names is agreed upon, there is no barrier to the occurrence of common nouns, but this is open to consideration.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti chose the view that foreign words do occur, and he argued for it by what is soundly reported from Abu Maysara, the distinguished Successor (tabi'i), who said: "In the Qur'an there is from every tongue." Similar was reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Wahb ibn Munabbih.

It has been mentioned that the wisdom behind the occurrence of those words in it is that it encompasses the sciences of the earlier and later peoples and the reports of everything. Therefore it must contain an indication to the varieties of languages, so that its comprehensiveness of everything may be complete. So from every language its sweetest, lightest, and most commonly used word for the Arabs was chosen. Also, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to every nation, it was fitting that his Book, with which he was sent, should contain something from the tongue of every people. Ibn al-Naqib alluded to the first aspect.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qasim ibn Sallam, after relating the view of the jurists (fuqaha') that foreign words occur, said: "The correct position of the people of Arabic is to affirm both views together. These letters are originally foreign, as the jurists said, but the Arabs came upon them and Arabized them with their tongues, turning them from the words of the non-Arabs into their own words, and so they became Arabic. Then the Qur'an was revealed. These letters have become mixed with the speech of the Arabs. So whoever says they are Arabic is truthful, and whoever says they are foreign is truthful." Al-Jawaliqi, Ibn al-Jazari, and others inclined to this view. What pertains to this discussion will come, God willing, in surah Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so consider this carefully and reflect.

Page 175

Al-Jubba'i argued from the verse that the Qur'an is created, in four ways. The first: it is described as "sent down" (inzal), and the eternal (qadim) cannot be described thus. The second: it is described as being Arabic, and the eternal is neither Arabic nor Persian. The third: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾, indicates that He, glory be to Him, is able to send it down in a non-Arabic form, and this is clearly indicative of its being originated (huduth). The fourth: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾, indicates that it is composed of verses and words, and whatever is composed is originated, since necessarily the second part does not exist while the first part exists.

The Ash'aris answered all of this by saying that at most it follows that what is composed of letters and words is originated, and that is not disputed. What we claim to be eternal is something else, which we call the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi). It is not described by being sent down, nor by being Arabic or otherwise, nor by being composed of letters or other things. What would benefit you here was already presented to you in the introductions, so do not be heedless.

﴿So that you may understand﴾: that is, so that you may comprehend its meanings and encompass the wonders contained in it, or so that you may employ your intellects in it and thus know that it is beyond the capacity of human beings, containing what testifies that it has been sent down from the One who creates powers and capacities. This is an explanation of the wisdom of sending it down in that attribute. Several scholars stated that *la'alla* (perhaps/so that) is used here in the sense of the causal *lam*, by way of the subordinate metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya). Its purpose from this is clear. Taking it to mean hope on the part of the addressees, although permissible, does not suit the context.

Al-Jubba'i claimed that the meaning is: He sent it down so that you may understand its meanings concerning religious matters, so that you may know the proofs indicating His unity and what He has obligated upon you. In this is evidence that He, may He be exalted, intended from all of them faith and righteous deeds, both for those in whom this came about and those in whom it did not. And in it is that the verse is far removed from being used as evidence for what he mentioned, as is not hidden.

Page 176

﴿We relate to you﴾: that is, We inform you and narrate to you, from *qassa atharahu* (he followed his trail), when one follows something. It is as if the narrator follows what happened and mentions it bit by bit. In the same sense, it is recited: ﴿the best of stories﴾, that is, the best of narrating. Its accusative (*nasb*) is in the sense of the verbal noun (*masdar*), either because it is annexed to a verbal noun, or because it was originally an adjective of a verbal noun, meaning: a narrative, the best of narratives. Together with the explanation of the actual events, there is an implication (*iham*) of what is ugly and defective in the narratives of the People of the Book. The object is omitted, meaning: the content of this Qur'an, and what is intended by it is this surah. Likewise in His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿by what We have revealed﴾, that is, because of Our revelation.

﴿to you this Qur'an﴾. The specification of its title as Qur'an is to confirm that the narration is not by way of inspiration (*ilham*) or unrecited revelation (*wahy ghayr al-matluww*). Perhaps the word ﴿this﴾ (*hadha*) is to indicate the magnification of what is referred to.

It has been said: in it there is an indication of the difference between this Qur'an and what is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, in that what is meant by that is the whole collection. But this requires reflection. Its being the best is because it is narrated in the most wondrous, splendid and beautiful methods, and the most marvellous, outstanding and fitting styles, as is not hidden from anyone who has studied the story in the books of the earlier people, even if he cannot distinguish the worthless from the valuable, nor tell the left from the right. It is also permitted that this mentioned thing be the object of *naqussu* (We relate).

Several scholars have stated that the verse is an instance of *tanazu' al-fi'layn* (competition between two verbs), and the Basran school is preferred here. As for the wording, it is evident. As for the meaning, it is because the Qur'an, as you have heard, the surah, and the act of revelation being applied to it, is more evident than the act of *naqussu* in relation to its containing the story; and what is more evident is more fitting to have the explicit verb applied to it. In this there is an exaltation of the Qur'an and a presentation of its inimitability and excellence of expression, which is not present in applying *naqussu* explicitly. It is also permitted to treat one of the two verbs as if it were intransitive, and it is possible that ﴿the best﴾ (*ahsan*) is the direct object of *naqussu*. The word *qasas* is either a form *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ul* (the thing narrated), like *naba'* and *khabar*, or a verbal noun used as a name for the object, like *khalq* and *sayd*. Meaning: We relate to you the best of what is narrated of the reports, which is the story of the family of Ya'qub, peace be upon him.

Page 177

The reason for its being the best is that it contains an envier and one envied, an owner and a slave, a witness and one witnessed, a lover and a beloved, imprisonment and release, fertility and drought, sin and pardon, separation and reunion, sickness and health, departure and journeying, humiliation and honour. It has also made clear that there is no repeller of Allah's decree, and no preventer of His measure; and that when He, Glorified is He, decrees for a person good and nobility, even if all the people of the world gathered to prevent it, they would not be able to do so; and that envy is the cause of failure and loss; and that patience is the key to relief; and that planning comes from intellect, and by it the affairs of livelihood are set right; and other matters that the fingers of the writer cannot describe.

It has been said: it is *ahsan* only because most of those mentioned in it had their end in happiness. It has also been said: what is narrated is the reports of the earlier nations and the past generations, not only the story of the family of Ya'qub, and what is meant by this Qur'an is that which contains those. And *ahsan* is not an elative (*ism al-tafdil*), but has the meaning of *hasan* (good), as if it were said: "the good story", by the construction of an adjective to its noun, meaning: the good narrative. This interpretation is, according to the majority, what we have mentioned. It has been said: because it is of such goodness, the motives to transmit it are abundant, and therefore it was not repeated as other stories were. It has been said: the reason for this is the temptation of a woman and women by the most wondrously beautiful of people, and this fits with the non-repetition, because it involves veiling and concealment. Al-Hakim, in his *Mustadrak*, has authenticated the hadith forbidding teaching Surat Yusuf to women. Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq said: Allah, Exalted is He, only repeated the stories of the prophets and presented this story in a single manner as a sign of the inability of the Arabs, as if the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, had said to them: "If it is from my own invention, then do with the story of Yusuf what I have done with the other stories." This is a good view, but it leaves unresolved the question why the specification of Surat Yusuf for this requires explanation, for presenting the story of Adam, peace be upon him, for example, in a single manner would similarly contain an indication of this, for the same reason. Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti said: a aspect of presenting it in this way has become apparent to me, which is that it was revealed in response to the request of the Companions that it narrate to them, so it was revealed in full and complete, so that they might obtain the purpose of stories, namely comprehensiveness and the refreshment of the soul by complete knowledge. What is wrong with this is not hidden. It seems that, for this reason, he said: The strongest answer to be given is that the stories of the prophets were repeated because their purpose is to convey the destruction of those who denied their messengers, and there is a need for this, like the repetition of the disbelievers' denial of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. So whenever they denied, a story was sent down warning of the descent of punishment, as it befell those who denied. For this reason He, Glorified is He, said in several verses: ﴿So the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾, and ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾. The story of Yusuf was not intended for this purpose. By this too the answer is obtained as to why the story of the People of the Cave, the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, the story of Musa with al-Khidr, and the story of the sacrificed one were not repeated. Then he said: If you say: the story of the birth of Yahya and the birth of Isa, peace be upon them both, has been repeated twice, and it is not of the kind you mentioned, I reply: the first is in Surat Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn, which is Meccan, revealed as address to the people of Mecca, and the second is in Surat Al 'Imran, which is Medinan, revealed as address to the Jews and the Christians of Najran when they came; and for this reason the mention of disputation and mutual invocation (*mubahala*) is connected to it. End of quotation.

It has been objected that the story of Adam, peace be upon him, was repeated, although its purpose is not to convey the destruction of those who denied their messengers. It was answered that although its purpose is not to convey what has been mentioned, nevertheless it contains a deterrence from disobedience to the degree that it does, so it is the most similar story to those stories which were repeated for that reason. Understand this.

﴿And indeed, you were before it﴾: that is, before Our revealing that to you, ﴿among the unaware﴾ of it, it had not occurred to your mind, nor had it struck your hearing. This is a justification for its being revealed, as some verifiers have stated. In such constructions the usual practice is to omit the *waw*. The expression of lack of knowledge by unawareness is to honour the rank of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. Likewise, the shift away from *ghafilan* (unaware) to what is in the sublime wording is in the view of some. It is possible to say: when a thing is wondrous and has a kind of strangeness, when one comes upon it, it is said to the addressee: "You were unaware of this," so it may be intended to point to the strangeness of that story, and it would then function as an emphasis of what came before, except that there is in it what is not hidden. The *an* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, its noun is the pronoun of the matter, and the *lam* is the distinguishing *lam*. The clause ﴿you were﴾ and so on is the predicate of *in*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When Joseph said﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb "remember" (udhkur), according to its (the adverb's) usage; and mentioning the time is a metonymy for mentioning what happened in it. The discourse is a beginning in fulfilling what He, glorified be He, promised. Makki reported that the governing element of (idh) is "the heedless" (al-ghafilin).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is permissible that the governing element in it be "we relate" (naqussu), and this was related from al-Zajjaj, in the sense of "we relate to you the situation when..." (idh) etc. It is for absolute, bare time, disregarding the consideration of past tense. In both views there is what there is.

Abu Hayyan preferred to keep it in its original meaning, and that its governing element is "he said: O my son" (qala ya bunayya), as you say: "When Zayd stood up, 'Amr stood up." This is not free from remoteness. Al-Zamakhshari permitted it to be a substitute for "the best of stories" on the assumption that it is made an object, and it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). It was objected that if it were a substitute for the object, the time would be what is related, and there is no sense in that. It was answered that what is meant is what it necessitates, namely the relating of Joseph's (peace be upon him) speech, for relating the time of the saying necessitates relating the saying.

It was objected that it would then be a substitution of part or whole, not inclusion. It was answered that this follows only if the time means the saying itself, which is either the very thing related or part of it. But if it remains in its own meaning and is made related by virtue of what is in it, the objection does not arise.

Moreover, they did not permit the substitution on the assumption that "the best of stories" is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). They justified this by the invalidity of the meaning in that case and by the existence of an obstacle in Arabic grammar. As for the first, the thing related at that time is not the relating; as for the second, "the best of relating" is a verbal noun, so if the adverbial were a substitute and that is the intended thing in relation, it would also be a verbal noun, which is impermissible because it cannot be interpreted as a verb. It was raised against this that a verbal noun may be used as an adverb, as in "I came to you at sunrise," and the adverb may also be a verbal noun and an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) by standing in for the verbal noun, as in his saying: "Your eyes did not close the night of one with sore eyes." They have stated explicitly, as in al-Tashil and its commentaries, that "layla" is an absolute object, i.e., "the closing of a night." What was mentioned about the interpretation as a verb is one of the empty fancies. Yes, when it stands in place of the verbal noun, then whether it is a substitution of inclusion is a doubtful point, but that is a different matter from what was mentioned. On the first view, although the time does not include the relating, it includes the thing related, so why is substitution not permitted with this connection? It was answered that such a connection does not validate substitution. It is reported from al-Radi that inclusion is not like the inclusion of a container over the contained, but rather that it indicates it in general and calls for it in some way, such that the soul, on hearing the first, remains eager for the second, awaiting it, so the second comes clarifying what was left general. If it is not so, it is a substitution of error (badal ghalat). On this basis it is said, regarding the impermissibility of substitution: the soul longs for the mention of the time of a thing, not for the mention of a time that accompanies it, and the time of saying is not the time of relating.

"Yusuf" is a non-Arabic proper name, not an Arabic derivative from "asaf" (grief), though it was named for the grief of his father over him, or his grief over his father, or the grief of one who sees him at his separation because of his great beauty, as has been said. Otherwise it would be triptote, since it has nothing but the quality of being a proper name. Nor should one suppose that it has the pattern of a verb as well, since we have no imperfect verb whose first and third letters are vowelled with damma. The same is said of "Yunus." It was read with a fatha and a kasra on the sin, as is common in non-Arabic names in their modifications, not as an imperfect verb built for the passive or active from "aasafa", because the well-known reading attests to its non-Arabic character. It is not permissible that it be non-Arabic and also non-non-Arabic, as several have said. However,

page 178

In the Sihah, it is stated that Ya'fur, son of the poet al-Aswad, if you say it with a fatha on the ya', you do not make it triptote, because it is like "yaqtulu." Yunus said: I heard Ru'ba say: "Aswad ibn Ya'fur," with a damma on the ya', and this is triptote, because the resemblance to the verb has departed from it. End of quotation.

They stated explicitly that this is the view of Sibawayh, and that al-Akhfash disagreed with him and prohibited its triptotic inflection because of the damma being an accidental vowel by way of imitation. On this basis it may be said: it is Arabic, and it is barred from triptotic inflection on the reading with fatha and kasra because of being a proper name and the pattern of the verb; likewise on the reading with damma, according to what al-Akhfash says, and committing that its third letter's damma is imitation of the damma of its first letter. It was answered that if it were Arabic, disagreement would have arisen concerning it as it did with Ya'fur, and the evident thing is that its non-Arabic character is established in their view; that is why they insisted on barring it from triptotic inflection for that reason and for being a proper name, and no attention is paid to that possibility.

Talha ibn Musarrif read "yu'safu" with a hamza and a fatha on the sin. Other vowelings with damma and kasra together with the hamza have also been transmitted, so there are six readings in it. "To his father" (li abihi): Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. In the Sahih, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.'"

A lineage as though upon it is light from the sun of forenoon, and from the light of dawn a pillar.

("Ya abati"): its origin is "ya abi," then the feminine ta' was substituted for the ya', because of their correspondence in each being one of the letters of augmentation, and it is added to the noun at its end. For this reason Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir changed it to ha' in pause, while the rest differed and kept it as ta' in pause, and it was vowelled with kasra because it is a substitute for the ya', which is the sister of kasra, so it was moved by a vowel corresponding to its origin, not in order to indicate the ya', lest that be like combining two substitutes, or a substitute and what it substitutes. Al-Zamakhshari made this kasra the kasra of the ya' shifted onto the ta' after the letter before it was made fatha, because the fatha of the letter before the feminine ta' is obligatory. Ibn Amir, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj read it with fatha, because its origin, the ya', when moved, is moved with fatha. It was also said: because the origin of "ya abat" is "ya abata," where the ya' was changed to alif, then deleted, and its fatha kept as evidence of it. This was criticized: "ya abata" is weak, like "ya abati," to the extent that it was said to be specific to poetic necessity, as in his saying: "O father, perhaps He will raise you or lift you up."

Al-Farra', Abu Ubayda and Abu Hatim said: the deleted alif of "ya abata" is for the lamentation (nudba). This was rejected, since the context is not one of lamentation. From Qutrub: the origin is "ya abatin" with tanwin, then it was deleted, and address is a domain of deletion. This was rejected because tanwin is not deleted from the accusative vocative, as in "ya darriban rajulan." It was read with damma on the ta', treating it as nouns of the feminine ending with ta' without regard to substitution. You know that the damma of a vocative construct is anomalous. It was not made sukun, although the ba' which stands as a substitute for it is made sukun, because it is a sound consonant treated as a noun, so it must be vowelled, like the kaf of address.

Some claimed that the ya' was changed to ta' because it indicates intensification and glorification, as in "'allamah" and "nassabah," and father and mother are the seat of glorification. On this view there is no deletion and no substitution, and the ta' is then a noun. They stated that a noun that is one letter and is replaced does not leave nominal status. The Kufans said: the ta' is merely for the feminine, and the ya' of attribution is presumed; this is refuted by the non-hearing of "ya abati" in common usage, and likewise the hearing of its fatha, as has been said. It was objected that the ta' of "lat" is feminine according to the majority, and likewise the ta' of "rubbat" and "thummat"

page 179

and it is with fatha. "Inni ra'aytu" (I saw): i.e., in a dream, as the statement of Ibn Abbas and others requires, and likewise His, glorified be He, saying: "Do not relate your vision" (la taqsus ru'yaka). And "this" is the interpretation of my vision, for the verbal noun of ra'a in the sense of dream is ru'ya, and the verbal noun of the visual sense is ru'ya in the common usage. For this reason al-Mutanabbi was faulted for his saying: "Your vision is sweeter in the eyes than closing them."

Al-Suhayli and some lexicographers went that ru'ya is heard from the Arabs in the sense of seeing at night and in general. Some argued that ra'a is oneiric by saying that if it occurred while awake, and it is something beyond custom, it would have spread and been counted as a miracle for Ya'qub (peace be upon him), or a preparatory sign (irhas) for Yusuf (peace be upon him). It was answered that it may have occurred in a short span of the night while people were heedless. The truth is that it is oneiric, and such a possibility is not to be considered.

Abu Ja'far read "inniya" with a fatha on the ya' "ahada 'ashara kawkaban" (eleven stars). They are: Jirban, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Qabis, Amudan, al-Faylaq, al-Musbih, al-Fazi', Wathhab, Dhu al-Ktaffayn, and al-Daruj. It was transmitted from Jabir that "Sinan the Jew came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Tell me, O Muhammad, about the stars that Joseph saw.' He was silent, then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and informed him of that. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Will you believe if I inform you?' He said: 'Yes.' So he (ﷺ) enumerated what was mentioned, and the Jew said: 'By Allah, these are their names.'"

Al-Suhayli narrated similarly from al-Harith ibn Abi Usama, except that he mentioned "al-Nath" instead of "al-Musbih." A group of exegetes and historians narrated the first report, and al-Hakim authenticated it, saying it meets the condition of Muslim. Abu Zur'a and Ibn al-Jawzi said: it is munkar and fabricated.

al-Hasan, Talha ibn Sulayman and others read "ahada 'ashar" with sukun on the 'ayn, to avoid successive vowels and to make clear that the two words are treated as one word. "And the sun and the moon" (wa al-shams wa al-qamar) is a conjunction with what precedes.

Some claimed the waw is for accompaniment (ma'iyya), but this is not so. Specifying them by mention and their not being included under the generality of the stars is because they are distinguished by nobility, and their mention is delayed because their prostration is more eloquent and higher in rank. It is of a type that such-and-such does not know, nor do the people of his town. The sun is placed before the moon according to the Qur'anic practice whenever it combines the sun and the moon, and that is either because it is greater in bulk, brighter in light and more beneficial than the moon, or because it is higher in place than it and its orbit is wider than its orbit according to what the astronomers and many others claim, or because it is the one that bestows light upon it, as many have asserted, and he took support for this from His, glorified be He, saying: "It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light." The discourse was given in this style and the number was not omitted, because the principal purpose is that the dream correspond to those who are in their situation, and by omitting the number that is lost. "I saw them prostrating to me" (ra'aytuhum li sajidin). Al-Bahr inclined to hold that "ra'aytuhum" is an emphasis of what preceded, as a renewal of the covenant, as in His, exalted be He, saying: "Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?" Al-Zamakhshari preferred that it is a new statement (ta'sis), and that the discourse is an answer to an implied question, as if Ya'qub (peace be upon him) said to him when he said "I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon": "How did you see them?" asking about the state of seeing them, and he said: "I saw them prostrating to me." It seems he did not hold that the visual dream sense (ra'a) takes two objects like the cognitive sense, so as to necessitate that the second object of the first verb be deleted; and he held that it takes one object like the visual sense, so there is no deletion, and "prostrating" is a circumstantial state (hal) in his view, as his statement indicates. The well-known view among the majority is that it takes two objects and the second is not deleted by way of abbreviation.

He permitted that his view may be that it takes the objects mentioned, but he holds that deletion, which they prohibited, is permissible, and you know

page 180

that what he understood from it in the sea is free from contradiction. The "theory" (the attribution of reason) is a known feature of the Noble Book. These plural-of-nonrational-things (*muta'atifat*) were given the treatment of rational beings in the pronoun, as the attribute (*sifah*) was applied to them with a description of rational beings, namely prostration (*sujud*). This holds whether the intended meaning is humility or actual prostration. Giving a thing that is connected to another, in some respects, a ruling of that other's rulings, in order to show the effect of the connection and closeness, is common in both old and modern speech. According to what has been said, the expression is a metaphor (*isti'arah*, a figure in which a comparison is implied) of the kind called *makniyyah* (implicit), by attributing the mentioned things to a people of rational beings prostrating. The pronoun and the prostration are an indication (*qarinah*), or one of them is an indication of the imaginative type (*takhyiliyyah*), and the other is an embellishment (*tarshih*).

A group of philosophers went to the view that the stars are living, rational beings. They cited this verse and its like as evidence, and many apparent texts of the Book and the Sunnah support them. Holding this view does not deny anything that is among the necessary matters of the religion. The placing of the prepositional phrase first serves to show care and concern, along with what it contains, according to what has been said, for the sake of observing the verse endings (*fawasil*). It is said that this vision occurred on a Friday night. Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Munabbih that it was the Night of Power (*Laylat al-Qadr*). It is probably not contradictory, since it is clearly possible for one night to be both the Night of Power and a Friday night. It was raised as an objection that it occurred on the Night of Power, since that is among the special privileges of this community. It was answered that what is among the special privileges is the multiplication of the reward for deeds performed in it, to the extent that Allah, glory be to Him, has related. According to what is narrated from Wahb, his age when he saw this was twelve years.

It is said he was seventeen years old. He had earlier seen, when he was seven years old, that eleven long staves were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and that a small staff leapt upon them until it uprooted them and overcame them. He described this to his father, who said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." The interpretation of these eleven staves is exactly the interpretation of the eleven stars, since each of them refers to his brothers. In the first vision there is nothing that points to what the sun and the moon point to in the second vision. There is no necessity to hold that the two dreams are one, by saying that he saw eleven things in each, except that in the first they were staves and in the second they were stars. The conjunction of the sun and the moon with what precedes them would then be of the type of the conjunction of Michael and Gabriel, peace be upon them both, with the angels, as the statement of some of them seems to imply. The sun was interpreted as his father and the moon as his mother, in consideration of place and station.

This was narrated from Qatadah and from al-Suddi: that the moon was his maternal aunt, because his mother Rachel had died. The claim that Allah, exalted is He, revived her afterward in order to confirm his dream is of no concern. It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that the sun was his mother and the moon his father, and this is an interpretation based on feminine and masculine gender. The sun may be interpreted as sovereignty, gold, or a beautiful wife; the moon as a commander; and the stars as chiefs, and likewise as scholars.

It is narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that the vision of the moon may be interpreted in seventeen ways: a king, a vizier, a king's companion, or a chief; or a noble, or a slave girl, or a young man, or a false matter, or a governor, or a corrupt scholar, or an esteemed man, or a father, or a mother, or a wife, or her husband, or a child, or greatness. Perhaps this is based on the difference of the one who sees and the manner of the vision. Some have claimed that he, peace be upon him, had not seen the stars, nor the sun and the moon, but had seen his brothers and his parents, and that he expressed them by these things by way of explicit metaphor (*isti'arah tasrihiyyah*). This is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning and almost counts as the speech of one who is asleep. The apparent meaning of what many commentators have transmitted supports the view that he, peace be upon him, saw the stars, the sun, and the moon descending and prostrating to him, and he related that to his father.

[p. 181]

﴿He said, "O my little son!"﴾ He diminished him out of affection. The grammarians call this kind of diminutive the diminutive of endearment (*tasghir al-tahbib*). How elegant is the saying of one of the later poets:

*He made the pearl in his mouth diminutive, but it is a diminutive of endearment.*

It is possible that this was for that reason and also because of his young age. The reading of Hafs with a fatha on the *ya'* (*yaa bunayya*) is the reading of Hafs, and the rest read it with a kasra. The sentence is a resumption (*isti'naf*) based on an implied question, as if it were said: "What did the father say after hearing this wondrous vision from his son?" So it was said: He said, "O my little son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a plot," meaning, lest they devise a great stratagem to destroy you, from which you cannot escape, or a secret scheme against which you cannot stand in defense. He said this to him because he, peace be upon him, knew from his vision that God Most High would bring him to a lofty station of wisdom, would choose him for prophethood, and would bless him with the honor of both abodes. So he feared for him the envy and enmity of the brothers. He said this to him in order to protect them from falling into what is not fitting regarding him, and to protect him from enduring hardships and suffering sorrows. This was so even though he was confident that they could not change what the vision indicated, and that God, glorified is He, would certainly fulfill it, and in hope that it would be attained without hardship. This is not in any way the forbidden backbiting (*ghibah*).

The *ru'ya* (vision), the verbal noun of *ra'a* in the sense of a dream indicating what occurs in sleep, whether or not it was seen, according to the well-known view, and the *ru'yah* (sight), the verbal noun of *ra'a* in the sense of visual perception indicating a particular kind of perception, are distinguished by the two feminine forms. Similar to this is *qurbah* (act of drawing near) for spiritual nearness through worship and the like, and *qurba* (kinship) for relational nearness. Its reality, according to the people of the Sunnah, is as Muhyi al-Din al-Nawawi said, quoting al-Mazini: God, glorified is He, creates in the heart of the sleeper beliefs just as He creates them in the heart of the one who is awake, and He, glorified is He, creates what He wills; neither sleep nor wakefulness prevents Him. He, glorified is He, has made those beliefs a sign of other matters that He creates later. Then, what becomes a sign of what is pleasing He creates without the presence of Satan, and what becomes a sign of what is harmful He creates in his presence. The first is called a *ru'ya* (vision) and is attributed to Him, Exalted is He, as an attribution of honor. The second is called a *hulm* (dream) and is attributed to Satan, as is common in attributing what is disliked to him, even though all of it is from Him, Exalted is He. Based on this, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) came: "The vision is from God Most High and the dream is from Satan."

In the Sahih, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you sees a vision that he loves, it is from God Most High, so let him praise God Most High and let him relate it. But when he sees other than that, something he dislikes, it is only from Satan, so let him seek refuge in God Most High from the accursed Satan and from its evil, and let him not mention it to anyone, for it will not harm him."

It is authentically reported from Jabir that the Messenger of God, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, said: "When one of you sees a vision that he dislikes, let him spit three times to his left, let him seek refuge in God Most High from the accursed Satan, and let him turn over from the side on which he was lying."

It is not far-fetched that God Most High made what has been mentioned a cause of safety from what is disliked, just as God made charity a cause for averting calamity, even though we do not know the wisdom of the connection between spitting to the left, turning from the side one was lying on, and causation in this case, for example. It has also been said: they are the reports of the angel entrusted with the spirits if they are true, and the whisperings of Satan and the self if they are false. This has been attributed to the scholars of hadith. The two statements may be combined by saying that the intended meaning of the one who said they are beliefs that God Most High creates in a heart, etc., is that they are beliefs created in that way through the medium of the angel's report or through the whispering of Satan, for example. Among the Ash'arites, the well-known view is that effects are created by Him, Exalted is He, at the occurrence of causes, not by them. So reflect.

Some of the philosophers said: it is the imprinting of the image descending from the horizon of the imaginative faculty (*al-mutakhayyilah*) onto the common sense (*al-hiss al-mushtarak*). True ones of these occur through the soul's connection with the realm of dominion (*malakut*), because of the affinity between them, when the soul is free, at least minimally, from managing the body. Then it imagines what is fitting for it from the meanings present there. Then the imaginative faculty represents it in a form that suits it, sends it to the common sense, and it becomes something seen. If that form is strongly proportionate to that meaning, such that the difference is only one of universal and particular, it dispenses with interpretation; otherwise it needs interpretation.

[p. 182]

Some of the great Sufis mentioned something close to this, namely: the vision is one of the properties of the realm of the restricted image, called the faculty of imagination (*khayal*), which may be affected by the heavenly intellects and the rational souls that perceive universal and particular meanings. So in it appear forms suitable to those meanings. It may also be affected by the estimative faculties (*al-quwa al-wahmiyyah*), which perceive only particular meanings, so a form suitable to them appears in it. This may happen because of a disorder in the temperament of the brain, or it may happen because the soul directs the estimative faculty toward producing one of the forms, as when someone imagines the form of his beloved who is absent from him with strong imagination, so the form appears in his imagination and he sees it. This is the first beginning of divine revelation for the people of special favor, because revelation only happens by the descent of an angel, and its first descent is in the imaginative realm, then in the sensory realm. It is authentically reported from A'isha, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "The first thing with which the Messenger of God, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, was begun in revelation was the true vision, and he would not see a vision except that it came like the break of dawn."

The thing seen, as some of them said, whether it is in its original form or not, may come about by the will of the one seen, or by the will of the one who sees, or by the will of both together, or it may come about without the will of either of them. The first is like the appearance of an angel to one of the prophets, peace be upon them, in some form, and the appearance of perfected people to some of the righteous in forms other than their own. The second is like the appearance of a spirit of the angelic or human spirits by the perfected one's bringing it down to his world, so that it may reveal the meaning of something whose knowledge is specific to it. The third is like the appearance of Gabriel, peace be upon him, to the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, by his bringing him down and by the Truth, glorified is He, sending him to the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace. The fourth is like Zayd, for example, seeing the form of 'Amr in sleep without intention or will from either of them. The vision of Yusuf, peace be upon him, was of this kind, because it is evident that if it had been by the will of the brothers, they would have known it, and then there would have been no meaning to the prohibition of relating it. And what indicates that it was not by his intention is his saying afterward: ﴿My Lord has made it true.﴾

This being said, what is reported from the theologians (*mutakallimun*) is that they are baseless imaginings. This is extremely strange after the testimony of the Book and the Sunnah to their validity. Some of the verifiers explained this by saying that what they meant is that what the sleeper imagines as perception by sight is not truly sight, and what he imagines as perception by hearing is not truly hearing. Thus that does not contradict the truth of these things in the sense that they are indicators of some matters, just as that very thing or something resembling and representing it is. The discussion of this has already passed, so be attentive.

The well-known view, in which the reports agree, is that the true vision is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood. The reasoning for this, according to a group, is that he, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, remained, as A'isha, may God be pleased with her, indicated, for six months seeing revelation in dreams, then the angel came to him while he was awake. Six months in relation to twenty-three years is one part of forty-six parts.

Al-Halimi mentioned that revelation came to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in forty-six kinds, such as the inspiration into the heart (*naft fi al-ru'*), the angel appearing in the form of Dihya, may God be pleased with him, for example, and hearing something like the sound of a bell, and other things. That is why he, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, said what he said. Al-Hafiz al-'Asqalani mentioned that the true vision being a part of such-and-such of prophethood is only in regard to its truthfulness and nothing more; otherwise it would be permissible for its owner to be called a prophet, which is not the case. It has already been mentioned to you that some reports contain something that contradicts what is in this report regarding the number of parts. Perhaps the intended purpose of all of that, as has been said, is to praise the true vision and to draw attention to the elevation of its status, not the specific number, nor the literal reality of partition.

Ibn al-Athir said in *Jami' al-Usul*: A few narrated that it is one part of forty-five parts. There is a reasonable connection for this: the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, did not complete sixty-three years, meaning that he, peace and blessings be upon him, died in the course of the sixty-third year. The report that it is one part of forty parts would be understood as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, having lived sixty years, and this is a report of some of them. It was also reported that it is one part of seventy parts, and I do not know a reason for that.

You know that seventy is often used for abundance, so perhaps that is the reason. The purpose is to point to the abundance of the parts of prophethood. So reflect.

As for "his brothers" here, according to what has been said, it means the eleven brothers whose plots and schemes he feared, who were sons of his paternal half-family: Yahudha, Ruwbil, Shim'un, Lawi, Rinalun, Yashjur, and Dinah, sons of Ya'qub by Liyya, daughter of Layan ibn Nahir, who was his maternal cousin; and Dan, Yiftali, Jad, and Ashir, his sons by two concubines, Zulfa and Bilha. These are the ones alluded to by the stars. As for Binyamin, who is the full brother of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and whose mother was Rahil, whom Ya'qub, peace be upon him, married after the death of her sister Liyya or during her lifetime, since joining two sisters was not forbidden at that time, he is not included under this prohibition, since no harm from him is to be feared and no disgrace from him is to be dreaded. He was not with them in the vision, since he was not with them in the prostration.

It has been objected that the well-known view is that the paternal half-brothers (*banu 'illatihi*, the sons of his father by other wives) are ten, and that none of them is named Dinah. Some people counted Dinah among the sons of Ya'qub, but they said she was the sister of Yusuf. Building the discussion on this is plainly corrupt. Indeed, she hardly enters the category of "brothers" except by way of *taghlib* (the predominance of the masculine gender), because the word is the plural of *akh* (brother), which is specific to males. So perhaps the preferred view is that what is meant by "brothers" includes both full brothers and half-brothers, and Binyamin is counted in place of Dinah to complete the eleven matching the visible stars. The prohibition against relating the dream to him, even though he was not one whose harms are feared, is a matter of precaution and closing the door to possibility. Among what is well known: every secret shared by more than two spreads. The view must commit to the occurrence of the prostration from him as from the rest of his family. Attributing the plotting to the brothers is by way of the majority, so there is no difficulty, thus it is said.

This, with the reading of "paternal half-brothers," is preferable to what has been said: that by his brothers is meant those excluding Binyamin and Dinah, because those two are not feared for mischief, nor is their harm imagined. Then they are nine, and the number is completed by his father and his mother or his maternal aunt. The mention of the sun and the moon would then be like the mention of Jibril and Mikail after the angels, and in it there is a magnification of their matter, for in that there is what there is.

The accusative of (يَكِيدُوا) is by an implied *'an* in answer to the prohibition. It is transitive with the *lam*, although it is one of the verbs that are transitive by themselves, as in His saying: ﴿So plot against me﴾, because it is made to imply what takes a preposition, namely *ihtiyal* (scheming), as we have indicated. This is to emphasize the meaning by conveying the meaning of both verbs together, the implying and the implied. And since the aim is emphasis, and the context calls for it, he emphasized the verb with the verbal noun and then affirmed it afterward by the causal clause. Making the *lam* superfluous, like making the verb transitive both directly and by the particle, is contrary to the apparent sense. It has been said that the prepositional phrase is one of the complements of the emphasis, in the sense of "they plot a plot for you," but this is nothing. Some made the *lam* causal, in the sense: "they do it for your sake and for your destruction, a firm or hidden plot." He claimed this style is more emphatic than saying "so they plot against you a plot," since it contains no indication that the act itself is the intended infliction. It also has a kind of contrariness to the apparent sense. Understand.

The majority read ﴿رُؤْياكَ﴾ with a hamza and without *imala*. Al-Kisa'i read ﴿رُؤْياكَ﴾ with *imala* and without a hamza, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man an open enemy﴾, i.e., to this kind, ﴿clearly hostile﴾, manifest in enmity. So he spares no effort in embellishing matters to your brothers and stirring envy in them, until he drives them to what has no good in it, even though they grew up in the house of prophethood.

[Page 184] The apparent sense is that these people were in such a state that Satan could have a path over them, and what supports this is that they were not prophets. The matter is disputed. What most of the earlier and later scholars hold is that they were not prophets at all. As for the earlier generation, nothing has been transmitted from the Companions that any of them said they were prophets, nor is it preserved from any of the Successors either. As for the Successors of the Successors, it is transmitted from Ibn Zayd that he said they were prophets, and a small group followed him. As for the later scholars, the exegetes are divided. Among them is one who said the view of Ibn Zayd, such as al-Baghawi. Among them is one who went to great lengths to refute it, such as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir. Among them is one who related both views without preference, such as Ibn al-Jawzi. Among them is one who did not address the question but mentioned something that indicates they were not prophets, such as his explanation of *al-Asbat* as those among the Children of Israel who were given prophethood, and "what was revealed to them" as "what was revealed to their prophets," like Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi and al-Wahidi. Among them is one who mentioned none of that but explained *al-Asbat* as the sons of Ya'qub, so some people took it as a statement that they were prophets, though it is not explicit in that, since he may mean by "the sons" his descendants through his own sons.

Shaykh Ibn Taymiyya mentioned in a work of his specifically on this matter what its summary is: What the Qur'an, the language, and reasoning indicate is that the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) were not prophets. Neither in the Qur'an, nor from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor from any of his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), is there any report that Allah made them prophets. Those who argued that they were made prophets relied on His saying in the two verses of al-Baqarah and al-Nisa': "and the Asbat," and they explained that as the sons of Ya'qub. The correct view is that by them is not meant his own sons, but his descendants, just as they are called "Children of Israel," and just as all people are called "Children of Adam." And His saying: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾, and ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations﴾, is explicit that the Asbat are the nations of the Children of Israel, and each tribe is a nation. They have stated that the Asbat among the Children of Israel are like the tribes among the Children of Isma'il. The root of *sibt*, as Abu Sa'id al-Darir said, is one tree, intertwined, with many branches. So there is no sense in calling the twelve sons "Asbat" before offspring spread out from them. Therefore, restricting the Asbat in the verse to his own sons, peace be upon him, is an error that neither the wording nor the meaning indicates, and whoever claimed it has clearly erred. The correct view is also that they were called Asbat from the time of Musa (peace be upon him), and from then prophethood was among them, for no prophet was known before him except Yusuf. What supports this is that when He mentioned the prophets from the descendants of Ibrahim, He said: ﴿And from his descendants, Dawud and Sulayman﴾, and the verses that follow. He mentioned Yusuf and those with him, but did not mention the Asbat. Had Yusuf's brothers been made prophets as he was, they would have been mentioned as he was. Also, Allah mentioned for the prophets (peace be upon them) praises and commendation suited to prophethood, even before it. The hadith says: "The most noble of people is Yusuf son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, a prophet, son of a prophet." Had his brothers been prophets, they would have shared with him in this nobility. When He related their story and what they did to their brother, He mentioned their confession of sin and their request for forgiveness from their father, and He did not mention of their merit anything suited to prophethood, even before it. Nor did He mention from them a manifest repentance, as He mentioned of one whose sin was less than theirs. He did not mention, of any prophet before or after prophethood, that he did such grave deeds as disobedience to a parent, severing kinship, enslaving a Muslim and selling him into lands of disbelief, manifest lying, and other things He related of them. Indeed, if there were no proof that they were not prophets other than the emanation of these grave acts from them, it would suffice, because prophets, according to most scholars, are protected from such things both before and after prophethood. These are also matters that one below the age of puberty cannot bear, so the excuse that they were done before prophethood is not valid, and that would not prevent later prophethood. Also, the historians mention that all of Yusuf's brothers died in Egypt, and he too died there, but he bequeathed that he be transported to Syria, and Musa (peace be upon him) transported him. It is not mentioned in the Qur'an that a prophet came to the people of Egypt before Musa other than Yusuf. Had there been a prophet among them, he would have been mentioned. This is weaker in indication than what came before, as is not hidden.

[Page 185] The summary is that the error in claiming their prophethood came from supposing that they were the Asbat, which is not so. Rather, the Asbat are a great community. Had the Asbat meant the sons of Ya'qub, He would have said "and Ya'qub and his sons," for that is clearer and more concise. But He expressed it thus as an indication that prophethood came among them from the time they were divided into tribes, in the era of Musa (peace be upon him). So let this be noted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

Furthermore, when he (peace be upon him) alerted him to the great significance of his dream and warned him of what he warned him about, he began to interpret it (ta'bir) and explain it (ta'wil) in a general manner, saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾, meaning: He will select you and prefer you for prophethood, as related from al-Hasan; or for prostration to you, as related from Muqatil; or for great affairs, as al-Zamakhshari said. This encompasses what has preceded, and likewise it encompasses enriching his family and removing famine from them through his blessing, and other things besides. Perhaps the best of the opinions is the middle one. The root of ijtiba' (choosing, selecting) is from jabaytu al-shay' (I gathered the thing), when you gather it for yourself, and they interpreted it as "choosing," because only what is chosen is selected.

Some have mentioned that God Most High's choosing (ijtiba') of a servant means singling him out with a divine overflow (faid ilahi) from which various kinds of honours result without any effort on the servant's part. This is specific to the prophets (peace be upon them) and those who approach them among the truthful (siddiqin), martyrs and righteous. The thing referred to by "thus" is either the choosing for a dream like that one, so the likened and the likened-to are different, or the verbal noun of the verb mentioned, which is then both the likened and the likened-to. ("Thus," كَذَلِكَ) is in the position of accusative as an attribute of an implied verbal noun, and the verification of this has been put forward. It has also been said here that the prepositional phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is thus, and the matter is not thus. Nor is the tenderness hidden in mentioning the Lord (al-Rabb) as an attribute joined to the pronoun of the addressee. He (peace be upon him) did not explicitly specify the details of what the dream indicates, out of fear of its being spread abroad, as has been said. ﴿And He will teach you﴾: a group of scholars held that this is a separate, independent statement, not included under the comparison. By it he (peace be upon him) intended to affirm and confirm his statement, and to reassure Yusuf (peace be upon him) about what he informed him of through interpretation and explanation; that is, "and He will teach you ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾," meaning that kind of knowledge, or a suitable portion of it, so that you will come to know the reality of what I am saying. The affirmation of what has preceded, and the urging to accept what will follow, is not hidden. The reason given for its not falling under the comparison is that the apparent sense would be to liken "choosing" to "choosing," and "teaching" is not "choosing," so it is not likened to it. This was examined: teaching is a type of choosing, and a type is compared with a type.
