It was also said that the reason is that the meaning would become "and He will teach you a teaching like the choosing with a dream like this," and its awkwardness is not hidden, since choosing is the aspect of resemblance between the likened and the likened-to, and this was not considered in teaching.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: there is no obstacle to making it fall under the comparison, with the meaning that by that is the honouring through that dream; that is, just as He has honoured you with these good tidings, He honours you with choosing and teaching. There is no need in that to make it two comparisons and to posit "thus" twice. You know that what comes to the mind is the conjunction (ataf), and there is no harm in what this verifier established for its explanation. Yes, for the resumptive (isti'naf) there is a sound aspect, even if it is not what comes to mind. The apparent meaning is that by "the interpretation of events" is intended the interpretation of dreams, since they are unseen reports through which God Most High creates beliefs in the heart of the sleeper as He wills, and there is no restriction upon Him, Most High. Or (it means) the stories of the angel if they are true, or of the soul or the Devil if they are not so. al-Raghib mentioned that ta'wil is from the first (sense), which is return (al-ruju'), and that is returning a thing to the goal intended from it, whether knowledge or action. The first is like His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God﴾, and the second is like the poet's saying: "For the separation before the day of parting there is an interpretation." The first also came in the sense of the policy whose outcome is observed; it is said: "Alanaa wa'il 'alaynaa" (the sense of "a refuge against us"). End quote.

Ta'wil has become current for taking a thing away from its apparent meaning. "Al-ahadith" (events, reports) is a broken plural of hadith, contrary to analogy, as they said: "batil" and "abatil" (falsehood and its plural). It is not a collective noun (ism jam') of it, because the grammarians stipulated for the collective noun that it not be of a pattern peculiar to the plural, such as mafa'il. Among those who explicitly stated that it is a plural is al-Zamakhshari in al-Mufassal, and this is what he meant by "collective noun" in al-Kashshaf, for he, like others, often applies the term "collective noun" to a plural that is irregular, so there is no contradiction between his two statements. It has also been said that it is the plural of uhdutha (a saying, a rumour), and this was refuted: uhdutha is a comical tale like a fable, so it does not suit here, nor does it suit the hadiths of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) to be the plural of uhdutha. Ibn Hisham said: uhdutha is from hadith what is talked about, and it is used only in an evil sense. Perhaps the matter is not as they mentioned, for al-Mubarrad explicitly stated that it occurs in a good sense, and he recited the verse of Jamil, which is among what has become famous and widespread:

"And whenever I came to Su'da to visit her, I saw the earth folded up for me and its distant parts drawing near,
Among the modest, white-skinned women, whose companion loved, when a tale ended, that she would repeat it."

It has also been said that they formed hadith into uhdutha and then formed the plural of that as ahadith, like qatili or aqtil and aqatil. That the intended meaning of "the interpretation of events" is the interpretation of dreams is what is related from Mujahid and al-Suddi; and from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is the outcomes of affairs; and from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning is the clarification of the meanings of the reports of the prophets, the earlier nations, and the revealed books.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "events" is the newly created matters of spiritual and corporeal beings, and the interpretation of them is the manner of reasoning by them to the power, wisdom and majesty of God Most High. All of these are contrary to the apparent meaning, in my view. ﴿And will complete His favour upon you﴾: by joining the favour of this world with the favour of the Hereafter; or by adding to the prophethood obtained through choosing the kingship, making it a completion of it; or by adding to teaching deliverance from trials and hardships. The mention of teaching is placed in the middle because it is among the necessary consequences of prophethood and choosing, and in observance of the order of existence in the external world, and because teaching is a means to completing the favour, for his interpreting the dreams of the two companions of the prison and the dream of the king became a pretext for deliverance from prison and connection with the supreme leadership.

Some have explained choosing as bestowing high ranks such as kingship and dignity in the hearts of creatures, and completing the favour as prophethood. This is supported by the fact that completing the favour is an expression for that by which a favour becomes complete and perfect, free of aspects of deficiency; and for a human being nothing achieves this except prophethood, for all human stations are deficient in comparison with it.

It is permitted that the dream itself be counted among God Most High's favours upon him, so that all the favours reaching him in accordance with it are its fulfilment, a complete fulfilment of that favour; but this is not free of remoteness. It has also been said: the intended meaning of choosing is the outpouring of what prepares him for every good and honour; by teaching the interpretation of events is meant teaching the interpretation of dreams; by completing the favour upon him is meant delivering him from trials in the most complete manner, such that together with his deliverance from them he will be among those who submit to him; and in teaching interpretation there is an indication of his being made a prophet, for that cannot be except through revelation. But it is objected that explaining choosing by what was mentioned is not apparent, and that teaching being an indication of prophetic appointment is within the realm of prevention, and what was mentioned as evidence does not establish it. For the apparent meaning is that his brothers knew the interpretation, otherwise his father (peace be upon him) would not have forbidden him from recounting his dream to them for fear of their scheming. That they were prophets at that time is something no one has held, nor is it likely that anyone would hold it at all. Yes, they mentioned that one does not know interpretation as it should be known except one who knows the correspondences between images and their meanings, and knows the levels of souls that appear in the presence of their imaginings according to them, for the judgments on a single image differ in relation to individuals of differing levels. This is rare to find, and error in interpretation has been established among great scholars. Abu Hurayrah related that "a man came to the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) and said: 'I saw a canopy from which ghee and honey were dripping, and I saw people gathering with their hands, some taking much and some taking little, and I saw a rope or a cord from the sky to the earth, and I saw you, O Messenger of God, take hold of it and rise; then another man took hold of it and rose; then another man took hold of it and rose; then another man took hold of it and rose; then another man took hold of it and was cut off, then it was joined to him and he rose.' Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him) said: 'O Messenger of God, may my father and mother be your ransom, by God, you must let me interpret it.' The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Interpret it.' He said: 'As for the canopy, it is the canopy of Islam; as for what drips of ghee and honey, it is the Qur'an, its softness and its sweetness; as for those who take much and those who take little, they are those who take much of the Qur'an and those who take little of it; as for the rope connecting the sky to the earth, it is the truth you are upon, you hold to it, and God will raise you; then another man after you will take hold of it and rise by it; then another after him will rise by it; then another after him will rise by it; then another will take hold of it and be cut off, then it will be joined to him and he will rise by it. Tell me, O Messenger of God, did I hit the mark or did I err?' The Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) said: 'You hit part of it and erred in part.' He said: 'I swear by my father and mother, you must tell me, O Messenger of God, where did I err?' The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Do not swear.'" End quote. Except that one may claim that the intended meaning of teaching is teaching in the most perfect manner, such that whoever errs in interpreting does not err by it; but this requires that the man be such that he knows the correspondences and the levels of souls, and commits to the claim that this cannot be except for a prophet. It was chosen that the intended meaning of choosing is the selection for prophethood, that teaching interpretation is what is apparent, that completing the favour is his deliverance from hardships, and that his (peace be upon him) saying: ﴿O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾ is a general indication from him of the interpretation of dreams, as is not hidden to one who has discernment; and it also contains good tidings. This is a continuation of it with what is greater in the eyes of Yusuf (peace be upon him). The place of teaching in relation to it is not hidden.

The summary of the meaning: just as He has honoured you with this good tidings indicating the prostration of your brothers to you and the elevation of your rank over them, He honours you with prophethood and the knowledge by which you know the interpretation of the likes of what you saw, and the completion of His favour upon you, ﴿and upon the family of Ya'qub﴾ by deliverance from hardships, which in the case of Yusuf (peace be upon him) is not hidden, and in the case of the family of Ya'qub. By them is meant his household, from his sons and others. Its root is ahl; it has been said its root is awl. We have verified this in more than one book. It is used only for those who have standing absolutely, and is not added to what does not reason, even if it has standing, unlike ahl; so one does not say "ali al-hijam" (the family of the cupper) or "ali al-haram" (the family of the sanctuary), but "ahl al-hijam" and "ahl al-haram." Yes, it may be added to what is treated as rational, as in the words of 'Abd al-Muttalib: "And give victory over the family of the cross and its worshippers today, your family."

In this there is a refutation of Abu Ja'far al-Zubaydi, who claimed that it is not permissible to add it to a pronoun because he had not heard it used as a construct with a pronoun. Ya'qub, like his son, is a non-Arabic name with no derivation; so what has been said, that he was named so because he emerged from his mother's womb after his brother Esau, is not acceptable to the scholars of the Hijaz, nor to the famine and drought and scattering of the family, and other things that are general or specific. Some explained "al" as "sons," and completing the favour as appointment to prophethood, and made the summary of the meaning: He bestows upon you and upon the rest of Ya'qub's sons the prophethood. And this has been cited as evidence that they became prophets afterwards.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 6 (part 2 of 2):

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that Yusuf's (peace be upon him) seeing his brothers as stars by whose light one is guided is among the blessings of Allah Most High upon them, because it indicates that their affair will end in prophethood. Thus, everything among their perfections that moves from potential to actuality will, in accordance with that, be the complete fulfilment of that blessing without doubt. You know that what has been mentioned is not fit to serve as evidence that they became prophets, because of the possibilities you have come to know.

صفحة 188

And when a proof is touched by possibility, the inference is invalidated by it. Their seeing stars by whose light one is guided is far from being evidence that their destiny is prophethood. It is only evidence that their destiny is to be guides for people, and that is something prophethood does not necessarily entail. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided." We do not deny that those people became guides after Allah Most High bestowed on them repentance; indeed, by my life, they were then among the greatest of their Prophet's companions. It may also be said: if their seeing stars indicated that their destiny is prophethood, then his mother's seeing a moon would be more indicative of that, and no one holds this.

Some have said: there is no objection to taking "the family of Ya'qub" to mean all his sons, and "the completion of blessing" to mean completing it through prophethood. But it does not thereby follow that their prophethood is established afterward, since it is possible that "and He completes His blessing upon you" [means] through prophethood, "and upon the family of Ya'qub" [means] through something else, such as deliverance from what is disliked, for example. This is like your saying: "I have bestowed favour upon Zayd and upon 'Amr," which does not require that the bestowal upon both be of one kind, since the statement is true even if you bestowed upon Zayd a position and upon 'Amr the giving of a thousand dinars, or freed him from a tyrant, for example. This is obvious.

Some preferred to understand "the family" as including the sons, on the ground that if the intended meaning were only the sons, the more evident and concise expression would be "and upon your brothers" instead of what is in this sublime arrangement. It has been said: he chose that wording over it because "brothers" would immediately suggest the brothers against whom he was forbidden to seek retribution, so Benjamin would not be included, whereas the intention is to include him. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "the family of Ya'qub" is his followers, those who were upon his religion.

It has been said: it refers to Ya'qub alone, on the understanding that "family" means the person himself. The weakness of both these views is not hidden, and the latter is the more remote of them. As for one who took the completion of blessing as an allusion to kingship, he made the conjunction [of "the family of Ya'qub"] on the basis that they would benefit from its traces of honour, status and wealth. This is it.

"Just as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq." That is, a completion like the completion of His blessing upon your two fathers before this time, or before you. The two noble names are an appositive for "your two fathers." Describing them as "father" even though they were his grandfather and great-grandfather is to indicate the complete connection of his line with the prophets (peace be upon them). And mentioning the principle that "the child is the secret of his father" is so that his heart may be reassured by what he was told. The completion of blessing upon Ibrahim was either through prophethood, or through taking him as a close friend (khalil), or through saving him from the fire of his enemy, or through [sparing] him the slaughter of his son, or through more than one of these. Upon Ishaq it was either through prophethood, or through bringing Ya'qub out of his loins, or through saving him from slaughter and ransoming him with a great sacrifice, according to the report that he was the one who was slaughtered, which many have held; its verification, if Allah Most High wills, will come later. The matter of the comparison under all the other possibilities is easy, since it is not required that it be in every respect. Limiting the mention of the one compared to the completion of blessing, without addressing election (ijtiba'), is a case of sufficiency (ikhtisar), as has been said, for the completion of blessing necessarily presupposes a prior blessing that calls for election. And his (peace be upon him) knowledge of what he was told, which the dream did not indicate, was either by insight (firasa) — and a father's insight into his child is often correct, whatever the father may be — so what do you suppose of his insight if he was a prophet, or [by] revelation? It is also claimed that the dream was used as evidence for all of that.

"Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing," knowing everything, so He knows who deserves the things mentioned. "All-Wise," doing everything as wisdom requires, so He does what He does in accordance with the patterns of His knowledge and wisdom. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to confirm the preceding sentences.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, there were in Joseph and his brothers﴾ — that is, in their stories. The apparent meaning is that the "brothers" here are the same as the "brothers" mentioned earlier. A group of scholars held that they were the paternal half-brothers (banu 'illat) of Joseph. It is permissible that by them here is meant everyone who was among the men of that account, since Benjamin also has a share in the story. This is considered unlikely, according to what has been said, by (they said) which comes next. ﴿signs﴾: great markers of tremendous importance, indicating the immense overpowering power of
Page 189
Allah the Exalted and His dazzling wisdom. ﴿for those who ask﴾: for everyone who inquired about their story and came to know it; or for those who seek the signs and take lessons from them, for they are the ones who take note of them and benefit from them, to the exclusion of others who fall under His words, the Exalted: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they turn away from it﴾. So the "story" here means the account itself. Or it refers to the Prophethood of him, upon him be blessings and peace, whom they asked about their story, as you know from the explanation of the occasion of revelation. So the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, informed them of it as it actually was, without hearing it from anyone and without reading a book. In this case, "story" means its narration. As for the plural "signs" in this case, it has been said: it is to indicate that the narration of each part of the story is a clear sign sufficient to demonstrate his Prophethood, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. It has also been said: it is due to the multiplicity of aspects of inimitability, in wording and in meaning. Some of the great scholars claimed that the verse is an instance of ellipsis (al-iktifa'), and the intended meaning is "signs" for those who ask and those who do not ask. A parallel to this is His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿alike for those who ask﴾. Its beauty lies in the strength of the speech's indication of what is omitted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the intended meaning of "those who ask" is people in general, but it was turned away from that to urge learning such a story, because of the greater lessons it contains. Both opinions are not free from remoteness.

The people of Makkah, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid read ﴿āyatun﴾ in the singular, and in the codex of Ubayy: ﴿'ibratun li-l-sā'ilīn﴾ ("a lesson for those who ask").

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 12, verse 8:**

﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother [Benjamin] are dearer to our father than we are"﴾. The mention of Benjamin is specified by the possessive "his brother," because he shared with Joseph brotherhood from both the mother's and the father's side, and this kind of brotherhood is stronger than brotherhood from only one of them. They did not mention Benjamin by name, to imply that Jacob's (peace be upon him) love for him was on account of his full brother Joseph (peace be upon him). For this reason, they did not harm him in any way like what befell Joseph (peace be upon him). The lam (ل) here is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), and "Joseph" is the subject (mubtada'), with "and his brother" conjoined to it. The statement of the Exalted: "dearer to our father than us" is the predicate, connected to it. The word "dearer" (aḥabb) is a comparative form (af'al al-tafḍīl) derived from a passive verb, which is an irregular usage (shudhūdh). For this reason it governs "to" (ilā), as they mentioned: the comparative of love and hatred governs the subject in meaning with "ilā," and the object with "lam" or "fī." You say: "Zayd is dearer to me (ilayya) than Bakr" if you love him more; and "dearer to me (liyya) or in me (fiyya)" if he loves you more than others. The comparative is not made dual, even though the two being described are two, because the comparative form "af'al min kadhā" is not differentiated between singular and what is above it, nor between masculine and feminine. This is unlike "the two brothers," for distinction is obligatory in the definite (with the article) and permitted in the construct form when the intention is to prefer it over the one it is attached to. And if the intention is to prefer it absolutely, then distinction is necessary. The lam of initiation is used to affirm and emphasize the content of the sentence, meaning that the greatness of his love for them both is an established fact without doubt. ﴿And we are a band﴾, meaning: while we are a group capable of serving him and striving for his benefit, unlike the two of them. The word "ʿuṣba" and "ʿiṣāba," according to what is transmitted from al-Farra', means ten or more; they were so named because affairs are "ʿuṣiba" (bound) by them, i.e., tied together so that they become strong.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the ʿuṣba is more than ten. In another narration from him, it is between ten and forty. From Mujahid, it is from ten to fifteen.

From Muqatil, it is ten. From Ibn Jubayr, six or seven. It was said: from one up to ten. It was said: up to fifteen. From Ibn Zayd, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba, it is a group in general, having no singular from its own form, like "nafar" and "rahṭ." It was said: three is a nafar, and when they increase they are a rahṭ up to nine, and when they increase beyond that they are an ʿuṣba. One does not say "ʿuṣba" for fewer than ten. Al-Nizal ibn Sabra transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah honor his countenance, that he read "ʿuṣbatan" in the accusative case. In that case the predicate is omitted, and "ʿuṣbatan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in it, meaning: "we gather as a band." This was estimated so that the circumstantial phrase would indicate the omitted predicate, because of the meaning of gathering contained in it.

Page 190

Ibn al-Munir claimed that the speech follows the pattern of: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is poetry," and the estimate is "we are we, a band." The predicate was omitted because it is equal to the subject and does not exceed it in wording, so omitting it avoids repeating the same word, while the context indicates what is omitted. There is no problem with a circumstantial phrase occurring after "we," because with the estimate mentioned it becomes a complete sentence with the grandeur it possesses. Similar estimation is made in ﴿They are purer for you﴾ according to the reading in the accusative, but it is objected that grandeur comes only from repetition, so omission is not permissible, and the indication of the omitted element is not clear.

It is transmitted from Ibn al-Anbari that this is like what the Arabs say: "Innama al-ʿAmiri ʿammatuhu" (the ʿAmiri is only his paternal aunt), meaning: he takes care of that. The indicator of the omitted element is "ʿammatuhu," for the form (fi'la) denotes the state in which a person continues, so he necessarily takes care of it. The better view is to consider the parallel of the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"O Lahdham, your judgment is established (musammaṭan)."

He meant, as al-Mubarrad said: "your judgment is for you, established," meaning firm, enforced, not rejected. This has become common among them, but they mention that it contains irregularity in two respects. The verse according to the reading of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his countenance, is more irregular than that, as is not hidden from one who is trained in the science of Arabic grammar.

﴿Indeed our father is﴾, meaning: in preferring those two over us in love, despite our superiority over them and their being incapable of managing affairs, ﴿in clear error﴾, meaning: a mistake in judgment and a departure from the path of just balance, which is fitting in placing each of us in his proper position. ﴿Clear﴾ means evident in its condition. The error is treated as a place (ẓarf) for his being fixed in it. Describing it as "clear" indicates that this, in their view, is not appropriate. The emphasis (in "indeed") is for greater attention.

It is reported that he (peace be upon him) loved Joseph more because of what he saw in him of signs (of goodness), and his brothers were envious of him. When he saw the dream, his love for him doubled, so he could not bear to be apart from him, and he would embrace him at every moment to his chest. Perhaps his heart sensed the separation, so their envy doubled because of that, until it drove them to what Allah the Exalted related about them. Some have said: the reason for the increase of his love for Joseph and his brother (peace be upon him) is that they were young and their mother had died. The love of the young is something inherent in human nature. It was said to the daughter of al-Hasan: "Which of your sons do you love most?" She said: "The young one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers." Some poets have composed verses about love for a young child, both in ancient and modern times. Among these is what the minister Abu Marwan ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Idris al-Jaziri said in a poem he sent to his children while he was in prison:

"And their youngest is ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, for I fold up for his separation a longing that has not grown less,

that one is foremost in the heart, even if he becomes as the little finger for you in lineage and origin;

indeed the five fingers are equal together, but the ring belongs to none of them except the little finger;

and when the youth loses his youth, the love of sons rises over him, and there is no love like the love of the youngest."

It is objected that if the source of the increase of love were what was mentioned, then Benjamin would have had a greater share of it, because he is younger than Joseph (peace be upon him), as is indicated by their saying that their mother died in giving birth to him. As we have indicated, the verse points to his love being on account of his full brother Joseph. What should be relied upon is that he (peace be upon him) loved him more than them only because he saw in him signs of goodness that he did not see in them, and that love increased after the dream, confirming those signs for him. There is no blame on a father for preferring one of his children over another in love for a reason like this. Many have stated that love is not among the things that fall under human capacity, and a person is excused in what does not fall under it. Yes, his sons supposed that what he did (peace be upon him) was from ijtihad (independent reasoning), and that he had erred in that. A mujtahid may err and be correct, even if he is a prophet. By this is resolved what is said: if they had believed that their father was truly a messenger from Allah the Exalted, how could they object, and how could they criticize his way and find fault in what he was upon? And if they were denying that, it would entail their unbelief, Allah forbid, which no one has said. The resolution is evident.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 9:

﴿Kill Yusuf or cast him out to some land.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is part of what is related after His words, glorified is He: ﴿When they said﴾. Some of them said it, addressing the others, and they were all content with that, except the one who said: ﴿Do not kill him﴾, and so on. It is also possible that each of them said it, addressing the rest, and the exception is the same exception. Some have claimed that the speaker was a man other than them whom they consulted about this, but this contradicts the apparent meaning and has no firm basis. The apparent meaning is that the speaker gave them a choice between the two matters: killing or casting out.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning is: some said, ﴿Kill Yusuf﴾, and others said, ﴿cast him out﴾. Ṭarḥ (casting) is throwing and dropping a thing; it is said: "ṭaraḥtu al-shay'" (I threw the thing away, I put it far off). From this is the verse of ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward:

"Whoever is like me, burdened with dependents and straitened of wealth, will cast himself into every place."

The word ﴿land﴾ (arḍan) is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition, as al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya held, meaning: cast him into a land far from the land in which he is. It was also said: it is accusative as a second object of ﴿cast him out﴾, being implicitly construed with the sense of ﴿set him down﴾, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Cause me to alight at a blessed place﴾. It was also said: it is accusative as an adverb of place. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others rejected this, arguing that what is accusative as an adverb of place must be indefinite, and since the intended meaning is a land far from his land, there is no indefiniteness. This was answered with a point that is not free from scrutiny. The sum of the meaning: kill him or banish him, for banishment is like killing in achieving the aim while being safe from his sin. By my life, they mentioned two bitter matters, for estrangement is a grief, what a grief it is! And by God, how well said the one who said:

"They made the saying fair and said: 'It is exile,' but exile for the free is slaughter."

﴿Your father's face will be free for you﴾: ﴿yakhlu﴾ is jussive as the answer to the imperative. "Face" (wajh) is the well-known organ. In the words there is an allusive metonymy for the purity of love. From here it was said: that is, he will turn to you with one undivided turning, not looking away from you toward others. The intended meaning is the safety of his love for them from anyone who shares it with them and contends with them for it. "Face" has been explained as "essence," with the metonymy for its state, since the transition to the intended meaning takes two steps on the first reading and one step on this one. It was also said: "face" means essence, and in the words there is a metonymy for turning toward and devoting oneself to arranging their affairs and managing their matters, because his being free for them indicates his freedom from preoccupation with Yusuf, peace be upon him, so he would occupy himself with them and organize their affairs. The more apparent of these is probably the first.

﴿And you will be﴾: jussive, coordinated with the answer to the imperative; and in the accusative after the waw, with ʾan implied, that is: there will combine for you the freedom of his face and the state of being. ﴿After him﴾: that is, after Yusuf, in the sense of after finishing with his matter, or after his killing or casting out. So the pronoun refers either to Yusuf or to one of the two verbal nouns understood from the two verbs.

﴿A righteous people﴾: by repentance and by seeking release before God, exalted is He, from the sin you have committed, as is related from al-Kalbi, and this is the view of the majority. Thus the righteousness meant is religious righteousness between them and God, exalted is He. It is possible that this is meant, but between them and their father, by making excuse, and although this contradicts religion because it is a lie, it agrees with it in that they hope for their father's pardon and forgiveness, so that they may, as it is said, escape disobedience to their father. It is also possible that worldly righteousness is meant, that is, be righteous in your worldly affairs, for after this your affairs will be ordered for you through your father's face being free. The choice of the second person in ﴿for you﴾ and what follows is for emphasis in moving them to accept, for a person's concern for his own affairs and his care in obtaining his benefits is more complete and more perfect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 10:

﴿A speaker among them said﴾ He was Yahudha (Judah), and his opinion regarding him was less evil than the opinion of others, and he is the one who said: ﴿Then I will not leave the land﴾ etc. This was related by al-Suddi.

Qatada and Ibn Ishaq said: he was Ruhbil (Reuben). And it is reported from Mujahid that he was Shim'un (Simeon), and it was said: Dan. Some of them said: one of these two is the one who said: ﴿Kill Yusuf﴾ etc., while the one who said ﴿Do not kill Yusuf﴾ was someone else, and perhaps the most correct view is that he was Yahudha.

It was said: no one among them was named explicitly, out of concealing the wrongdoer, and each of them was not free from wrongdoing, even though its degrees differed. The claim that, on this basis, no one should name any of them explicitly, following the Book, is worthless, because that is a place of tafsir (exegesis), and in it naming is something required. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), as if a questioner asked: Did they agree on what was put before them of the two courses of action, or did anyone among them oppose them in that? So it was said: ﴿A speaker among them said: Do not kill﴾ etc. The use of "Yusuf" rather than a pronoun is to arouse their compassion for him and to magnify the killing of him, though he himself is [a party to it]; it is related that he said to them: "Killing is a great matter," and he did not explicitly forbid them the other course of action, but left it to the preferability of what he put before them, by his saying: ﴿And throw him into the depths of the well﴾, that is, to its bottom and its depth. It was named so because it is hidden from the eye of the one who looks, and from this comes the word for a grave: ghaya(ta). Al-Minkhal al-Sa'di said:

When one day they hide me in my ghaya(ti), then travel with my journey among the clan and the family.

Al-Harawi said: the ghaybah in the well is like a cave, or a niche in the well above the water, in which what is inside is hidden from the eyes. And al-jubb is the well that has not been lined with stone; when it is lined, it is a bi'r. Al-A'sha said:

Though I were in a well eighty cubits deep, and I climbed the causes of the heavens by a ladder.

It is pluralized as jubab, jibab and ajbab. It was named jubb because it was cut (jubba) out of the earth, that is, cut off. Soon, God willing, the discussion of its feminine and masculine forms will come.

Nafi' read ﴿ghayabat﴾ in both places, as if the well had ghayabat (recesses), which indicates its spaciousness; or he meant by al-jubb the genus, that is, in some of the recesses of the well. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿ghayyabat﴾ with the yeh doubled, which is an intensive form. Its pattern, as transmitted by the author of al-Lawami', may be fa''alat, like hammamat, or fay'alat, like shaytanat in the plural of shaytanah. Al-Hasan read ﴿ghayabah﴾ with fatahs, as in its origin being a verbal noun like ghalabah; it may also be the plural of ghA'ib, like sani' and san'ah. In the reading of Ubayy, may God be pleased with him, it is ghaybah with a sukun on the yeh, as a verbal noun used to mean "the absent one."

﴿Some caravan will pick him up﴾, that is, will take him in a manner of preservation from loss and destruction, for iltiqat (picking up) is taking a thing exposed to loss, so it is said. In Majma' al-Bayan it is: to find a thing and take it without intending to; and from this is his saying: "a watering place I came upon by chance (iltiqatan)."

﴿Some of the caravan﴾, that is, some of a company travelling in the land; and the article in "al-sayyarah" is as in "al-jubb" and "ma fihima." In "some" there is a kind of indefiniteness, to achieve what he intends in making his speech appealing by agreeing with their purpose, which is the removal of Yusuf, peace be upon him, from them in such a way that his trace is not known and his news is not related. Al-Hasan read ﴿taltaqitu﴾ with the feminine, in accordance with the meaning, as in his saying:

When some of the years (ta'arrafatna) suffice the orphans, the loss of the father of the orphan.

And there came: "some of his fingers were cut," and they treated this as a case of the genitive noun taking the feminine from the genitive noun it is attached to, like his saying: "as the spear's tip (sharaqat) was reddened with blood."

﴿If you are doers﴾, that is, if you are determined and resolved to do with him what separates him from his father; or, if you are doers by my counsel and opinion, then throw him etc. He did not decide the matter for them, but put this before them, to win their hearts, to direct them to his opinion, and to guard against their ill opinion of him. Since this was likely to prompt a questioner to ask: what did they do after that, did they accept his opinion or not? the answer was given by way of resumption, in a manner that included within it their acceptance of it, by what will come, God willing, in his words, glorified is He: ﴿And they resolved to put him in the depths of the well﴾. So it was said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 11:

﴿Qālū yā abānā﴾ They addressed him, peace be upon him, with this (term) to stir up the chain of kinship and to remind him of the bond of brotherhood, so that by this they might bring about his relenting from his opinion regarding his protecting him from them, since he sensed their envy. So it is as if they said: ﴿What is wrong with you﴾, i.e., what is the matter with you, ﴿that you do not trust us﴾, i.e., do not make us trustworthy ﴿with Yusuf﴾, although you are his father, we are his sons, and he is our brother, ﴿while we are indeed his sincere well-wishers﴾, desiring good for him and being solicitous toward him; there is nothing in us that would undermine that. The clause ﴿do not trust us﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and likewise the clause ﴿while we are indeed his sincere well-wishers﴾. The interrogative (mā laka, "what is wrong with you") carries the sense of wonder (taʿajjub). The speech clearly indicates that they had previously made a request that Yusuf go out with them, and his father did not consent to that.

The majority of readers recited ﴿lā taʾmannā﴾ with idgham (assimilation) and ishmām. It has been explained as pressing the two lips together with a slight parting between them, indicating the vowel movement alongside clear idgham, as occurs in pausal forms; this is what is known among them, though it is difficult here. Ishmām is also used for giving a kasra a trace of ḍamma, as they said in qīla, and for mixing one of two letters with a trace of another letter, as they said in al-ṣirāṭ. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with both of them, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Zuhrī, and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited with idgham without ishmām, and the intention of negation is evident. Ibn Hurmuz recited with a ḍamma on the mīm together with idgham; this ḍamma is transferred to the mīm from the first nūn after its vowel was removed.

Ubayy, al-Ḥasan, Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif, and al-Aʿmash recited: lā taʾmannunā, with clear pronunciation (iẓhār) and a ḍamma on the nūn according to the original form, though this differs from the script of the muṣḥaf, since it has a single nūn. Ibn Wathhāb and Abū Razīn recited: lā tīmannā, with a kasra on the letter of present-tense prefix according to the dialect of Tamīm; Ibn Wathhāb softened the hamza after the kasra, while Abū Razīn did not soften it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh related from ʿĀṣim that he recited in this manner in the presence of ʿUbayd ibn Faḍla, who said to him: "You have committed a grammatical error (laḥanta)." Abū Razīn said: "The one who recites in the dialect of his own people has not committed a grammatical error."

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾: (ghadan) is in the accusative as a temporal adverb (zarf zamani, an adverb of time). It is used for the day following your day, and for future time in general. Its original form is ghadaw, and its final radical has been dropped. It has also come in its full form. The meaning is: send him with us tomorrow to the desert.

﴿He will enjoy himself﴾ (yartaʿ): i.e., he will expand in eating fruits and the like. The basic meaning of ar-rataʿ is to eat and drink whatever one wishes in abundance and ease. It is said: "rataʿa" meaning he remained in abundance and luxury. Abundance is called ratʿah, with the taʾ vowelled either with a sukun or with a fatha. Ar-Raghib mentioned that ar-rataʿ is literally said of the eating of beasts, and is used figuratively of a human when a great deal of eating is meant. Upon this is the saying of [the poet]: "And when he is left alone in the protected pasture, he feeds freely."

﴿And he will play﴾ (wa yalʿab): by racing, shooting arrows, and the like, things by which one trains for fighting the enemy. The intended meaning is not frivolous play, for otherwise Yaʿqub, upon him be peace, would not have allowed them to do it. They expressed it this way because it was in its form, to make true what they had suggested about Yusuf's being in their company, by portraying him in the image that suits his condition, upon him be peace, namely his young age.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read yartaʿ and yalʿab with the ya' and the jazm (jussive). The two Ibns (Ibn ʿAmir and Ibn Kathir?) and Abu ʿAmr read them with the nun and the jazm. The two Harami readers (al-Haramiyan) pronounced the ʿayn with a kasra. There is a difference of transmission from Qunbul regarding affirming and omitting the ya'. It is narrated from Ibn Kathir: "nartaʿ" with the nun, and "yalʿab" with the ya'. This is the reading of Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad. Al-ʿAla' ibn Sayyabah read "yartaʿi" with the ya' and kasra on the ʿayn, jussive, with the final radical omitted, and "yalʿabu" also with the ya' and damma on the ba', as either a new sentence or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "and he plays."

Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Muhaysin read "nurtaʿ" with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the ʿayn, from "artaʿna," and "nalʿab" also with the nun. Abu Raja' did likewise, except that he used the ya' (yuntaʿ/yalʿab) in both. Both readings are with the object omitted, meaning: "we make the livestock or other things graze." In all these readings the verbs are in the active voice.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "yurtaʿu" and "yulʿabu" with the ya' and the passive voice in both. This is explained as: the deputy subject is the pronoun referring to "ghad" (tomorrow), and the original is "yartaʿu fihi wa yalʿabu fihi." Then the preposition was dropped and the verb was extended to the pronoun, so it became "yurtiʿuhu" and "yulʿibuhu." Then it was put into the passive, so the pronoun that had been in the accusative, because it became the deputy of the subject, was concealed.

As for whoever pronounced the ʿayn of the first verb with a kasra, it is, in his view, from mura'ah (mutual watching over), according to what is narrated from Mujahid, i.e., some of us watch over and guard one another.

Ibn Zayd said: it is from ra'y al-ibl (the herding of camels), i.e., we train in herding and guarding property. Or it is from grazing plants and pasture, and the meaning is that we graze our livestock, except that it is attributed to them metaphorically, or it is a figurative use for their eating by grazing. Ibn ʿAtiyyah judged the reading with the affirmed ya' to be weak, and said: its affirmation in a position such as this is not permitted except in poetry, like the saying of [the poet]:

"Has there not come to you, while the news spreads, what the milch-camel of the Banu Ziyad has encountered?"

It was also said: the assumption of dropping the vowel from the ya' and similar letters for the jussive is a dialect, and it is not a matter of necessity at all.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan that he used to read "nalhu" and "nalʿab." ﴿And indeed we are to him guardians﴾: i.e., from anything harmful befalling him. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), and the governing element in it is the imperative verb or the answer. This is not from the category of governance (bab al-aʿmal, the rule of which verb governs a shared noun), as Abu Hayyan said, because a circumstantial phrase cannot be omitted, and in that category the governed item must be made into a pronoun when the first verb governs. They emphasized their statement with various kinds of emphasis: presenting the clause as nominal, adorning it with "inna" and the lam, attributing the guarding to all of them, and placing "lahu" before the predicate, as a stratagem to achieve their aim.

[p. 194]

﴿Qal﴾ [He said.] This is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*), as if a questioner asked: "What did their father say to them?" So it was said: He said, ﴿"Truly, it grieves me that you should take him away"﴾ because of the severity of his separation from him and the weakness of my patience concerning him. When the lam that enters the predicate of *inna* is followed by a present-tense verb, it was said that it restricts the meaning to the present. This is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words. It was also said that it may refer to the present and to other times. They cited the verse ﴿"Truly your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection"﴾ as evidence. It was also said that it refers to the present if there is no indicator otherwise, and with an indicator it can refer to other times. They counted the verse under discussion among these cases. Some of them took it to refer to the present here. This raises an objection: the going away is in the future, so the verb would precede its agent, which is impermissible, since the agent is its effect, and it is not conceivable that an effect precedes its cause.

It is answered that the intended meaning is "the intention or expectation that you take him away." So the speech contains an elided *mudaf* (a noun governed in a construct phrase), namely the agent, and the going is not a future matter but a present state. Omitting the agent is not forbidden in such a case, because what they have stated is that it is forbidden only when nothing stands in its place, and here something does stand in its place. It is not necessary that the one standing in its place be the *mudaf ilayhi* (the second term of the construct), as was supposed. Rather, if something else stood in its place, omission would also be permissible. From here, the estimate "the intention of you (plural) that you take him away" is correct. It is possible that this estimate is of meaning, not of grammatical parsing (*i'rab*).

Some of them said: The objection can be removed without the need to posit an elided *mudaf*, by saying that the going grieves him in terms of his conception of it, as was said regarding its parallel in the final cause. Shihab (al-Khafaji) said: "That verification, I think, is that what they said in directing the objection is a fallacy with no basis. The requirement that the agent be existent at the existence of the verb applies only to the real agent, not to the grammatical or linguistic agent. The verb may precede it, whether the verb is a present-state, as in the case we are discussing, or past, just as the agent in such a construction may be a nonexistent matter, as in the poet's words:

*"Whoever is pleased not to see what hurts him, / let him not take for himself anything he fears losing."*

No one has said that such a construction requires interpretation (*ta'wil*). Grief and sorrow, like joy and happiness, can be felt toward a thing before it occurs, as Ibn Hilal explicitly stated in his *Furuq* (Differences). There is no need for interpretation, estimation, or treating mental existence as external existence, whether one holds this view or accepts it. Such a thing is not recognized by the people of Arabic or by the language. If you insist on contention regarding it, then let it be a figurative use in the attribution to what is future, because it is now a cause of grief." End of Shihab's words.

You know that they stated that the act of the agent, when it is a deliberate action, is either something that subsists in him or something that proceeds from him. Subsistence of a thing in what does not yet exist, and its proceeding from it, is not conceivable. Accordingly, interpretation in a manner that makes subsistence or proceeding valid, in the apparent sense of the one lacking it, is obligatory. So it was said. Reflect on this.

Ibn Hurmuz and Ibn Muhaysin read *liyahzunni* (with the two identical consonants merged) with idghaam (assimilation). Zayd ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them) also read it this way. He also read *tadhhabu bihi* as a quadriliteral from *adhhaba*. According to Abu Hayyan, it is explained by the extra *ba'* in *bihi*, just as some explained *tunbitu bi-al-duhn* ("it grows with oil") in the reading of the one who vowels the *ta'* with a *damma* and the *ba'* with a *kasra*. The meaning would be: "It grieves me that you cause him to go away."

﴿"And I fear that the wolf will devour him"﴾. The wolf is a well-known animal. He specified it in mention because the land, as it is said, was full of wolves. It was also said: because it is a small, weak, insignificant beast of prey. So he, peace be upon him, drew attention by his fear for him from it to his fear for him from what is greater than it in devouring, by way of a fortiori argument. Because of the wolf's insignificance, al-Rabi' ibn Dhaba' al-Fazari specified that it is the one he fears, given the age he had reached, in his words:

*"The wolf, I fear it if I pass by it / alone, and I fear the winds and the rain."*

It was also said: because he, peace be upon him, saw in a dream that a wolf had attacked him, and so he was wary of it. Perhaps this wariness was because the prophets, peace be upon them, by their complete affinity with the world of the dominion (*malakut*), have their occurrences be the very occurrence itself. Otherwise, in sleep, a wolf is interpreted as an enemy.

Some claimed that he, peace be upon him, symbolized by the wolf one of them. He, peace be upon him, is too exalted to not know what kind of dream that vision is, since among dreams there are some that need interpretation and some that do not, and the perfect person knows this. This was objected to: it is possible that the matter was hidden from him, just as such a matter was hidden from his grandfather Abraham, peace be upon him. This is based on what our shaykh Ibn al-Arabi, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned, that his dream, peace be upon him, of slaughtering his son was from a dream that is interpreted as slaughtering a ram, but this was hidden from him. The meaning of this is not hidden. What is mentioned in some reports is that he, peace be upon him, saw in his dream as if he were on the summit of a mountain, and as if Joseph were in the bottom of a valley, and then ten wolves surrounded him, wanting to eat him. He repelled one of them, then the earth split and Joseph disappeared into it for three days. I have not found any reliable chain for the narration of this dream in general, and there is no need for us to rely on it, given the strain of speech involved in it. In sum, what he, peace be upon him, said in this matter was a suggestion of the answer without intent, and it is in the style of His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿"What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?"﴾ And calamity is entrusted to speech.

[Page 196]

Abu al-Shaykh and others reported from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not suggest answers to people, lest they lie. The sons of Jacob did not know that the wolf eats people, but when their father suggested it to them, they lied and said: 'The wolf ate him.'"

Grief is the pain of the heart over losing the beloved, and fear is the agitation of the soul at the arrival of something disliked. For this reason, he attributed the first to the going away with him, which causes loss, because of the continuation of his companionship and his constant association with Joseph, peace be upon him. And he attributed the second to what is expected to happen, namely the wolf's devouring. The root of *al-dhi'b* (wolf) is with a hamza, which is the dialect of the Hijaz, and several readers recited it that way.

Al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Abu Ja'far, Warsh, al-A'sha, and others read it with the hamza changed to a *ya'* because it is sukun (quiescent) and preceded by a kasra. This is the analogical form in such cases. Some have mentioned that Ibn Kathir recited it with the original hamza, as did Nafi' in the narration of Qalun, and Abu Amr in pause, while Ibn Amir and Hamzah, in continuous speech, changed it and in pause also changed it. Perhaps this is because the meeting of two quiescent letters in pause, though permissible, is better when the first is a long vowel letter.

Nasr said: "I heard Abu Amr not hamzating it." The apparent meaning is that he meant in general, so the earlier statement would be a narration and this a different one. Its plural is *adhu'ub*, *dhi'ab*, and *dhu'ban*. According to al-Zamakhshari, its derivation is from *tadha'abat al-rih* (the wind blew from every direction). Al-Asma'i said: the derivation of *tadha'abat* is from the wolf, because the wolf does this to its enemy. It was said: this is more appropriate, and for this reason *tadha'abat al-rih* is counted as a metaphor in *al-Asas*. But it was objected to: deriving a verb from non-derived nouns, such as *ibil* (camels), is rare and contrary to analogy.

﴿"And you were heedless of him"﴾ because you were busy with pasturing and play, or because of your little concern for guarding him.

They said: ﴿Even if the wolf devours him while we are a group﴾. That is, while we are a company worthy of having affairs entrusted to us and of having calamities averted by our opinions and our arrangements. The *lam* that enters upon the conditional is *muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (a *lam* that prepares the way for an oath). His statement, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed we would then be losers﴾ is a *jawab* (response) that stands in place of the apodosis of the conditional. "Loss" (*khasar*) may mean destruction, used figuratively for weakness or for deserving it, or for deserving to have a curse called down upon oneself with it. That is: we would be weak and incapable, or deserving of destruction, with no sufficiency or benefit in our lives according to us, or deserving to be cursed with loss and ruin, so that it is said: "God cause them loss and ruin," since the wolf devoured their brother while they were with him. It is also permissible that it bears its literal meaning, that is: if we are unable to protect him, and he is the most precious thing to us, then our livestock have perished and we have lost them. They limited their answer to the fear of their father, peace be upon him, of the wolf devouring him, although he had mentioned two reasons for not letting him go with them: his grief at being separated from him, and his fear for him from the wolf. This is because the wolf is the stronger cause for prevention, not grief, since the period of separation is short, based on their quick return with him. Or because his grief at the going is only out of fear for him, so the negation of the second implies the negation of the first. Or because they disliked that, since it was the cause of their envy of him, and for this reason they paid it a deaf ear.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 15:

﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾, meaning they resolved firmly ﴿to put him into the depths of the well﴾. It is said that it was a well three farsakhs (about nine miles) from the place where Ya'qub (Jacob) (peace be upon him) lived in Canaan, which is among the regions of al-Urdunn (Jordan). It is also said that it lay between Egypt and Madyan, and that it was in the land of al-Urdunn itself. Some claimed that it was the well of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), but this was refuted on the grounds that the reasoning based on a caravan picking him up and their coming in the evening of that day rules it out, since there are many stages between the dwelling of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) and Bayt al-Maqdis. The answer to *lamma* (when) is omitted, to signal that it is evident and to indicate that its details cannot be contained by the expression. Its summary is: "they did what they did." Some scholars supplied it as "their trial became great," and this is better than a supplied phrase such as "they put him in it." It is also said that there is no omission and that the answer is ﴿We revealed to him﴾, with the *waw* being superfluous, but this is not correct.

Wahb and others among the people of biography and reports (ahl al-siyar wa al-akhbar, the historians of the prophetic narratives) said: The brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) said, "Do you not long to go out with us to our livestock, so that we may hunt and race?" He (peace be upon him) said, "Yes." They said, "Ask your father to send you with us." He said, "I will do so." So they entered upon Ya'qub with their whole group and said, "O our father, Yusuf has wished to go out with us to our livestock." Ya'qub said, "What do you say, my son?" He said, "Yes, my father. I see from my brothers gentleness and kindness, so I wish that you would permit me." Ya'qub disliked being separated from him and loved to please him, so he permitted him and sent him with them. When they went out with him, they began carrying him on their necks while Ya'qub watched them. When they were far from him and had brought him into the desert, they threw him to the ground, revealed to him what was in their hearts of enmity, spoke harshly to him, and began beating him. Whenever he came to one of them and sought help from him, that one would strike him. When he realized what they had resolved upon, he began calling out, "O father! If only you could see Yusuf and what has befallen him from his brothers, it would grieve you and make you weep. O father! How quickly they have forgotten your covenant and neglected your charge!" He wept intensely. Then Ruben seized him, threw him down on the ground, sat upon his chest, and wanted to kill him. Yusuf said to him, "Gently, my brother, do not kill me." He said, "O son of Rahil, you are the one of the dreams! Let your dream save you from our hands!" He twisted his neck. Then Yusuf sought help from Yahudha (Judah) and said to him, "Fear Allah, the Exalted, concerning me, and stand between me and the one who wants to kill me." The bond of brotherhood moved Yahudha, and he was softened toward him. So he said, "O my brothers! Did you not pledge this to me? Shall I not show you something that is easier for you and gentler on him?" They said, "And what is that?" He said, "Throw him into this well. Either he will die, or some of the caravan will pick him up." So they set off with him to a well there, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. They began lowering him into it, and he clung to its edge. They tied his hands and stripped off his shirt. He said, "O my brothers! Return my shirt to me so that I may cover myself with it in the well." They did not do so. Then they threw him into it. He said to them, "O my brothers! Will you leave me alone?" They said, "Call upon the sun, the moon, and the stars, and they will keep you company."

It is also said: They put him in a bucket and lowered him, and when he reached halfway down they let go of him, intending that he should die. There was water in the well, so he fell into it, and then he stood upon a rock within it.

It is related that when they threw him into the well, he began to weep. They called out to him, and he thought that it was mercy that had come to them, so he answered them. They wanted to crush him with a rock in order to kill him, but Yahudha prevented them. With Ya'qub was the shirt of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), which Allah, the Exalted, had clothed him in from Paradise when he was cast into the fire. He had placed it in a silver case and hung it around the neck of Yusuf when he went out with his brothers. When he was in the well, an angel brought it out and dressed him in it, and the well was illuminated for him. It is related from al-Hasan that when he was thrown into it, its water became sweet, and it sufficed him in place of food and drink, and Jibril (peace be upon him) came down to him to comfort him. When evening came, he got up to leave, and Jibril said to him, "I fear that you will be lonely when you leave." He said, "When you desire something, say: 'O helper of those who seek help, O aid of those who call for aid, O reliever of the distress of the afflicted, You see my place and know my state, and nothing of my affair is hidden from You.'" When Yusuf (peace be upon him) said this, the angels (peace be upon them) surrounded him, and he found comfort in their company.

Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Ta'ifi said: When he (peace be upon him) was thrown into the well, he said, "O Witness who is not absent, O Near One who is not distant, O Victor who is not vanquished, grant me relief from what I am in." It is also said that he used to say, "O God of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, have mercy on my weakness, my lack of resources, and my young age."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Yusuf was thrown into the well, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said, 'O boy, who threw you into this well?' He said, 'My brothers.' He said, 'And why?' He said, 'Because of my father's love for me, they envied me.' He said, 'Do you want to get out of here?' He said, 'That is up to the God of Ya'qub.' He said, 'Say: O Allah, I ask You by Your hidden and guarded Name, O Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour, that You forgive me, have mercy on me, make for me a relief and a way out from my affair, and provide for me from where I expect and from where I do not expect.' So he said it, and Allah, the Exalted, made for him a relief and a way out from his affair, and provided him the kingship of Egypt from where he did not expect it." Then he (peace be upon him) said: "Persist with these words, for they are the supplication of the chosen and the righteous." Other reports also exist. The narrations concerning how he was cast in and what was said to him and by him are numerous. They contain what would soften rocks, but none of them has a sound chain of transmission on which one may rely. And Allah knows best.

﴿And We revealed to him﴾. The pronoun refers to Yusuf, meaning: We informed him at that time, giving him good news of what his affair would come to and removing his loneliness and consoling him. According to Mujahid, this was by inspiration (ilham). It is also said that it was by being cast into his heart in true dreams (mubashshirat al-manam). Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said that it was by sending Jibril (peace be upon him) to him. The content of the revelation is what is contained in the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs﴾, which is also good news to him of deliverance: that is, you will indeed be delivered from what you are in of evil condition and narrow circumstances, and you will indeed inform your brothers of what they did to you, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ that you are Yusuf, because of the difference between your two states: your present state, and your state on that day when your rank is elevated, your royal authority is great, and your condition is far removed from their imaginings. It is also said that it is because of the long time that has passed, which changes forms and alters appearances. The first explanation is the one included in the consolation. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the brothers of Yusuf entered upon Yusuf, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. A drinking cup was brought, and he placed it on his hand and then struck it with his finger. He said, "This cup tells me that you had a brother from your father called Yusuf, whom he favoured over you. You took him away and threw him into the depths of the well, then you came to your father and said that the wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." Some of them said to others, "Indeed this cup is telling him about your affair." Then Ibn 'Abbas said: We do not think that this verse, ﴿You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs﴾ and so on, was revealed except concerning that.

It is permissible that ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ be connected to the revelation, in the sense that We gave him company through the revelation and removed from his heart the loneliness that they had caused him, while they do not perceive this and suppose that he is lonely with no one to keep him company. This is also related from Qatadah.

This revelation took place when he (peace be upon him) was six years old according to al-Dahhak, twelve or eighteen years old according to al-Hasan, and seventeen years old according to Ibn al-Sa'ib, who is the one the Jews claim. Other views have been stated. Whoever reflects upon the verses will find that the stronger view is that he (peace be upon him) had not yet reached maturity at that time. On all the views, he (peace be upon him) was not forty years old at the time of the revelation. Indeed, most prophets (peace be upon them) were commissioned at the age of forty, though revelation came to some of them, such as Yahya and Isa (peace be upon them both), long before that.

Some claimed that the pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to Ya'qub (peace be upon him), but this is not correct, as is not hidden.

Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) recited *la-yunabbi'annahum* with the *ya'* of the third person, and likewise in the codices of Basra.

Salam recited it with the *nun* (first person plural), as a threat to them. So the words of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ are connected only to ﴿We revealed﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari said and those who followed him. But this has been critiqued: it is also permissible that it be connected to the words ﴿You will surely inform them﴾, and that the informing by Allah, the Exalted, mean the bringing of their deed to his knowledge (peace be upon him) while they do not perceive that. This was answered by saying that this is based on the apparent sense, and that Allah's informing does not combine with their not perceiving what He informed them of, except with an interpretation, such as: "We will make them know the great extent of what they committed before, while they do not perceive what is in it."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 16:

﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ That is, at that time. It is, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, from the prayer of Maghrib (sunset prayer) until al-Atamah (the late night, i.e., the time of the 'Isha' prayer), and al-'Ishan (the two 'ishas) are al-Maghrib and al-'Atamah.

It is reported from al-Hasan that he recited ﹙'Ushayyan﹚ with a damma on the 'ayn, a fatha on the shin, a shadda on the ya', and tanwin, and it is a diminutive of 'ashiyy, which is from the decline of the sun until the morning. It is also reported from him that he recited ﹙'Ushan﹚ with a damma and a short vowel (qasr), like dujan, so its accusative is as a circumstantial accusative (hal). It is the plural of a'sha according to some, and 'asha according to others. Its origin is 'ushah, like mashin and mushah, so the ha' was deleted for lightness. It was objected to these two (views) that such deletion is not permissible, and that af'al (the pattern) of fa'la' is not made plural as fu'al with a damma on the fa' and a fatha on the 'ayn, but rather fu'l with a sukun on the 'ayn. For this reason it was said: its origin was 'ashw, then the vowel of the waw was moved to the letter before it, since it is a sound consonant with sukun, then it was deleted after being changed into an alif because of the meeting of two sukuns. And if what they wept about on that day is considered, a person does not become blind from it. This was answered by saying that the intention is hyperbole regarding the intensity of weeping and wailing, not its literal reality, meaning their sight nearly weakened from the abundance of weeping. It was also said: it is the plural of 'ashwah, with the 'ayn having three vowels, and it means riding a matter without insight, as one says: he stepped on it in a 'ashwah, i.e., an ambiguous matter that places him in confusion and affliction. Thus it is an emphasis of their lying, and it is a specification (tamyiz) or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). It was also permitted that it be the plural of 'ashwah with a damma, in the sense of a flame of fire, as an expression for their haste out of joy at what they had done of the great deed, and they fabricated the lie (iftaʿalu min al-ʿadhihah). It was also permitted that (ʿishaʾan) according to the reading of the majority be the plural of ʿashin, like ra'in and ri'a', and its accusative would be as a circumstantial accusative. The first (view) is apparent. As for why they came at nightfall, either because they had not reached their place except at that time, or so that they would be more able to make excuses, due to the darkness in which shame is lifted. For this reason it was said: Do not seek a need at night, for shame is in the eyes; and do not make excuses for a sin in the daytime, lest you stammer in your excuse. And did they come in the evening of the day on which they went, or in the evening of another day? The apparent meaning of the words of some is the first, and some went to the second, based on what is narrated: that he, peace be upon him, remained in the well for three days, and his brothers were grazing around him, and Yahudha (Judah) used to bring him food.

And in the speech there is an ellipsis according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), and the estimation is ﴿And they came to their father﹚ without Yusuf ﹙ʿishaʾan yabkun﹚, that is, pretending to weep, that is, showing weeping with artifice, because it was not from sorrow, but it resembles it, and many liars do the same. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi who said: A woman came to Shurayh to dispute over something and began to weep, so they said: O Abu Umayyah, do you not see her weeping! He said: The brothers of Yusuf came to their father at nightfall, weeping. Al-A'mash said: No weeping person is believed after the brothers of Yusuf. In some reports it is related that when Ya'qub, peace be upon him, heard their weeping, he said: What is wrong with you? Has something happened to the sheep? They said: No. He said: Then what has befallen you, and where is Yusuf?

﴿They said: "O our father, we went off racing one another"﴾. That is, competing with one another in running on foot, according to what is related from al-Suddi. Or it means competing in shooting arrows, as al-Zajjaj said. Or it means engaging in tasks we share among ourselves, such as watering, pasturing, and gathering firewood. Or it means hunting and seizing game, as has been said. What al-Zajjaj said is preferred because of the reading of Abd Allah: "We went off to shoot arrows at targets" (*innā dhahabnā nantadil*). An objection to the first view is that racing on foot would not be permissible for them, since it is one of the activities of children, which have no benefit. It is answered that this is denied, and its benefit is training in running for fighting the enemy and for defending against the wolf, for example. In sum, *nastabiq* means *natasābaq* (racing one another). The *iftiʿāl* (reflexive) and *tafāʿul* (reciprocal) forms may share a meaning and be equivalent, as in *intiḍāl* and *tanāḍul* (both meaning competing in archery) and similar pairs.

﴿And we left Joseph by our belongings﴾. That is, by what is used for enjoyment: garments, provisions, and other things. ﴿So the wolf devoured him﴾ immediately after that, without a period of time in which one usually checks and attends to the goods. Since a person ordinarily sets down his belongings only in a place considered safe from dangers, leaving him (peace be upon him) beside them is not counted as negligence or as failure to keep the guarding that was required, especially since they were not absent from him. So it is as though they said: "We did not fall short in guarding him, nor were we heedless of watching over him. Rather, we left him in our place of safety and gathering, in our sight, and we did not part from him except for a short time, with only a brief distance between us and him." This is what Shaykh al-Islam said. Apparently they did not intend anything beyond the fact that the wolf ate Joseph, and they did not intend an allusion by it. What has been said, that they meant to say that the wolf ate the belongings, is not to be considered, because it departs from the straightforward meaning without any reason.

﴿And you will not believe us﴾, that is, you will not accept what we say in this statement. ﴿Even if we were﴾ in your sight and in your belief ﴿truthful﴾, that is, described as truthful and trustworthy because of your excessive love. How then, when you hold a bad opinion of us and do not trust our word? It has been said that this interpretation is necessary, for if the meaning were "even if we were truthful" in reality, its implied counterpart would be "how much less if we were lying in it," and then their admission of lying would follow. It has already been noted that in such constructions the purpose is to confirm the preceding judgment in every situation. So it is as though it were said here: "You will not believe us in any state whatsoever." Reflect and consider this.

﴿And they brought his shirt with false blood﴾, that is, blood that is a lie, or it is described with the verbal noun for emphasis, as though it were the lie itself and its very essence. This is like saying of a liar: "He is the lie itself and falsehood in person." Among examples of this is the verse of the poet:

*Pour out upon your bachelors some of your daughters, for there is no provision in the Book of God that the bounty be withheld.*

*And among them is a bounty whose place we know; they are generous with it, and you are stingy with it.*

Some interpreters take *kadhib* to mean "falsified blood" (*maktūb fīhi*), since the verbal noun may be interpreted in this way. Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with them both, read *kadhiban* in the accusative. It is explained as a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of *jāʾū* ("they came"), interpreted as "lying." It has also been said that it qualifies *damin* ("blood") as "falsified." But this faces the objection that a circumstantial qualifier from an indefinite noun is contrary to analogy. It is also permitted that it be an object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*), meaning they came with that for the sake of lying. Aisha, may God be pleased with her, and al-Hasan read *kadibin* with a *dāl* (unmarked). This is not a substitution of *dhāl* by *dāl*, but a separate dialect form meaning "turbid," "fresh," or "dry," and so it is one of the words with contrary meanings (*addād*). The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: the meaning is "having a *kadib*," that is, a mark, because *kadib* is a whiteness that appears on the nails of young men and leaves a mark on them, so it is like an engraving. This is called *fūf*. Some scholars of verification did not accept the assumption of an elided *mudāf* (possessive noun), and took this as an eloquent simile (*tashbīh balīgh*) or a metaphor (*istiʿāra*), since blood on the shirt resembles the *kadib* in that its color differs from the color of what it is on.

His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿upon his shirt﴾, according to what Abu al-Baqa went to, is a circumstantial qualifier of *damin*. Regarding the permissibility of placing a circumstantial qualifier before its governed noun when that noun is in the genitive by a non-redundant particle, there is disagreement. The correct view, as al-Saffaqsi said, is that it is permitted, because this is common in their speech. In *al-Lubab* it says: it does not precede its governed noun in the genitive according to the more correct view, as in "I passed by Hind sitting," unless the circumstantial qualifier is an adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*). But the truth is what Ibn Malik chose, namely that placement before is permitted absolutely. Al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him said that it is in the position of the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning "they came above his shirt," as you say "he came on his camels with loads." According to *al-Kashshaf*, he meant that *ʿalā* is in its literal sense of elevation, and it is an *ẓarf laghw* (a non-essential adverbial). Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr* denied that the governing verb is "came," because that would imply the upper position is an adverb of place for the ones who came. It is answered that the adverbial status is not with regard to the subject but with regard to the object.

In some marginal glosses it is said that it is better to say "they came taking control of his shirt." His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿with blood﴾, is a circumstantial qualifier of the shirt, and the meaning is "they took control of the shirt, being stained with blood, having come." This, it has been said, is better than "they came taking control," because of what has been established regarding *tadmin* (implicit inclusion of one verb's meaning in another). The matter is easy, for if the implied verb is taken as the principal and the stated one as the circumstantial, or vice versa, either is permitted. When context requires one of them, it is preferred. It was held as more likely that it is an adverb of place for the transitive "came," and the meaning is "they brought, with false blood, above his shirt." Its soundness is not hidden.

Then that blood was the blood of a young goat that they slaughtered and smeared on the shirt with its blood, as narrated from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatada that they took a gazelle, slaughtered it, and smeared its blood on the shirt. When they brought it, he began turning it over and said: "I see no trace of fang or claw on it. This wolf is compassionate!" In another report, he took the shirt, threw it over his face, and wept until he stained his face with the blood of the shirt. He said: "By God, I have never seen a wolf more gentle than this one, which ate my son without tearing his shirt." It is also reported that he wept, cried out, and fell unconscious. They poured water over him, but he did not move. They called to him, but he did not answer. Judah placed his hand over the openings of his breath, but he sensed no breath and no pulse moved in him. He said: "Woe to us from the Judge of the Day of Judgment! We have lost our brother and killed our father." He did not recover until the cool of dawn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 18:
