﴿He said: "Rather, your souls have embellished for you an affair."﴾ That is, adorned and made easy (zayyanat wa-sahhalat) ﴿an affair﴾ among the matters, an abhorrent thing that cannot be described and cannot be recognized. The root of taswil (embellishment/suggestion, tasweel) is the fixing of something in the soul together with desire for its accomplishment.

Al-Raghib said: It is the soul's adorning for itself what it is eager for, and the depicting of the ugly in the form of the beautiful.

Al-Azhari said: It seems that taswil is a form of tafˁil from the sawal of a person, which is his wish that he seeks, so it makes the false and other things appear beautiful to its seeker. Its root is hamzated. It has also been said that it is from al-sawal (with two fathas), which is a slackening in the sinew and the like, as if the one who embellishes, from his excessive greed, has had his sinew slackened. In the speech there is an ellipsis, according to what is in al-Bahr, meaning: the wolf did not eat him. ﴿Rather, your souls have embellished...﴾ etc. As for his knowledge, peace be upon him, of their lying, it is said that it came from the safety of the shirt from being torn, which is one of three signs in the shirt: the second being Ya'qub's return to sight by placing it upon his face, and the third being that it was torn from behind, for it was a proof of Yusuf's innocence. To this is added his standing by the dream indicating his reaching a lofty rank, below which the stars are humbled. It has also been said, contrary to what they claim, that it is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, said what was reported from Qatadah, some of them said: "Rather, the robbers killed him." He said: "How could they have killed him and left his shirt, while they had more need of his shirt than of killing him?!" Perhaps, despite this knowledge, he, peace be upon him, only grieved because he feared for him harm and hardships other than death. It has also been said that he grieved only at separation from him, and separation from loved ones is what cannot be borne, and for this reason it has been said:

Were it not for the separation of loved ones, death would not have found for our souls any paths.

There is no harm in saying that his grief was caused by separation from him and fear that some harm would befall him. ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ That is, so my affair is beautiful patience, or so my patience is beautiful patience, as Qutrub said; or so what I do is that, as al-Khalil said; or so it is patience, etc., as al-Farra' said. And "patience" in all of these is the predicate of an omitted subject. Or "beautiful patience" is more excellent and more beautiful, being a subject whose predicate is omitted. Is the omission in such a case obligatory or permissible? There is a difference of opinion about this. Similarly they differed regarding a single utterance in which it is valid to consider the omission of the subject and retention of the predicate, and to consider the reverse: is the first consideration preferable or the second?

Ubayy, al-Ashhab, and Isa ibn Umar read ﴿fa-sabran jamilan﴾ with the accusative for both, and likewise in the codex of Anas ibn Malik; this is also reported from al-Kisai. It is explained as meaning "fa-asbir sabran" (so be patient with patience), taking "isbir" as an imperfect verb attributed to the first-person speaker. This has been objected to, on the grounds that the accusative in such a case is good only with the imperative. Some undertook to estimate it here as meaning that he, peace be upon him, had turned to addressing himself and said: "Patience, beautiful patience," meaning "so be patient, O soul, with beautiful patience." Beautiful patience, according to what al-Hasan reported from him (may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him), is that in which there is no complaint, i.e., to creation; otherwise Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah﴾. It has also been said that his eyebrows fell over his eyes, so he would lift them with a band; he was asked about the reason for this, and he said: "The length of time and the abundance of griefs." Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Do you complain to other than Me?" He said: "O Lord, it is a sin, so forgive it."

It has also been said that what is meant by His saying ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ is: "How can I make myself beautiful to you in my patience, so that I do not associate with you with a gloomy face and a frowning brow, but rather I remain as I was with you?" This is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought﴾, that is, the One from whom aid is sought, and it is an invocation from him, peace be upon him, for continuous seeking of help. ﴿against what you describe﴾ is connected to "the One whose help is sought." And "description" is mentioning a thing with its attribute; it may be true or false, and what is meant here is the second, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾. Indeed it has been said that the form has become predominant in this sense. The meaning of his, peace be upon him, seeking help from Allah the Exalted against their lying is his asking Him, glorified is He, to manifest that it is a lie through the safety of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and reunion with him. So the mention of seeking help here is similar to ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ after his saying later: ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. It is reported in some reports that Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said on the day of the slander: "By Allah, if I swear, you will not believe me, and if I offer an excuse, you will not accept my excuse; my example and yours is like the example of Ya'qub and his son. And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe." Then Allah the Exalted revealed in her defense what He revealed. It has also been said that what is meant is that He, the Exalted, is the One whose help is sought to bear what you describe of Yusuf's destruction; as if he, peace be upon him, after saying "beautiful patience," asked Him, the Exalted, for help in patience, because the carnal drives call to the display of distress, and they are strong, while the spiritual drives are beautiful patience; so it is as if a struggle occurred between the two attributes, and unless help comes from Him, glorified and exalted, victory is not achieved. Thus his saying "So patience is beautiful" runs in the manner of ﴿You alone we worship﴾, and ﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ runs in the manner of ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾. Perhaps the first is safer from talk and disputation. Imam al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, has a discussion at this point, namely: patience with the decree of Allah the Exalted is obligatory, but patience with the oppression of oppressors and the plots of schemers is not obligatory; rather, what is obligatory is to remove it, especially when the harm returns to another. So it would have been fitting for Ya'qub, peace be upon him, to search and strive to free Yusuf, peace be upon him, from the affliction and hardship if he was alive, and to establish retribution if it is true that they killed him. Indeed it may be said that the obligatory duty that was incumbent upon him was to strive in seeking him and freeing him, because the apparent meaning is that he was knowing that he was alive and safe, according to His saying: ﴿And thus your Lord chooses you and teaches you the interpretation of events﴾, for the apparent meaning is that he said it by revelation. Also, he, peace be upon him, was of great rank, of exalted status, esteemed in souls, renowned in the horizons; so if he had exerted himself greatly in seeking and inquiry, it would have become apparent and widely known, and the cause of deception would have vanished. What, then, is the reason for his, peace be upon him, abandoning the inquiry, despite his utmost desire for Yusuf's presence and his extreme love for him? Is patience in this situation anything but blameworthy by reason and by law? Then he said: The answer is that we say: there is no answer to that except that it may be said that He, glorified and exalted, prevented him from seeking, to intensify the trial and make the matter more severe. Also, perhaps he knew from circumstantial evidence that his sons were strong and that they would not allow him to seek and inquire, and that if he exerted himself greatly in the search, they might proceed to harm him and kill him. Also, perhaps he, peace be upon him, knew that Allah the Exalted would protect Yusuf from affliction and trial, and that his matter would be exalted in the Hereafter; then he did not want to expose the concealment of his sons, and he was not content to cast them onto the tongues of people. This is because if one of two sons wrongs the other, the father falls into severe torment: for if he does not take retribution, his heart burns over the wronged son, and if he takes retribution, his heart burns over the son from whom he takes it. A parallel to this is what the poet alluded to in his saying:

My people are they who killed my brother Umayym, so when I shoot, my arrow strikes me.
And if I pardon, I will pardon a great fault, and if I lash out, it breaks my bones.

When Ya'qub, peace be upon him, fell into this affliction, he saw that the more correct course was patience, silence, and entrusting the matter entirely to Allah the Exalted, especially if we say that he, peace be upon him, knew that what had occurred could not be remedied until the Book reaches its appointed term.

صفحة 203

﴿وجاءَتْ﴾ (*And there came*): this begins the account of what happened to Joseph, peace be upon him, in the well, after finishing the mention of what had occurred between his brothers and their father. That is, *and there came to the well* ﴿سَيّارَةٌ﴾ (*a caravan*), a company traveling from Madyan toward Egypt. This was after three days had passed from the time he was thrown in, according to one opinion. It was said that it was on the second day. The apparent meaning is that the well was on their usual route.

It was also said that it was in a remote desert far from inhabited areas, so they lost their way and came upon it. ﴿فَأرْسَلُوا﴾ (*So they sent*) to it ﴿وارِدَهُمْ﴾ (*their water-drawer*), the one who comes to the water and draws it for them. This was Malik ibn Dhu'r al-Khuza'i.

Ibn Atiyya said: "The *warid* (water-drawer) here may refer to one person or to a group." End quote. The apparent view is the first. The feminine in ﴿جاءَتْ﴾ and the masculine in ﴿أرْسَلُوا﴾ and ﴿وارِدَهُمْ﴾ are according to the wording and the meaning respectively. The use of the verb "came" (*jā'a*) hints at the honor of Joseph, peace be upon him, with his Lord, glory be to Him. The object of the verb is omitted, as is the object of "sent," because it is evident. For the same reason, the object is omitted in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿فَأدْلى دَلْوَهُ﴾ (*so he lowered his bucket*), meaning he sent it down into the well to draw water. It is said: *dalā al-dalw* means he pulled up the bucket when it was full. The word *dalw* (bucket) is among the feminine nouns by lexical transmission (*samā'iyya*), so its diminutive is *duliyya*, and its plurals are *adul*, *dilā'* and *duliyy*.

Ibn al-Shihna said: The bucket with which water is drawn is feminine, though it may be made masculine. As for *dalw*, a verbal noun from *dalawtu* and a kind of movement, it is masculine. Similarly in gender, *jubb* (well/pit) is, according to al-Farra', as transmitted from him by Muhammad ibn al-Jahm, both masculine and feminine. Some have said it is masculine only. As for *bi'r* (well), it is feminine only according to the well-known view. Its diminutive is *buwayra*, and its plurals are *ābār*, *abŭr*, *abu'ur* and *bi'ār*.

In the speech there is an ellipsis: *fa-adlā dalwahu fa-tadallā bihā Yūsufu fa-kharaja* (*so he lowered his bucket, and Joseph clung to it and came out*). ﴿قالَ﴾ (*he said*) is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nāf*), answering a question that the situation demands.

﴿يا بُشْرى هَذا غُلامٌ﴾ (*O good news! This is a boy!*) He called out "good news" as glad tidings to himself, or to his people and companions, as if he had made it like a person and called to it. So it is a implicit metaphor (*isti'āra makniyya*) and imaginative (*takhyīliyya*), meaning: O good news, come, for this is the time of your presence. It was also said that the one addressed is omitted, as in "O would that" (*yā layta*), meaning: O my people, look and listen to my good news. It was also said that this expression is used for giving good news without intending a call.

Some claimed that *Bushrā* is the name of a companion of his, whom he called to help him bring him out. This was narrated from al-Suddi, but it is not correct.

Readers other than the Kufans recited *yā bushrāya* with the *iḍāfa* (possessive form). Hamza and al-Kisa'i made the *fatḥa* on the *rā'* into *imāla* (a vowel inclination). Warsh recited between the two pronunciations.

It is narrated from Nafi' that he recited *yā bushrāya* with the pronoun-suffix *yā'* (*ya' al-iḍāfa*) pronounced with sukun, which requires meeting of two unvowelled letters contrary to its usual rule, and he excused this by saying he treated the connected speech as if it were pausal. Similar cases are numerous in the Qur'an and elsewhere. It was also said this was allowed because the long *alif* stands in place of a vowel because of its length.

Abu al-Tufayl, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Jahdari recited *yā bushrayy* (with the *alif* changed to *yā'* and assimilated into the *yā'* of possession). This is a dialect of Hudhayl and others. Among examples of this is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*They outran their longing and went to excess in their desire, so they were struck down, and every side has its place of falling.*

People also say *yā sayyidī* and *mawlayy* (O my lord, O my master).

The word *ghulām* (boy) is very often applied to the one between two years old and puberty, and it may be applied to a complete man, as in the words of Layla al-Akhyaliyya about al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi:

*A youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink.*

The apparent view is that the *tanwīn* in it is for magnification (*tafkhīm*). He deserved this, for he was among the most beautiful of boys. Al-Baghawi reported from him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, that he said: "Joseph was given half of beauty." (ﷺ)

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "Joseph and his mother took two-thirds of beauty." Al-Tha'labi narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: "Joseph had a beautiful face, curly hair, large eyes, a balanced build, fair complexion, thick forearms and calves, a slender belly and a small navel. When he smiled, you saw light in his smile, and when he spoke, you saw the rays of light from his front teeth. No one could describe him. His beauty was like the light of day at night, and he resembled Adam, peace be upon him, on the day He created him, before he committed the sin."

It is said that the sides of the well wept over him when he came out of it. Perhaps this is from the figure of speech where "the house wept over the loss of so-and-so."

The apparent view is that the words of the water-drawer ﴿يا بُشْرى هَذا غُلامٌ﴾ were said upon seeing him. It was also said that when he came to his companions he shouted this.

﴿وأسَرُّوهُ﴾ (*And they concealed him*): the water-drawer and his companions hid him from the rest of the caravan, so that they would not see him and desire him. It was said that they concealed the matter of him, and that he was found in the well, and they told the rest of the caravan: "The people of the water gave him to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt."

It was also said that the pronoun refers to Joseph's brothers. This is because some of them returned to verify his situation, saw him with the caravan, informed their brothers, and they came to them and said: "This is a runaway slave of ours." So they bought him, and Joseph remained silent for fear that they would kill him. In one report they said in Hebrew: "Do not deny that you are a slave, or we will kill you." So he acknowledged it, and they bought him from them.

It was also said that Yahudha (Judah) used to bring him food. He came to him on the day he was taken out and did not find him in the well, but found him with the caravan, so he informed his brothers, and they came to them and said what they said.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the pronoun refers to the brothers. It was said that this is the more suitable reading for the singular *qāla* (*he said*) and the plural of the pronoun in *asarrū* (*they concealed*), and it fits the threat that comes shortly after, if Allah wills. There is no disruption in the composition. It is not hidden that the apparent view is the one mentioned first.

The accusative of His words, glory be to Him, ﴿بِضاعَةً﴾ (*as merchandise*) is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), meaning: they concealed him while he was goods for trade. In *al-Farā'id* it is stated that *asarrūhu* was made to include the meaning of *ja'alūhu* (they made him), meaning they made him merchandise, keeping him secret, so it is an object.

Ibn al-Hajib said: It is possible that it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*), meaning for the sake of trade. Its condition is not missing, because the subject of the verb and the subject of the verb it is given as a reason for are one, for the meaning is that they concealed him for the sake of obtaining wealth through him. It is not permissible that it be a specification (*tamyīz*). It is from *al-bid'* in the sense of cutting off. The word *biḍā'a* (merchandise) seems to be so named because it is cut off from wealth and made for trade. From the same root come *bid'* (a number between three and ten, or more than five and less than ten) and *badī'a* (an island cut off from the mainland). Al-Raghib considered in *biḍā'a* that it is a substantial piece of wealth kept for trade, and he did not consider the abundance of it as a condition.

﴿واللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (*And Allah is Knowing of what they do*): nothing of their secrets was hidden from Him, glory be to Him. Many have stated that this is a threat to Joseph's brothers for what they did to their father and their brother, and for their selling him, while he was exposed to being sold and bought.

[Page 204]

﴿And they sold him﴾. The pronoun (the subject) is either for the brothers, in which case *shara* means "sold" (*baa'a*), or for the caravan, in which case it means "bought" (*ishtara*), as in the line:

*(And I bought) a cloak, would that after one cloak I had been its headpiece*

and in the line:

*Had this death been ransomable with a ransom, I would have bought Abu Zayd with all that my hand possesses*

He also allowed that, on this second reading, it could mean "sold," on the basis that they sold him when they had picked him up from some of them. ﴿For a paltry price﴾: *bakhs* means deficiency, and it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. "deficient," meaning underweight. Al-Raghib allowed that it could mean *bakhis* (a participle of the same root), i.e. one that falls short of its value by a clear deficiency. Muqatil said: "counterfeit, lacking in its standard." Qatadah said: "*bakhs* is injustice, because they wronged him in selling him." Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, among others, said: "*bakhs* is the unlawful, and that was unlawful because it was the price of a free man. The unlawful was called *bakhs* because it is stripped of blessing (*mabkhus al-barakah*), i.e. its blessing is diminished." His words, glorified is He: ﴿dirhams﴾ is an apposition to *thaman* (price), i.e. not dinars. ﴿Counted﴾, i.e. few. Counting is used as a metaphor for scarcity, because a large amount was weighed among them. The number of these dirhams in most narrations was twenty dirhams. In a narration from Ibn Abbas it was twenty-two; in another from him, twenty, plus a garment and two sandals; and it was said thirty, plus a garment and two sandals; and it was said eighteen, with which they bought socks and sandals; and it was said ten. And from Ikrimah it is related that they were forty dirhams. What several have mentioned does not contradict this, namely that their custom was not to weigh anything less than an *uqiyyah*, which is forty dirhams, since there is no denial in it that forty may be counted.

﴿And they were in regard to him﴾, i.e. regarding Joseph, as is the apparent meaning, ﴿of those who were indifferent﴾, i.e. those who turned away from him. The pronoun in "they were" (*wa-kanu*), if it refers to the brothers, is clear. If it refers to the caravan, who were sellers, their indifference toward him is because they had picked him up, and one who has picked up something is careless about it and does not mind what he sells; also because he fears that a rightful owner may come forward and seize it from his hand, so he sells it to the first bidder at the lowest price. And if it refers to them as buyers, i.e. they bought him from some of them or from the brothers, their indifference is because they believed he was a runaway slave, and so they feared to risk what was theirs in him. It was also said that the pronoun in "in it" (*fihi*) refers to the price, and their indifference to it is because of its poor quality, or because their only aim was to remove Joseph, peace be upon him. This is evident if the pronoun in "they were" refers to the brothers. The prepositional phrase, according to what is reported from Ibn Malik, is connected to a deleted element indicated by "the indifferent," meaning: they were indifferent to him, being of the indifferent. This is because the *al-* in "the indifferent" is a relative pronoun (*ism mawsul*), and the content of the relative clause may not precede it, and because what follows a preposition does not govern what comes before it. Then is "of the indifferent" in that case an attribute of the deleted "indifferent" that is emphasizing, as you would say: "a scholar of the scholars"? Or a specifying attribute, meaning: indifferent, to the point that their indifference reached the level of their being counted among the indifferent, because the indifferent person may not be firmly established among the indifferent until he is counted among them when they are counted? Or is it a second predicate? All of this is possible. It is not an apposition to the deleted element, because *min* is present with it. Some have estimated the deleted element as "I mean, and I am among the indifferent." Ibn al-Hajib, in his *Amali*, said: it is connected to the relative clause, and the meaning is clearly that without doubt. They only avoided this because they understood that the relative clause does not govern what precedes the relative pronoun at all. There is a difference between the relative clause of *al-* and others, for this one has the form of a particle that is treated as part of the word, so there is no prohibition on placing its complement before it. Thus there is no need to say that its connection to what was mentioned is the view of al-Mazini, who made *al-* in such cases the definite article, and it seems he did not regard fronting the complement of the genitive as impermissible; otherwise the removal of the difficulty would not be complete by what he mentioned.

Some have claimed that it is necessary, after the active participle has operated, without a dependence, that there be a heedlessness in its place, because the point of disagreement is its operation on the subject and the direct object, not on the prepositional phrase, which is sufficient for it as a trace of the verb. Some later scholars said: the attribute here relies on the subject of "they were," which is originally a predicate of the subject, and reliance on that is considered valid among them. In al-Radi, on the words of Ibn al-Hajib, "and reliance on its companion," by its companion he means the subject, either in the present, as in "Zayd is a hitter, his two brothers," or originally, as in "Zayd was a hitter, his two brothers," "I thought you a hitter, your two brothers," and "indeed Zayd is a hitter, his two boys." On this view there is no need, in answering, to take the prepositional phrase out of the ruling of the subject and direct object; although it has a good basis, it is disputed by those who deny it. Some people hold fast to a generality that allows a wider scope for adverbs and prepositional phrases than for other elements, in order to answer the objection raised against connecting the prepositional phrase here to the attribute in the genitive that serves as the relative clause of *al-*, whatever it may be. So let this be understood.

That said, the common view is that the sellers were his brothers and the indifferent were them. And in some reports it is said that when they sold him they told the merchant: "He is a thief and a runaway, so bind him and assign to him a black slave." When the time of their departure came, he wept, peace be upon him. The merchant said to him: "Why are you weeping?" He said: "I want to reach those who sold me, to bid them farewell and greet them with the greeting of one who will not return to them." The merchant said to the slave: "Take him and go with him to his masters so that he may bid them farewell, then join him to the caravan. I have never seen a boy more dutiful to his masters than this one, nor people more harsh than them." So the slave went ahead with him to his brothers. One of them was awake, guarding the sheep. When Joseph reached him, stumbling in his chains, he threw himself upon him and wept. He said to him: "Why have you come?" He said: "I have come to bid you farewell and greet you." Their brother cried out to them: "Stand up for the one who has come to greet you with the greeting of one who does not hope to see you ever again. Woe to you because of this farewell!" So they stood, and Joseph began to fall upon each of them, kissing and embracing him, saying: "May God Most High preserve you; if you wrong me, may God Most High shelter you; if you drive me away, may God Most High have mercy on you, even if you do not have mercy on me." It was said: the sheep gave birth to what was in their wombs from the terror of this farewell. Then the slave took him and sought the caravan. While he was on his mount, he passed by the grave of his mother Rahil in the cemeteries of Canaan. When he saw the grave, he could not restrain himself and threw himself upon it, embracing it, weeping and saying: "O mother! Raise your head from the dust so that you may see your son in chains. O mother! My brothers threw me into the well, separated me from my father, and sold me for the lowest of prices, and they did not show pity for my young age, nor did they have mercy on me. So I ask God Most High to gather me and my father in the abode of His mercy; indeed He is the Most Merciful of the merciful." The slave turned and did not see him, so he returned and found him at the grave. He said: "By God, your masters spoke the truth: you are a runaway slave!" Then he struck him a severe blow, so that he fainted. Then he came to, and said to him: "Do not blame me. This is my mother's grave. I came down to greet her, and I will never return to what you dislike." Then he raised his eyes to the sky, having rolled in the dust, with tears on his face, and said: "O God, if I have any sin that has marred my face before You, then by the sanctity of my noble forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, forgive me and have mercy on me, O Most Merciful of the merciful." At that, the angels cried out to God Most High. Then the Blessed and Most High said: "O My angels, this is My prophet and the son of My prophets, and he has sought help from Me, and I am his helper and the helper of those who seek help. O Gabriel, reach him." So Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended and said: "O friend of God, your Lord sends you greetings and says to you: 'Be patient; you have made the angels of the seven heavens weep. Do you want Me to overturn the sky upon the earth?'" He said: "No, O Gabriel, be gentle with the creation of my Lord, for He is forbearing and does not hasten." Then he struck the earth with his wing, and a red wind blew, the sun was eclipsed, and the dusty earth grew dark, so that the people of the caravan could not see one another. The merchant said: "Dismount before you perish. I have passed along this road for many years, and I have never seen the like of today. Whoever among you has committed a sin, let him repent of it, for this has befallen us only because of a sin we have committed." Then the slave informed him of what he had done with Joseph, and said: "O my master, when I struck him, he raised his eyes to the sky and moved his lips." The merchant said to him: "Woe to you! You have destroyed us and destroyed yourself!" Then the merchant approached him and said: "O boy, we wronged you when we struck you; if you wish to take retribution from us, here we are before you." Joseph said: "I am not of a people who take retribution when they are wronged. Rather, I am of a household that, when they are wronged, pardons and forgives. I have pardoned you, hoping that God Most High will pardon me." The darkness cleared, the wind subsided, the sun shone out, and it lit up the eastern and western parts of the earth. They traveled until they entered Egypt in safety. It is said that this merchant was Malik ibn Dhu'r, who had drawn him out of the well; and it was said to be someone else.

It is related that when he arrived with him in Egypt, he sold him for twenty dinars, a pair of sandals, and two white garments. It was also said: he was taken to the market for sale, and they haggled over his price until it reached his weight in musk, his weight in silver, and his weight in silk. He was bought for that by the *'Aziz* who was over the treasuries of Egypt in the service of its king. It was also said that he was the king's baker, his cupbearer, the keeper of his animals, and the well-known keeper of the prison. The one relied upon is the first, and his name was Qatfir, or Atfir, or Qantura. The first is related from Ibn Abbas, and it is what is meant in His words, glorified is He:

[p. 207]

﴿The one who bought him from Egypt said﴾. This purchase is not the earlier purchase, which was for a base price. The claim that the two are the same is very weak; otherwise the phrase ﴿from Egypt﴾ would have little value. The king at that time was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid al-'Amaliqi, who died during the lifetime of Yusuf, peace be upon him, after he had believed in him. He was succeeded by Qabus ibn Mus'ab, whom Yusuf invited to faith, but he refused.

It has also been said that the king in his time was the Pharaoh of Musa, peace be upon him, who lived four hundred years, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Yusuf had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾. It has also been said that the Pharaoh of Musa, peace be upon him, was one of the descendants of the Pharaoh of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and that the verse is an address to the descendants about the circumstances of their fathers. This is the correct view. The apparent state of the Aziz is that he was a disbeliever.

Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), relied on this from the fact that an idol was in his house, as is mentioned in some narrations.

Mujahid said he was a believer. Perhaps his meaning is that he believed afterwards, for otherwise his being a believer on the day of the purchase is hardly acceptable. Yes, he took care of the matter of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and for this reason he said ﴿to his wife﴾, Ra'il, daughter of Ra'abil. This is what is related from Mujahid.

al-Suddi said: Zulaykha, daughter of Tamlikha. It has also been said: her name was Ra'il and her epithet was Zulaykha, and it has also been said the reverse.

The first prepositional phrase, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is connected to ﴿bought﴾, as in your saying "I bought him from Baghdad", meaning "in it" or "with it". Or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun ﴿the one﴾ or from the pronoun in ﴿bought﴾, meaning "being from the people of Egypt". The second prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿said﴾, as we have indicated, not to ﴿bought﴾. The content of the saying is ﴿Honour his residence﴾, meaning: make his place of dwelling and stay honourable, i.e. good and pleasing. This is a metonymy for honouring him, peace be upon him, himself in the most eloquent and complete manner, because whoever honours a place by cleaning it, furnishing it and the like, has honoured his guest with everything by which he is honoured.

It has also been said: al-mathwa (residence) is superfluous, as one says "the high assembly" and "the lofty station", and the meaning is: take good care of him and attend to what the honouring of a guest requires. ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ in the management of our affairs when he is trained in matters and knows their courses. ﴿Or we may adopt him as a son﴾, meaning we may adopt him and make him in the place of a son. It is reported that she was barren. Perhaps the separation (in the sentence) is to prevent a void.

Some claimed that the disjunction is to prevent combination, in the sense: perhaps we will sell him and benefit from his price. This is nothing. This statement came from the Aziz because he perceived in him signs of right guidance and nobility. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said in what Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Hakim related, and which al-Hakim authenticated along with a group: The most perceptive of people are three: the Aziz, when he perceived in Yusuf and said to his wife: ﴿Honour his residence; perhaps he will benefit us﴾ and so on; the woman who came to Musa and said to her father: ﴿O father, hire him﴾; and Abu Bakr when he appointed Umar as successor.

﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land﴾, meaning We made for him a place in it. One says: "makkanahu fihi" meaning "He established him in it", and "makkana lahu fihi" meaning "He made for him a place in it". Because the two are close and mutually implied, each is used in the position of the other. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established in the land as We have not established you?﴾ The intended meaning of "place" here is rank and status, not mere distance, nor the inner surface of the container touching the outer surface of the contained, nor anything else of what some philosophers held, whether true or false. The demonstrative refers to what is understood from the preceding speech and the sense of distance in it, to magnify it. The particle "ka" (like/as) is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (masdariyya), meaning: just as We made for him an honourable dwelling in the house of the Aziz, or a lofty place in his heart, so that he ordered his wife, above all others in his entourage, to honour his residence, We made for him an exalted rank in the land of Egypt. The making mentioned has been explained as making him distinguished among the people of Egypt and beloved in their hearts, on the basis that this is what leads to the goal mentioned in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾

[p. 208]

meaning some of the interpretation of dreams, whose principal sources are the dream of the king and the two companions of the prison. This meaning is related from Mujahid, and it is the apparent one, as his saying, peace be upon him, indicates: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾. Whether it is taken as coordinated with an implied purpose that the discourse leads to and the arrangement requires, as if it were said: "Likewise this wondrous establishment: We established Yusuf in the land and made the hearts of its people entirely the places of his love, so that there would follow from that what follows of what took place between him and the wife of the Aziz, and that We might teach him some of the interpretation of events, which leads to the highest rank and the great leadership", or whether the coordinated element is omitted to indicate that it is not intended, or it is made a cause of an omitted element, as if it were said: "For this profound wisdom We did this establishment, and not for anything else that has no good outcome." Perhaps the omission of the coordinated element is to indicate that it is not intended.

Some of the verifying scholars chose that ﴿that﴾ refers to the verbal noun of the verb mentioned after it, and the particle "ka" is superfluous to emphasize the grandeur of the matter referred to, according to what they mentioned regarding ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾. What is intended is the establishment in the heart of the Aziz or in his house. That this is an establishment in the land, in the sense that he became powerful in it, is because what these affairs depend upon is the establishment on the side of the Aziz. As for the establishment on the side of all the people, its reaching them is only by way of its being included in that establishment. It is not hidden that to take "establishment in the land" as "establishment in the heart of the Aziz or in his house" is contrary to what is apparent, and likewise to take it as what preceded. Perhaps what is apparent is to take it as his being made a king who disposes of the land of Egypt by command and prohibition, except that in making the mentioned teaching a goal of it there is an obscurity, because that making is among its effects and results that branch from it, not the reverse. Nor has it been known from him, peace be upon him, in the course of his affairs, that he acted according to the requirement of the dream that warns of events before they occur, as a known precedent that would justify making it a goal of that. What occurred of the discussion about the years was rather action according to the requirement of the earlier known dream, and a desire that Our teaching him might become manifest, as you see. It seems that whoever held this view, because it is the apparent one, intended by the teaching of the interpretation of events the making understood of the profound secrets of the divine books and the subtle details of the ways of the prophets, peace be upon them. Then the meaning becomes: We established him in the land of Egypt so that he might dispose of it with justice, and that We might teach him the meanings of the books of Allah the Exalted, their rulings, and the subtle details of the ways of the prophets, peace be upon them, so that he might judge among its people by them. The general teaching of those events, although not later than his establishment in that sense, yet the teaching of each particular meaning that happens within events and the guidance to the truth in each calamity among calamities, is later than that and suitable to be its goal. Some of them included the deliverance under the indication of this, and in it there is a discussion, so reflect.

﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾: He is not prevented from what He wills, nor is He disputed in what He intends. Rather, His command for a thing, when He wills it, is only that He says to it "Be," and it is. The matters of Him, glorified be He, related to Yusuf, peace be upon him, enter into the generality of the verbal noun in construct, entering not in the first place, or being in charge of the matter of Yusuf, peace be upon him, so that He manages it and does not entrust it to another. Ibn Jubayr went to the view that the pronoun of "His affair" refers to Allah the Exalted, and al-Qurtubi went to the view that it refers to Yusuf, peace be upon him. In any case, the statement according to what is in al-Kashf (of al-Zamakhshari) is a concluding remark (tadhyil). As for the first view, it is because it runs in the manner of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ from its preceding context, because since He is dominant over all His affairs, none contends with Him and nothing that He wills is prevented from Him, His will was the establishment of Yusuf and such and such, and the occurrence of his being suckled as two infants. As for the second view, its meaning is that He is dominant over His affair, managing it with His subtle craftsmanship and abundant kindness. When the river of Allah the Exalted comes, the river of Ma'qil is annulled, so where does the plotting of the brothers and others, like the wife of the Aziz, stand? It is like his saying:

"And why should I mount it, if I do not dismount from its predecessor? I mean, leave the fighting, and I was the first to dismount."

[p. 209]

The verse according to the first view is explicit in the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah, the adherents of the prophetic tradition and community) ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ that the matter is so in what they do and what they leave undone, claiming that they have some share in the matter. And how could they? Rather, the whole matter belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Or they do not know the subtleties of His craftsmanship and the hidden aspects of His grace. The intended sense of "most of the people" has been said to be the disbelievers, and this has been reported from Ibn Atiyya. It has been said: the people of Egypt; it has been said: the people of Makkah; it has been said: "most" here means "all", and what is meant is that all people do not have knowledge of His unseen. The better course is to keep it on what is understood from it, and not to restrict its explanation to what the earlier sayings included, but rather it is intended to refer to whoever has been denied knowledge of what preceded, whatever it may be. And it is not far-fetched that the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) enter into its generality.

﴿And when he reached his full maturity (ashudd)﴾ means: when he reached the time when the growth and strength of his body were complete, which is the age when the body stops growing in any significant way, that is, between thirty and forty. Al-Qadi al-Nahwi Muhadhdhib al-Din Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib al-Khaymi was asked about it and said: it is thirty-five years, and its completion is forty.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from seventeen years up to about forty. From Mujahid and Qatadah, and it is also transmitted by Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, that it is thirty-three, or thirty, or twenty-one. Al-Dahhak said: twenty. Ibn Qutaybah reported that it is thirty-eight.

Al-Hasan said: forty. The well-known view is that a person's body stops growing when he reaches that age, and when the body stops, the powers, the dispositions and the character also stop. For this reason it has been said:

When a man reaches forty and has not
Restraint or modesty before what he desires,
Then leave him, and do not grieve over what has passed,
Even if life's causes are drawn out for him by length of years.

It has also been said: the furthest limit of ashudd is fifty-two. The view that ashudd is the end of youth and strength before decline begins was held by Abu Ubaydah and others of the trustworthy lexicographers, and some of the scholars of verification (muhaqqiqun) regarded it as the strongest. According to Sibawayh, it is a plural whose singular is shiddah, like ni'mah and an'um. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said it is the plural of shadd, like sakk and asukk, and fals and aflus. According to what Abu Hatim mentioned, this requires that it be feminine, because every plural on the pattern af'ul is feminine.

It is claimed on the authority of Abu Ubaydah that the word has no singular from its own form among the Arabs. Al-Farra' said: the people of Basra claim that it is a singular noun but of a pattern that is rare among singulars, and we have seldom seen a noun of the pattern af'ul that is not a plural.

﴿We gave him judgment (hukm)﴾ means wisdom (hikmah). In the language of the Sharia, wisdom is beneficial knowledge that is confirmed by action, because without action knowledge is not counted as valuable, and action contrary to knowledge is foolishness. Or it means judgment between people. ﴿And knowledge (ilm)﴾ means the knowledge of the interpretation of dreams. It is mentioned separately because it is not included in what precedes it, or it is singled out because it is something of great importance, and Joseph, peace be upon him, had a complete specialization in it, so it is said.

Some have explained wisdom as prophethood and knowledge as understanding of the religion. It has also been said: wisdom is restraining the self from its desires and guarding it from what is not fitting, and knowledge is theoretical knowledge. It has also been said: by wisdom is meant judgment between people, and by knowledge is knowledge of the aspects of public benefit, for when people brought their disputes to the Aziz, he ordered him to judge between them, because of the intellect and soundness of judgment he saw in him.

From Ibn Abbas: judgment is prophethood and knowledge is the Sharia. Their indefiniteness (in the Arabic) is for magnification, meaning judgment and knowledge whose essence cannot be grasped and whose measure cannot be estimated.

The view that the intended knowledge is the knowledge of the interpretation of narrations has been criticized, on the grounds that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And thus﴾, meaning like that wondrous recompense, ﴿We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning everyone who does good in his knowledge, rejects it, because that does not suit being a recompense for his good deeds, among which is enduring sorrows and hardships, unless it is restricted to the knowledge of interpreting the king's dream. For that, since it came at the end of the days of trial, could properly be counted among the recompense. As for the dream of the two companions of the prison, he, peace be upon him, remained in prison for several years after interpreting it. In linking the mentioned recompense to the doers of good there is an indication that good conduct is the cause for him, and an alert that God, exalted is He, gave him what He gave him only because he was a doer of good in his deeds and excellent in his affairs in the vigour of his early life. For this reason al-Hasan said: whoever does well in the worship of God, glorified is He, in his youth, God, exalted is He, will grant him wisdom in his old age.

An objection has been raised concerning what the linking of the judgment to a derived term of causation indicates, on the assumption that by wisdom is meant knowledge confirmed by action. For example, excellence in action is not possible except after knowledge of it, so if the knowledge confirmed by it were the cause of excellence, this would lead to circularity (dawr).

It has been answered that excellence in action can occur by another way, such as imitation and divine grace, and so it becomes a cause for knowledge of it through rational or transmitted evidence. Or the intended meaning is actions that do not depend on revelation, so that this becomes the cause for knowledge of what was prescribed for him of actions. Some of the scholars of verification said: the apparent view is that the two kinds of knowledge are different, as in the report: "Whoever acts on what he knows, God, exalted is He, will make easy for him the knowledge of what he did not know."

From al-Dahhak, the interpretation of "the doers of good" is "those who are patient in calamities."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him﴾. This is a return to explaining what happened to him, peace be upon him, in the house of the Aziz after he had ordered his wife to honour his lodging. The words of the Exalted, ﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾, up to here, are a parenthetical interjection, brought as a sample of the story, so that the listener may know from the outset that what he, peace be upon him, encountered of the trials which will be narrated to him in detail has a beautiful end and a praiseworthy outcome, and that he, peace be upon him, was a doer of good in his deeds, and nothing proceeded from him that would compromise his integrity. ORIGINAL: والمُراوَدَةُ المُطالَبَةُ بِرِفْقٍ مِن رادَ يَرُودُ إذا ذَهَبَ وجاءَ لِطَلَبِ شَيْءٍ.

Note on the text: I have translated only the opening portion of the passage as it stands in your input, and I have not gone beyond it.

Ibn Abi Ishaq (his view). It was objected to that it involves applying "Rabb" (Lord) to other than God Most High. If it is meant in the sense of Creator (al-Khaliq), then it is invalid, because a noble prophet could not apply that to a created being. And if it is meant in the sense of master (al-sayyid), then he, peace be upon him, is in reality a slave belonging to Him. For this reason, although there is clear scrutiny of what was mentioned, al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan) chose that the pronoun refers to God Most High, that "rabbi" (my Lord) is the subject of "inna" (indeed), that "ahsana mathwaya" (He made my abode good) is a second predicate, or that it is the predicate, and the first is a substitute for the pronoun. That is: indeed He, Most High, my Creator, made my abode good, by way of a turn of the heart; so how could I disobey Him by committing that great immorality? Within it is a warning to her against the punishment of God Most High. He also permitted, on the assumption that "Rabb" means Creator, that the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n) as well. Whichever is the case, restricting the mention to this state without addressing what it requires, namely the refraining from what she invited him to, indicates that this level of explanation is sufficient to show its impossibility and that it is something that does not fall under occurrence at all.

God Most High's words: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed.﴾ are a rationale following a rationale for the aforementioned refraining. Al-falah (success) is attainment of victory and reaching one's aim, and it is of two kinds: worldly and otherworldly. The first is attaining the worldly good by which life in this world is made pleasant, which is continuance, wealth, and honor. The second consists of four things: continuance without end, wealth without poverty, honor without humiliation, and knowledge without ignorance. For this reason it was said: there is no life except the life of the Hereafter. The meaning of aflaha is "entered into success," like asbaha and its sisters. Perhaps the intended meaning here is the otherworldly success. By "the wrongdoers" is meant everyone who wrongs, whoever he may be, so those who repay good with evil and those who disobey God's command enter into it first and foremost. It was also said: the adulterers, because they wrong themselves, and wrong the one who is violated concerning his family. It was also said: the traitors, because they wrong themselves as well and wrong those who trusted them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, that is, desired to be intimate with him, in that case, for them. This holds whether the verb is used in the general sense of intending and wanting, or in the sense of firm resolve and fixed determination, which is what is meant here. It is not connected with concrete objects.

The meaning is that she intended the intimacy and resolved upon it with a firm resolve, which no deterrent could turn her from after she had begun its preliminaries and done what she did, as Allah the Exalted has related. Perhaps she also undertook other acts there, such as stretching out her hand toward him, seeking an embrace, and other things that compelled him, peace be upon him, to flee toward the door. The emphasis is to remove what might be imagined, namely the possibility that she had given up what she was doing because of the warnings in his words, peace be upon him. ﴿And he desired her﴾, that is, he inclined toward intimacy with her by the demands of human nature, like the inclination of a fasting person on a hot day toward cold water. Such a thing hardly falls under obligation. It does not mean that he, peace be upon him, intended her by a deliberate choice, because that is a blameworthy matter, and the verses testify that he, peace be upon him, was not characterized by it. He was described with the word "desire" only because it occurred alongside her desire in the wording, by way of rhetorical correspondence (mushakalah), not because of any resemblance, as some have said. Their difference has been pointed out, as many have said: the wording did not join them in one clause, such as "they both desired intimacy" or "each of them desired the other." The first was emphasized and the second was not.

﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, that is, His overwhelming argument that demonstrates the complete ugliness of fornication and the evil of its way. Seeing it means his complete certainty in it and his witnessing of it reaching the level of the certainty of direct observation (ʿayn al-yaqin). It was also said that seeing the proof means the arising of moral restraint and the recollection of circumstances that deter one from committing what is forbidden. It was also said that it was the sight of the words ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way﴾ written on the ceiling. The answer to "had he not" (law-la) is omitted, and the context indicates it: that is, had he not witnessed the proof, he would have acted according to the demand of his natural inclination. But since he was witnessing it, he continued in what he was upon, according to the requirement of the proof. This is what some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) have held regarding the meaning of the verse. It is a view that affirms that he, peace be upon him, had a desire, but one that was not blameworthy.

In al-Bahr it is said that nothing of the kind of desire for her ever occurred from him, peace be upon him, at all. Rather, it is negated because of the existence of the sight of the proof, as you would say: "I committed the sin, had Allah not protected you." We do not say that the answer to "had he not" precedes it, although no evidence proves that this is impossible. Indeed, the explicit conditional particles that govern their answers differ on whether their answers may precede them. The Kufans held that it is permissible.

Among the leading Basran grammarians are Abu Zayd al-Ansari and Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad. Rather, we say that the answer to "had he not" is omitted because what precedes it indicates it, as the majority of the Basrans say regarding the Arab saying: "You are a wrongdoer if you do such-and-such." They take it to mean "If you do such-and-such, then you are a wrongdoer." Their saying "You are a wrongdoer" does not indicate that wrongdoing is established. Rather, it is affirmed on the assumption that the act exists. Likewise here, the sense is: ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, he would have desired her. So the desire would have existed on the assumption that the seeing of the proof did not occur. But he did see the proof, so the desire was negated. The "proof" means what he possessed of knowledge demonstrating the prohibition of what she desired, and that it was not possible for him to desire it, let alone fall into it. No attention is paid to the words of al-Zajjaj: "If the statement were 'and he would have desired her,' it would be distant, so how much more so with the omission of the lam, since he imagined that the word of the Exalted, ﴿he desired her﴾, is the answer to 'had he not.' We have not said this. We have said that it is evidence of the answer, not the answer itself." It may be said that the lam is not obligatory, since the answer to "had he not" may come in the past tense both with the lam and without it. One says: "Had it not been for Zayd, I would have honored you," and "Had it not been for Zayd, I honored you." Whoever holds that what is mentioned is the answer itself is not far off. Likewise, no attention is paid to the words of Ibn Attiyah: "The view of those who say that the statement is complete at the word of the Exalted, ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, and that the answer to 'had he not' is in His word, ﴿and he desired her﴾, and that the meaning is ﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, he would have desired her, so Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not desire her, is refuted by the language of the Arabs." The discussion of what he said, "is refuted by the language of the Arabs," and the statements of the early scholars (salaf) is long.

Those who held that permissibility is valid have argued from its occurrence in the language of the Arabs. For the Exalted has said: ﴿She had almost revealed it, had We not fortified her heart﴾. His word ﴿she had almost﴾ and so on is either the answer, according to what that speaker held, or it is evidence of the answer, according to what we have established.

As for the statements of the early scholars, what we believe is that nothing from them has been authenticated, because they are mutually contradictory statements that refute one another, and they are damaging even for some of the wicked among the Muslims, let alone for those who are attested to be infallible. Moreover, what has been narrated is not supported by the language of the Arabs, because it requires that the answer be omitted without evidence, since on that basis they did not supply "he would have desired her." The language of the Arabs indicates only that the omitted element should be of the meaning of what precedes the condition, because that is what serves as evidence for it.

Among those who held that the vile desire truly occurred from him, peace be upon him, is al-Wahidi, for he said in the book al-Basit: "The exegetes whose knowledge is trusted, whose narrations are relied upon, and who took the interpretation from those who witnessed the revelation, said: Yusuf, peace be upon him, also desired this woman with a real desire, and sat with her in the position of a man with a woman. When he saw the proof from his Lord, every desire left him."

Abu Jaʿfar al-Baqir said, with his chain going back to ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "She longed for him, and he longed for her." His longing for her was that he desired to untie the drawstring.

From Ibn Abbas: he untied the money belt and sat in the position of one who circumcises. Also from him: she lay back for him, and he sat between her legs removing his clothes. They narrated various accounts of the proof. Among them is what Abu Nuʿaym narrated in al-Hilya from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, that she went to an idol adorned with pearls and rubies in a corner of the house and covered it with a white cloth between herself and it. He, peace be upon him, said: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before my god that he should see me in this state." He said: "You are ashamed before an idol that neither eats nor drinks, and I am not ashamed before my God who watches over every soul for what it has earned?!" Then he said: "Do not let her touch me ever." That is the proof he saw. Among them is what Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Abbas: that Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, appeared to him, and he struck his chest with his hand. Among them is what he narrated from Qatada: it was mentioned to us that Yaʿqub appeared to him biting on his two fingers and saying: "O Yusuf, will you desire the deeds of fools while you are recorded among the prophets?" Among them is what he narrated from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, who said: "A call came: O son of Yaʿqub, do not be like the bird that has feathers, which when it commits fornication sits without feathers." He did not respond to the call, but sat, then raised his head and saw the face of Yaʿqub biting on his finger, so he stood up in fear, ashamed before his father. And other accounts.

Imam al-Razi criticized what was mentioned, saying that this disobedience, which they attributed to Yusuf, and God forbid, is among the most ugly and detestable sins. Its like, if attributed to the most wicked of Allah's creatures and the furthest of them from every good, would be disdained. How then is it permissible to attribute it to this truthful and noble one? Moreover, Allah the Exalted testified that the essence of evil and the essence of indecency are turned away from him. With this testimony, how can the claim that the greatest evil and indecency is attributed to him, peace be upon him, be accepted? Also, if this vile desire had truly occurred from him, peace be upon him, as they claim, and the verse included it, then following it with the word of the Exalted, ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and indecency﴾, would be outside wisdom. For even if we grant that it does not indicate the negation of disobedience, it does indicate at least a great praise. It is well known that it does not befit the wisdom of Allah the Exalted to narrate his committing a great disobedience and then praise him and commend him with the greatest praises and commendations. Also, the great ones, like the prophets, when a slip or lapse comes from them, regard it as grave and follow it with the display of remorse, repentance, humility, and seeking exoneration. So if Yusuf, peace be upon him, had committed this outrageous indecency, it would be impossible that he did not follow it with that, and if he had followed it, it would have been related. Since we do not know that any sin at all came from him in this event, and moreover, everyone connected with this event has declared Yusuf's innocence of disobedience, as is not hidden from anyone who has a heart or who listens attentively while being present. Whoever considers the word of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, he is of Our sincere servants﴾, finds it the clearest witness to his innocence, peace be upon him. And whoever adds to it the word of Iblis, ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾, finds Iblis acknowledging that he did not lead him astray or misguide him from the path of guidance. How could he not be, when he, peace be upon him, is among the sincere servants of Allah the Exalted by the testimony of Allah the Exalted? He excepted them from the generality of ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾.

At this point it is said to the ignorant who attributed that shameful act to Yusuf, peace be upon him: if they are followers of Allah the Exalted, then let them accept Allah's testimony to his purity, peace be upon him. And if they are followers of Iblis, then let them accept his testimony. Perhaps they will say: "We were his students at the beginning until we graduated, and we surpassed him in folly," as al-Hariri said:

I was a man from the army of Iblis, until the matter reached the point where Iblis became one of my soldiers.
If he had died before me, I would have excelled after him in the ways of wickedness, which no one excels in after me.

Whoever examines the proofs carefully and is fair will conclude that nothing remains in the hand of al-Wahidi or of whoever agrees with him except mere boasting and the enumeration of the names of exegetes. He finds with them no argument for their claim that contradicts what the clear verses testify, except feeble narrations.

Al-Tibi, may Allah sanctify his resting place, after quoting what Muhyi al-Sunnah related from some of the people of spiritual realities (haqaiq), that desire is of two kinds, a settled desire, which is that accompanied by resolve, determination, and consent, like the desire of the wife of al-Aziz, and a passing desire, which is a fleeting thought and inner talk without choice or resolve, like the desire of Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: this interpretation is the one that must be followed and adopted as a doctrine, even if the exegetes have related what they related. This is because following the decisive text and the innocence of the infallible from that vice, and attributing the shortcoming to the narrators, is more appropriate to adopt. Moreover, the masters of meticulous transmission did not narrate in their books anything traced back to the Prophet regarding this, and most of those narrations, indeed all of them, derive from the questions of the People of the Book. End of quotation. Indeed, al-Hakim has authenticated some of the narrations on which those who attributed that vile act to him relied, but al-Hakim's authentication is judged to have no weight among those who weigh evidence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 24 (part 2 of 2):

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), after quoting a portion of these reports, the author says: "All of that is nothing but fabrications and falsehoods that ears reject and minds and intellects refuse. Woe to the one who chews them over, fabricates them, or hears them and believes them." Then the Imam (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned, in his interpretation of the noble verse, after denying that it indicates desire, the following in substance: "Even if we grant that desire occurred, we say that it is necessary to supply a particular verb that makes the object of the desire, since the persons themselves cannot serve as that object, and what they claim, that she intended to commit the indecency with him, is not determined. Rather, we supply something else that differs from what they supplied. We say: the meaning is that he desired to repel her from himself and to prevent her from that vile act, because that is what his condition requires, peace be upon him. The expression 'hamamtu bi-fulan' has come with the meaning 'I intended him and repelled him.' In the first case, one supplies the intimacy, the enjoyment, and the like, because that is what suits her condition." If they say: "Then the words of the Exalted, ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, would serve no purpose," we say: "On the contrary, it contains the greatest benefits, and its explanation is from two aspects."

The first is that the Exalted informed Yusuf that if he were to desire to repel her, she would do to him what would bring about his destruction. So refraining from that preserved his soul from destruction.

The second is that if he had busied himself with repelling her, she might have clung to him, and his garment would have been torn from the front. It was in Allah's knowledge, the Exalted, that a witness would testify that if his garment were torn from the front, he would be the aggressor, and if it were torn from behind, she would be the aggressor. So He informed him of this meaning, and therefore he did not busy himself with repelling her, but fled from her, until the testimony became a proof for him of his innocence of sin.

Some of the Sufi masters, may Allah sanctify their secrets, adopted the supposition of repulsion. In al-Sha'rani's al-Jawahir wa al-Durar: "I asked our shaykh about the words of the Exalted, ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾, what is this desire that has been left vague? People have spoken about it in ways that are not fitting for the ranks of the prophets, peace be upon them. He said: 'I do not know.' I said: 'The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn Arabi), may Allah sanctify his secret, mentioned that an unrestricted expression indicates the unity of the meaning, but that is a majority rule, not a universal one. The truth is that she desired him, peace be upon him, so that she might compel him to what she wanted from him, and he desired her so that he might compel her to repel what she wanted from him. So the shared element is the aim of compulsion, from him and from her, but the ruling differs.'" That is why she said: ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾, and nothing in the surah at all indicates that he sought to seduce her. End of quotation.

The Imam also permitted interpreting the desire as lust, and it was mentioned that it is used in common language, for one says of what he does not desire: "This does not concern me," and of what he desires: "This is the most important thing to me." This is what we pointed to at first. However, he (may Allah have mercy on him) took the desire in both places to mean this, and then said: "So the meaning of the verse is: she lusted after him and he lusted after her, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have acted." This is something for which there is no call, since there is no prohibition in attributing blameworthy desire to her. Apparently, desire in this sense is metaphorical, as the sayyid al-Murtada stated explicitly in his Durar, and not literal, as the apparent sense of the Imam's words suggests. Abu Ali al-Jubba'i and others took this interpretation, and it is related from al-Hasan. In sum, one should not rely on what is widespread in the reports, nor turn away from what the excellent verifiers have adopted. Beware of attributing that abomination to that noble person, after Allah, the Exalted, has uncovered from the sight of your insight, so that you see the proof of your Lord without a veil.

﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil﴾. It was said: "evil" is the betrayal of the master. ﴿And immorality﴾ is fornication, because it is extremely ugly. It was said: "evil" refers to the preliminaries of immorality, such as kissing and looking with lust. It was said: it is the bad matter in general, so the betrayal mentioned and other things enter into it. The kaf, as has been said, is in a position of nasb (accusative). The indication is to the firm establishment necessitated by the showing, which is implied by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, meaning: "Like that firm establishment, We established him, ﴿that We might turn away﴾," and so on.

Ibn Atiyya said: the kaf is connected to an implied element, its estimate being: "Our acts and decrees took place ﴿thus that We might turn away﴾." Abu al-Baqa estimated: "We observe him thus." Al-Hawfi estimated: "We showed him Our proofs thus." All permitted that it be in a position of raf' (nominative), so it was said: "That is, the matter, or his protection, is like that." But al-Hawfi said: the nasb is better because of the demand of the prepositions for verbs or their meanings. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr preferred that the indication refers to the seeing implied by "ra'a" or the opinion implied by "al-ra'y." The verbal noun of al-ra'y has come like that of al-ru'ya, as in his words:

"And the sight of the young man's eyes, your father, gives abundantly, so that is for you."

The kaf is in a position of nasb governed by what is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Had he not seen﴾, etc. It is also connected to ﴿that We might turn away﴾, meaning: "Like the seeing or the opinion, he sees Our proofs, ﴿that We might turn away﴾," and so on. Other views have been stated. Among what should not be paid attention to is what was said: that the prepositional phrase is connected to "hamma," and that there is inversion and reordering in the speech, its estimate being: "And she certainly desired him, and he desired her thus. Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, that We might turn away from him..." etc. The effect of expressing it with what is in the noble composition, rather than "li-nasrifahu 'an al-su' wa al-fahsha'," is not hidden, as it indicates the refutation of one who attributes to him what was attributed, and we seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted.

Al-A'mash read "li-yasrifa" with the third-person masculine (yā' of absence), attributing the turning away to the pronoun of the Lord, the Exalted. ﴿Indeed he is of Our sincere servants﴾: this is a justification of what preceded from the content of the sentence by way of confirmation. The "mukhlasun" are those whom Allah, the Exalted, has purified and chosen for His obedience, by protecting them from what would harm it. The apparent meaning is the judgment that he is chosen for the obedience of the Exalted. It may be possible, as was said, that the intended meaning is that he is of the offspring of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, concerning whom the Majestic and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure quality﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Ibn Amir read "al-mukhlisin" wherever "al" occurs, with a kasra on the lam, meaning those who made their religion sincere for Allah, the Exalted. It is not hidden what the expression by the nominal sentence indicates of his, peace be upon him, being included in the line of those servants who are such from the very beginning, not that this happened to him after he had not been so. In this, for people of understanding, there is that which cuts off the excuse of those who cling to the skirts of those reports which Allah, the Exalted, did not send down any authority for.

[p. 217]

[Page 218]

﴿And they raced each other to the door﴾ is connected to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾, and so on. His saying, exalted is He, "Thus" (kadhalika), and so on, is an interjection placed between the two conjoined clauses to affirm his purity, peace be upon him. The meaning is: she desired him, and he refused, and ﴿they raced each other to the door﴾, that is, they raced toward the door, in the sense that each of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the wife of the Aziz intended to get there before the other. He wanted to leave, and she wanted to prevent him from leaving. It was also said that the racing on her part means that she hastened after him, but he expressed it this way for emphasis. Here he used the singular "door" although he had used the plural earlier, because the intended door is the outer door (al-bab al-barrani), which is the way out. It was raised as an objection: how could they race toward it when there were inner doors before it, given what they mentioned that the doors were seven in number?

It is answered that it is narrated from Ka'b that the locks of those doors would fall apart when Yusuf, peace be upon him, approached them, and they would open for him. It is also possible that those closed doors were not arranged one after another, but were in different directions, all of them exits for the place where they were, so they raced to the door from which he would exit. The word "door" is in the accusative by extension (ittisa'), because the basic construction of istabaqa is that it takes "ila" (to), but it came this way in the manner of ﴿And when they measure out to them﴾ (83:3) and ﴿Moses chose from his people seventy men﴾ (7:155). It was also said that he construed istibaq with the meaning of initiating (al-ibtida'), so it took its complement directly.

﴿And she tore his shirt from behind﴾ may be coordinated with "they raced" (istabaqa), and it may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as Abu Hayyan said, meaning: "and she had torn." Qadd means cutting and splitting, and its most common usage is for what is lengthwise, which is the intended meaning here, based on what has been said: she pulled him from behind and the shirt was torn down to its bottom. Qatt is used for what is crosswise. On this basis, what was said describing Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, applies: that when he went along a length he qadda, and when he went across he qatta. It was also said that qadd here means splitting in general. This is supported by what is transmitted from Ibn 'Atiyya that a group read "wa-qutta" (and was cut), and this is found in the codex of al-Mufaddal ibn Harb.

It is transmitted from Ya'qub that qadd is restricted to what occurs in leather and in a sound garment. The qamis (shirt) is well known, and its plurals are aqmisa, qumus, and qumsan. Attributing the tearing, in whatever sense, specifically to her, although the strength of Yusuf, peace be upon him, also played a part in it, is either because she was the final component of the complete cause, or to indicate her great effort in preventing him from going out and her exerting her utmost in that, for fear of losing the beloved, or for fear of exposure.

﴿And they found﴾, that is, they came upon. Abd Allah read it this way. ﴿Her master﴾, that is, her husband. It is fay'al from sada yasudu, and its use became common for the owner and for the chief. At that time, as it has been said, the woman would call her husband "my master," and so he did not say "their master." In al-Bahr it is said that it was not attributed to both of them because he was not truly the owner of Yusuf, due to his freedom. ﴿At the door﴾, that is, at the outer door. It was said: they found him intending to enter with a cousin of hers. ﴿She said﴾ is a resumptive clause answering a question of someone who asks: "What happened when they found the master at the door?" So it is said: she said, ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your family﴾, meaning adultery or the like.

﴿Except that he be imprisoned, or a painful punishment﴾. Apparently "ma" is negative, "jaza'" is the subject, and "man" is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun in construction as a genitive, and the infinitive clause is the predicate. "Aw" is for classification, and what follows is coordinated with that infinitive: that is, his recompense is nothing but imprisonment or a painful punishment. It is said that this refers to striking with a whip. It is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that it means shackling. It is also permitted that "ma" be interrogative, so "jaza'" is the subject or the predicate, meaning: what is his recompense other than that, or that. She came in that state, in which the keen-minded person is bewildered, when her husband saw her in that condition by a stratagem that combined her two aims: clearing her name from what appeared in the outward situation, and drawing Yusuf, peace be upon him, away from his opinion of resisting her and not complying with her desire, by casting terror into his heart from her plotting, in hope of getting him to succumb to her under compulsion when she despaired of that, willingly as she said: ﴿And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned, and he will surely be among the humiliated﴾ (12:32).

Then she made the issuing of the said intention from Yusuf, peace be upon him, a settled matter, taken for granted, needing no report of its occurrence, and that what she was doing was for the purpose of realizing its recompense. She did not state the name explicitly but used a general expression to magnify the matter and to exaggerate the threat, as if that were a consistent rule regarding everyone, whoever he might be. She also reminded herself of the title of being the wife of the Aziz, to magnify the affair and to incite him to achieve what he aims at by the dictate of anger and zeal. Thus did more than one scholar explain it.

The Imam (al-Razi) in his tafsir mentioned something that contains a kind of disagreement with this, saying: In the verse there are subtleties. The first is that her intense love for Yusuf, peace be upon him, moved her to observe two delicate points in this place. She began with mentioning imprisonment and delayed mentioning punishment, because a lover does not strive to cause pain to the beloved. Also, she did not say that Yusuf, peace be upon him, must be requited with one of these two matters, but mentioned it in a general way, to protect the beloved from being mentioned with evil and pain. Also she said, ﴿Except that he be imprisoned﴾, and what is meant is that he be imprisoned for a day or less, as a form of leniency.
