As for permanent detention, it is not expressed by this phrase, but rather it is said: he must be made one of the prisoners. Do you not see how Pharaoh spoke when he threatened Moses, peace be upon him:
﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the prisoners﴾ (26:29).

The second is that when she witnessed from Yusuf, peace be upon him, that he kept himself chaste from her, although he was in the prime of youth, full strength, and extreme desire, her belief in his purity and integrity was greatly magnified. So she was ashamed to say, "Yusuf intended me with evil," and she did not find it in herself to accuse him by this lie explicitly, but was content with this allusion. Would that the Hashwiyya had been content with what she was content with! But they did not, and after nearly four thousand years they described him with what they described him of ugliness. Far be it from him.

The third is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, wanted to strike her and push her away from himself, and that would have been, in her view, an evil. So her saying, "What is the recompense," and so on, is in the manner of an allusion. Perhaps in her heart she wanted him to move to repel her and prevent her, while outwardly she gave the impression that he had intended her with what is not fitting. (End of his purpose, and in it there is what there is of considerations.)

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read ﴿or a painful punishment﴾ in the accusative, as a verbal noun (masdar), as al-Kisa'i said: meaning, "or he will be punished with a painful punishment," except that this is omitted because it is evident. This reading fits better with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that he be imprisoned﴾. The reason for the difference of expression in the well-known reading has not become clear to me in a way that can be relied upon. But Allah, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book, so reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 26:**

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf), an answer to the question: "What did Yusuf (peace be upon him) say at that point?" It is said: he said, ﴿"It was she who sought to seduce me from myself."﴾ That is, she sought to make me consent to her, not that I intended any evil by it, as she claimed. He (peace be upon him) said this only to clear himself of the accusation and to ward off harm from her, not to expose her.

Using the pronoun of absence (ghaybah) for her, rather than the second person or a demonstrative, is said to observe good manners, while also hinting at turning away from her. Yet there is discussion about this pronoun and others like it. Ibn Hisham, in one of his glosses on Ibn Malik's poem (the Alfiyya), mentioned the verse:

*"So what is for the one absent or present..."*

etc. Let one consider ﴿hiya rawadatni﴾ (she sought to seduce me), where *hiya* is by agreement a pronoun, yet it does not refer to an absent person but to one who is present. The same applies to ﴿O father, hire him﴾. The first is an attached pronoun (muttasil) and the second a detached one (munfasil). Likewise the statement of one who addresses a person about a matter concerning another who is present with him: "I told him: fear God, Most High, and I commanded him to do good." It may be said that the pronoun in these cases has been given the status of the absent. Similarly, in the reverse case: news reaches you about an absent person, and you say, "Woe to you, O so-and-so, do you do such-and-such?" treating him as if he were present. In that case it is said that the definition derived from what has been mentioned applies only to the pronoun in terms of its lexical positing (wad').

End of quotation. Al-Siraj al-Balqini said in his treatise entitled *Nashr al-'Abir li-Tayy al-Damir* (The Spreading of Perfume to Fold the Pronoun): the explanatory referent of a pronoun of absence is either explicitly stated, or omitted because its referent is present, either sensorially or cognitively. The sensory type is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿hiya rawadatni﴾ and ﴿O father, hire him﴾, as Ibn Malik mentioned. Our shaykh Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it is not as he illustrated, because these two pronouns refer to what precedes them. The pronoun in ﴿hiya rawadatni﴾ refers to "the household" in her words: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intends evil to your household?﴾ Since she had alluded to herself by that expression and did not say "me" in place of "your household," he (peace be upon him) referred to her with the pronoun of absence, saying ﴿she sought to seduce me﴾, and did not address her with "you sought to seduce me," nor did he point to her with "this one sought to seduce me." All of this is by way of good manners in speech and modesty in address, which befit the prophets, peace be upon them. Thus the noun appeared in the form of the pronoun of absence out of courtesy toward the Aziz and modesty before him. The pronoun in ﴿hire him﴾ refers to Musa, so its explanatory referent is explicitly stated by name. Ibn Malik seems to have imagined that this is a place of indication, because the owner of the pronoun is present with the addressee, and so he thought the explanatory referent could be dispensed with due to the sensory presence of its referent, and so the pronoun took the place of a demonstrative. The correct view is what we have stated. This is his statement.

I hold that what Ibn Malik said is more probable than what the shaykh said, because when two people have a dispute before a judge, the claimant says to the judge: "He owes me such-and-such." The defendant says: "He knows that he has no right over me." The pronoun in *huwa* here refers to the sensory presence of its referent, not to the words "he owes me," as is most readily understood. Also, what he (Abu Hayyan) said about the pronoun in ﴿hire him﴾ is objected to: Musa (peace be upon him) had not been mentioned before when he was with the daughter of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), yet she said ﴿O father, hire him﴾, and the person she intended by the pronoun was the man present who had shown her great strength and trustworthiness. Furthermore, one who quarrels with his wife and says to those present, whether her family or others, "She is divorced," his wife is divorced, because the condition that Ibn Malik established is met, and this does not accord with what the shaykh established, as is clear. In sum, although the interpretation he gave applies to the two verses, it can hardly be applied to others. Understand this.

﴿And a witness from her family testified.﴾ Many have said that he was her paternal cousin's son (ibn khaluha, her maternal nephew), and that he was an infant in the cradle, whom God, Exalted is He, made speak to testify to Yusuf's innocence (peace be upon him). It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Four spoke in the cradle while they were infants: the son of Pharaoh's daughter's hairdresser, the witness of Yusuf (peace be upon him), the companion of Jurayj, and Isa son of Maryam (peace be upon both of them)."

Al-Tibi objected to this, saying: "It is refuted by the restrictive force (dalalat al-hasr) in the hadith of the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Only three spoke in the cradle: Isa son of Maryam, the companion of Jurayj, and a child who was nursing from his mother. A rider of fine appearance passed by, and his mother said: "O Allah, make my son like this." The child left the breast and said: "O Allah, do not make me like him."'" End of quotation.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti rejected this, saying: "This is from him in keeping with his habit of not being acquainted with the chains of hadith. The hadith mentioned earlier is sound. Ahmad related it in his Musnad, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and he graded it sound, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hakim also related it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and said: 'It is sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim).' In the hadith of the two Sahihs referred to just now there is an addition to the four: 'the child who was nursing from his mother, when a rider passed by...' etc., so they become five, and they are more than that. In Sahih Muslim, a child spoke in the story of the People of the Trench. I have gathered those who spoke in the cradle, and they reached eleven, and I put them in verse:

*The Prophet Muhammad spoke in the cradle, and Yahya, Isa, al-Khalil, and Maryam,*
*And the infant of Jurayj, then the witness of Yusuf, and a child of the People of the Trench, reported by Muslim,*
*And a child who passed by the slave-girl who was said to commit fornication and did not speak,*
*And the hairdresser's child in the time of Pharaoh, and in the blessed time of al-Hadi it is concluded."*

End of quotation. In this regard, al-Tibi did not reject the criticism of the hadith he mentioned, as he supposed. Rather, he meant that there is a contradiction between the hadith that indicates restriction and other reports, which requires reconciliation. In al-Kashshaf, after mentioning the hadith of the four and what al-Tibi objected to, it is said that al-Zamakhshari transmitted a fifth in the chapter of al-Buruj. If this also is established, then the correct view is to take "in the cradle" as a qualifier and emphasis, meaning that it was at the beginnings of childhood. In this report it is taken as absolute, that is, whether it was at the beginning or later, such that his speech is one of the miracles. It is not hidden that this is a distant reconciliation.

It has also been said: he was the paternal cousin of her husband, who was at the door with her husband, and he was a man with a beard. This does not contradict the statement of Qatadah that he was a wise man from her family, of sound opinion, whom the king consulted and took counsel from. It is also permitted that he was one of her family who was in the house with them without their noticing him, so he saw what had passed between them, and God, Exalted is He, angered him on behalf of Yusuf, so he spoke the truth. It was related from Mujahid that the witness was the shirt torn from behind, but this is nothing, as is not hidden.

God, Exalted is He, made the witness one of her family. It has been said: so that it would be a stronger proof of his innocence (peace be upon him), more effective in removing the accusation, and more binding upon her. This is specific to the case when the witness was not the child whom God made speak, who makes everything speak. As for when it was that child, mentioning that he was from her family is to explain the reality, for the testimony of a child is a decisive proof, and there is no difference in it between relatives and others.

It was objected that the testimony of a relative in general being stronger is not something one should doubt. He was called a witness because he performed his testimony in such a way that through his speech the words of Yusuf were established and her words were invalidated. It was also said: he was named so because he pointed to the witness, which is the tearing of the shirt. Mujahid, in what Ibn Jarir related from him, interpreted "testimony" as "judgment," meaning: a judge from her family judged.

﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾, that is, from in front of Yusuf, peace be upon him, or from the front of the shirt. The particle ﴿in﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah), ﴿kana﴾ is the verb of the condition, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿then she has told the truth﴾ is the answer to the condition. It is understood with ﴿qad﴾ (indicating a completed action), since otherwise the particle ﴿fa-﴾ would not enter into such a construction. Ibn Kharuf reported that such a construction is based on an elided subject (mubtada'), and that the whole sentence, not the past verb alone, is the answer to the condition. In al-Kashshaf, the conditional ﴿in﴾ here is like your saying: "If you have done good to me, then I have done good to you before," said to someone who reminds you of his kindness; its meaning is "if you remind me of kindness, I will remind you of mine." Likewise, here the intended meaning is that he should know that his shirt was torn, or something similar. Otherwise, it is clear that the verb is in the future sense, and ﴿kana﴾ contradicts this. It was said: this is based on the view of some that ﴿kana﴾ is strong in indicating time, so the conditional particle does not turn its past into the future; otherwise every past verb that the condition enters upon would be turned into the future without any need for interpretation. This was objected to: interpretation is necessary here, and the occurrence of knowledge and the like is made to be the two parts of the conditional, as if one said: "If he knows, or it becomes apparent that it is so, then truthfulness has become apparent." The same can be said of the second conditional that follows, even if ﴿kana﴾ is one of the verbs that the conditional particle turns into the future like other past verbs, because the meaning is not that the truth or falsehood in the future depends on the shirt being in this or that state, but that the appearance of one of the two, truth or falsehood, depends on the occurrence of knowledge of its being so; and this is evident. Is this interpretation a matter of estimation (taqdir) or of something else? There is disagreement about it. What the words of some careful scholars point to is that knowledge of a thing in such a case is treated as the occurrence of that thing, because of the necessary connection between them, as it is said: "What thing is hidden?" And it was answered: "What does not occur, so let it be understood."

Then, the object of ﴿truthfulness﴾ is what her speech indicates, namely that Yusuf intended her harm, and this is the object of the ﴿falsehood﴾ attributed to her afterwards. Both of them relate to the relation contained in the speech by way of its explicit meaning, and they relate to the relation it contains by way of what it implies. So it is as if it were said: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth﴾ in her claim that Yusuf intended her harm, ﴿and he is among the liars﴾ in his claim that she sought to seduce him. ﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind﴾, that is, from behind Yusuf, peace be upon him, or from behind the shirt, ﴿then she has lied﴾ in her claim, ﴿and he is among the truthful﴾ in his claim. Both conditional sentences are reported speech: either with an implied saying, meaning he testified saying, or he said, "If his shirt..." etc., as is the doctrine of the Basrans; or the verb "testified" is taken as a kind of speech, so that it may govern sentences, as is the doctrine of the Kufans. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun in the second conditional is to show independence while maintaining greater clarity. The two sentences ﴿and he is among the liars﴾ and ﴿and he is among the truthful﴾ are emphatic, because from the words ﴿then she has told the truth﴾ one knows his lying, and from the words ﴿then she has lied﴾ one knows his truthfulness. As for how the tearing of the shirt from behind indicates her lying: she pursued him and pulled his garment, so it tore. As for how its tearing from the front indicates her truthfulness, it is on two grounds. The first is that if he was pursuing her while she was pushing him away from herself, his shirt would be torn from the front by the pushing. The second is that he rushed toward her to overtake her, stumbled in the place of his shirt, and so it tore. Thus it is in al-Kashshaf.

[p. 222]

Ibn al-Munir objected to the first ground: what was established regarding his pursuit of her may equally be applied to her pursuit of him. For she would only tear his shirt from the front on the assumption that he had seized her until they were facing each other, and then she pushed him away from herself. This same thing could be applied if she were the pursuer: she pulled him until they were facing each other, then pulled his shirt toward her from the front. Rather, this is more apparent, because what generally causes a shirt to tear is pulling, not pushing. As for the second ground, what has been mentioned could equally apply if she were the pursuer while he was fleeing from her, so that his shirt tore as he hastened to flee. End of quotation.

It was answered to what he mentioned first that it is not valid, because that hurried situation admits only the easiest and quickest possibility. On the supposition that she was pursuing him, tearing from behind is the only option, because it is the less severe of the two pullings. Then we do not suppose that the fleeing man turned back to push her, or that as she caught up she pulled him. Such a supposition has no basis in that situation. So when it is established that the tearing indicates this kind in general, the matter is determined. As for what he mentioned second, it was answered that the evident thing, on the supposition that she was the pursuer, is that when the fleeing man stumbles, the pursuer clings to him, and when they are separated after that, this possibility remains.

The commentator who was objected to (al-Fadil al-Mut'aqqib) mentioned that the correct view in this matter is to say: if the witness mentioned was a child whom God caused to speak in the cradle, as is reported in some hadiths, then the verse is about his mere speech before its proper time. Even if he had said, "Yusuf spoke the truth and she lied," that would suffice as proof of his truthfulness, peace be upon him, just as the mere report of Jesus, peace be upon him, in the cradle was a proof of Mary's truthfulness. Therefore, there is no need for a relation between the sign that was set up and what is consequent upon it, for the essential thing in proofs is their establishment, not their relevance. Even if it is close to it and has been perceived from a point it does not notice. This, and God knows best, was that he should have stated what he saw, thus confirming Yusuf, peace be upon him, and denying her. But he wanted not to be the one who exposed her, and he was certain that the shirt had been torn from behind, so he set it up as a sign of his truthfulness and her lying. Then he mentioned the other case, that it was torn from the front, while knowing that it had not been torn in that way, in order to remove from himself any suspicion in his testimony and to avoid the intention of exposure, and to be fair to both of them. Therefore he mentioned a sign of her truthfulness, whose negation is known, just as he mentioned a sign of his truthfulness, whose existence is known. He presented both in one manner, and he used the passive form ﴿was torn﴾ in both places, to conceal the one who tore it. He mentioned the sign of her truthfulness first, to remove suspicion, and trusting that the second sign is the one that actually occurred, so the order of mention does no harm.

The summary is that the principal basis of this witness is only the last sign, and the relevance in it is clear. As for the first sign, it is not intended in itself; it is like a preface mentioned as a prelude to the second, so no comparable relevance was sought for it. But if the wise man whose opinion the king used to seek was the witness, then it is necessary to seek relevance on both sides, because it is the principal part of a wise man's testimony. The closest possibility of relevance is that a shirt torn from behind is evidence of his turning away from her, and a shirt torn from the front is evidence of his turning toward her with his face. It is not hidden that such an aspect is not suitable as the object of a wise man's consideration, who attends only to certainties. So it is better to say: it is possible that this wise man was acquainted with the reality of the situation through one of the possible means. This becomes easier if we say that he was her cousin. He was then certain of the non-existence of the antecedent of the first conditional and of the existence of the antecedent of the second. Among the necessities of this certainty is the conviction of the non-occurrence of the consequent of the first and the occurrence of the consequent of the second. So it was in fact a report of her lying and his truthfulness, peace be upon him. But he presented his testimony in a manner safe from injury and reproach, by framing it as a conditional that apparently remains undecided between benefit to her and benefit to him, though in reality there is no doubt about it, as was indicated. And regarding the first conditional not being intended in itself, the scholar Ibn Kamal went on to point out, reproaching the heedlessness of al-Qadi al-Baydawi, when he said: the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾ and so on, is one of the cases of leniency in one of the two halves of the speech, because the other is determined according to the speaker, by treating the possible as if it were the evident, since tearing by pulling is also possible in this case. Whoever overlooks this says: "Because it indicates that he intended her, so she pushed him away from herself," and so on to the end of the words of al-Baydawi. The summary of this, according to what some of our shaykhs, may God have mercy on them, established, is that the speaker knows with certainty that the tearing was from behind, but he mentioned the tearing from the front although it is possible that it was caused by her pulling him toward her side, just as its being caused by her pushing him is among its possibilities. He treated this possibility as the evident, to emphasize and magnify the establishment of what the second conditional indicates regarding his truthfulness and her lying. That is, we judge her truthful and him a liar merely by the occurrence of the tearing at the front, even if it is possible for it to have other causes than her pushing. But this tearing did not occur at all, so there is no truthfulness for her. This is like when it is said to you: "Did you convey to Zayd that statement on this day?" And you say: "If you spoke with Zayd on this day, then your saying this is true." Your speaking with him on this day in general does not indicate the truth of their claim, because it is possible that you spoke with him about something other than that statement. But you said that in order to affirm that you did not convey that statement to him.

Here our shaykh, the scholar Sibghat Allah al-Haydari, may God sanctify his grave, also mentioned that the evident point is that the indication of each of the two halves is according to what it indicates in terms of its agreement with what its speaker claimed. For she was saying: "He sought me while facing me, so I saved myself from him by pushing or by fleeing," and he was saying: "She was the one seeking, so I fled from her, and she pursued me and pulled my garment, so it tore." Thus the tearing at the back indicates that he was turning away from her, not facing her, and the reverse is the reverse. Then he based on this that what Ibn Kamal mentioned is heedlessness of the disputation by argument, and this is a subtle interpretation of the noble verse. However, the claim that the dispute occurred by argument in the manner that he, may God have mercy on him, mentioned has no witness, and the one who makes the claim must provide evidence that it is unlikely by reason that she would say: "He sought me while facing me, so I saved myself from him," and then his shirt tore from the front, which is what his claim requires, that the evident point is that the indication of each of the two halves and so on, because it is clear that her lying would become evident at once in that case.

In sum, it was said: the factors weakening this witness are many. Some of them you know, and some of them you know with little attention. From here they said: this is a matter of considering a sign, and for this reason the verse was cited as evidence, as Ibn al-Furs said: whoever sees judgment by scholars based on signs and indications, where witnesses are not present, such as lost property, theft, deposit, the boundaries of walls and roofs, and other such matters.

The Imam mentioned that the signs of the woman's lying were many and reached the level of certainty. So they added this other sign not in order to rely on it for judgment, but so that it would function as a reinforcement and a preponderating factor. And God knows best.

Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿min qubul﴾ and ﴿min dubur﴾ with a sukun on the ba' in both, and with tanwin. This is the dialect of the Hijaz and Asad. Abu Ya'mur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-'Utaridi, Abu al-Zinad and others read ﴿min qubul﴾ and ﴿min dubur﴾ with three damma. The first two, and al-Jarud in a narration from them, read with sukun on the ba' in both, together with their being built on damma. They treated them, like qabla and ba'da, as built forms after the omission of the genitive complement and the intention of its meaning. Abu Hatim objected to this: it is poor in Arabic, and building occurs only in adverbs of time and place, whereas these two words are fully inflected nouns and not adverbs. And Ibn Ishaq is reported to have read ﴿min qabal﴾ and ﴿min dabar﴾ with fatha. It was said: it seems he treated them as proper names for the two directions, so he did not inflect them, because of their being proper names and feminine by virtue of the direction.

[Page 224]

﴿When he saw his shirt torn from behind﴾, i.e., the Sayyid (the lord of the household), though it has been said it was the witness. The verb is from seeing, either with the eye or with the heart, meaning: when he knew his shirt was torn from behind, ﴿he said: Indeed, it is﴾, i.e., this tearing and rending, as al-Dahhak said, ﴿of your guile﴾, i.e., arising from your scheming, O women, and your deceit, and caused by it. This is a rebuke to her and an affirmation of him, peace be upon him, in the most subtle manner, as if it were said: You are the one who solicited him, yet he did not comply and fled, so you seized him and tore his shirt. So he is truthful in ascribing the solicitation to you, and you are lying in attributing the evil to him. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the matter over which they quarrelled, which is an expression for the intention of evil that was ascribed to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the plotting of his punishment by her saying: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your family?﴾ etc. The meaning is that this is of the same kind as your deceit and scheming. It has also been said that it refers to the evil itself, which is the same thing even if it is not a scheme, but it necessarily accompanies it. Al-Mawardi said: it refers to this matter, which is her desire for Yusuf, peace be upon him. Taking it as "scheming" is also a metaphor (majaz), as in the previous view. Al-Zajjaj said: it refers only to her saying ﴿What is the recompense﴾ etc. The Allamah Abu al-Su'ud preferred the first view, and he laboured to justify it, and he raised objections to the views that follow it.

Perhaps what we have mentioned is closer to good taste and requires less strain than what he laboured to justify. In any case, the address is general to women in general, and that it is addressed to her and her female attendants, as has been said, is not correct. Generalizing the address serves to alert that scheming is a deep-rooted disposition in them:

*Do not think that Hind alone possesses treachery as her nature,*
*for the nature of every coquette is Hind.*

﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾. For it is more subtle, more clinging to the heart, and more forceful in its effect on the soul. Moreover, it may bring about shame that men's scheming does not bring. Among the mistresses of palaces, this quality is most pronounced, since they have more leisure than others, together with the constant arrival of schemes upon them; thus they are complete and comprehensive. Because of the greatness of women's scheming, Iblis, may the curse be upon him, took them as means to lead astray whoever was hard for him to mislead. In a report: "Satan never despaired of anyone without coming to him through women." It is related from some scholars that he said: "I fear women more than I fear Satan, for He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾, and He said to women: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great﴾. Also, Satan whispers secretly, while they confront [their schemes] openly." It is not hidden that his use of the two verses as evidence is based on the apparent generality of both. Similar to this is what the soul contracts and expands for; that amount suffices for it. The fact that the weakness of Satan's plot is in comparison to God's plot does not harm the argument, and the greatness of their guile is only in comparison to the guile of men. As for what has been said, that what is mentioned here is related from Qitfir and therefore cannot be used as evidence in any way, it is nothing, because He, glorified is He, related it without disapproval, so there is no fault in using it as evidence, as is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 29:**

﴿Yusuf﴾: the particle of address (*harf al-nida'*) has been dropped from it, because of his nearness (to the speaker) and his complete alertness to the speech. Addressing him by his name brings him close and is gentle toward him, peace be upon him.

Al-A'mash read (*Yusufa*) with a fatha. According to what Abu al-Baqa' said, the more likely reading is that he treated it according to the original form of the vocative (*al-munada*), as in the line of poetry:

*O ʿAdiyy, indeed the Awaqi have protected you.*

It is also said that this reading was not transmitted correctly from al-A'mash. It is also said that he treated pausing as if it were continuation (*ajra al-waqf majra al-wasl*) and moved the vowel of the hamza to the preceding letter, from the words of God the Exalted: ﴿Turn away from this﴾, meaning: turn away from this matter, keep it hidden, and do not speak of it, for your truthfulness and the purity of your garment have become clear. This is like what God has related in ﴿Allahu akbar, ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah﴾ with the connecting and the fatha. It was also read as (*A'rada*) in the past tense, so that *Yusuf* is then the subject (*mubtada'*) and the clause after it is the predicate (*khabar*). Perhaps the intended meaning is the command in its most complete form, which returns to the meaning: "Turn away [from this, O Yusuf], and you, O woman, ask forgiveness." Abu al-Baqa' considered this reading weak, because the more appropriate thing for it is to say: ﴿and ask forgiveness﴾ for ﴿your sin﴾ that proceeded from you and became established against you, ﴿for indeed you were﴾ because of that ﴿among the sinners﴾, meaning among the people who deliberately commit sin, or of their kind. It is said: *khati'a yakhta'u khata'an wa khit'an* when one commits sin deliberately, and *akhta'a* when one sins without intention. Al-Raghib mentioned that *al-khata'* is deviation from the right direction, and it has kinds. The first is that one intends what it is not good to intend and then does it; this is the complete error for which a person is held accountable. The second is that one intends what is good to do, but what he does happens contrary to what he intended; this one is correct in intention but wrong in action. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever exerts himself in judgment and errs, he has a reward." The third is that one intends what is not good to do and it happens that the result is other than that; this one is wrong in intention but correct in action. It is not hidden that the meaning we have mentioned returns to the first kind of these types. The emphasized clause (*al-jumla al-mu'akkada*) is in the position of giving a reason (*ta'lil*) for the command and the reminder, and it uses the masculine form to give precedence to the males over the females. The possibility that it is said that the meaning is "You are of the lineage of sinners, so that corrupt vein flowed in you from them," is very remote. This address is said to be from (the witness) al-Shahid al-Hakim, and this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The seeking of forgiveness is understood as asking pardon and pardon from the husband. It is possible that the intended meaning is asking forgiveness from God the Exalted. It is said that those people, although they worshiped idols, nevertheless affirmed the Creator and believed that evil deeds have a bad consequence from Him, glorified is He, if He does not forgive them. The proof that they affirmed the Creator is also that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾. The apparent speaker of that is the ʿAziz. Perhaps, as it was said, he was a forbearing man; this was narrated from al-Hasan. For this reason he was content with this measure of taking her to account. It was also narrated that he was little given to jealousy, and this was a kindness from God the Exalted toward Yusuf, peace be upon him. In al-Bahr it is said that the soil of the region of Qitfir required that. And how does this compare with what happened to one of the kings of the Maghrib, who was in a session of enjoyment with his intimate companions, while a slave-girl sang to them from behind a curtain. One of his close companions asked her to repeat two verses she had sung. Shortly afterward, the head of the slave-girl was brought in cut off on a basin, and the king said to him: "Repeat the two verses from this head." That man was struck with dismay and fell ill for the duration of the king's life.

﴿وقالَ نِسْوَةٌ﴾ The well-known view, which Abu Hayyan adopted, is that it is a broken plural (jam' taksir, a plural formed by internal change of the word's pattern) of paucity (li-l-qillah), like ṣibyah and ghilmah. It has no singular from its own form, but only from its meaning, which is imra'ah (woman).

Ibn al-Sarraj claimed that it is a collective noun (ism jam', a noun that denotes a group without being a regular plural). In either case, its feminine marking is not real (ghayr haqiqi), and there is no regard for the fact that its singular is feminine in reality, because with the occurrence of what opposes that, it is not like other nouns. For this reason its verb is not made feminine. There are two dialectal forms for its nun: kasr (kasra), which is the well-known one, and ḍamm (ḍamma), and al-Mufaḍḍal, al-A'mash and al-Sulami read it with ḍamm, as al-Qurtubi said. So one should not heed whoever denies this. In that case it is definitely a collective noun, without disagreement. It takes the plural forms nisā' and niswān for multiplicity. According to what was narrated from Muqatil, they were five women: the wife of the baker, the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the doorkeeper, the wife of the jailer, and the wife of the keeper of the animals.

Al-Kalbi narrated that they were four, with the wife of the doorkeeper omitted.

﴿فِي المَدِينَةِ﴾ (in the city) is meant to refer to Egypt. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-l-majrur) stands in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) of "women," as some of them have inferred. They were described with this because the provoking of their speech in this respect is stronger, since they were characterised by what strengthens the side of truthfulness. For the speech of the Bedouin women, because of their distance from the places of gathering and from knowledge of the true circumstances of the urban women of the palaces, is not paid attention to, and so it does not provoke in that manner.

The majority, according to the preferred view, takes it as connected to qāla (said). The meaning of their saying being "in the city" is its spreading and dissemination there. This has been objected to on the basis that it goes against the apparent meaning.

﴿امْرَأتُ العَزِيزِ﴾ (the wife of al-Aziz). ʿAzīz, originally, is one who overpowers and is not overpowered, as if it were derived from ʿazza, meaning he came to be in ʿizāz, which is hard ground that is difficult to tread. It is also applied to the king. Perhaps they used to apply it at that time among themselves to everyone whom the king appointed over a particular office of the offices that have importance. So it was among his special, high-ranking, and secure men. In this sense it is intended here, because by it is meant Qaṭfīr. According to the well-known view, as you know, he was only over the treasuries of the king, and the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid. It was said: what is meant by it is the king, and Qaṭfīr was the king of Egypt and Alexandria.

Their attributing her to him by this title, rather than explicitly naming her or him, was so that her status as one of the people of high standing would appear, and this would help in spreading the news, on the principle that souls are more inclined to hear the reports of people of high standing.

It was also said, and this is the preferred view, that this is for the purpose of intensifying the blame of her by their saying ﴿تُراوِدُ فَتاها عَنْ نَفْسِهِ﴾ (she solicits her young man from himself), meaning she seeks to have intercourse with him and strives for that. Their choice of the present tense form (muḍāriʿ) indicates the continuation of the soliciting, as if it had become a habit for her. The fatā (young man) among people is the tender one among the youths. Its origin is fatiyy with a yāʾ, because they say in the dual (tathniyah), which returns things to their roots, fityān. So the futūwah (youthfulness) on this basis is an anomaly. Its plural is fityah and fityān. It was said that it is both yāʾī and wāwī, like kanawtu and kanaytu, and it has many parallels. It is also applied to the slave and the servant, because most servants are youths.

In a hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my slave-girl'; let him say 'my young man' and 'my young woman'." It was applied to Yusuf, peace be upon him, here because he used to serve her. It was also said that because her husband had given him to her, he is her slave according to the women's claim. Their referring to him, peace be upon him, with that and attributing him to her, not to al-Aziz, is to make clear the stark difference between them that arises from servanthood and mastery, or ownership and being owned. All of this is to reinforce the intensification of blame mentioned earlier. For a woman who has no husband, or who has a base husband, may be excused for soliciting lovers, especially if they are of high rank. But one who has a husband, and what a husband, soliciting another man, especially one with whom she has no suitability (kafa'ah), and persisting in that, is the utmost of error and the extreme of misguidance.

﴿قَدْ شَغَفَها حُبًّا﴾ (he has pierced her with love), meaning his love pierced the shaghaf (membrane) of her heart, which is its covering. It was said: it is a thin skin called "the tongue of the heart," until it reached her heart. By this, the intensification in describing her love for him is achieved. It was also said: the shaghaf is the black spot (suwaydāʾ) of the heart. The intensification in that case is clear. To this view goes what was narrated from al-Hasan, that the shaghaf is the inner part of the heart, and what was related from Abu ʿAli, that it is its middle part. The verb is with a fatḥah on the ghayn (shaghafa) according to the majority.

Thabit al-Bunani read it with a kasrah on it, and this is the dialect of Tamim. ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, his son Muhammad, and his son Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Sha'bi, and Awf al-A'rabi read shaʿafahā (with a fatḥah on the unpointed ʿayn). This is a narration from Qatadah, Ibn Hurmuz, Mujahid, Humayd and al-Zuhri. It was narrated from Thabit al-Bunani that he also read it so, except that he pronounced the ʿayn with a kasrah. It derives from sha'afa al-baʿir, when he smeared the camel with tar and burned it. So the meaning is that his love reached her heart, and it nearly burned.

From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"The slanderers disobey, and love was at times what adorns for the one smitten what he has done."

Al-Raghib mentioned that it derives from sha'fat al-qalb, which is its head at the place of the attachment of the sinews. It is also said: the mountain's top is also called sha'fah. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that al-shaghaf is deadly love, and al-sha'f is a love less than that. They both narrated from al-Sha'bi that al-shaghaf is love, and al-sha'af is madness. They also both narrated from Ibn Zayd that al-shaghaf is in love and al-sha'af is in hatred. This meaning is not admissible here according to this reading.

In the book Asrar al-Balaghah, in the section on the arrangement of love: the first stage of love is hawa (inclination), then ʿalaqah (attachment), which is love that clings to the heart, then kalaf (intense ardor), which is the intensity of love, then ʿishq (passion), which is the name for what exceeds the measure named love, then sha'af with an unpointed letter, which is the burning of the heart together with a pleasure one finds in it, and likewise lawʿah and lāʿij, then shaghaf with a pointed letter, which is that love reaches the shaghaf of the heart, then jawā, which is inner hawa, then taym, which is that love enslaves him, then tabl, which is that love makes him ill, then tadallaha, which is the loss of reason from love, then hayyum, which is that a man goes off in his direction because hawa overcame him. End of quote.

Some arranged this in a different pattern, and Allah knows best. In any case, the sentence is either a second predicate (khabar thani) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (tu– rāwidu) or from its object. Its purpose is the repetition of blame and the emphasis of reproach by clarifying the variation of her inner states, like her outer states. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it is a resumptive sentence (isti'nafiyyah), and then, according to what was said, it is in the position of a reason for the continuation of the soliciting. But this is not so, because if it is considered from the standpoint of the "that" (al-inniyyah, the fact of existence), it would lead to inferring the less evident from the more evident. And if it is considered from the standpoint of the "why" (al-limmiyyah, the cause), it would contain an inclination to paving the way for an excuse on her behalf, and this context does not call for that.

The accusative of ḥubban (love) is a specification (tamyīz, an accusative clarifying what is vague), and it is transferred from the subject, since the original is "shaghafahā ḥubbuhu" (his love pierced her), as was indicated. The two grammarians, Hamzah, Hisham and Ibn Muhaysin assimilated the dal of qad into the shin of shaghafahā.

﴿إنّا لَنَراها﴾ (Indeed, we see her), meaning we know her. So the seeing is of the heart, and its use in the sense of knowledge is literal, just as its use in the sense of sensory perception by sight is. If by it is meant visual seeing, and then it is used figuratively for knowing, it would be more eloquent in conveying that her state in what she did of soliciting and excessive love was established.

﴿فِي ضَلالٍ﴾ (in manifest error), great, away from the path of right guidance and correctness, or the ways of reason, ﴿مُبِينٍ﴾ (manifest), clear, such that its being error is not hidden from anyone, or making her affair evident among people. So the tanwin is for magnification. The sentence confirms the content of the two preceding sentences which were stated for blame and censure, and it records against her that in her affair she is in a great mistake. The women did not say "indeed she is in manifest error" to indicate, as it was said, that this judgment did not proceed from them without basis, but from knowledge and opinion, with a hint that they were far removed from the likes of what she was in. The blaming for the shaghaf is valid. It was said: because it is voluntary in terms of its beginnings, as its speaker indicates:

"She jested with him, so she loved him, and love's beginning is jest."

Otherwise, what is not in one's power should not be blamed, as al-Busayri indicated with his words:

"O one who blames me in chaste love, I apologise to you; if you were fair, you would not blame."

It was said: the blaming for it is in terms of indulging in it and abandoning its treatment, for they stated that this is among the ailments, and they mentioned treatments for it, and among the best of what is mentioned for it is remembering the faults of the beloved and reflecting on its consequences. For it has been said:

"If the lover reflected on the ultimate end of the beauty that captivates him, he would not be captivated."

The full discussion of this point should be sought in its proper place.

[Page 226]
[Page 227]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿When she heard of their scheming﴾: that is, of their backbiting and their evil talk. Calling this "scheming" is because it resembles scheming in being concealed. It has also been said: she had asked them to keep her secret, but they divulged it and exposed her affair. It has also been said: they intended by that remark to anger her, so that she would show Joseph to them, in order to reveal her excuse, and they would thereby gain the sight of him. On these two opinions, "scheming" is used in its literal sense. ﴿She sent for them﴾, inviting them. It was said: she invited forty women, among them the five or four mentioned, and this is narrated from Wahb. The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to those women who were speaking about her. ﴿And prepared﴾, that is, readied ﴿for them a mutaka'﴾

[Page 228]

That is, that on which they would recline, such as cushions and pillows, as is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It derives from *ittika'* (reclining), which means leaning toward one of the two sides. Its origin is *mawtaka'*, since it comes from *tawakka'tu*, and the *waw* was changed to *ta'* and assimilated into a similar letter. It is also narrated from the Scholar (al-Hibr, i.e. Ibn 'Abbas) that *al-mutaka'* is the place of food, because they used to recline in the manner of affluent and arrogant people, and for this reason it was forbidden. Ibn Abi Shayba has transmitted from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Prophet ﷺ forbade a man to eat with his left hand and to eat while reclining." It has also been said that the word refers to the food itself. Al-Utbi said: it is said, "We reclined at so-and-so's place," meaning we ate. From this is the line of Jamil:

*"So we remained in blessing, and we reclined, and we drank the lawful from its jugs."*

On this understanding it is either a noun of the object (meaning "one reclined upon") or a verbal noun meaning "reclining." The word expresses, by way of *majaz* (figurative usage), the posture in which the affluent eater sits. It has also been said that it is of the category of *kinaya* (metonymy). From Mujahid it is said that it refers to food which is cut with a knife. Scholars differ on its specific identity. It was said it was meat, since they did not tear meat with their teeth but ate it cut with knives. It was said it was citron, banana and melon. It was said it was *al-zamaward*, which is thin bread wrapped around meat and other things, or something resembling citron. It seems that what is cut with a knife was called by this name because the custom of one who cuts something is to lean upon it, so it becomes something "leaned upon."

Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read *muttaka'* with a doubled *ta'* and without hamza, on the pattern of *muttaqan*. In that case it is either from *ittika'* with the hamza lightened, as they say *tawaḍḍaytu* for *tawaḍḍa'tu*, or it is a *muf'ala* form from *awkaytu al-siqa'* (I tied the waterskin tightly with its cord), and the meaning is: she prepared for them what is tightened by leaning or by cutting with a knife. Al-A'raj read *matka'* on the pattern of *maf'al*, from *taka'a yatka'u*, meaning "he reclined." Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read *muttaka'* with a long vowel and hamza. It is a *muf'al* form from *ittika'*, except that the fatha was lengthened so that an *alif* was produced from it, which is common in their speech. From this is his saying:

*"You, among the calamities, when you hurl (them), and far from blaming men, are not distant."*

And his saying:

*"He spurts from the nape of a camel of strong build, a sorrow of ... like a noble stallion."*

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Qatada and others read *mutkan* with a damma on the *mim*, a sukun on the *ta'*, and tanwin on the *kaf*. This is also narrated from Ibn Hurmuz. It is citron according to al-Asma'i and a group, and the singular is *matka*. He recited:

*"So she sent to the sons of her father a matka, which she caused to walk, the strong-limbed, hard-stepping (mare)."*

It has also been said: it is a name that covers everything that is cut with a knife, such as citron and other fruits. He recited:

*"We drink sin openly from the cup, and we see the matk among us borrowed."*

It derives from *matak al-shay'* in the sense of *batakahu*, that is, he cut it. Al-Khalil's explanation of *mutk* with a damma on the *mim* is honey. Abu 'Amr's explanation is pure drink. Al-Kisa'i related three vowelings of its *mim*, and explained it as *fālūdhaj* (a sweet confection). Al-Mufaddal likewise related the three vowelings, but explained it as *zamaward*, and he mentioned that with a damma it means the table-spread or wine in the dialect of Kinda. With a fatha, Abdullah and Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read it. In the verse, according to all the readings, there is an ellipsis: that is, *so they came and sat*. ﴿And she gave each one of them a knife﴾.

Some of the verifiers said: it is not far-fetched to call this *wāw* the *wāw* of *faṣīḥa* (the eloquent *wāw* that indicates an omitted clause). She gave each one of them that so that she might use it to cut what is customarily cut, from what had been placed before them and brought close to them. Her purpose in this was what would happen of their cutting of their own hands, so that she might rebuke them with proof.

It has also been said: her purpose was that, and also to terrify Joseph, peace be upon him, by her scheming: when he came out before forty women gathered together with daggers in their hands, it would make him think they would attack him, so he would be fearful of her scheming constantly, and perhaps he would comply with her desire. [Page 229] According to al-Sijistani, the word *sikkīn* (knife) is masculine. He said: I asked Abu Zayd al-Ansari, al-Asma'i and others whom we met, and all of them made it masculine and denied its feminine. From al-Farra' it is said that it is both masculine and feminine, and this is narrated from al-Lihyani and Ya'qub. Some prohibited saying *sikkīna*. Yet something contrary to this was recited from al-Kisa'i, namely his saying:

*"The wolf has his knife in his jaw, then a sheath whose blade is in its throat."*

﴿And she said﴾ to Joseph, peace be upon him, while they were occupied with handling the knives and using them on what was in their hands. The conjunction with *wāw* perhaps indicates that her saying *"Go out before them"*, that is, *"Show yourself to them"*, was not immediately after the arrangement of their affairs, so that her purpose with them would be completed.

The apparent view is that she did not order him to go out except simply so that they would see him, and thus her aim would be attained. It has been said: she ordered him to go out before them for the sake of service or to greet them, and she had concealed along with that what she had concealed. It is narrated that she dressed him in white garments on that day, because beauty is at its finest in whiteness. ﴿So when they saw him﴾, this is conjoined with an implied clause required by the command to go out, and which the discourse implies: that is, *so he went out before them and they saw him*. It was omitted, it is said, to make the suddenness of their seeing him sharper, as if it would be lost by mentioning his going out before them. In this there is an indication of the speed of his compliance, peace be upon him, with her command in matters whose harm he did not witness, from the deeds of the serpents. A similar case is *"Coming (ātin)"*, as has passed just now.

﴿They were struck with awe at him﴾, that is, they magnified him and were astonished by the sight of his surpassing, splendid, delightful beauty, for the excellence of his beauty over the beauty of every beautiful one was like the excellence of the moon on the night of the full moon over the rest of the stars.

Ibn Jarir and others have transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "I saw Joseph on the night of the Ascension like the moon on the night of the full moon." It is related that when he, peace be upon him, walked through the alleys of Egypt, his face shone on the walls as the sunlight is seen. It came from al-Hasan that he was given a third of beauty. In a narration from Anas, traced to the Prophet: "He, peace be upon him, and his mother were given half of beauty." And the report has preceded that he, peace be upon him, resembled Adam, peace be upon him, on the day his Lord created him. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, it is that the meaning of *akbarna* is *ḥiḍna* (they menstruated). From this is his saying:

*"He comes to women in their states of purity, and does not come to women when they become (menstruating) with great menstruation."*

Perhaps the menstrual period was called *ikbār* (great [menstruation]) because puberty is known by it, so it is as if it brings the young to the age of the elderly. So it is in origin a metonymy or a figurative usage. The pronoun on this view is either a pronoun for the verbal noun, so it is as if it were said *akbarna ikbāran*, or it is a pronoun for Joseph, peace be upon him, with the preposition dropped, meaning they menstruated on his account, because of the intensity of their lust. And a woman, as al-Wahidi claims, when her lust intensifies, menstruates. From this al-Mutanabbi took his saying:

*"Fear God, and conceal this beauty with a veil, for when you appear, the unmarried maidens menstruate in their chambers."*

It has been said: the *hā'* is for pausal sound (*sakt*). This was rejected: it is not moved, and it is not retained in continuous speech; and treating continuous speech as pausal, and vocalizing it as if it were a pronoun, as in his saying, *"Alas, my two hearts, for the one whose heart is ... (shabam)"*, is weak in Arabic, even if that line is authentically transmitted.

In *al-Kashf* he objected to the first two derivations, saying: removing the preposition is weak, because it is only applied to adverbs, attributes and relative clauses, owing to the verb's indication of the place of deletion. But in such a case as this, it does not apply. And the verbal noun is not of its figurative usage, since the context is not for emphasis. He claimed that the correct view is the last one. Everything he mentioned falls within the scope of prohibition, as is not hidden.

Abu 'Ubayda denied that *akbarna* comes with the meaning of *ḥiḍna*, and said: we do not know this in the language, and the line is a fabricated, invented one, which the scholars of poetry do not recognize. Similar was transmitted from al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and several other verifiers. The narration of this from Ibn 'Abbas was transmitted by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim through the route of Abd al-Samad. Even if this is narrated from his father 'Ali, from his father Ibn 'Abbas, it is not to be relied upon, for they have said: he, may God have mercy on him, was not among the transmitters of knowledge.

From al-Kumayt the poet, *akbarna* is explained as *amnayna* (they became secure). Perhaps the discussion of this is like the discussion of what preceded, in its analysis and acceptance. As for me, I do not consider al-Kumayt among the horsemen of this field or the knights of that matter.

﴿And they cut their hands﴾, that is, they wounded them with the knives in their hands, from the extreme of their astonishment and the movements of their limbs departing from the path of choice, until they did not know what they had done and did not feel the pain that had reached them. This is like your saying, "I was cutting the meat, and I cut my hand." It is a literal sense of cutting according to some. In *al-Kashf* it is said that it is a figurative sense according to the most correct view. The intensive form (*taḍ'īf*) indicates multiplicity, either in relation to the multitude of those cutting, or in relation to the multiplicity of cuts in the hand of each one of them.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Mujahid that he interpreted *taqti'* (cutting) as *al-ibanah* (clarifying, making evident). The first meaning comes to mind more quickly, and taking *aydi* (hands) to mean the known limbs is something whose opposite can hardly be understood. Among the strange things is what is narrated from Ikrimah, that the intended meaning of "hands" here is the sleeves (*akmam*). I think the origin of this is merely a sense that cutting falling on the hands in the apparent meaning is unlikely. By my life, if what he said were presented to the least intelligent people, they would find it unlikely.

﴿And they said﴾, declaring God, glorified be He, exempt from attributes of deficiency and incapacity, and marvelling at His power, exalted and majestic, over such a wondrous creation. ﴿Ḥāshā lillāh﴾ (Far be it from God!). Its origin is *ḥāshā Allāh* with an alif, as Abu 'Amr recited it in continuous speech, and its final alif was dropped for lightness. It is said to be a particle (*ḥarf*) laid down for both exception (*istithnā'*) and exculpation (*tanzīh*) together. Then it was transferred (*nuqila*) and made a noun with the meaning of exculpation, stripped of the meaning of exception, and it was not given tanwin (the nunation ending), in observance of its original source from which it was transferred. They often observe this. Do you not see that they said *jalastu min 'an yamīnih* ("I sat from his right side")? They made *'an* a noun and did not subject it to *i'rāb* (case-inflection, the grammatical declension of endings). They also said *ghadat min 'alayhi* ("she went forth from upon him"), and did not keep the alif of *'alā* with the pronoun, as they kept the alif of *fatā* in *fatāhu* ("his young man"). All of this is observance of the original form. The *lām* is for specification (*bayān*), so it is connected to a deleted element.

It was objected, in *al-Baḥr*, to the claim that it conveys both exception and exculpation, that this is not known among the grammarians, and that there is no difference between *qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan* ("the people stood except Zayd") and *ḥāshā Zaydan* ("except Zayd"). This was countered by saying that the grammarians' not mentioning this does no harm, because that is the task of the lexicographers (*lughawiyyūn*), not theirs. Some objected to the claim of transfer, saying that a particle (*ḥarf*) cannot become a noun unless it is transferred and named with it and made a proper name (*'alam*). In that case it may take both *ḥikāyah* (quotation, i.e. remaining unchanged) and *i'rāb*. For this reason Ibn al-Ḥājib made it a verbal particle (*ism fi'l*) with the meaning of "God is free of evil." Perhaps the entry of the *lām* is like its entry in ﴿Hayhāt hayhāt limā tū'adūn﴾ (Far, far is what you are promised). That the meaning is on the basis of a verbal noun (*maṣdariyyah*) does not refute this, because it has been said that verbal particles are laid down for the meanings of verbal nouns, and this is what is transmitted from al-Zajjāj. Yes, al-Mubarrad, Abu 'Alī, Ibn 'Aṭiyyah, and a group went to the view that it is a past-tense verb meaning "kept away" (*jānib*), originating from *ḥāshiyat al-shay'* (the edge of a thing), and *ḥashyuh*, that is, its side and region. In it is a pronoun for Joseph, and the *lām* is for causation (*ta'līl*), connected to it. That is, he kept himself away (*jānab Yūsuf mā qurifa bihi*) for God, that is, for the sake of his fear and watchfulness of Him. The meaning intended is exculpation and distancing, as if he had gone to one side from what he was accused of, because of the signs of protection (*'iṣmah*) and the majesty of prophethood seen in him, peace be upon him. It is not hidden that on this view the sense of wonder is lost.

It was cited as evidence that it is a noun by the recitation of Abu al-Simal, *ḥāshan lillāh* (with tanwin), and he (the cited authority) allowed that it might be a verbal particle with tanwin as in *ṣahin* (a particle for calling a camel to halt). Similarly, with the reading of Ubayy and 'Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with both of them), *ḥāshā Allāh* with the genitive, like *subḥāna Allāh* (Glory be to God). Al-Fārisī claimed that *ḥāshā* in this case is a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*) intended for exception, as in the verse:

*(Except) Abī Thawbān, indeed Abū Thawbān*
*is not a dullard nor a fool.*

This was refuted on the ground that nothing preceding it here is stated as excepted from. A narration from al-Ḥasan states that he recited *ḥāsh lillāh*, with sukūn on the *shīn* both in continuous speech and in pausal form, with the *lām* of the genitive on the sacred name, on the basis that the fatḥah followed the alif in its deletion, since it is like an accident attaching to it. This reading was declared weak, because in it there is a meeting of two sakins against the rule. In another narration from him he recited *ḥāshā al-Ilāh*. Al-A'mash recited *ḥashā lillāh*, deleting the first alif.

Al-Mubarrad, Ibn Jinnī, and the Kufans argued that *ḥāshin* may be a verb through its inflection by deletion, as is known from these readings, and that its present tense has also come from it, as in the words of al-Nābigha:

*I see no doer among people who resembles him,*
*nor do I except (anyone) from the peoples, from any one.*

Their intention was to refute Sībawayh and most of the Basrans, who denied that it is a verb and said that it is always a particle, like *illā*, except that it governs the excepted noun. It seems the Basrans had not heard of its being used with the accusative, as in the verse:

*Except Quraysh, for God has preferred them.*

They sometimes answer the argument from inflection by deletion by saying that deletion may enter a particle, as in their saying *amā wallāhi* and *am wallāhi*. Yes, it was also refuted by saying that it occurs before the preposition. Opposed to this view is what al-Farrā' held: that it is never a particle at all, but always a verb with no subject, and that the genitive following it is as in *ḥāshāya innī muslimun ma'dhūr* ("Far be it from me, indeed I am a Muslim, excused"). The verse mentioned a moment ago is with an implied *lām*. The truth is that it is sometimes a verb, so it puts the following word in the accusative and has a subject, which is a pronoun hidden in it necessarily, referring either to a part understood from the speech or to the verbal noun understood from the verb. For this reason it is not dualised, pluralised, or feminised. And it is sometimes other particles, and the following word is in the genitive, and it is not connected to anything, like the superfluous particles according to Ibn Hishām, or it is connected to what precedes it of a verb or its equivalent according to some. It does not enter upon anything except when it is a verb, unlike al-Kisā'ī's claim that this is permitted when it is in the genitive. And when it comes before the genitive *lām*, it is a verbal noun (*ism maṣdar*) synonymous with exculpation. The full discussion belongs in its proper place.

﴿mā hādhā basharan﴾ (This is no human). They denied humanity of him, because of what they witnessed of his beauty, which has no known parallel in the human species. They restricted him to the angelic by their saying: ﴿in hādhā illā malakun karīm﴾, that is, *mā hādhā illā malakun karīm* (This is none other than a noble angel), meaning: honourable, abounding in excellences. This is based on what is fixed in human natures, that no living being is more beautiful than an angel, just as it is fixed in them that nothing is uglier than Satan. For this reason everyone who is extreme in beauty or ugliness is still likened to these two, even if no one has seen them. They recited for one of the Arabs:

*I am not for a human, but for an angel*
*who descended from the air of the sky, descending.*

Much of what belongs to this category appears in the poetry of the later poets (*al-muḥdathīn*), and among it is his saying:

*When they are confronted, they are angels in beauty,*
*and if they are fought, they are demons (ʿafārīt).*

Their purpose in this is to describe him as being at the furthest degrees of beauty and perfection, suited to their natures. It is known from what has been established that the verse is no proof that the angel is more excellent than the children of Adam, as Abu 'Alī al-Jubbā'ī and his followers thought. Al-Fakhr (al-Rāzī) supported this with what he supported it with, and there is no pride (*fakhr*) in him. Others than one went to the view that the purpose is to exculpate him, peace be upon him, of what was levelled against him in the most perfect manner. They began that with *ḥāshā lillāh* (Far be it from God!), according to what is common in such cases.

In the commentary on *al-Tashīl* it is stated that their usage is that when they wish to clear someone of an evil, they begin by clearing God, glorified be He, of evil, and then they clear the one they wish to clear, on the meaning that God, exalted be He, is too exalted to fail to purify him of what harms him. This makes it more emphatic and more eloquent. The preferred view is what was indicated first, and it is what the context and the preceding and following passages require. Yes, this usage is clear in what will come, God willing, in His saying, exalted be He, concerning the women: ﴿Ḥāshā lillāh mā 'alimnā 'alayhi min sū'﴾ (Far be it from God! We know no evil in him). Here *mā* acts in the manner of *laysa* (is not), and this is a dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, because it resembles it in negating the present, according to what is well known concerning *laysa*, that it is for that, or in absolute negation, on the basis of what al-Raḍī said, that it occurs for negating both past and future. The prevailing practice of their dialect is to put the predicate in the genitive with *bi-*, to the extent that the grammarians found no evidence for the accusative in their poetry except the saying:

*And I am the warner, with a free-born, musawwadah woman*
*whose armies reach you, with her commanders.*
*Her sons surround their father,*
*they have made the breasts rage, though they are not her sons.*

Al-Zamakhsharī calls this dialect the ancient Ḥijāzī dialect, and the dialect of the Banū Tamīm in such a case is the nominative. On this basis came his saying:

*And one slender of waist, I said to him: "Declare your lineage,"*
*so he answered: "The killing of the lover is forbidden."*

Ibn Mas'ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, recited in their dialect. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah claimed that no one recited with it here. Al-Ḥasan and Abu al-Ḥuwayrith al-Ḥanafī recited *mā hādhā bi-shirā* with the preposition *bi-* and the kasrah on the *shīn*, on the basis that *shirā*, as the author of *al-Lawā'iḥ* said, is a verbal noun put in place of the object: that is, *mā hādhā bi-mushtarin*, meaning he is not one who is bought, in the sense that he is too noble for such a thing to befall him.

This reading was also transmitted by 'Abd al-Wārith from Abu 'Amr, except that it was transmitted from him that, along with it, he also made the *lām* in *malik* kasrah. Al-Ḥasan and Abu al-Ḥuwayrith were also transmitted by Ibn 'Aṭiyyah with the kasrah. The intention is to bring him into the category of kings afterwards, so in the fact that he is fit for kingship there is a clear correspondence between the two sentences. Perhaps some did not see that whoever recited this also recited *malik* with the kasrah on the *lām*, so he said: to achieve correspondence between them in interpretation, that is, "This is not a bought slave, base," and on both estimations it is not said that this reading contradicts the requirement of the context. Yes, it does contradict the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, because it was not written with a *yā'* in it.

[Page 233]

﴿She said: "That is the one⁠—﴾ The *fa'* here is *fasiha* (the *fa'* that signals an implied condition in the sentence). The address is to the women. The demonstrative, as the context requires, refers to Yusuf, peace be upon him, by the description she has just given him: his surpassing beauty and perfection, which place him beyond the ranks of human beings and limit him to the status of an angel. Or it refers to him by the description of what they have mentioned, together with the praise and the cutting of their hands because of him. So the demonstrative is the subject (*mubtada'*) and the relative pronoun is its predicate (*khabar*). The meaning is: "If the matter is as you have said, then that is the noble angel who surpasses human ranks in beauty, or the one for whose sake you cut your hands, whom you magnified and described with what you described him, ﴿the one about whom you blamed me⁠﴾," that is, you rebuked me for being infatuated with him. Or the demonstrative refers to him by the description they used earlier in their words, "The wife of the Governor has fallen in love with her Canaanite slave." In that case the demonstrative is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject, and the *fa'* entered on it after the omission. The relative pronoun is an attribute of the demonstrative. The meaning is: "So he is that Canaanite slave whom you imagined in yourselves and spoke about, concerning him and concerning me, what you said. Now you know who he is and what your words about us were." It has also been said that she meant: "This one is that Canaanite slave whom you imagined in yourselves, then blamed me for, in the sense that you did not picture him as he truly is. Had you pictured him as you have now witnessed him, you would have excused me for being infatuated with him." The demonstrative used for distant things is used here although the one referred to is close and present. It has been said that this is to elevate his rank in beauty and to make his place in it seem remote, and to indicate that because of his rarity, someone like him is unlikely to be found.

It has also been said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was not present at the time of the blame, but he was present at this statement. If the demonstrative refers to him by the earlier time, it remains in its original use. If the later time is considered, he is near, and the demonstrative used for distant things is employed to raise his station by treating him as distant. The possibility that he, peace be upon him, was further away from them at the time of this statement, so that they would not be increased in bewilderment and temptation, and for this reason he was pointed to with that (distant) demonstrative, is weak.

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the demonstrative refers to Yusuf's love, with the pronoun in "about whom" (*fihi*) referring to it. On this view he made the demonstrative refer to an absent thing, in its proper use. But this is far-fetched in view of what follows: ﴿And I did indeed seek to seduce him from himself⁠﴾. This is her admission, after establishing her proof against them and clarifying her excuse before them, while they themselves had been afflicted by the same thing that afflicted her. The meaning is: "By God, I did indeed seek to seduce him, just as you have said and heard." ﴿But he refused⁠﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, he sought chastity (*'ismah*), held fast to it, and refused me.

In al-Kashshaf it is said that *ista'sama* is an intensive form, indicating a strong refusal and intense self-restraint, as if he were in protection (*'ismah*) and was striving to increase it. Similar forms are *istamsaka* (he held fast), *istawsa'a al-fatq* (the tear became wide), *istajma'a al-ra'y* (the opinion was gathered), and *istafhala al-khatb* (the matter became grave). End of quotation.

In al-Bahr it is said: what the morphologists (*al-sarfiyyun*) mention concerning *ista'sama* is that it has the same meaning as *i'tasama*. As for *istamsaka*, *istawsa'a* and *istajma'a*, the *istaf'ala* form here also corresponds to the *iftaʿala* form, and the meaning is *imtasaka*, *ittasa'a* and *ijtama'a*. As for *istafhala*, the *istaf'ala* form here corresponds to the *tafa''ala* form, that is, *tafahhala*, like *istakbara* and *takabbara*. So the meaning of *fa-'stʿasama* is that he refused what she wanted from him. The *'ismah* is interpreted as refusal when the meaning is taken as seeking, because refusal is its lexical meaning. It has been said that his fleeing from her was a sign of this refusal, for he first refused her verbally, and then, when this did not benefit her, he sought to protect himself from her by fleeing. The meaning of *'ismah* here is not what God placed in some of His prophets, peace be upon them, which prevents them from inclining toward sins, for that is a later conventional meaning that did not exist before, and even if it did, it would not be the intended meaning, as is clear. The emphasis of the sentence by an oath, although its content, her seeking to seduce him, is something the women had already spoken of, is to show her joy in this.

It has also been said that the emphasis is in view of the coordinated clause, which is the refusal. It is as if she arranged it this way because of the strength of what motivated him to do otherwise: he was in the full vigour of youth, he was much in her company, she was seeking to seduce him, and the barriers were removed, so that in her view the matter fell within what would be denied and disbelieved by the one who reports it. Therefore she emphasized it for this reason. But this, as you see, is weak.

The verse is evidence that nothing proceeded from him, peace be upon him, of the kind with which the storytellers (*al-qassas*) have blackened the faces of the pages. Would that al-Suddi had shut his mouth from saying, after the untying of his trousers, "﴿but he refused⁠﴾."

Then, after she had admitted to them what they had heard, and had told them about it, and had shown his turning away from her and his refusal, which she displayed, she mentioned that she was still as she had been, and that neither blame nor refusal turned her from it. So she said: ﴿And if he does not do what I command him⁠﴾, that is, what I command him concerning the future, just as he did not do it in the past. ﴿*Ma*⁠﴾ is a relative pronoun, and the clause after it is its relative clause, and the returning pronoun is the *ha'*. The preposition has been omitted from it, so that it is attached directly to the verb. This is common with *amara* (to command). Such as the line: "I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded." The first object of *amara* is either left unstated, because her intention is the obligation to comply with what she commanded in general, as has been said, or it is omitted because the verb *yaf'alu* indicates it, and it is a pronoun referring to Yusuf, that is, "what I command him to do."

It has been permitted that the existing pronoun is the one referring to Yusuf, and that the returning pronoun to the relative pronoun is omitted, that is, "what I command him with." The omission is taken as gradual, since they stipulate in omitting a returning pronoun governed by a preposition that it must be governed by the same preposition that governs the relative pronoun, in form, meaning and dependence. When the gradual omission is considered, the omitted word is in the accusative. The same applies to similar cases.

Ibn al-Munir said in his tafsir: this preposition is one whose omission is familiar, so the returning pronoun is not assumed except as an accusative separate pronoun, as if it were said: "Yusuf was commanded it," because two pronouns of the same kind cannot be joined. It is also permissible that *ma* is a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), so the pronoun mentioned belongs to Yusuf, that is: "If he does not do my commanding of him." The meaning of the verb "to command" is the verb that results from its cause and requirement. It is either a metaphorical attribution or the omission of a modifier. She expressed her seeking to seduce him by "command," to show that her rule over him was in effect, and to demand that he comply with her command. ﴿He will surely be imprisoned⁠﴾, with the heavy *nun*. She chose to build the verb in the passive voice, following the custom of kings. It has been permitted that this is a vagueness, to indicate the swiftness with which this follows from his failure to comply with her command, as if no act by any agent intervenes between them.

﴿And he will surely be among the humbled⁠﴾, with the light *nun*. That is, among the abased and the belittled. It comes from *saghira* (to be small), like *fariha* (to be happy). The verbal noun of *saghara* is *saghar* with two fatha, *sughran* with a damma then a sukun, and *saghar* with fatha. This is in regard to measure. As for size and bulk, the verb is *saghura*, like *karuma*, and its verbal noun is *sighar*, like *'inab*. Some have made *saghar* a verbal noun for this as well, and likewise *saghar* with fatha on the *gh*. The well-known form is the first.

She emphasized the imprisonment with the heavy *nun*. It has been said this is because it is certain. What follows it she emphasized with the light *nun*, because it is not certain. It has also been said that this state is one of the consequences and necessary results of imprisonment, so she contented herself with the light *nun* for its emphasis after having emphasized the first with the heavy one. A group read both with the heavy *nun*, but this contradicts the orthography of the *mushaf*, because the *nun* is written there with an *alif*, like *nasfa'an*, according to the rule for pausing. It is pronounced in pause with an *alif*, as in the words of al-A'sha: "Do not worship Satan, but worship God." In reality this is because it resembles tanwin in pronunciation, being a single, unvowelled *nun* attached to the end of the word.

The *lam* that enters on the conditional particle is a preparatory *lam* for an oath, and its answer serves in place of both answers (the oath's and the condition's). The severity of what she threatened is not hidden, especially since humiliation has a great effect on the souls of free people, who sometimes prefer death to it and to what leads to it. It has been said: she did not mention the painful punishment she mentioned in ﴿What is the recompense for one who intends evil against your household⁠﴾ and so on, because at that time she was fresh in her anger and was disclaiming that she was the one who had sought to seduce him, so the severity of punishment fitted that place. But here she was in a state of hope and expectation, and because of her excuse before the women, she had softened toward him, so she threatened him with imprisonment and what belongs to it and follows from it. It has also been said that her words ﴿and he will surely be among the humbled⁠﴾ were said in place of her earlier words ﴿a painful punishment⁠﴾. Its humiliation would be by the fetter, or by beating, or by other means.
