But it is possible that by humiliation and painful punishment she meant only what happens by beating with whips, or what happens with it or with other things, or she meant by humiliation what happens by beating and by painful punishment what happens with it or with other things, or the reverse. Whichever is the case, what she demanded here is greater than what she hinted at there, because of the *wa* (and) here and the *aw* (or) there. Perhaps she went to such lengths in front of those women to increase her anger, since her lie and his truth had become evident, and he was persisting in refusing to quench her thirst. And so that she would inform Yusuf, peace be upon him, that she was not acting in fear or secrecy from anyone in this matter, so that his stratagems would be constrained, his excuses would fail him, the women would advise him, and guide him toward complying with her. So reflect upon this.

[p. 235]

﴿He said﴾: an explanatory resumptive clause (*istinaf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question), as if a questioner asks, "What did Joseph do then?" It is answered: (He said), speaking privately to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿My Lord, the prison﴾, in which she promised to put me, is ﴿more preferable to me﴾. The word *sijn* means a place of confinement. ʿUthman and his freedman Tariq, Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Hurmuz, and Yaʿqub read (*as-sijn*) with a fatha on the *sin*, as a verbal noun from *sajanahu*, meaning "he confined him." In both readings it is a subject (*mubtada*), and its predicate is what follows it. Another reading has (*Rabbu*) with a damma and (*as-sijni*) with a kasra on the *sin* and in the genitive, as an annexation (*idafa*). In that case *Rabbu* is the subject and the predicate is the same predicate. The meaning, as has been said, is: meeting the companion of the prison, or enduring his affair. ﴿Is more preferable to me﴾, that is, more deserving of choice in my view, because in it there is a small hardship that passes away, followed by many lasting comforts. ﴿Than that to which they invite me﴾, namely their compliance, which leads to wretchedness and painful punishment. The comparative form is not used in its proper sense, since he, peace be upon him, had no trace of love for what they invited him to. Rather, he and the prison were two evils, the lesser and nearer of which to being chosen was the prison. The expression of choosing by "love" is to cut off her hope of his assistance in her aim, out of fear of imprisonment. Mention of only the prison (and not humiliation) is because humiliation follows from it, as has been said. It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, was content with mentioning the prison without mentioning humiliation, because it fulfils the purpose, which is to cut off her hope of assistance, out of fear of what she threatened, since she thought the prison was harder on him than humiliation, on the assumption that he was truly her servant and that young men are not burdened by such things as the prison's burden. Since the harder thing would be more beloved to him than what they invite him to, the lesser thing would be more beloved to him by a fortiori reasoning. In this there is clear prohibition. The attribution of the invitation to them (the women) is because they frightened him away from disobeying her and made obedience to her attractive to him. It is reported that they said to him: "Obey your mistress and fulfil her need, so that you may be safe from her punishment, for she is the wronged one and you are the wrongdoer." It is also reported that each of them asked for a private meeting to advise him, and when she was alone with him she invited him to herself. From ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with both of them, it is reported that each of them sent to him secretly asking for a visit. The attribution of this to them is because they also invited him to themselves, either explicitly or by allusion.

In a report mentioned by al-Qurtubi: when he, peace be upon him, said, ﴿My Lord, the prison is more preferable to me﴾, and so on, Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "O Joseph, you have brought harm upon yourself. Had you said, 'Well-being is more beloved to me,' you would have been granted well-being." For this reason the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, rejected the one who asked for patience. Al-Tirmidhi related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal that the Prophet, peace be upon him, heard a man saying: "O Allah, I ask You for patience." He, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "You have asked Allah for trial, so ask Him for well-being."

﴿And unless You turn away﴾, that is, and if You do not avert ﴿from me their plotting﴾ in making that beloved to me and making it appealing to me, by making me firm in what I am upon of chastity and purity, ﴿I shall incline towards them﴾, that is, I shall lean, by the natural disposition and the rule of the appetitive faculty, towards answering them by complying with them, or towards themselves, which is a metonym for their compliance. This is a seeking of refuge by him, peace be upon him, in the gentle kindnesses of Allah the Exalted, following the way of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the righteous, in restricting the attainment of good and deliverance from evils to the threshold of Allah the Exalted, and in stripping themselves of strength and power. It is also an exaggeration in seeking His gentle kindness, may He be glorified, in averting their plotting, by showing that he has no power to resist, like the words of one seeking help: "Rescue me, or I perish." It does not mean that he, peace be upon him, was asking to be compelled, forced into chastity and purity, while in himself there was a motive calling him to evil. Thus Abu al-Suʿud has established it, and it is a subtle meaning. He took it from the words of al-Zamakhshari. But al-Qutb and others said: this is a flight into Mu'tazilism (*al-iʿtizal*, the rationalist school that holds human beings create their own actions), and an allusion to the answer to the Ashʿaris' use of this verse to prove that the servant does not turn away from disobedience unless Allah the Exalted turns him away. Al-Imam has established this with what he established, so let it be consulted and considered. The original form of *illa* is *in la*, composed of the conditional *in* and the negative *la*, as we have indicated, and the *nun* has been assimilated into the *lam*. (*Asbu*) comes from *sabā yasbū sabwan wa sabwatan*, meaning he inclined towards desire. From it comes *al-saba*, the particular wind, because souls incline towards it for the goodness of its breeze and its spirit. It is a jussive imperfect verb, in response to the condition. The conditional clause is coordinated with his words, ﴿the prison is more beloved﴾. The first was given as a nominal sentence and the second was not, because his preference for the prison over what they invite him to was established and constant, whereas the averting that is sought is not of that kind. It is also read (*asbu*) from *sababtu sabābatan*, meaning I was passionately in love. In al-Bahr it says that *al-sababa* is excess of longing, as if the one who has it pours himself into what he desires. The verb is also construed to include the sense of inclining, and for this reason it takes *ila*: that is, "I shall incline, being drawn towards them."

﴿And I shall be among the ignorant﴾, that is, those who do not act upon what they know, because whoever has no benefit from his knowledge is equal to one who does not know. Or it means among the foolish, by committing the vices to which they invite me, because the wise do not commit ugliness. So *al-jahl* here means foolishness, the opposite of wisdom, not the lack of knowledge. Among this is his saying:

*Ala la yajhalanna ahadun ʿalayna fa-najhalu fawqa jahli al-jahilina*
"Let no one act ignorantly towards us, lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 34:

﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾ meaning: He answered his supplication, which was contained in his saying: ﴿And if You do not turn away from me their scheme, I might incline toward them﴾ and so on, in the most eloquent manner. For it carries the force of his saying, "Turn it away from me," and is even stronger than it in seeking the turning away, as you know. In attributing the response to the Lord, with the pronoun referring to him (peace be upon him), there is a manifest display of kindness, which is not hidden. What further enhanced the fitness of this was that he (peace be upon him) opened his speech by calling upon Him, the Exalted, with the title of Lordship. ﴿So He turned away from him their scheme﴾ according to his supplication, by making him steadfast in chastity and purity and by placing a barrier between him and disobedience. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the supplication of those who humble themselves before Him, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their conditions, of what their intentions conceal, and of what is good for them, none other than Him, glorified is He.

﴿Then it appeared to them﴾, that is, it became apparent to al-Aziz and his companions, who were in charge of loosing and binding affairs, that they might be content with keeping Yusuf, peace be upon him, imprisoned and turning away from the matter. ﴿after they had seen the signs﴾, which should have deterred them from that change of mind. These were the evidences indicating his innocence, peace be upon him, and his purity: the tearing of the shirt from behind and the cutting of the women's hands. Qatadah limited himself to these two, as transmitted from him by Ibn Jarir. In this there is the use of the plural for two, and the matter is easy. From Mujahid, however, it is reported that he limited it to the tearing of the shirt alone, because the cutting is not, in that case, one of the evidences indicating innocence at all. The plural is then taken as a plural of honour (li-l-ta'zim), or the definite article (al-) is taken as generic (al-jinsiyyah), and this would negate the meaning of plurality. It is said, and it is as you see. Some have justified counting the cutting among the evidences by saying that his beauty, peace be upon him, was enchanting to women in a single gathering, and at the first glance it indicates that their enchantment was the greater, and that the solicitation came from them and not from him. Some have also counted his steadfast refusal, peace be upon him, toward the women when they invited him to themselves, for al-Aziz and his companions had heard it and were certain of it, until it became as though they had witnessed it. The indication of innocence in this is evident.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ikrimah, who said: I asked Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about the signs. He said: No one has asked me about them before you. Among the signs: the tearing of the shirt and its trace on his body, and the trace of the knife. Thus Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, counted the trace among the signs, which was not mentioned previously. From here it is said: it is permissible that there are signs other than those mentioned, whose mention was omitted, just as the mention of many of the miracles of the prophets, peace be upon them, was omitted.

The subject of (badā) is a pronoun that refers either to the ‘badā’ (emergence/change of mind), the verbal noun of the verb mentioned, or to the meaning of ‘opinion’, as in his saying:

*Perhaps you, and the one whose meeting is a true promise,*
*a change of mind has come upon you concerning that young she-camel.*

Or it refers to the imprisonment (al-sijn, with fatḥ), which is understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿they must imprison him﴾. The clause of the oath and its response is either an object of a hidden saying that falls as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of their pronoun, and this is the view of al-Mubarrad, or it explains the hidden pronoun in (badā), in which case it has no place in the i'rab.

It is also said that the clause ﴿they must imprison him﴾ is the response to (badā), because it is one of the verbs of the heart (af‘āl al-qulūb), and the Arabs treat it as the oath and receive it with what they receive the oath with. Some claimed that the content of the clause is the subject of (badā), as they said regarding His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Has it not become clear to them how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾, that the subject is the content of the clause, that is, the multitude of Our destruction and the manner of Our action. The apparent sense of Ibn Malik's words in his commentary on al-Tashil is that the subject in that clause is, by its being interpreted as a singular noun, since he said: The attribution (isnād) in this section is permitted by way of interpretation, just as it is permitted in the section on the subject (mubtada’), such as ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. However, the majority of grammarians do not permit this, as has been verified in its proper place.

Al-Mazini preferred the first aspect regarding the subject. It is said: and (badā lahum badā’) was good, although (ẓahara lahum ẓuhūran) would not be good, because (badā’) has been used in non-verbal-noun senses, as you know. Abu Hayyan preferred the last aspect, that it refers to the earlier imprisonment, on the recitation of the one who read the sīn with fatḥ. The more preferable is that it refers to the imprisonment understood from the clause, that is, their decided imprisonment of him, saying: (By Allah, they must imprison him). That emergence occurred through the woman's bringing down her husband, his submission to her, his love for her, and his placing the reins of his affair in her hand.

It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, refused her and she despaired of him, she said to al-Aziz: This Hebrew youth has disgraced me among the people. He tells them that I solicited him for himself, but he refused, and he describes the matter as he chooses, while I am confined and secluded. So either you permit me to go out, and I will apologize to the people and deny him, or you imprison him just as I am imprisoned, and he was imprisoned. Ibn Abbas said: He was commanded concerning him, peace be upon him, so he was mounted on a donkey, the drum was beaten with him, and it was proclaimed in the markets of Egypt that Yusuf the Hebrew solicited his mistress, so this is his reward. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, as Abu Salih said, whenever he mentioned this, would weep. She intended by this the fulfilment of her threat, so that his stubbornness would be softened by it and his obstinacy would submit to her, since the cords of her hope had been severed regarding his being drawn in by displaying her beauty herself and by her helpers.

Al-Hasan recited (la-tasjununnahu) in the second-person form, either by addressing al-Aziz and whoever was with him, or al-Aziz alone as a mark of honour, or by addressing with it al-Aziz and those among his companions of opinion who were directly involved in the imprisonment and confinement. ﴿for a time﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Until the talk ceases and what spread in the city of the indecency is forgotten. This is the apparent view according to al-Aziz. As for her view, it is until the prison humbles him, subjects him to her, and the people suppose that he is the offender. It is said: the ḥīn here is five years, and it is said: rather seven.

Muqatil said: He, peace be upon him, was imprisoned for twelve years. The more preferable view is that one should not assert a specific quantity, but should assert only a long period. The ḥīn, according to most scholars, is a period of time that is not fixed, applying to both its short and long span, and it has been used in other senses, as we have mentioned in our commentary on al-Qadiriyyah.

Ibn Mas'ud recited (ʿattā), replacing the ḥāʾ of ḥattā with an ʿayn, and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. He had taught the recitation in this way until Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to him that he should teach it in the dialect of Quraysh, (ḥattā) with the ḥāʾ.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 36:

﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ They were two servants of the great king, al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid. One was his baker and the keeper of his food, and the other was his cupbearer and the keeper of his drink. The king had become angry with them because a group of the nobles of Egypt had planned to deceive the king and assassinate him. They promised the two servants money on condition that they poison his food and drink, and they agreed to this. Then the cupbearer regretted it and retracted. The baker accepted the bribe and poisoned the food. When it was brought before the king, the cupbearer said: "Do not eat, O king, for the food is poisoned." The baker said: "Do not drink, for the drink is poisoned." The king said to the cupbearer: "Drink it," and he drank it and it did not harm him. He said to the baker: "Eat from your food," but he refused. So some of it was fed to an animal, and it died. The king ordered them imprisoned, and it so happened that they were put into the prison with him. Perhaps the reason he expressed the entry with the verb "entered" (dakhala), which is apparent in that the entry was by choice, although it was not so, is to indicate, as has been said, that when they saw Yusuf, the matter of the prison became easy for them, because love for him had settled in their hearts.

[Page 238]

*And the desire of every soul is where its beloved is.*

Indeed, more than one narrator has related from Ibn Ishaq that when they saw him, they said to him: "O young man, by Allah, we have loved you since we saw you." He said to them, peace be upon him: "I beg you by Allah the Exalted not to love me, for by Allah, no one has ever loved me without trouble entering upon me because of his love. My aunt loved me, and trouble entered upon me because of her love. Then my father loved me, and trouble entered upon me because of his love. Then the wife of this companion of mine loved me, and trouble entered upon me because of her love for me. So do not love me; may Allah the Exalted bless you both." But they insisted on loving him, by Allah, wherever he was.

It has also been said: he expressed it this way when he mentioned (ma'ahu, "with him"), which indicates that he, peace be upon him, was characterized by what is attributed to the two of them. What is appropriate concerning him is to attribute the entry to the place, in accordance with his saying, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to.﴾ Not the causing of entry, which indicates the removal of choice. Had he expressed it as "caused to enter" (adkhala), that would have indicated attributing the causing of entry to him, so there was no alternative to expressing it as "entered," giving preference to his side, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning is that (ma'a, "with") indicates companionship and accompaniment of the doer of the action at the beginning of his undertaking of the action, so it indicates that their entry was accompanied by his, and that they were all imprisoned together at one hour. It has been objected that this is refuted by His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon﴾, relating from Bilqis, since their submission was not concurrent with the beginning of Solomon's submission, peace be upon him. It was answered that the reading of it as metaphorical there is due to a distinguishing indicator, and there is no such indicator in what we are discussing, so it is read literally. What supports this is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned concerning His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And when he reached with him the effort﴾, that it is an explanation connected to an omitted element, because connecting it to (balagha, "reached") is impossible, or to (al-sa'y, "the effort") in meaning or in wording.

The author of al-Kashf said: it is not necessary that what is related about her is determined, because of the accompaniment of the doer. So it is permissible to mean "I have submitted to Allah and His Messenger," for example. The placing of (ma'a, "with") first is to indicate that she used to think that she was upon a religion before, and that she was a Muslim in what she used to worship of the sun. This indicates that it is a submission that is counted, from the effect of following his prophet, not a submission like the first, which is invalid. This meaning is correct, and it is better to read the verse upon it. If it is read upon the accompaniment of the doer, there is no alternative to an omitted element, such as "with the arrival of his call and the manifestation of his miracle," because the difference between accompaniment and mere joining is known by necessity. End of quotation.

Some have distinguished between an extended action, such as submission, and others, such as entering, by saying that the first does not require their concurrence at its beginning, unlike the second. This, as has been said, returns to joining and is not at all part of accompaniment. Moreover, in that case there is no need for interpretation in the verse ﴿And when he reached with him the effort﴾. It has been chosen that concurrence is the basic meaning, and one should not turn away from it as long as it is possible. So reflect.

The placing of the doer after the object, as has been mentioned more than once, is due to giving importance to what is placed first and creating anticipation for what is delayed, so that it settles in the soul at the moment of its arrival with great firmness. Perhaps the placing of the adverbial phrase before "the prison" is because concern with the matter of accompaniment is stronger than concern with the matter of the prison itself, since accompaniment is the source of what happened. It has also been said: it was placed first because delaying it would give the impression that it is a predicate placed before the subject, and the sentence would be a circumstantial clause of the subject of (dakhala, "entered"). It was objected that the outcome of the first construction is the companionship of the two young men with him at the time of their entry, and the outcome of the second is the companionship of the two young men with him at the time of his entry. Both matters return to their entering and his entering as companions. So understand.

The sentence, as has been said, is joined to an omitted element that the mind naturally infers, as if it were said: "When this seemed right to them, they imprisoned him," then ﴿And there entered with him﴾, and so on. He (al-Sajn, "the prison") was read with a fatha on the sin, meaning the place of imprisonment.

*(Qala, "He said")* is a resumptive sentence built upon the question of one who says: "What did they do after they entered?" So it is answered that *(qala)* ***one of them*** — he is the cupbearer, and his name was Binnu — ﴿Indeed I see myself﴾, meaning I saw myself in a dream. The expression with the present tense is to bring the past images to presence: ﴿pressing wine﴾, meaning grapes. It is reported that he said: "I saw a vine, beautiful, having three branches, on which were clusters of grapes, and I used to press them and give the king to drink." He named it by what it would turn into, because wine is not something that is pressed, since pressing a thing means extracting from it its liquid by force. That grapes turn into wine, and that what it turns into is its water by its nature, does not harm, because that is what is intended from it, and what is other than that is not considered. So there is no double figurative usage with respect to the common usage of it. It has been said: in the language of Ghassan, wine is a name for grapes; it has also been said: in the language of Adhari'an. Ubayy and Abd Allah read: "I press grapes." Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: it is necessary to take that as explanation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex; the established and transmitted reading of both of them is ﴿pressing wine﴾. End of quotation. Al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh, through several chains, have indeed transmitted this reading from the second (Ibn Mas'ud), and they mentioned that he said: "By Allah, I took it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in exactly this way." So understand.

Ibn Atiyyah said: it is permissible that the description of the wine as pressed is because pressing is for its sake, so that is not a metonymy of the first kind. The well-known view is that it is a metonymy, as al-Farra' said: it is feminine, though it is sometimes made masculine. It is reported from al-Sijistani that he heard the masculine form from trustworthy eloquent speakers. The Hulmiyyah grammarians treated it as operating like verbs of the heart, in permitting that its doer and its object be two pronouns referring to the same meaning, and they did not permit this in other than what was mentioned, so one does not say: "Hit me" or "honor me." Its summary is: I see myself pressing wine.

﴿And the other said﴾, and he was the baker, whose name was Mijlath: ﴿Indeed I see myself carrying upon my head bread﴾. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "crumbled bread (tharidan)."

﴿Of which the birds eat﴾. This, as has also been said, is an explanation, not a reading. It is reported that he said: "I saw that I was coming out of the king's kitchen, and upon my head were three baskets with bread in them, and the birds were eating from the top of them." Bread is well known; its plural is (akhbaz). It is the object of (uhmilu, "I carry"), and the adverbial phrase is connected to (uhmilu). Its being placed after it is for the reason already mentioned. It has been said: it is connected to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause from it. The clause (ta'kulu, "eats") and what follows is a qualifier of it, or a resumptive sentence built upon the question.

﴿Inform us﴾, meaning tell us, ﴿of its interpretation﴾, meaning of its explanation and what its matter will come to. The pronoun refers to the two dreams, according to the interpretation of what was mentioned, or what was seen. The pronoun has been treated as if it referred to that by way of metaphor, since the demonstrative pronoun is used to point to something plural, as the pointing has already been mentioned more than once. This is when they both said it together, or when one of them said it on behalf of both together. But when each of them said it after relating what he had seen, the referent is not plural. This possibility is not excluded by the first-person plural form, since it may be that it occurs within the narration and not within the narrated account, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, for they were not addressed all at once, but each one was addressed at a different time with a singular form specific to him.

﴿Indeed we see you﴾, an explanation for their presenting their dream to him and asking him about it, peace be upon him. That is, indeed we believe you to be ﴿among the good-doers﴾, meaning among those who excel in the interpretation of dreams. When they saw him, some of the people of the prison recounted their dreams to him, and he interpreted them in a good manner. He, peace be upon him, when he entered the prison, had said: "I interpret dreams and I am skilled at it." Or (among the good-doers) means among the scholars, as in the saying of Ali, may Allah honor his face: "The worth of every person is what he excels at." This was because they heard him mentioning to the people what indicated his knowledge and excellence. Ibn Abi Hatim and others transmitted from Qatadah, who said: When Yusuf reached the prison, he found in it people whose hope had been cut off, whose trials had grown severe, and whose sorrow had lasted long. So he began saying: "Rejoice and be patient, you will be rewarded, for this has indeed a reward." They said: "O young man, may Allah bless you. How beautiful is your face and how beautiful is your character and your form! Blessing has come to us through your neighborhood, in a way we would not wish that we had been otherwise since you came to us, because of what you tell us of reward, expiation, and purification. So who are you, O young man?" He said: "I am Yusuf, son of the chosen one of Allah, Ya'qub, son of the sacrificed one of Allah, Ishaq, son of the friend of Allah, Ibrahim." The prison officer said to him: "O young man, if I could, I would free your way, but I will treat your residence well. So stay in whichever houses of the prison you wish."

Or ﴿among the good-doers﴾ toward the people of the prison, meaning: then treat us well by relieving our distress, if you are able to do so. This is the view taken by al-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bayhaqi, and others transmitted from him that he was asked: "What was Yusuf's goodness?" He said: "Whenever a person fell ill in the prison, he would attend to him. Whenever a place became crowded for him, he would make room for him. Whenever he was in need, he would gather for him."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 37:

﴿He said: "No food will come to you that you are provided with in the prison, except that I will inform you of its interpretation (ta'wil) before it comes to you."﴾ In the prison, according to your regular custom. ﴿Except that I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) relating to the most general of circumstances, meaning: no food will come to you in any circumstance except in the circumstance of my informing you of it, by making clear to you its essence (mahiyyah), its manner (kayfiyyah), and all its other conditions, ﴿before it comes to you﴾. Its summary is: no food will come to you except that I will have told you, before its coming to you, that food will come to you, with such and such a description. The application of the term "ta'wil" to this, although its real meaning in the well-known usage is the explanation of expressions whose intended meaning is contrary to the apparent sense, by clarifying the intended meaning, by way of metaphor (isti'arah), since this resembles the explanation of what is obscure (mushkil); or it is, with respect to the vague food, in the position of the ta'wil (interpretation) with respect to what was seen in a dream, and something similar to it.

What makes this metaphor pleasing is its correspondence (mushakalah) with what occurred in their own words: "Inform us of its ta'wil" (nabbi'na bi-ta'wilihi). That the intended meaning of ta'wil is the matter that will become (al-amr al-a'il al-ma'al), based on the fact that in origin it is the making of one thing return (ya'il) to another thing, and just as it is permissible to intend the second meaning by it, it is permissible to intend the first meaning by it, and the meaning would be: "I would inform you of what the speech will lead to (yu'awwalu ilayhi)." But the report that corresponds to reality is far off, indeed it is hardly worth considering, as is not hidden from the just. It seems that he, peace be upon him, wished to present to them the Tawhid, to make it attractive to them, and to make Shirk with God, exalted is He, ugly to them, before answering what they had asked him regarding the interpretation of their dreams; then he would answer them concerning that.

This is a method that every person of intellect should follow with the ignorant and the sinners: when one of them asks him for a ruling, he should first offer guidance and advice, and call him to what is more important for him and more obligatory upon him than what he asked about, and then give him the ruling. Perhaps that was obligatory for him, peace be upon him, so he first described himself with what is above the knowledge of scholars, namely the report of unseen things, and made it a transition (takhallus) to what he intended, like the well-known transitions among them. The report of the unseen is suitable for what they asked of him, the interpretation of their dreams, and that whoever is like this will undoubtedly be truthful in other matters. The specification of food for mention among all the other unseen things strengthens the matter of suitability, as is not hidden. It also suits what he intended of calling to Tawhid, because his truthfulness, his prophethood, and his being among those who are approved by God, exalted is He, in their sayings and their deeds, were established. In God's recounting of this there is guidance for whoever has a heart. It also incorporates the point that a scholar describing himself so that he may benefit thereby is not forbidden, and this is not counted as prohibited self-praise (tazkiyah).

To the interpretation of the coming (al-ityan) as coming in wakefulness (al-yaqazah), many of the eminent scholars went, as I have mentioned, and it is related from Ibn Jurayj. Some of them took it to mean coming in a dream. Al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq said: when he, peace be upon him, knew from the vision of the baker that he would be executed, he began another discourse to console them (tansiyah) regarding the matter of the dream, and to make them hopeful (tama'iyyah) regarding their faith, so that the one to be killed would receive his share of faith and his afterlife would be safe for him. So, with the great extent of his knowledge of interpretation, he said: "No food will come to you in your sleep, which you see as food you are provided with, except that I will inform you of what its matter will lead to in wakefulness, before that appears."

It is not hidden that the hadith of the mentioned hopefulness (tama'iyyah) is something without harm, but the hadith of consolation (tansiyah) is not free from objection. In another report from Ibn Jurayj, transmitted by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others from him, there is something close to this hadith from one aspect, for he said: "He, peace be upon him, disliked interpreting for them, so he answered them that he had knowledge of the food that would come to them, and he did not state what their vision indicated, out of compassion for the one of them who would perish. When the king wished to kill a person, he would prepare a known food for him and send it to him. When they were not satisfied with that and asked him for interpretation as well, he called them to Tawhid, out of dislike for interpreting also. When they still were not satisfied, he interpreted for them and made clear what their vision indicated." And this is as you see. Whatever the case, the pronoun in ta'wilihi returns to the food. It is permissible, on the basis of the two visions they recounted to him, to take the meaning: "No food will come to you that you are provided with, according to your custom, except that I will inform you of the interpretation of what you related to me before that appointed food comes to you." The intended meaning is the report of the matter in advance of the announcement. But this is contrary to the apparent sense, and the report in advance is something with little relevance to what he is about. It may be said: the pronoun may return to what they related, and the food that is provided may be what they saw in sleep. This also has its problems, but the interpretation according to these two aspects does not need interpretation; rather, by it is intended what was intended by its ta'wil in their speech. Likewise, the hidden pronoun in (ya'tikuma) returns to the food, and its return to the interpretation, though nearer, is remote.

Then, peace be upon him, informed them that this knowledge of his is not from the sciences of soothsayers and astrologers, but is a divine bounty which He gives to whom He wills. So he said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾. It is related that they said to him: "From where do you have this knowledge you claim, and that you are not a soothsayer or an astrologer?" It was also said that they said: "This is soothsaying or astrology." So he said: that is, that interpretation and unveiling of unseen things. The sense of distance in "that" is to indicate the remoteness of his station and the loftiness of his rank. ﴿Of what my Lord has taught me﴾, by revelation or by something similar through which knowledge is attained, as it is for the saints, the people of unveiling, may God be pleased with them. Some restricted themselves to the first and claimed that the verse is evidence that he, peace be upon him, was then a prophet. Whatever the case, the meaning is that this is part of what God, exalted is He, has taught me, or of that kind which only the chosen ones attain. By this he indicated to them that he had great knowledge; what they had heard was but a drop from its flood and a flower from its blossoms.

His saying: ﴿Indeed I have forsaken the creed of a people who do not believe in God﴾ is a resumption (isti'naf) that occurred as an answer to a question arising from what preceded, and as a justification for it, as if it were said: "Why has your Lord taught you those sublime sciences?" He said: "Because I have forsaken the religion of disbelief upon which they agreed, of Shirk and the worship of idols."

It was also said: it is a justification for the teaching that occurred as a relative clause (silah), and this leads to the meaning that it is of what my Lord taught me for this reason and not another, and this is not intended.

It was also said: it is a justification for the content of the declarative sentence. Against this: what was mentioned is not a cause for the mentioned interpretation being a part of what his Lord taught him, or being of its kind, but rather for the teaching itself. The intended meaning of "forsaking" is refraining, for he was never defiled by that at all, as is made clear by what will come from his speech, peace be upon him, shortly, God willing. But he expressed it thus in order to win them over, so that they would abandon that creed they hold in the best manner. The expression of their disbelief in God, exalted is He, by the negation of faith in Him, glorified is He, is for the sake of stating explicitly that their worship of Him, exalted is He, together with the worship of idols, is not faith in Him, exalted is He, as they claim. By "those people" he meant those characterized by the attribute mentioned, wherever they were. It was said: the people of Egypt, for they were worshippers at that time. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter﴾ and what is in it of recompense ﴿they are disbelievers﴾, that is, specifically, not others of the Canaanites who were upon the creed of Abraham, peace be upon him, according to what the placing of the separating pronoun here suggests, according to some. It was mentioned that placing the pronoun is for specification, and its repetition for emphasis. Perhaps he emphasized their denial of the return (al-ma'ad) because it was stronger than their denial of the origin (al-mabda'), so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 38:

﴿And I follow the religion of my forefathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾ is within the scope of a causal clause (ta'lil, a clause giving the reason for what precedes). It is as if he said: "I have attained what I have attained only because I did not follow the religion of a people who disbelieved in the Origin and the Return, and I followed the religion of my noble forefathers who believed in that." He (peace be upon him) said this to encourage his two companions toward faith and monotheism, and to repel them from the polytheism and misguidance they were upon. He mentioned his abandonment of their religion before his following the religion of his forefathers (peace be upon them), because clearing away (takhliyah) precedes adorning (tahliyah).

Some scholars permitted that there is no causal clause here, and that the first sentence is rather a new sentence (mustanfa'ah) mentioned as a preparation for the call, and the second is a declaration that he is from the household of prophethood, so that desire for him may grow. In the words of Abu Hayyan there is something that implies this is the apparent meaning, but it is not so.

Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli and the Kufans read (ابائي) (ʾābāʾī) with the ya' silent (ʾābāʾī, with sukun on the yāʾ), and this is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. (ما كان) means: it was not correct and not proper, let alone that it should occur, (لنا) for us, the company of prophets, because of the strength of our souls. It was also said: that is, the people of this house, because of God Most High's abundant care for us. ﴿That we associate anything with God﴾, that is, any thing whatsoever, whether an angel, a jinn or a human, let alone the idol which does not hear or see. The (من) in (من شيء) is an added particle for emphasis on the object, to stress the generality. It is also possible that the meaning is "any part of polytheism, whether little or much," so that by (شيء) is meant the verbal noun (the act of associating), and the generality remains as it is. From the generality of this there follows the generality of its related matters.

(ذلك) that is, the monotheism indicated by the negation of the validity of polytheism, ﴿is of the bounty of God upon us﴾, that is, it arises from His support for us through prophethood and revelation in its various kinds. What is meant is that it is a bounty upon us directly, ﴿and upon mankind﴾ through our mediation, ﴿but most people do not give thanks﴾, that is, they do not affirm God's unity. Since He expressed that by this title, He expressed the monotheism it requires by (giving) thanks, because it, together with being one of the effects of the support mentioned, is a thanksgiving to God, Mighty and Majestic. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun referring back to "mankind" for the sake of greater clarification and explanation, and to cut off the supposition that it refers back to the totality of mankind, and what was alluded to by (بنا, through us), which might imply that the non-thankful are not exclusively from mankind. There is in this such corruption as there is.

It is also permitted that the meaning is: this monotheism arises from God Most High's bounty upon us, in that He set up for us proofs which we look into and by which we infer the truth. He has set up similar proofs for all other people as well, without any difference, but most of them do not look into them nor infer by them, following their desires, so they remain disbelievers, not thankful. The bounty on this view is rational (ʿaqlī), and on the first view it is transmitted (samʿī).

Abu al-Su'ud permitted that one may say: the meaning is that this monotheism is of God Most High's bounty upon us, in that He gave us intellects and faculties which we use for the proofs of monotheism that He laid out in the self and in the horizons. He has given all other people a similar thing as well, but most of them do not give thanks, that is, they do not turn those powers and faculties to that for which they were created, and they do not use them in the proofs of monotheism mentioned, the horizonal, the self-based, the rational and the transmitted. End of quotation.

You may also say: it is possible that the demonstrative reference is to what was indicated, namely [Page 243] "that (which) you two (are asking about)," and what is meant is what is understood from what came before of his knowledge of the interpretation of dreams. The (من) in His saying (من فضل الله) is partitive, and he would have informed about it first that it is among what his Lord taught him, and second that it is part of God Most High's bounty upon him and upon his forefathers directly, and upon mankind through them, because they interpret their dreams for them, so they uncover what was obscure to them and remove from them what occupied their minds, together with the benefit in that which no one denies except a sleeper or one feigning sleep. Whoever considers the benefits, specific and general, that follow from the interpretation of the king's dream will not doubt that the knowledge of interpretation is among God Most High's bounties upon mankind, but most of them do not give thanks for God Most High's bounty in general, or for His bounty upon them in the existence of those to whom they return for the interpretation of their dreams. This would be like your saying to someone who asks you about Zayd: "That is my brother, that is my beloved." But here he interposed what he interposed and varied the expression, so he used the demonstrative first, joined with their address, and did not use it so the second time, and he used the Lord with a pronoun first and the sublime name second. It is also possible that what is referred to in both places is the reporting of unseen matters in general, and the rest of the verse on this view, I do not think is problematic. On both views, the causal explanation of attaining that honour, by his abandoning the religion of the disbelievers and following the religion of his noble forefathers, is not contradicted by the report that this is of God Most High's bounty upon him and upon those with him, as is not hidden. Yes, taking the demonstrative to refer to what was mentioned and directing the verse toward it as it has been directed is not free from remoteness.

Some people took the demonstrative to refer to prophethood, and there is in this also what there is.

Furthermore, al-Imam (al-Razi) made it necessary that what is meant in his saying (لا يشكرون, they do not give thanks) is: they do not give thanks to God Most High for the blessing of faith. Then he said: It is related that one of the People of the Sunnah entered upon Bishr ibn al-Mu'tamir and said: "Do you give thanks to God Most High for faith or not? If you say no, you have opposed the consensus (ijma'), and if you give thanks to Him, how do you give thanks for what is not an act of His?!" Bishr said: "We give thanks to Him for having given us capacity, intellect and instrument. As for our giving thanks to Him for faith, while it is not an act of His, that is false." Speaking became difficult for Bishr, so Thumamah ibn al-Ashras entered upon them and said: "We do not give thanks to God Most High for faith; rather God Most High gives thanks for it on our behalf, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Those, their striving is appreciated﴾." Bishr said: "When speech became difficult, it became easy." Al-Rahmah (the author of the objection) pursued this against him, saying that what Thumamah committed himself to is false and is on the edge of the thumam (a worthless weed), by the explicit text of this verse, because He, glorified is He, made clear in it that the absence of associating is of God Most High's bounty, then He made clear that most people do not give thanks for this blessing, and He mentioned that in the manner of reproach. This indicates that it is obligatory for a believer to give thanks to God Most High for faith, lest he enter into the reproach. Then the proof is strengthened and the evidence is completed. End of quotation.

Perhaps the correct view regarding the verse is what has preceded, so let it be understood.

O my two fellow prisoners! (Literally "O my two companions in the prison." The idafa here is loose: the original is "يا صاحِبَيَّ فِيهِ," with "السجن" attached to the vessel-noun as a broad usage, as in their saying: "O thief of the night, (you) people of the house.") Perhaps he addressed them by the title of companionship in a place of sorrows and abodes of grief, where affection is pure and sincere counsel is unmixed, so that they would turn to him and accept his words. It is also possible that "companionship" means residence, as one says "the companions of the Fire" and "the companions of the Garden," because they are constantly in that place. The idafa is of the kind of attributing a thing to what is like an object, according to Abu Hayyan, and to the object according to others, and there is no looseness in this. It has also been said that there is looseness here too, and that he attributed them to the prison rather than to himself because they were disbelievers; but there is room for consideration in this. Perhaps in calling them by this, in this manner, there is an encouragement for them to acknowledge the truth, as if he had said to them: "O residents of this hard place and this narrow abode, I am going to mention to you a matter, so say the truth regarding it and do not deviate from it, for you are under hardship, and one in such a state should not deviate from the truth." He used the word "companion" as you have heard because "the companion of the prison," in common usage, is the jailer or the king. The address with "yā," according to the well-known view that it is for the distant, is an indication of their heedlessness and bewilderment in the valleys of error. He, peace be upon him, dealt with them gently in returning them to the truth and guiding them to guidance, in that he presented to them, in the form of a question, what indicates the falsehood of what they were upon, so that their natures would not recoil from the sudden shock of abandoning what they had been accustomed to for a long time and what their forefathers had followed generation after generation. So he said: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ "Separate" means many and multiplied, each of them ruling you in turn. The speech, as Abu Hayyan explicitly states, is on the omission of a modifier, meaning: is the worship of separate lords better ﴿for you﴾, or ﴿Allah﴾, that is, or the worship of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿the One﴾ who is singular in divinity, ﴿the Subduer﴾ the Overpowering whom no one can overpower, exalted is He. This is better than what al-Khattabi said, that He is the One who subdued the tyrants by punishment and creation by death.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that this is a parable coined for the worship of Allah alone and the worship of idols. Al-Qutb objected that this would be valid only if the two were sometimes attributed to various lords and sometimes to one Lord, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah strikes a parable: a man in whom are partners at odds...﴾ (39:29), but here they are attributed to lords and to Allah, Exalted is He, so how can it be a parable? He answered that "Allah" is interpreted as a single lord because it stands in contrast to "lords," and He expressed the single Lord by "Allah, Exalted is He," because worship is confined to Him, glorified is His majesty.

Al-Tibi also said: there is a difficulty in this, because the apparent meaning of the verse is the negation of the equality of idols and their worship with Allah, Exalted is He, and His worship; so where is the parable? Then he said: but the estimate is: many diverse masters who enslave one slave is better than one Master, the Subduer; so it was placed in the position of the Lord, and "the Master" is Allah because He is opposed to His saying "lords," so it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah strikes a parable: a man in whom are partners...﴾.

Al-Kashf established what made clear that it is a sound parable with no difficulty in it. The truth is that it is apparent in negating equality, and that making it a parable requires interpretation, as you have heard from al-Tibi; yet it is not free of subtlety, and perhaps it is preferable, even though it requires what it requires. Interpreting "separation" as separation in number and multiplicity is what many have taken. Some interpreted it as difference in size, smallness, shape and the like, which come to them through the influence of others upon them, and took it as an indication that they are subdued and powerless.

As for multiplicity, it is indicated by the plural "lords," considering that it is a plural. Thus the mention of "the One" on this view stands against what was indicated by multiplicity, and "the Subduer" stands against what was indicated by being subdued and powerless. The meaning is: Are many, called by you "lords," powerless, subdued, affected by others, better, or Allah, that is, the Possessor of this glorious name, the One, to whom multiplicity is impossible in any way, the Subduer, besides whom there is no existent except that it is subjected under His subjugation and power, helpless in His grip.

It has also been said that what is meant by "separate" is those differing in kinds and natures, such as angels, jinn and inanimate things, for example; and it may be meant that there is no connection among them and no agreement. Often this is used as a metaphor for weakness and disorder of condition. The Imam has derived from the verse more than one proof against the invalidity of idol-worship, and the apparent sense of his words is that he did not regard it as a parable, so let this be considered. Then he, peace be upon him, added to the guidance by showing that their gods fall from the level of consideration altogether, let alone divinity, and he expressed this in the most complete manner, saying, addressing them generally and those who follow their religion among the people of Egypt, as is apparent; and it has been said: generally; and it has been said: those with them among the people of the prison.

[Page 245]

﴿What you worship besides Him﴾, i.e., besides God, Exalted is He, anything, ﴿but names﴾, i.e., empty words that have no referent in external reality, because what has no instance to which the name applies has no existence at all. So their worship was directed only at those words. ﴿Which you have named﴾, i.e., made into names, ﴿you and your fathers﴾, out of pure ignorance and error. ﴿God has sent down no warrant for them﴾, i.e., for that naming, which entails worship, ﴿no authority﴾, i.e., no proof indicating its validity. It was also said: they used to apply the name "gods" (ʾālihah) to their false objects of worship and claimed a proof for that. So they are answered: you have named what no reason or transmitted report indicates deserves this name, and then you proceeded to worship it on the basis of the name you attached to it. The objects named are not mentioned in order to train the reader in what the context requires, namely to remove them from the rank of existence, and to signal that their naming is void just as their worship is void, since the names have no named referent, just as the worship has no worshipped object. This applies also to those who claim that they worship God, Exalted is He, while imagining Him to be a great body sitting upon the Throne or something similar, which reason and transmitted text both declare Him free of. ﴿Exalted is God far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.﴾ This is because what the sublime name was established for in reality is not what they imagined; rather it is something beyond that, and it is the One who deserves worship. What they themselves posited for Him is not a god in reality, nor deserving of worship. It is that which they worshipped, so in reality they worshipped nothing but a name that has no referent in external reality, because what exists externally is one thing, and what they assigned the name to is another.

﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, i.e., the ruling concerning worship that derives from that naming and concerning its validity is not in anyone's hands except God's authority, because He alone deserves worship in His own essence, being the Necessary Existent in Himself, the Originator of all, and the Owner of all affairs. ﴿He has commanded that you worship none but Him﴾, i.e., that you worship no one except Him, as reason also requires. The clause is a resumptive sentence answering an implicit question arising from the preceding clause, as if it were said: "What has God ruled regarding this matter?" and it was answered: "He has commanded…" etc. It was also said that the clause is in the position of a causal explanation for an omitted element, as if it were said: since the ruling concerning the matter of worship belongs only to Him, worship belongs only to Him, Exalted is He; or [it is said] for one who commands worship of Him, while He does not command that and does not assign it to another, because He, Exalted is He, ﴿has commanded that you worship none but Him﴾. But this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

It is also permitted that this sequence of clauses in this arrangement serves to block every avenue for justifying the validity of idol worship for them in the most thorough manner. For if they say: "God has sent down a proof for that," they are answered with His words, ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾. If they say: "Our elders ruled for us in that," they are answered with His words, ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾. If they say: "Since no proof has come down concerning that, and there was no ruling from anyone else, the matter remains suspended, for the absence of a proof indicating validity does not entail a proof indicating invalidity," they are answered with His words, ﴿He has commanded that you worship none but Him﴾. ﴿That﴾, i.e., His singling out for worship, ﴿is the upright religion﴾, the established one indicated by the rational and transmitted proofs. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that this is the upright religion, either because they are ignorant of those proofs, or because they know nothing at all, so they worship names they coined themselves, turning away from what reason requires and what the guidance of transmission leads to. The source of this aversion is the fixation on the familiar and the restriction to the sensible, which is ingrained in most natures. From this came anthropomorphism (tashbīh) and corporealization (tajsīm), and the attribution of worldly events to the sun, the moon, the rest of the stars, and similar things.

Then, after he had established the truth and explained it to them both, the extent of his vast knowledge, he began to inform them of what they had asked him about. Because this is a separate topic from what preceded it, he separated it by repeating the address, and said: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you﴾. By this he meant the cupbearer. He, peace be upon him, did not specify him, relying on the indication of the interpretation, together with his regard for good companionship. ﴿He will give his lord﴾, that is, his master, ﴿wine to drink﴾. It is related that he, peace be upon him, said to him: "As for what you saw of the vine and its goodliness, it is the king, and the goodness of your state with him. As for the three branches, they are three days that will pass while you are in prison, and then you will come out and return to what you were."

It was read as (fa-yusqī), with a damma on the yā' and the active form from asqā. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: saqā and asqā have the same meaning. In the Seven (the seven canonical readings), it was read (nasqīkum) and (nusqīkum), with a fatḥa and a ḍamma. What is well known is that saqāhu means he handed him something to drink, and asqāhu means he provided him with a drink. The reading with a ḍamma on the yā' is attributed to ʿIkrima and al-Jaḥdarī. Some have mentioned that ʿIkrima read (fa-yusqā) in the passive, and (rayyihi) with a yā' and a kasra on the rā'. What is meant by it is that with which one is quenched, and it is the second object of (li-yasqī). The first object is the pronoun standing in for the subject, referring back to someone. In that case (khamran) is put in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz).

﴿As for the other﴾, who was the baker, ﴿he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head﴾. It is related that he, peace be upon him, said to him: "As for what you saw of the three baskets, they are three days that will pass, and then you will come out and be crucified." (﴿It has been decreed﴾) means it has been completed and settled. ﴿The matter about which you both inquire﴾ is what their state will come to, and what their dreams indicate of the salvation of one of you and the destruction of the other. The meaning of their inquiring about it is their asking about it. A group of scholars, including al-Ḥākim, who graded it as ṣaḥīḥ (sound), related from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The two companions of Yūsuf did not see anything; they only made up dreams to test his knowledge. When he interpreted their dreams, they said: 'We were only playing and did not see anything.' So he, peace be upon him, said: (It has been decreed the matter)," and so on, meaning: the interpretation has occurred. It was said: what is meant by the matter is what they were accused of, and the statement then has an elided modifier, meaning: the outcome of that.

Some verifying scholars (muḥaqqiqūn) held that what is meant by it is the two dreams they had seen, and he denied that the matter means what their affair would come to. He said: because inquiry (istiftāʾ) occurs about an incident, not about its ruling. One says: "He asked the jurist (istaftā al-faqīh) about the incident," meaning he requested from him an explanation of its ruling, and one does not say: "He asked him about its ruling." Likewise iftāʾ (giving a legal opinion): one says: "He gave a ruling (afta) on the particular incident with such-and-such," and one does not say: "He gave a ruling on its ruling with such-and-such." Among what is clear in this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O chiefs! Give me your opinion about my dream﴾. The meaning of their asking about it is their request for its interpretation, by their saying: ﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾. He expressed that by the matter, and the request for its interpretation by inquiry, in order to magnify its importance and exalt its affair, since inquiry occurs in perplexing events whose ruling is difficult and whose answer is unclear. The choice of the present-tense form is because they were about to inquire until he, peace be upon him, gave them the answer they desired. The attribution of the decreeing to him, although it is one of the states of its outcome, is because in reality it is the very same outcome, and it had already appeared in the world of images (ʿālam al-mithāl) in that form. As for his using the singular while their dreams were two, it follows what they used in their saying: ﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾. It is not because the matter is what they were accused of and imprisoned for, from the poisoning of the king, for they did not inquire about that, nor about what is its form, but about what is the form of its outcome and its end. So reflect. End.

It was objected: there is no barrier to the matter meaning the outcome, as the attribution of the decreeing to it apparently requires, and many have gone to this. The particle (fī) is taken to indicate causality, like its use in his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat." The meaning of inquiring about it would then be inquiring because of it, that is, requesting an explanation of the ruling of the two dreams on its account, and they only asked for that so that their state and the outcome of their affair would become known.

If you refuse this, then what barrier is there to the inquiry being about the matter, given that inquiry occurs about an incident, and here the incident is the two dreams, since there is a unity between the matter and that incident, as he himself claimed, and by which he justified the attribution of the decreeing to the matter in the sense he understood it, although it is one of the states of its outcome? It is not for him to say that attributing the decreeing is valid when considering identity, but considering identity is invalid in connecting the inquiry. For once identity between two things is considered, it is valid to attribute to one what belongs to the states of the one but not to attribute to that other what belongs to the states of the first; this would be preferring one without a preferring factor. Denying that out of obstinacy is an insult to reason. What is preferred is the view of the many, for in it lies the safety of one who removes his sock before reaching water, as is not hidden from one who makes tayammum towards the Kaʿba of fairness. Also, what he mentioned as the reason why interpreting the matter as what they were accused of and imprisoned for is invalid is not free from weakness. Moreover, that was an indirect criticism of the author of al-Kashshāf, and he, according to al-Ṭībī, did not mean by the matter anything except the outcome. Yes, the beginning of his statement is apparent in what he mentioned, and the matter in it is easy. Perhaps the reason for the call to reflect on the words of this verifier is the whole of what we have mentioned, so reflect.

Then, this information may be meant as a reply to the two of them, according to what is reported in the narration, and it may be meant as a confirmation and affirmation of his interpretation. There is no difficulty for the first view in that there is no reason for the cupbearer to deny it, for we say: on the assumption that they both lied about it, it may be for the sake of safeguarding the feelings of his companion, the baker.

It has come in some reports: "The one who denied was the baker." In that case the matter is clear. This has been used as evidence for what is famous, that a dream occurs as it is interpreted, and for this reason it was said: "A dream is on the wing of a bird; if it is interpreted, it falls."

﴿وقالَ﴾ أي يوسف عليه السلام.

﴿لِلَّذِي ظَنَّ أنَّهُ ناجٍ﴾ عُدِلَ به عن صيغة المضارع مبالغةً في الدلالة على تحقيق النجاة، حسبما يفيده قوله: ﴿قُضِيَ الأمْرُ﴾ إلخ. وهو السر في إيثار ما عليه النظم الكريم على أن يُقال: "للذي ظنّه ناجيًا". ﴿مِنهُما﴾ أي من صاحبيه. وإنما ذُكر بوصف النجاة تمهيدًا لمناط التوصية بالذكر، بما يدور عليه الامتياز بينه وبين صاحبه المذكور بوصف الهلاك. والظانّ هو يوسف عليه السلام لا صاحبه، وإن ذهب إليه بعض السلف (السلف: الصحابة والتابعون وأئمة القرون الأولى)، لأن التوصية لا تدور على ظن الناجي، بل على ظن يوسف عليه السلام، وهو بمعنى اليقين، كما في قوله تعالى: ﴿الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أنَّهم مُلاقُو رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ونظائره، أي الذين يوقنون أنهم ملاقو ربهم.

ولعل التعبير به من باب إرخاء العنان والتأدب مع الله تعالى، فالتعبير على هذا بالوحي، كما ينبئ عنه قوله: ﴿قُضِيَ الأمْرُ﴾ إلخ. وقيل: هو بمعناه، والتعبير بالاجتهاد، والحكم بقضاء الأمر أيضًا اجتهادي. واستدل به مَن قال: إن تعبير الرؤيا ظنيٌّ لا قطعيٌّ. والجارُّ والمجرور إما في موضع الصفة لـ"ناجٍ"، أو الحال من الموصول، ولا يجوز أن يكون متعلقًا بـ"ناجٍ"، لأنه ليس المعنى عليه.

﴿اذْكُرْنِي﴾ بما أنا عليه من الحال والصفة.

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ﴾ أي سيدك. رُوي أنه لما انتهى بالناجي في اليوم الثالث إلى باب السجن قال له: أوصني بحاجتك، فقال عليه السلام: حاجتي أن تذكرني عند ربك، وتصفني بصفتي التي شاهدتها.

﴿فَأنْساهُ الشَّيْطانُ﴾ أي أنسى ذلك الناجي بوسوسته وإلقائه في قلبه أشغالًا حتى يذهل عن الذكر. وإلا فالإنساء حقيقةً لله تعالى. والفاء للسببية، فإن توصيته عليه السلام المتضمنة للاستعانة بغيره سبحانه وتعالى كانت باعثةً لما ذُكر من إنسائه.

﴿ذِكْرَ رَبِّهِ﴾ أي ذكرَ يوسفَ عليه السلام عند الملك. والإضافة لأدنى ملابسة. ويجوز أن تكون من إضافة المصدر إلى المفعول بتقدير مضاف، أي ذكرِ إخبارِ ربِّه.

﴿فَلَبِثَ﴾ أي فمكث يوسف عليه السلام بسبب ذلك القول أو الإنساء ﴿فِي السِّجْنِ بِضْعَ سِنِينَ﴾. البِضع ما بين الثلاث إلى التسع، كما رُوي عن قتادة، وعن مجاهد أنه من الثلاث إلى السبع، وقال أبو عبيدة: من الواحد إلى العشرة. ولا يُذكر، على ما قال الفراء، إلا مع العشرات دون المائة والألف. وهو مأخوذ من البِضع بمعنى القطع. والمراد به هنا في أكثر الأقاويل سبعُ سنين، وهي مدة لبثه كلها فيما صححه البعض، وسنتان منها كانتا مدة لبثه بعد ذلك القول. ولا يأبى ذلك فاءُ السببية، لأن لبث هذا المجموع مسبَّبٌ عما ذُكر. وقيل: إن هذه السبع مدة لبثه بعد ذلك القول، وقد لبث قبلها خمسًا، فجميع المدة اثنتا عشرة سنة. ويدل عليه خبر: «رَحِمَ اللَّهُ تعالى أخي يوسفَ، لو لم يقل: ﴿اذْكُرْنِي عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ﴾ لَما لبث في السجن سبعًا بعد خمسٍ». وتُعقِّب بأن الخبر لم يثبت بهذا اللفظ، وإنما الثابت في عدة روايات أنه ما لبث في السجن طولَ ما لبث، وهو لا يدل على المدعى. ورَوى ابنُ حاتم عن طاوس والضحاك تفسيرَ البِضع هنا بأربع عشرة سنة، وهو خلاف المعروف في تفسيره. والأولى ألّا يُجزم بمقدار معيّن، كما قدّمنا. وكون هذا اللبث مسبّبًا عن القول هو الذي تظافرت عليه الأخبار، كالخبر السابق، والخبر الذي رُوي عن أنس قال: «أوحى الله تعالى إلى يوسف عليه السلام: من استنقذك من القتل حين همّ إخوتُك أن يقتلوك؟ قال: أنت يا رب. قال: فمن استنقذك من الجُبّ إذ ألقَوْك فيه؟ قال: أنت يا رب. قال: فمن استنقذك من المرأة إذ همّت بك؟ قال: أنت يا رب. قال: فما بالُك نسيتني وذكرتَ آدميًا؟ قال: يا رب، كلمةٌ تكلم بها لساني. قال: وعزتي لأُدخلنّك في السجن بضع سنين»، وغير ذلك من الأخبار. ولا يُشكل على هذا أن الاستعانة بالعباد في كشف الشدائد مما لا بأس به، فقد قال سبحانه: ﴿وتَعاوَنُوا عَلى البِرِّ والتَّقْوى﴾، فكيف عُوتب عليه السلام في ذلك؟ لأن ذلك مما يختلف باختلاف الأشخاص، واللائق بمناصب الأنبياء عليهم السلام تركُ ذلك والأخذُ بالعزائم. واختار أبو حيّان أن يوسف عليه السلام إنما قال للشرابي ما قال ليتوصل بذلك إلى هداية الملك وإيمانه بالله تعالى، كما توصل إلى إيضاح الحق لصاحبيه، وإن ذلك ليس من باب الاستعانة بغير الله تعالى في تفريج كربه وخلاصه من السجن. ولا يخفى أن ذلك خلاف الظاهر، وموجبٌ للطعن في غير ما خبر. نعم، إنه اللائق بمنصبه عليه الصلاة والسلام.

وجوّز بعضهم كون ضمير ﴿أنْساهُ﴾ و﴿رَبِّهِ﴾ عائدَيْن على يوسف عليه السلام، وإنساءُ الشيطان ليس من الإغواء في شيء، بل هو ترك الأَوْلى بالنسبة لمقام الخواص الرافعين للأسباب من البين. وأنتَ تعلم أن الأول هو المناسب لمكان الفاء، ولقوله تعالى الآتي: ﴿وادَّكَرَ بَعْدَ أُمَّةٍ﴾ (وتذكّر بعد مدة).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 43:

﴿And the king said﴾. He was ar-Rayyan, and he was a disbeliever. The application of this title to him is evidence for what has been said: that it is permissible to call a disbeliever "king" (malik). Some scholars prohibited this, and similarly prohibited saying of him "amir" (commander), arguing that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius, "the Great One of the Romans," and did not write "King of the Romans" or "their commander," because of what that implies of his being upon the truth. They took this as a case of recounting a title whose ruling has passed and whose time has elapsed, and the like of this does no harm. That is, he said to those around him: ﴿Indeed, I see﴾, i.e., "I saw." The choice of the present tense expresses the narration of a past situation: ﴿seven fat cows﴾, full of flesh and fat, from "samina" (to be fat), in the pattern of "samia," samanah, with a fatha, and samanan, like 'inab, so he is sami' and samin. It is mentioned that samin and samina are pluralized as simān, so it is like kirām, the plural of karim and karimah; one says rijal kiram and niswah kiram. ﴿Devouring them﴾, i.e., they devoured them. The shift to the present tense is to bring the image before the mind, as a matter of wonder, and the clause is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "the cows" or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) for them. ﴿Seven lean ones﴾, i.e., seven cows extremely emaciated, from their saying: "a naṣl a'jaf," meaning slender. It is the plural of 'ajfā’, contrary to the analogical rule; the analogical form would be 'ujf, like ḥamrā’ and ḥumr, since fa'lā’ and af'al are not pluralized on the pattern fi'āl. However, they formed it on the pattern of (simān), and they sometimes form a word on its opposite, as in their saying: 'adūwah with the ha’ in place of ṣadīqah, and fa'ūl in the sense of fā'il does not take the ha’. They made (simān) agree with the specified noun, so it is in the genitive as an adjective of it, and it was not put in the accusative as an adjective of the counted number-specification, because the description of its specification is in meaning a description of it. They have mentioned that when the specification is described, the specification is by kind, and when the specified is described, the specification is by genus. There is no doubt that the first is better and more eloquent, since the kind includes the genus; it is thus more effective in removing the intended ambiguity of the specification. Therefore what is in the noble text is preferred over other forms, and he did not say: (seven lean ones) with the genitive construction, and he made it an adjective of the implied specification according to the analogy of what precedes it, because the specification is for the clarification of the genus, the reality and the description. It does not indicate it; rather it indicates something that has a state and a description. Therefore they mentioned that the specification is by the bare genus noun, and not by a derived descriptive noun in eloquent speech. So you say: ʿindī thalāthūna Qurashiyyūn, and you do not say Qurashiyyīn in the genitive construction. As for your saying: thalāthat fursān and khamsat rukbān, this is because fāris and rākib have come to function like nouns, being used for the most part without a described noun.

The author of al-Fara'id objected that the basic form for numbers is specification by the genitive construction. So when seven is described by "lean," it is necessary to assume the omitted genitive complement, and each of the description and the assumption of the complement is against the basic rule. But when it is in a genitive construction, the adjective stands in the place of the described noun. So our saying "seven lean" is in effect our saying "seven cows lean." The specification required by the genitive construction is achieved through the construction with the adjective, since it stands in the place of the described noun. Just as "seven cows lean" is permissible, "seven lean" is permissible. It was not put in the genitive construction because it stands in place of "the cows," which is described by "lean," so it would be of the type of the construction of the described noun with its adjective, which is not permissible except by interpretation. Al-Qutb criticized this, saying: Grant that the basic rule for numbers is specification by the genitive construction, but since the mention of "seven fat cows" has preceded, it becomes clear that the seven lean ones are cows. So this seven is specified by what precedes it, and the specification by the genitive construction has been achieved. Therefore if it were put in the genitive construction with "lean," the lean ones would be standing in place of the cows in the specification, and the specification would be by the adjective, which is against the basic rule. As for the claim that the seven stands in place of the cows, this is only when it is described by "lean." But when it is put in the genitive construction, with the lean ones standing in place of the cows, it does not entail the construction of the described noun with its adjective. End quote. There is room for reflection here.

Al-Tibi mentioned in this context that it may be said: when the specification is described and then the ambiguity and generality of the number is removed by it, this indicates that both are intended in the mention, unlike when it is specified and then described. Rather, the description is more appropriate, because the specification is brought in only for the sake of the description. For this reason the specification was omitted in the three subsequent parallel phrases, and the context requires this, because the intended meaning is to show the trial of hardship after ease, and the explanation of quantity by number and of quality by the cows is secondary. Understand this. From this one learns the reason for the shift to what is in the noble text, instead of saying: "Indeed I see seven lean cows devouring seven fat ones," which is more concise.

It is said that the expression in this form is because it was the first thing he saw: the fat ones. It is narrated that he saw seven fat cows come out of a dry river, then there came out after them seven lean cows, and they swallowed the fat ones, and no sign of them appeared upon them.

﴿And seven green ears of grain﴾, whose grain had formed. ﴿And [seven] others﴾, i.e., and seven others, ﴿dry﴾, which had ripened and twisted around the green ones until they overcame them, so that no greenness remained in them, according to what has been narrated. Perhaps the omission of mention of the number is because what was mentioned about the state of the cows suffices. It is not permissible to coordinate "others" with "ears of grain," because coordination with the specification requires that both the coordinated and the coordinated-to be explanation of the counted thing, whether one says by extension or by repetition of the governing element, since the meaning on both views does not differ; the difference lies only in the verbal analysis. In that case there would be a contradiction in the verse, because the coordination requires that the ears of grain, green and dry, be seven, while the word "others" requires that they be other than seven. This is because their contrast in attribute, namely greenness and dryness, is explicit, and their sharing in being ears of grain; so the implication of the word "others" is a difference in number, and a contradiction results. On this basis it is correct to say: "I have seven men standing and sitting," in the genitive, because you have specified seven men described as standing and sitting, with some of them being thus and some thus. But it is not correct to say "seven men standing and other men sitting," for the reason you know. So the verse and the example in this matter are on one pattern, as the Kashshaf's statement requires. The author of al-Fara'id examined this and said: the correct view is
صفحة 250
that coordination is in the status of repetition of the governing element, not extension. So if "other men sitting" were coordinated to "standing men," then "seven" would be repeated in the coordinated element, meaning "and seven others," i.e., other men sitting, and this corrupts the meaning, because it is supposed that the men are seven. As for the verse, if it were repeated there and it said "and seven others," meaning "and seven other ears," it would be correct, because the green ones are seven and the dry ones are seven. Indeed, if this were taken according to the weaker view, namely extension, it would lead to the mentioned seven being specified by green ears and by other dry ears, and it would be corrupt, since the intended meaning is that each of them is seven, not that they together are seven. So the example and the verse are not on one pattern: on the repetition view the example is corrupt, and on extension it is correct; the verse is the reverse. Then he built on what he claimed, that the correct view is repetition, the permissibility of coordination.

He claimed that it is better for the coordination to be upon "green" and not upon "dry," so as to indicate another described noun, namely ears, and its described noun should not be assumed by the context. But it is not hidden that the discussion is only on the assumption that the specification of seven is what has been stated. On that assumption the contradiction arises. It is not built upon the supposition that they are seven or fourteen, so that it would be correct in the verse and not in the example; that is an error.

From this it appears that repetition and extension have no place in this supposition. Moreover, the preferred view is extension, as Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib stated and verified in more than one place. As for the argument from the verse for extension rather than assumption, were it otherwise the word "others" would be superfluous, and the speech of God Most High, which is inimitable, is to be protected from that.
