This is not sound according to what is in al-Kashf, because the one who holds the assumption claims the dominance of independence, and likewise the one who holds extension claims dominance in the contrasting element, as the imams of Arabic grammar stated. So the emphasis by "others" is not superfluous for the sake of the explicit texts, but rather is an elaboration (ītnāb) that falls in its proper place.

﴿O chiefs﴾: an address to the nobles, from among those thought to have knowledge. It is narrated that he gathered the magicians, the soothsayers and the interpreters, and said to them: "O chiefs."

﴿Explain to me my vision﴾: that is, interpret it, explain its ruling and what it will lead to as a final outcome.

It has been said: this is an address to his companions and the people of his counsel, and the expression of interpretation by "giving a fatwa" is to honor them and magnify the matter of his vision. ﴿If you are able to interpret visions﴾: i.e., you know the interpretation of the genus of visions with continuous knowledge, which is the transition from the image seen in a dream to what is its image and example among external and internal matters that occur in reality. From 'ubur, which is crossing over; one says "I crossed the river" when you cross it and pass beyond it. Similar is "awwaltuhā," i.e., I mentioned what it will lead to. The verb 'abartu al-ru’yā, with lightening of the middle, as a term ('ibārah) is stronger and better known among the people of the language than 'abbartu with doubling, to the extent that some of them denied the doubling. The poetry which al-Mubarrad cited in al-Kamil by one of the Bedouins refutes him, and it is:

I saw a vision, then I interpreted it, and I was a skilled interpreter of dreams.

The combination of the past and the future is to indicate continuity, as has been pointed out. The lam: it has been said that it is connected to an omitted element, and the intended meaning of that clarification is as if, when it was said "you interpret," it was asked: "for what?" and it was answered: "for visions." So it is the lam of clarification, as in "suqyan lahu." However, placing the clarified before the clarifier is not without some problem. It has also been said, and Abu Hayyan chose this, that it is for strengthening the verb mentioned, because it was weakened by being delayed. It is called the lam of strengthening, and it occurs in eloquent speech with a complement when it precedes its governing element absolutely, and with a complement of a non-verb when it is delayed, as in "Zayd is a striker for 'Amr." Whether it is initially superfluous is disputed. It has been said that it was brought in to make a transitive verb carry the meaning of an intransitive verb that takes the lam, that is, "if you are appointed to interpret it." It was also permitted that "for visions" be the predicate of "kāna," as one says "so-and-so was for this matter" when he is prepared for it in the future and capable of it. The clause "you interpret" is another predicate or a circumstantial clause. What is in this of artificiality is not hidden, and likewise what precedes it.

Abu Ja'far recited with assimilation in "al-ru'yā" and its kind, after changing the hamza to waw and then changing the waw to ya because it came before it as a sukūn; they stated that this is irregular, because the waw is a non-obligatory substitute.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 12, verse 44:**

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clarifying clause (*istiʾnaf bayani*), as if it were asked: "What did the chiefs say to the king when he said that to them?" So it was answered: "They said: it is ﴿a confusion of dreams﴾," meaning "it is *adghath* (bundles, confused mixtures) etc." *Adghath* is the plural of *dighth* (a bundle of mixed plants), which is less than a *huzma* (a large bundle) and more than a *qabda* (a handful), of mixed plants. It may also be used for what is of one kind, as in his saying:

*A slender maiden, as if she had laid on her bed*
*bunches of sweet basil on a morning of the north wind.*

From this usage is the phrase in His saying, ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (*dighth*) and strike with it﴾. It is related that Ayyub (peace be upon him) took a bundle of palm fronds and struck with it.

In the *Kashshaf*, it is said that *adghath al-ahlam* means their confusions and falsehoods, and what comes from them of the self's talk or the whispering of Satan. It has been used metaphorically for this, and its origin is what is gathered of mixed plants and their bundles. Its idafa (construct) is taken to mean "bundles *from* dreams" (in the sense of *min* = "of"). An objection was raised: when *adghath* is used metaphorically for false dreams, and the dreams are mentioned, and the implied word *hiya* refers to a particular vision, then both the metaphor's vehicle (*mustaʿar*) and its subject (*mustaʿar lahu*) are mentioned, and that prevents metaphor according to the correct view among them. Many have answered this objection in ways that are not free of scrutiny. Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) mentioned two explanations for this.

The first: he intends that the real meaning of *adghath* is mixtures of plants, so confusions and falsehoods in general, whether they are dreams or other things, are likened to it. This is supported by the statement in *al-Sihah* and *al-Asas*: "*dighth al-hadith*" means "mixing it." Then here, through the idafa, specific falsehoods are intended. So the two terms of the metaphor are the mixtures of plants and the fabricated falsehoods. The dreams and the king's vision lie outside these two, so mentioning them does no harm, just as when you say, "I saw the lion of Quraysh," where it is a *qarina* (indicator) or a *tajrid* (abstraction). His saying, "its confusions," is an explanation after the specification. His saying, "and it has been used for this," is an indication of the confusions.

The second: *adghath* has been used metaphorically for the confusions that occur within one single vision. So they are its parts, not its essence. Thus the vehicle is bundles of plants, and the subject is the parts of the vision. This is like when you use "rose" for "cheek," and then say, "I smelled the roses of Hind," for which it is not said that both terms were mentioned. [End of quotation.] Yet there is no concealing the artificiality and the resort to what is not apparent in it.

Some have inclined to consider ﴿adghath ahlam﴾ as being of the type of *lujayn al-ma'* (the silver of water, a figurative expression). There is no concealment that it is safe from the objection raised against al-Zamakhshari, except that the author of *al-Asas* has explicitly stated that this is metaphor (*majaz*), and what is understood from it is the customary metaphor, which is not applied to what was mentioned. Perhaps the matter in this is easy. *Ahlam* is the plural of *hulm* (with a *damma* or two *dammas*), meaning false sleep-visions, as stated by a group of scholars. Some said: *ru'ya* (vision) and *hulm* (dream) are expressions for what the sleeper sees in general, but *ru'ya* came to be used for what he sees of good and beautiful things, and *hulm* came to be used for the opposite. In the hadith: "The *ru'ya* is from God, the *hulm* is from Satan." Al-Turbashti said: among the Arabs, *hulm* is used in the sense of *ru'ya*, and the distinction is one of the terminologies which the Lawgiver (may God's blessings and peace be upon him) established to separate truth from falsehood, as if he disliked naming what is from God and what is from Satan by one name. So he made *ru'ya* an expression for the good part, because it indicates seeing something with the eye and with insight, and he made *hulm* an expression for what is from Satan, because the root of the word is used only for what is imagined to the dreamer in his sleep of fulfilling desire with what has no reality. [End of quotation.] This is a good statement. Among what supports the claim that *hulm* is used by the Arabs in the sense of *ru'ya* is the previous verse which al-Mubarrad recited, as is not hidden.

They said *adghath ahlam* in the plural although the vision was only one, for emphasis on describing it as falsehood. This is like saying: "So-and-so rides horses and wears silk turbans," for one who rides only one horse and has only one turban.

In *al-Fara'id*: since *adghath ahlam* is used metaphorically for what was mentioned, namely its confusions and falsehoods, and these are realized in one vision in terms of it being composed of things, each of which is a dream, so they were "dreams." Al-Shihab said: this is weak, although al-'Allama al-Tibi praised it. Yes, this is not the use of the plural for the singular, because that exists in this type, since the idafa means *fi* ("in"). Then it was transmitted from al-Radi that he said in the commentary on *al-Shafiya* that the plural of paucity (*jam' al-qilla*) is not a basic plural, because it is only mentioned where the paucity is to be expressed, so it is not used merely for plurality and genus as the plural of abundance (*jam' al-kathra*) is used. It is said: "So-and-so has good clothes," meaning "good garment," but one does not say "good garment" (in the plural form *hasan al-thawb*); and "how many garments do you have?" (*kam 'indaka min al-thawb aw min al-thiyab*), and one does not say *min al-athwab*. [End of quotation.] Then he said: al-Sharif has mentioned it in the commentary on *al-Miftah*, and it contradicts what they mentioned here, so consider it. Perhaps what was mentioned, after accepting it, is only in the plural of paucity that is accompanied by a plural of abundance, as he mentioned in the example, and not in this case, and the plural of paucity that is not accompanied by a plural of abundance, as here. For we have not found in the books of lexicography a plural of the singular of this plural other than this plural. Many have mentioned that when the plural of paucity is not accompanied by a plural of abundance, it is used in the manner of the plural of abundance. Then the excellence of the position of *adghath* together with *sanabil* (ears of grain) is not hidden. So, by God, how marvelous is the matter of the Revelation, how wondrous are the gardens of its eloquence!

﴿And we are not knowers of the interpretation of dreams﴾, i.e., of the false sleep-visions, ﴿knowers﴾, because they have no interpretation. Interpretation (*ta'wil*) is only for true dreams. This is either because dreams are commonly mixed with falsehoods, or because the *lam* (the definite article *al-*) is for previous reference (*lil-ʿahd*), and what is referred to is the bundles (*adghath*) among them. The statement is in the style of: "a road whose landmarks cannot be guided by." It is an indication of the major premise of a syllogism which they presented as an excuse for their ignorance, as if they said: "This is a false vision, and every vision of this kind, we do not know its interpretation, i.e., there is no interpretation for it until we know it. It produces: this is a vision with no interpretation."

It is also permitted that the intended meaning of *ahlam* is visions in general, with *al-* being for the genus, and the statement is an acknowledgment by them of the deficiency of their knowledge, and that they are not experts in the interpretation of visions, although they do have interpretation. Ibn al-Munir chose this and claimed that it is the apparent meaning. He said that the king's first statement to them, ﴿If you are able to interpret visions﴾, is evidence that they were not knowers in his knowledge of them, because he used the word of doubt, so their acknowledgment of deficiency came in agreement with the king's doubt, which he had put in the form of an inquiry about their being knowers. And the saying of the young man: ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so that I may return to the people, so that they may know﴾ is also evidence of this.

Some of the verifiers mentioned that their turning away from the expression used in the king's speech (which expresses merely the passage from the signifier to the signified) indicates this, since they did not say "interpreting dreams" or "their expression" but turned to *ta'wil* (interpretation), which indicates an act of manipulation, and the strain in this is due to the distance between the *ayl* (what returns) and the *ma'al* (outcome). It was objected that according to this, their saying ﴿confusions of dreams﴾ would remain without purpose, since it has no role in the excuse. It was answered that it is possible the intention of it is to remove the king's fear from that vision, so it does not remain without purpose.

Al-Sahib (the author) of *al-Kashf* said: the way of that is to make the first a self-standing answer and the second likewise, i.e., here there are two matters: one from the side of the dreamer, and the second from the side of the interpreter. The way of putting the adverbial phrase in relation to its governing word is: "We are people of opinions and plans, and our knowledge of that is firm, not of interpreting visions." Its way according to the first is clear, and he claimed that the situation agrees with it, and its occurrence in that style is a statement that is not weakened, contrary to what is in *al-Insaf*. It becomes stronger when choosing the second way, if the address is to his companions and the people of his counsel from among the people of loosening and binding, because the common state among people like them is ignorance of this kind of knowledge, which only certain individuals among people know.

﴿And the one of the two who was saved, and remembered after a time (ummah), said﴾: that is, one of the two companions of Yusuf, peace be upon him, namely the cupbearer. ﴿وادَّكَرَ (wa-ddakara)﴾ with the unpointed dal according to the majority of readers. Its original form is *idhtakara*, the ta was changed to dal, and the dal was assimilated into it.

al-Hasan read *idhdhakara*, changing the ta to a pointed dhal and assimilating the pointed dhal into it. The first reading is more eloquent. The meaning in both cases is that he recalled what had passed between him and Yusuf, peace be upon him. ﴿Ba'da ummah (after a time)﴾: that is, a span of time and a long period.

al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read *immatin* with a kasra on the hamza and a shadda on the mim, meaning a favour upon him after a favour. What is intended by this is his deliverance from killing and imprisonment and the bounty of his king upon him. On this basis came the line of verse:

"Ala la ara dha (immah) asbahat bihi / fatatrukuhu al-ayyamu wa-hiya kama hiya"

Ibn Atiyya said: what is intended is "after a favour" that Allah Most High bestowed upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, and this makes the expression close to its meaning, though its remoteness is not hidden.

Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, read *ummatin* and *amahin*, with a fatha on the hamza and a lightened mim, and a tanwin on the ha, from *amaha ya'mahu amahan*, meaning he forgot. The verbal noun also occurs as *amhun* with a sukun on the mim. It is reported from Mujahid, Ikrimah and Shabil ibn Azarah al-Dab'i that they read thus, and no weight is to be given to one who denied it.

The clause is a parenthetical insertion between the speech and what was said. It is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) of the relative pronoun or of its pronoun in the relative clause, which would require *qad* according to the well-known view. It was said that it is conjoined to *najā*, but this is not correct, as some verifiers have said, because the proper status of both the relative clause and the descriptive clause is that their attribution to the relative pronoun or the described noun should be known to the addressee just as it is known to the speaker. Hence it was said: descriptions before knowledge of them are informative statements, and informative statements after knowledge of them are descriptions. You know that his remembering after a time is known only through this clause, so there is no sense in placing it in the same chain of relative clauses as his deliverance, which was known beforehand.

﴿Ana unabbi'ukum bi-ta'wilihi (I will inform you of its interpretation)﴾: that is, I will inform you of the interpretation of that matter whose affair was hidden, by receiving it from one who has its knowledge, not from my own opinion. For this reason he did not say "I will give you a fatwa concerning that." He followed it with ﴿fa-arsilun (so send me)﴾ to the one who has its knowledge. By this he meant Yusuf, peace be upon him. He did not name him explicitly out of eagerness that he himself should be the one sent to, for if he had named him, they might have sent someone else. The plural pronoun is either because he meant only the king, but addressed him in the plural as a mark of honour, as is well known in addressing kings, or it is supported by what is reported: when he heard the people's speech, he knelt before the king and said, "In the prison there is a man, a learned one, who interprets dreams, so send me to him," and they sent him. The prison, according to what is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was outside the king's city. It was said that it was within it. Abu Hayyan said: people today mark the prison of Yusuf, peace be upon him, at the place of the Nile, between it and al-Fustat, eight miles. And Allah Most High knows the reality of the matter best.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Hasan that he used to read *ana atikum*, the present tense of *ata* from *al-ityan* (coming). He was told: it is only ﴿unabbi'ukum﴾. He said: Did he, then, used to inform them?! Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ubayy that he also read thus.

Page 254
In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is so in al-Imam also.

﴿Yusuf, O man of truth (al-Siddiq)﴾. There is an omission in the speech: the meaning is "so they sent him, and he came to him and said: O Yusuf." He described him with exaggeration in truthfulness, according to what he had known of him and tested of his conditions during his stay with him in prison, since he was eager to gain his traces and draw light from him. This belongs to the category of *bara'at al-istihlal* (the skill of the opening, the artful introduction). It also contains an indication that the one seeking a ruling (*mustafti*) should honor the one giving the ruling (*mufti*). From this it has been inferred that the two men did not lie to Yusuf about their dreams, and that they lied in their statement, "We were only joking" (if that is established).

﴿Give us a ruling about seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry﴾. That is, [give us a ruling] about the dream of that. He did not state it explicitly because its aim was clear from the context of their prior dealings and because the substance of the event indicates it, since such a thing does not occur in the world of witnessed reality. The meaning is: explain to us its outcome and its judgment. He expressed this as *ifta'* (giving a ruling), and he did not say, as he and his companion had said at first, "Tell us its interpretation (*ta'wil*)," magnifying his station, peace be upon him, since he witnessed his rank in virtue. He also did not say, "Give me a ruling," even though he was the one seeking it alone, indicating that the dream was not his own but belonged to another, one who has involvement in public affairs, and that he was in this matter an interpreter and envoy. For this reason he did not change the word "king." This is suggested by his saying: ﴿So that I may return to the people﴾, that is, to the king and those around him, or to the people of the land, so that I may inform them of what you have ruled ﴿so that they may know﴾ that, and act according to its requirements, or that they may know your excellence and your standing together with your present condition, so that you may be freed from it. According to Abu Hayyan, the clause on the first reading is like a reason for the return, and on the second reading it is like a reason for "give us a ruling." He did not state the matter definitively but said "perhaps I" and "perhaps they," in deference to him, peace be upon him, following the way of courtesy, and to avoid rash speculation, since he was not certain of returning:

So while a man is among the living, rejoicing, behold, he is the grave, which the winds erode.

Nor [is it certain] that they will know it, for perhaps they will not know it, either because of their lack of understanding or because they do not rely on it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 47:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive (mustaʾnaf) clause, in the same pattern as what has passed many times. ﴿You shall sow for seven years in succession (daʾaban)﴾. Ḥafṣ read the hamza with a fatḥa (daʾaban), while the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with sukūn (daʾban). It was also read dābban with an alif and without a hamza, as a lightening (takhfīf) of the hamza. In all of these, it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from the root d-ʾ-b. Its original meaning is fatigue (taʿab), and it is used as a metonym for a continuous habit (ʿādah mustamirrah), because such a habit arises from the constant pursuit of a task that entails fatigue. Its accusative case is that of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿tazraʿūn﴾, meaning "persistently" (dāʾibīn), or "those who have a habit" (dhawī daʾb). It is given in the singular because the original form of the verbal noun is singular. Alternatively, it is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of a deleted verb, meaning "you shall persist with persistence" (tadaʾabūna daʾaban).

The clause is also circumstantial (ḥāliyyah). According to al-Mubarrad, it is an absolute object of ﴿tazraʿūn﴾, and this, in his view, is analogous to "he sat the qurfuṣāʾ (a crouching posture)." But this is not correct. The peace be upon him had interpreted the sleek cows and the green ears of grain as seven years of abundance (makhāṣīb), and the lean cows and the dried ears as seven years of drought (mujdibah). He therefore informed them that they would persevere in farming for seven years and would exert themselves in it, for through this abundance (khiṣb), which is the fulfilment (miṣdāq) and interpretation of the sleek cows, would be realised. It was also said that the intended meaning is a command to farm in this manner, so the clause is a declarative in form (khabar lafẓan) but an imperative in meaning (amr maʿnan). It is expressed in the form of a report for the sake of emphasis on the obligation of its occurrence, as though it had already happened and been reported. This is supported by His words, exalted is He: ﴿so whatever you harvest﴾, that is, in each year.

﴿So leave it in its ear﴾, and do not leave it, lest the weevil (sūs) eat it, as is the condition of grain in Egypt and its surroundings when about two years pass over it. Perhaps he (ʿAlayhi al-salām) derived this from the green ears, which suits it being a command like it. It was said: for if that is not interpreted as a command, it would necessitate coordinating (ʿaṭf) an imperative upon a declarative, since "mā" is either conditional or a relative pronoun implying the sense of a condition. In any case, because the response (jazāʾ) is an imperative, it becomes an imperative clause coordinated upon a declarative one.

It is answered that we do not concede that a conditional sentence whose response is an imperative is itself imperative. And even if it were conceded, we do not concede the coordination; rather, the clause is a resumptive one, for their counsel and guidance toward what they ought to do, since this was not customary for them, just as the sowing was of that kind. Or it is the response of an implied condition, meaning: if you sow, ﴿then whatever you harvest﴾, and so on. Also, the imperative may bear the opposite of what they mentioned: that ﴿dhurūh﴾ means ﴿tadhurūh﴾ (leave it), and it is expressed in the form of an imperative because by his guidance it is as if he had commanded them to it. The verification is what is in al-Kashshaf, that the more apparent view is that ﴿tazraʿūn﴾ stays on its original sense, because it is the interpretation of the dream, as shown by his later words: ﴿then there will come﴾, and his words: ﴿so whatever you harvest, leave it﴾ are a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), out of his concern for their affairs before completing the interpretation. Within it is what reinforces the command of what precedes and what follows, as though it had already occurred; so he commands them with what is good for them. This is the inimitable composition (al-naẓm al-muʿjiz), end of quotation.

Some have mentioned that ﴿whatever you harvest﴾ and so on, on the assumption that ﴿tazraʿūn﴾ means "sow" (uzraʿū), is included within the expression, for the devouring of the seven lean (cows) of the seven sleek ones, and the prevalence of the dried green ears, indicates that they would eat in the years of drought what was gathered in the years of abundance. And the method of preserving it was taught to them by Yusuf (ʿAlayhi al-salām), so it remained for them throughout that period. It was also said that ﴿tazraʿūn﴾ on this assumption, and likewise what follows it, lies outside the expression. All of this, as you see, [is weak].

﴿Except a little of what you eat﴾, that is: leave that in the ear, except what is indispensable of the little that you eat in those years. In this there is guidance toward eating sparingly.

Al-Sulamī read ﴿mimmā yaʾkulūn﴾ with the yāʾ, in the third person, meaning "what people eat." The restriction of the exception to what is eaten, rather than to the seed, is because the seed is known from His words, peace be upon him: ﴿you shall sow for seven years﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 48:

﴿Then there will come after that﴾ i.e., after the seven years mentioned. He did not say "after them" (min ba'dihinna), intending to magnify their status. ﴿seven hard [years]﴾ i.e., seven years difficult for the people. The specification (tamyiz) is omitted because the first (seven) indicates it. ﴿they will consume what you have stored up for them﴾ i.e., what you have saved during those years of grain left in its ears for their sake. Attributing the eating to them, although it is in fact the state of the people during them, is metaphorical (majaz), as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and the day giving sight﴾. The lam in (lahunna, "for them") serves as a reinforcement (tarshih) of this metaphor. The motive for it was the correspondence (tatbiq) between the one expressed and the means of expression. It is also possible that the expression with this wording is for the sake of mushakalah (correspondence in wording) with what occurred in the event.

Some scholars interpreted the eating (al-akl) as destruction (al-ifna'), as in the saying: "The journey ate the meat of the she-camel," meaning it consumed it and carried it away. ﴿except a little of what you guard﴾ i.e., what you secure and set aside for the sowing season. It is derived from al-hisn, which is protection and refuge.

﴿Then there will come after that﴾, that is, after the years described above with the hardship and the consumption of stored grain, ﴿a year﴾. It is like "sanah" (year), but "'am" is more often used for a time of ease and abundance, while "sanah" is used for a time of hardship and drought. For this reason drought is expressed by "sanah." It seems that, out of avoidance of that and as a warning from the outset about the difference in circumstances between it and the earlier years, the word "'am" was used instead of "sanah." ﴿In it people will be given rain﴾, that is, rain will reach them, meaning rainfall, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and the majority said. It is thus from "ghatha," the triliteral defective verb. From it is the saying of the Bedouin woman: "Give us rain for our livestock" ("ghuthna mashiyatana"). Another person said: "The fleas have harmed us when the fleas..." It was also said that it is from "al-ghawth," meaning relief, and one says: "Allah gave us relief (aghathana Allah) when He supplied us by removing hardships after they had overshadowed us." In this sense it is quadriliteral and hollow (waw-based). ﴿And in it they will press﴾, from the well-known "'asr" (pressing), that is, they will press whatever is suitable to be pressed, such as grapes, sugar cane, olives, sesame and similar fruits, because of their abundance. Mentioning it, as some verifiers said, is despite the possibility of dispensing with it by mentioning the rain, which necessarily entails it customarily, just as He dispensed with mention of their processing of grains. This is either because the rain's entailing of pressing is not like its entailing of grains, since those mentioned depend for their goodness on other factors besides rain, or because of regard for the one asking the question, considering his particular circumstances, as good news for him. This is what the excellence of the placement depends upon, in the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the second person (taghlib), giving precedence to him over the people.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this was interpreted as "yahlubun" (they will milk), and it seems to be taken from the well-known "'asr," because in milking there is pressing of the udder so that the milk comes out. The repetition of "fihi" (in it) is either, as has been said, to indicate the difference in what occurs in it in time and in kind, or because the context is that of enumerating the benefits of that year, and for this reason both occurrences are placed before the governing verb. The context is an explanation that these things happen in that year, this and that, not an explanation that they occur in that year, as the postponement would indicate. It is also permitted that the fronting is for restriction, in the sense that their rain in those years is as nothing in relation to that year of theirs, and that the one in the last place is for the sake of the rhyme endings, while the first is for regard for his situation.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with both of them, al-A'raj and 'Isa al-Basrah recited (yu'sarun) in the passive voice. And from 'Isa, (tu'sarun) with the second person, also in the passive, from "'asarahu Allah," meaning He delivered him, that is, Allah the Glorified will deliver them from the hardship they are in. This fits with His saying: "the people will be given rain." It is also narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah and others that the active form was derived from "'asr" in the sense of deliverance as well. In al-Bahr, the explanation of "al-'asr" and "al-'usrah" (with a dammah) is "the place of deliverance." He recited the verse of Abu Zubayd about 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Thirsty, seeking help, not helped, though he had been a refuge for the one delivered."

Ibn al-Munir said: its meaning is "ya'sirun," from "a'sarat al-sahabah 'alaihim," that is, the time of the winds' pressing for it came, so that it might rain. The verb is then construed directly, as in "I pressed the lemon over the food," so the preposition was omitted and the verb was connected to its object directly. Or "a'sarat" was implicitly made to carry the meaning of "matarat" (rained), so it takes its construction. In al-Sihah: "'asara al-qawm" means they were rained upon. From this is the reading of some, "wa fihi ya'sirun." Its apparent meaning is that the word is coined for that, so there is no need to imply it. Al-Naqqash related that it was read as (yu'assirun), with the yā' vowelled with a dammah, the ṣād with a kasrah, and the shaddah, from "'assara" intensively, for multiplication. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, recited (wa fihi ti'issirun), with a kasrah on the tā', the 'ayn and the ṣād, and a shaddah. Its original form is "ya'tasirun," so the tā' was assimilated into the ṣād, its vowel was transferred to the 'ayn, and the vowel of the tā' was made to follow the vowel of the 'ayn. It is possible that this is from "i'tasara al-'inab" and the like (pressing grapes and the like), or from "i'tasara" in the sense of "najā" (to be delivered). From this is the saying:

"Even if my throat were choked by something other than water, I would be like the one choked, struggling for water in deliverance."

Then, as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatadah, the rulings of this blessed year are a knowledge that Allah the Exalted gave him, which was not among what he was asked about. The same was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. They meant that this was through revelation, which is the apparent meaning. Peace be upon him indeed provided at the end of his interpretation something that shows his excellence, in contrast to what he did first when answering the dream of his two companions, where he mentioned that at the beginning. The reason for this is clear. It has been said that this good news from him, peace be upon him, was not from revelation, but because it is the custom that the end of drought is fertility, or because it is the divine way that Allah the Glorified widens things for His servants after having constricted them.

[Page 257]

But it is objected that if this were so, he would have stated the good news in general terms. Furthermore, the restriction of the drought requires its change to a different kind of abundance, not what he said, especially according to what some readings imply regarding some people helping others, for that is not known except through revelation. Then, after he had given them the verdict, guided them and given them good news, he, peace be upon him, was anticipating the occurrence of what he had reported. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that after that, he, peace be upon him, used to prepare a meal for two people, and he would bring it to the man, who would eat half and leave half. Then one day he brought it to him and he ate all of it. He, peace be upon him, said: "This is the first day of the hardships."

Al-Balkhi used his interpretation of that to argue for the invalidity of the view that a dream is as it is interpreted first. They had said, "a confused medley of dreams" (adghath ahlam). Had what they said had any effect, he, peace be upon him, would have turned away from interpreting it. There is discussion about this, for Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Razin: "A dream is on the wing of a bird as long as it is not interpreted. When it is interpreted, it occurs. And you should not relate it except to a beloved friend or one of sound judgment." Perhaps if this is authentic, it implies that judging a dream as "a confused medley of dreams," and that it has no outcome, is not part of interpretation at all. Otherwise, reconciling what is here with the report is problematic.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is fitting that this be restricted to a dream that admits several meanings, so the interpreter explains it by one of them, and it then occurs in that way. They also used this as evidence for the validity of the dream of a disbelieving person, which is evident. They have mentioned etiquette for asking about dreams: among them, that this should not happen at sunrise, at sunset, or at night. They said: the interpretation of a dream while asleep is its interpretation in reality, so it needs no further interpretation afterwards. They said much about what relates to it, and most of what has been said is of a kind whose secret does not appear to me. I do not know much of that, except as a "confused medley of dreams."

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 50]

﴿And the king said﴾ after the envoy had come with the interpreter, and he had heard from him what he had heard concerning the smallest and the tiniest matters.

﴿Bring him to me﴾, because of what he saw of his knowledge, his virtue, and his telling of things that none knows but the All-Subtle, the All-Aware. ﴿So when the messenger came to him﴾, that is, Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿the messenger﴾, who was his companion who had asked him for the interpretation, and he said to him: "The king wants you to come out to him."

﴿He said: "Return to your lord﴾, that is, your master, who is the king, ﴿and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands﴾, that is, inquire of him about their affair and their condition. He did not say "ask him to investigate that," but rather urged the king to diligence in the inquiry, so that his innocence might become clear and his uprightness might be manifest. Asking about something that stirs a person and moves him to investigate is more effective, because he is averse to ignorance. Had he said, "Tell him to investigate," it would have been a provocation to him to search into that, and it would have been a boldness toward him, so he might have refused it and not paid attention to it. Peace be upon him did not raise the matter of the wife of the Aziz, although she was the original root of what he had suffered, out of courtesy and generosity; and for this reason that matter led her to acknowledge his uprightness and the purity of his reputation. It has been said: he avoided her deceit, since he believed she remained in her former error. As for the women, he hoped to bring them to speak the truth and to bear witness, by their own confession, that she had solicited him, and that he had abstained. Therefore he limited himself to describing them by the cutting of the hands, did not state their solicitation of him explicitly, and was content with alluding to it by his saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Knowing of their plot﴾, out of courtesy toward them, and to avoid evil speech on their part and their standing up, when they were summoned before the king to plead on their own behalf, whenever they heard that he attributed corruption to them. In the Kashshaf it is said that he, peace be upon him, meant by this that it is a great plot that none knows but Allah the Exalted; or he called upon the knowledge of Allah the Exalted to show that they had plotted against him and that he was innocent of what he had been accused of; or he meant a warning to them, that is: He knows their plot, so He will recompense them for it. End of quotation.

As for the restriction in the first interpretation, it is due to his nearness to Zayd, who knows, and to its suitability for conveying meaning to him; or it is due to what the context requires, because when he urged him to ask, then attributed knowledge of it to Allah the Exalted, that indicated His greatness, and that the full reality is not something hoped to be reached. But what cannot be wholly grasped should not be wholly abandoned. This is the preferred view, and it contains greater stimulation and an incitement to learn the matter. So according to it the sentence is a completion of his saying: ﴿ask him﴾ and so on. "Kayd" (plot) is a noun for what they plotted with. According to the second interpretation, it is a concluding statement, as if it were said: Make him aware of it, so that his innocence may become clear to him, for Allah, glory be to Him, knows that this was a plot on their part; and if it was a plot, then he must be innocent. "Kayd" here means the act. According to the third interpretation, it admits both meanings, and the sense is to stir the king to anger on his behalf and to take vengeance upon them. Otherwise the speech would not fit, nor would it agree with the generosity of Yusuf, peace be upon him, at which our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, marvelled. Indeed, more than one has reported, from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, from him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "I have marvelled at Yusuf and his generosity and his patience. Allah the Exalted forgives him when he was asked about the lean cows and the fat ones. Had I been in his place, I would not have answered them until I had stipulated that they bring me out. And I have marvelled at him when the messenger came to him and he said: ﴿Return to your lord﴾. Had I been in his place and remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have hastened to respond and would have raced them to the door, and I would not have sought an excuse, because he was forbearing, possessed of patience." As for his supplication for him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, it has been said that it is an indication of abandoning the stricter course (the 'azima) in favour of the concession (the rukhsa), which is giving precedence to the right of Allah the Exalted in conveying monotheism and the message over the clearing of his own self. The scholar al-Tayyibi regarded it as being of the kind of your saying to someone you venerate: "May Allah the Exalted be pleased with you, what is your answer to my speech?" It has also been said: It may be said that in clearing his self there is something of the right of Allah the Exalted, for when his innocence was established in their eyes, what followed it would fall upon acceptance. It has been mentioned that striving (ijtihad) to remove suspicions is obligatory, in the manner of avoiding standing in places of suspicion. The Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, has said: "Whoever believes in Allah the Exalted and the Last Day, let him not stand in places of suspicion."

Muslim reported, from the narration of Anas, that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, "was with one of his wives when a man passed by him, and he called him and said: 'This is my wife.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who did I suspect, when I did not suspect you?!' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Indeed Satan runs through the son of Adam as the blood runs.'" It seems that for this reason al-Zamakhshari, who had lost the use of a leg, established before the judges that his leg had not been cut off for any crime or corruption, but had fallen off from frostbite that had struck it during some journey. He used to display the judges' written certificate in every town he entered, out of fear of the accusation of evil. Perhaps, then, peace be upon him feared that he might leave without the matter of his sin being made clear, and that his innocence from what he had been imprisoned for and accused of might not be manifest; lest the envious should climb upon it to disparage his affair and make it a ladder to lower his standing, and the people should look upon him with contempt, so that his speech would not take root in their hearts and his call would not be followed by their acceptance. In that there is something of the emptying of the message of its fruit. As for what the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, mentioned: "Had I been in his place," and so on, it was an act of humility on his part, peace and blessings be upon him, and not that had he been in his place he would have hastened and rushed. Otherwise, his forbearance, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, and his endurance, and his concern for what follows from the people's acceptance of the commands of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, is a matter well known to the elite and the common folk.

Ibn 'Atiyya asserted that it is possible that peace be upon him meant by "the Lord" the Aziz, as was said concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed he is my lord, who has made my abode good﴾. In that there is an appeal to him and a rebuke to him. But this is not right. Similar to it is what has been said: that the pronoun in "their plot" does not refer to the women mentioned, but refers to the category (of women) in general. So understand.

Abu Haywa and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, in the narration (of the reading) "al-nuswa" (with a ḍammah on the nūn), and a group read "al-lā'ī" with a yā', and it is like "al-lā'" (the plural of "allatī"). [End of passage]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 51:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question, as has passed, as if it were said: "What happened after that?" So it was said: The king said, after the messenger had conveyed the report to him and had brought them (the women) before him: ﴿What was your affair﴾, that is, what was your matter (sha'n)? Its origin (asl) is a great matter which, because of its greatness, merits much discussion (takhatub) and being spoken about (khatb). ﴿When you sought to seduce Yusuf﴾ and deceived him ﴿concerning himself﴾, and tempted him to obey his mistress. Did you find in him any inclination toward you? ﴿They said: Hashasha lillah (Far be Allah from imperfection)﴾, declaring Him free of such (tanzih) and expressing wonder at his purity and chastity, peace be upon him. ﴿We know of him no evil﴾: they went to the utmost in negating any kind of evil from him, by the indefiniteness (of "su'") and the addition of (min). In al-Kashshaf, in explaining how the question assumed in the structure of the speech concerns their finding in him an inclination, the explanation is that it is a question about their state with him at the time of seduction, and its first part is inclination, then what follows from it. Taking it as a question claims complete purity, so the king's question is directed at it, for what follows cannot occur unless inclination is absent. Their answer corresponds to it, since their amazement at his purity is by way of the wonder at the power of Allah the Exalted to create a chaste character like him, so that the wonder at it is by way of metonymy (kinayah), and thus it is more eloquent and more eloquent still. Then their denial of knowledge absolutely, and of any aspect (tarf), whatever aspect of evil befell him, whatever evil, far less the witnessing of inclination toward them. Peace. And this is of great excellence.

What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned, that the women gave a good answer from which the innocence of themselves entirely appears, and they granted Yusuf, peace be upon him, some innocence, because when the king established against them that they had sought to seduce him, they answered in response to that and in declaring themselves innocent: ﴿Hashasha lillah﴾, and it is possible that it is in regard to him, peace be upon him. Their saying ﴿We know﴾ etc. is not a complete acquittal, but rather an explanation of the story in its true form, so that the error on their part becomes established, arising from heedlessness of what the Master, the author of al-Kashshaf, established.

﴿The wife of the Aziz said﴾, and she was present in the assembly. It is said: the women turned toward her to establish (the matter) against her. And it is said: she feared that they would testify against her for what she had said on the day they cut their hands, so she confessed, saying: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾, that is, it appeared and became clear after concealment. This was said by al-Khalil, and it is derived from ḥiṣṣah, which is a portion of a whole, meaning the portion of truth became distinguished from the portion of falsehood, and what is meant is the distinguishing of this from that. Al-Zajjaj also went to this view. It is said: it is from ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu when he uprooted it so that the skin of his head appeared, and upon that is his saying:

The egg has stripped my head bare, so I taste no sleep except a light doze.

This also returns to the meaning of appearance. It is said: it is from ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ba'īr when he laid down his chest so that he might be made to kneel. Ḥumayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali said, describing a camel:

He pressed his knees firmly upon the hard rocks, and he rose with a heavy burden of Salma, then became still.

The meaning is: now the truth has been established and settled. Al-Raghib and others mentioned that ḥaṣṣa and ḥaṣḥaṣa are like kaffa and kaffkafa, and kabba and kabkaba. It was also read in the passive (ḥuṣṣ/ḥuṣḥiṣa), in the sense that the truth was settled in its place and placed in its position. And (al-ān, "now") is among the indeclinable adverbs (ẓurūf mabniyyah) according to the well-known view. It is a noun for the present time in its entirety, like the time of the act of speech at the moment of uttering it, or the present time in part, as in this verse, and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Now Allah has lightened it for you﴾. It may, according to Ibn Malik, come out of its adverbial function, as in the hadith: "He is falling into the Fire now (al-ān), when he has reached its place," where al-ān is in the position of raf' as a subject (mubtada'), and ḥīna is its predicate. It is indeclinable because it is attached to a clause whose beginning is a past verb, and its alif is changed from waw, due to their saying in its meaning: al-awān. And it is said it is from ya', because it is from āna ya'īnu, when it draws near. And it is said: its origin is awān, the waw was changed to alif and then deleted because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. This is refuted by the fact that a waw before an alif is not changed, as in al-jawād and al-sawād. And it is said: the alif was deleted and the waw changed back to it, as in rāḥa and rawāḥ. They used it once as fa'al and another time as fi'āl, like zaman and zamān. They differed regarding the cause of its indeclinability. Al-Zajjaj said: it is indeclinable because it includes the meaning of indication, since its meaning is "this time." This is refuted by the fact that what includes the meaning of indication is like the demonstrative noun, and that does not take al. Abu 'Ali said: because it includes the meaning of the definite article lam, since it is used as definite but is not a proper name, and al in it is superfluous. This is weakened by the fact that including the meaning of a particle in a noun for brevity contradicts the addition of what is not considered significant, especially when the added element is not the one whose meaning is included. Al-Mubarrad and Ibn al-Sarraj said: because it deviated from its counterparts, since it is originally indefinite, used from the beginning of its formation with al, while the rule of al is to enter upon indefinite words. This was also the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Malik refuted it by the necessity of indeclinability of al-jamma' al-ghafir and similar words that from the beginning of their formation took al, and by the fact that if deviation of a noun from other nouns required resemblance to a particle and entitlement to indeclinability, then every noun that deviated from nouns by a pattern or otherwise would have to be indeclinable, which is invalid by consensus. He chose that it is indeclinable because of resemblance to a particle in its constant attachment to a single form, since it is not dualized, pluralized, or diminutivized, unlike ḥīna, waqt, zamān, and muddah. Abu Hayyan refuted him with what he refuted those before him. Al-Farra' said: it is indeclinable only because it was transferred from a past verb, āna, meaning ḥāna, so it remained in its indeclinable form by continuity, in the manner of "I forbid you from qīl and qāla." This is refuted by the fact that if it were so, al would not enter upon it, as it does not enter upon what was mentioned, and it would be permissible for it to be declined, as it is permissible for them. Some have gone to the view that it is declinable, in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). They cite the verse: "As if they two were full, they had not changed," with kasr of the nun, meaning from al-ān, so the nun and the hamza were deleted and it was put in the genitive, which indicates that it is declinable. This is weak, since the kasra may be a kasra of indeclinability, and al-ān may have two dialects in its indeclinability: fatḥ and kasr, as in shattān, except that fatḥ is more common and better known. In the commentary on the Alfiyyah by Ibn al-Sa'igh, the one who said that its origin is awān says that it is declined, as wa'nan is declined.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti chose the view that it is declinable, because no valid cause for its indeclinability has been established. So in his view it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and though min may enter upon it and be genitive, its exit from the adverbial function is not established. As for citing the previous hadith, there is dispute about it. Whatever the case, here it is connected to ḥaṣḥaṣa, meaning the truth became established at this time ﴿I sought to seduce him concerning himself﴾, not that he sought to seduce me concerning myself. She said that only after her confession, as emphasis on his innocence, peace be upon him. Likewise her saying: ﴿And indeed he is of the truthful﴾, that is, in his saying, when you falsely accused him: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me concerning myself﴾. It is said: what moved her to all of that was the intent to answer confession, since denial is of no use, with forgiveness. And it is said: when her love for him reached its extreme, she did not care about the violation of her veil and the exposure of her secret. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: she did not intend by her saying "now" etc. merely the manifestation of what became apparent by the testimony of the women, of his absolute purity, peace be upon him, in what their knowledge encompassed, without addressing his purity in all other situations, especially in what the dispute concerned in the presence of the Aziz, nor did she investigate her own state or what she had done in that matter. Rather, she intended the manifestation of what is established in reality and the confirmation, regarding the point of dispute, of his purity, peace be upon him, and her treachery. For this reason she said: ﴿I sought to seduce him﴾ etc., and by "now" she intended the time of her speaking these words, not the time of their testimony. End of quotation. So understand and reflect. Do you see above this rank any purity in which the adversaries could not refrain from testifying to it in its most complete form?

And excellence is what the adversaries testified to.

Would that he who attributed evil to him, and God forbid, had possessed a tenth of a tenth of the fairness that those witnessing women possessed.

﴿That﴾ [is so] that he may know, which is what many have held: that ﴿that﴾ refers to the steadfastness together with the whole story that precedes it, so it is part of Joseph's (peace be upon him) own speech, a summation (fadhlakah) by him of what he had earlier undertaken, namely the rolling up of his sleeves to show the purity of his conduct and the innocence of his honour. God Most High has related what happened in this matter in accordance with what actually occurred, while observing the concision that is the habit of the Qur'an, such as the omission in ﴿So he returned to his lord and informed him of the women's words﴾ and then ﴿He summoned the women and asked, "What was your affair?"﴾ and so on. Likewise, as has been said regarding ﴿The wife of the governor said﴾ and so on, the same applies here, because the meaning is: the messenger returned to him, saying, "The king has investigated the matter thoroughly, and the clear truth has become evident to him regarding your innocence, and that you did not stray in that slippery position, nor did any blame touch you." At that point he (peace be upon him) said: ﴿That﴾ [is so] ﴿that he may know﴾ the governor ﴿that I did not betray him﴾ in his absence (lit. his honour) ﴿in secret﴾, i.e. in his absence. It has been said that the pronoun in (yaʿlama, "he may know") refers to the king, and the pronoun in (akhunhu, "I betrayed him") refers to the governor. It has also been said that both refer to the king, because the betrayal of his minister is a betrayal of him. The bāʾ in "bil-ghayb" is either for accompaniment (mulabasah) or for location (zarfiyyah). On the first, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "akhunhu", meaning "I abstained from betraying him while I was absent from him"; or from its object, meaning "while he was absent from me", and these two are mutually implicated. It was permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from both, but this is not correct. On the second, it is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf laghw) attached to what precedes it, meaning ﴿I did not betray him﴾ in a place of absence, behind the curtains and closed doors. It may also be a circumstantial clause. ﴿And that God﴾, i.e. and so that he may know that God Most High.

﴿Does not guide the scheme of the betrayers﴾: i.e. does not make it take effect or succeed, but rather nullifies it and destroys it. Thus, "guiding the scheme" is a metaphor for making it effective. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: He does not guide the betrayers by means of their scheme. He has then attributed the negated guidance to the scheme, while in fact it applies to them, as a figurative usage for emphasis, because if the cause is not guided, it is understood that its agent is not guided by even stronger implication. In this there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) against the wife of the governor in her betrayal of his trust, and against those who were involved in betraying God Most High's trust when they helped her to imprison him after they had seen the signs indicating his purity (peace be upon him). It is also possible that, along with this, it is an affirmation of his trustworthiness (peace be upon him), in the sense: "If I had been a betrayer, God Most High would not have guided my scheme nor made it succeed." The expression of some of them suggests that affirmation and allusion cannot coexist, but the truth is that there is no obstacle to that. By "his scheme" he meant his rolling up of sleeves and his steadfastness in that. Calling it a "scheme" on the assumption of betrayal is literal in its proper sense, as is not hidden. Thus, what is in al-Kashshaf, that he called it a scheme by way of metaphor (istiʿārah) or figurative association (mushākalah), is not correct. It has also been said that the pronoun in (yaʿlamu, "he knows") and in ﴿I did not betray him﴾ refer to God Most High, meaning: "That God Most High may know that I did not disobey Him," i.e. so that He may make manifest that I am not disobedient, and honour me by it, and that it becomes a cause for raising my rank, and so that it may be shown that the scheme of the betrayer does not take effect, and that the final outcome belongs to the obedient, not to the disobedient. This is like His saying: ﴿That We may know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾. There are many other similar expressions in the Qur'an, except that God Most High informed about Himself in this way, whereas for others it has not occurred in the Noble Book. In this there is a kind of implication from which it is better to refrain; moreover, the context favours what came before.

(The twelfth part is complete, and there follows, God willing, the thirteenth part, whose beginning is ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾.)

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 53:**

[Page 2]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾, i.e., I do not purify it of evil. He, peace be upon him, said this out of humbling himself before his own soul, which was innocent of all evil, and out of humility before Allah, the Exalted, and out of avoiding self-praise and admiration of its state. This is in the manner of the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without boasting." Or it was a way of speaking of the blessing of Allah, the Exalted, and of making manifest His hidden secret concerning the actions of servants. That is, I do not ascribe this virtue to the soul by its own nature, apart from the grace of Allah, glorified is He, but rather it is by His grace and mercy, majestic is His glory. It has also been said that he indicated by this that his not being tempted was not due to the absence of natural inclination, but out of fear of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿Indeed, the soul﴾, human as it is, of which my soul is a part, in itself, ﴿is one that commands evil﴾, i.e., it is much given to commanding evil. The meaning is that it is much inclined toward desires, employing its faculties and instruments in attaining them. In many exegeses it is related that when he said, ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Nor when you resolved (to do it)." Then he said: ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾… etc. Al-Hakim related it in his History, and Ibn Mardawayh with a wording close to this, from Anas, raised to the Prophet. The same is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Hakim ibn Jabir, al-Hasan and others. If it is authentic, the "resolve" (hamm) in it is to be understood as an inclination arising from human appetite, not from a determined intention and purpose. It has been said that there is no obstacle to understanding it in the second sense, and it is said that it was a minor sin (saghirah), which is permissible for prophets, peace be upon them, before prophethood, and it is maintained that he, peace be upon him, was not then a prophet. Al-Zamakhshari regarded this and what resembles it as the fabrications of the falsifiers and their slander against Allah and His Messenger, and approved of this view. Ibn al-Munir deemed him most fitting for this, and he alluded to the Mu'tazilah by his saying: "This is the way of the falsifiers of every sect, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The majority hold that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), and "ma" is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), meaning: rather, it is the mercy of my Lord that turns evil away from it, in the manner that was permitted in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Nor will they be saved﴾ ﴿except by a mercy from Us﴾. It has also been permitted that it be an exception from the general category of times, with "ma" being a temporal verbal noun (masdariyyah zarfiyyah zamaniyyah), meaning: it commands evil at all times, except at the time of my Lord's mercy and His protection. The accusative here is on the basis of adverbial time (zarf), not on the basis of exception, as has been imagined. But in this there is an affirmative elision (tafrigh fi al-ithbat), and the majority hold that it is not permitted except after a negation or something similar. Yes, some have permitted it in an affirmative context if the meaning holds, as in "I read except on Friday." It was objected to this that it would entail that the souls of Joseph and other prophets, peace be upon them, were inclined to desires most of the time, unless this is understood as referring to the time before prophethood, on the basis of the permissibility of what was mentioned before it, or unless the intended meaning is the genus of soul and not each individual soul.

It was rebutted that the last point is not evident, because exception is the criterion of generality, and what was mentioned does not arise at all, because the intended meaning is the humbling of the human species, acknowledging incapacity were it not for protection. Moreover, the time of mercy may encompass a person's whole life for some people. End. Perhaps it is better to restrict oneself to what is in the realm of the supplement (al-'ilawah), so reflect. And it may be an exception from the soul, or from the concealed pronoun in "commanding," which refers back to it.

[Page 3]

That is: every soul commands evil, except the one upon which Allah, the Exalted, has mercy and whom He preserves from that, such as my soul. Or it is an exception from the omitted object of "commanding," meaning: it commands its possessor, except him upon whom Allah, the Exalted, has mercy. In this there is the use of "ma" for one who has reason, which is contrary to what is apparent. Let the distinction in this between it and the disjunctive exception be considered.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. (53) Great in forgiveness, so He forgives what afflicts souls by the requirement of their natures, and He is abundant in mercy, so He protects them from following the demand of that. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, together with the mention of the attribute of lordship, is for the cultivation of the beginnings of forgiveness and mercy. Perhaps the mention of what indicates the first (forgiveness) before what indicates the second (mercy) is because clearing away is prior to adorning. Al-Jubba'i went to the view, which Abu Hayyan preferred, that ﴿That he may know﴾ up to here is the speech of the wife of the Chief (al-'Aziz). The meaning: that acknowledgment and admission of the truth is so that Joseph may know that I did not betray him and did not lie about him in his absence, and yet I do not declare myself innocent of betrayal, given what I said and what I did to him. Indeed every soul commands evil, except a soul upon which Allah, the Exalted, has mercy with protection, such as the soul of Joseph, peace be upon him. Indeed my Lord is Forgiving to whoever seeks forgiveness for his sin and admits it, Merciful to him. Al-Alusi's sources... Sahib al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari) objected to this: its only basis is the apparent connection of form, which is not so, and how can she say: ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾ after it has become clear, and the spot of the piebald has not been hidden, that she is its mother, to whom its ... returns?

Some have defended her, saying that the matter of the causal clause (ta'lil) is apparent in it, and it is, on the assumption that it is from his speech, peace be upon him, not apparent, because the Chief's knowledge that he had not committed what she accused him of only calls for an investigation in general, not specifically for preceding the departure when the King summoned him. The apparent reading on that assumption is to make it his (Joseph's) saying. It was answered that the intended meaning is that his knowledge might appear in its most complete form, and this requires specificity. What supports the intention of the appearance of knowledge is that the origin of the knowledge was already present in the Chief before, when a witness from her family testified. In this there is room for consideration. It may be said that in verification and in giving precedence to the investigation over the departure there is something of respecting the rights of the Chief, in that he did not leave his household before the falsity of what he had made the cause for it became manifest, although the King had summoned him to it. It follows from that his knowledge that he had not betrayed him in anything at all, nor betrayed him in his household, because it is evident that he, peace be upon him, if he did not proceed with what might be imagined to be a violation of what had been firmly agreed, despite the strength of the motive and the abundance of the motives, then he is more worthy and more fitting not to proceed with other things. So the cause for verification, together with what follows it in the story, is the purpose of obtaining knowledge that he, peace be upon him, had not done anything by which he betrayed, whatever it was, together with what is conjoined to it. That knowledge is only produced by what was mentioned through the investigation, even after the departure, as is not hidden. Or it may be said that the intended meaning is that he might act according to the requirement of knowledge of what was mentioned, on the basis of the assumption that he had known that before, but he had not acted according to the requirement of his knowledge; otherwise he, peace be upon him, would not have imprisoned him for it. So he would make up for his shortcoming by turning away from condemning his affair, or by praising him, so that he might gain favor with the King, and people would honor him, so that its trees would bear fruit from his call, and its rivers would flow in the valleys of hearts. There is no doubt that this is among the things that follow from giving precedence to the investigation, as he did. And that is not something unbefitting his station, peace be upon him. Rather, the prophets, peace be upon them, very often do such things at the beginnings of their affairs. Our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to give the unbeliever who was the chief of his people what he gave, to promote his cause. And if his saying, peace be upon him, to his companion who was saved, ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾, is taken in this sense, as Abu Hayyan did, the two parts of the speech fit together most closely. Likewise if that is taken in the sense that the apparent meaning of the speech requires, and the reports converge upon it.

It has been said here: that was so that the Chief would not disparage his affair before the King, as a stratagem to carry out what he had decided, and that this would be among the efforts toward achieving what is required for his release. This is among the ways of striving to remove an obstacle, but it is something that does not befit the dignity of his station, peace be upon him.

[Page 4]

Perhaps the supplication for forgiveness in the earlier report, on this view, is an allusion to what was mentioned. It is said: he, peace be upon him, was not reproached for it as he was reproached for the first, because it was less than that, although the flood had already reached the highest hills. It is not hidden that his returning to what would call for even slight reproach, relative to his rank, after what had happened, is in extreme remoteness. From here it has been said: the better view is that what preceded is as it preceded, and this is to be understood as him, peace be upon him, intending by it the paving of the way for the call to Allah, the Exalted, as a making-up for what he had done before, and as following what is less than the preferable, considering his station, in the first place. It has been said: regarding the reason for the causal clause, other than that is meant. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Jurayj that this is from the inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) of the Qur'an, and he went to the view that it is connected to ﴿Ask him, what about the women who cut their hands...﴾ etc. Its apparent meaning is objectionable in ways that are not hidden. So reflect on all that we have mentioned, so that you may be on insight into your affair.

In the narration of al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir and Qalun from Nafi', they both read ("bis-su'") (with the hamza replaced by a waw), changing the hamzah into a waw.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 54:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself."﴾ That is, I will make him sincerely devoted to myself and specially mine. ﴿So when he spoke to him﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech; the sense is: "They brought him, so when..." and this is omitted to indicate the swiftness of the bringing, as if there had been no time at all between the command to bring him, upon him be peace, and the address with him. He was not present with the women in the assembly, as some have claimed, and some have taken the meaning of this command to be "bring him close to me." The pronoun hidden in (kallamahu) refers to Yusuf, upon him be peace, and the explicit pronoun refers to the king; that is, when Yusuf, upon him be peace, spoke to the king after being brought to him, and the king questioned him and saw the goodness of his speech, such that the report was confirmed by the reality. Abu Hayyan favoured that the first pronoun refers to the king and the second to Yusuf; that is, when the king spoke to him and saw the goodness of his answer and his discourse. ﴿He said, "Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted."﴾ That is, one of high rank and lofty station. ﴿Trustworthy.﴾ (54) Entrusted with everything. It was also said: safe from every hateful thing. Describing him with trustworthiness is more eloquent in honouring him. And ﴿today﴾ is not a measure of station and trustworthiness; rather, it is the present moment of speech, and the intention is to specify their starting point, to guard against their being after a while. The choice of "ladayya" (with us) over "'indahu" carries, as is not hidden, the concern for his matter, upon him be peace, and likewise the nominal form of the sentence and its emphasis. It is narrated that the messenger came to him and said: "Answer the king now without delay, cast off the clothes of the prison, bathe, and put on new garments." He did so, and when he rose to leave, he prayed for the people of the prison: "O Allah, incline toward them the hearts of the good, and do not blind them to the news, for they are the most knowledgeable of people about news in every land." Then he went out, and it was written on the gate: "These are the dwellings of affliction, the graves of the living, the gloating of enemies, and the testing of friends." When he reached the gate of the king he said: "Allah is sufficient for me against my worldly life, and Allah is sufficient for me against His creation; Your protection is mighty, Your praise is exalted, and there is no god besides You." When he entered upon the king he said: "O Allah, I ask You by Your goodness over his goodness, and I seek refuge in You from his evil and the evil of others." Then he greeted him in Arabic. The king said to him: "What is this tongue?" He said: "The tongue of my uncle Isma'il." Then he addressed him in Hebrew, and the king said: "And what is this tongue too?" He said: "This is the tongue of my fathers." The king knew seventy languages, so he spoke to him in them, and he answered him in all of them. He marvelled at him and said: "O truthful one, I wish to hear my dream from you." So he related it to him, upon him be peace, exactly as he had seen it, omitting a single letter. The king said: "I am more amazed at your interpretation of it than at your knowledge of it." So he seated him beside himself on the throne and entrusted his affairs to him. It was also said that he seated him before he related the dream. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: They mentioned that Qitfir died in those nights, and that the king married Yusuf to his wife Ra'il. When she was brought in to him, he said to her: "Is this not better than what you were seeking?" She said: "O truthful one, do not blame me, for I was a woman, as you see, beautiful, graceful and luxurious in dominion and worldly comfort, and my husband did not approach women, and you were as Allah, exalted, made you in your beauty and bearing, so my self overcame me in what you saw." They claim that he found her a virgin and he lay with her, and she bore him two sons, Ifraithim and Misha.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated from Wahb, who said: The wife of the Aziz had a need, and it was said to her: "If only you would go to Yusuf ibn Ya'qub and ask him." She consulted the people about this, and they said: "Do not do it, for we fear him for you." She said: "No indeed, I do not fear one who fears Allah, exalted is He." So she was brought in to him, and she saw him in his kingship, and she said: "Praise be to Allah, who made the slaves kings through His obedience." Then she looked at herself and said: "Praise be to Allah, who made the kings slaves through their disobedience." So he fulfilled all her needs, then married her as a virgin. The report...

In another narration, she confronted him on the road and said what she said, and he recognised her and married her, and found her a virgin, though her husband had been impotent. It has spread among the storytellers that she returned to him young and a virgin, as an honour to him, upon him be peace, after she had been a previous wife and no longer young; but this has no basis. The report of her marriage too is something not relied upon by the hadith scholars. And even supposing the marriage is established, the apparent sense of al-Hakim's report is that it took place only after he was appointed over what was entrusted to him of the treasuries. It is said that the statement of the Exalted, "..." indicates this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 55:**

﴿He said: "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land."﴾ That is, the land of Egypt. Some have said that its meaning is: "over your land, which is under your control." It was also said that by "the land" he meant the category of land, and by "its treasuries" the food that comes out of it. The word *عَلى* ('alā, "over") is, according to what has been said, connected to a verb implied as *مُسْتَوْلٍ* ("one who takes charge"). The meaning is: "Put me in charge of its affairs, in terms of its provision and its disposal." ﴿Indeed, I am a guardian﴾ of it against those who do not deserve it, ﴿knowing﴾ (55) of the ways of managing it. It was also said: knowing the time of hunger. It was also said: a guardian who keeps accounts, knowing the languages.

In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of a person praising himself with the truth when his situation is unknown, and for the permissibility of seeking public office when the one seeking it is able to establish justice and implement the rulings of the Sharia, even if it is under the authority of an unjust ruler or a disbeliever. It may even be obligatory for him to seek it when the establishment of an obligatory duty depends on his holding that office, for example, and he is the one specifically suited for it.

As for what is in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abd al-Rahman, do not ask for leadership. For if you are given it because you asked for it, you will be left to handle it alone; and if you are given it without asking, you will be helped in it," it applies to other than what has been mentioned.

It is narrated from Mujahid that [Yusuf] embraced Islam at his (peace be upon him) hand. Perhaps the reason he (peace be upon him) preferred that particular office was only to carry out what was most important among the matters of rulership at that time, namely managing the affairs of the years, because it is one of the branches of that office, not merely for the general benefit, as has been said.

It has come in a narration that when the king spoke with him (peace be upon him) and he related the king's dream to him, the king said: "What do you think, O Truthful One?" He said: "Sow a large amount of crops in the years of abundance. For if you sow them on a stone, it will grow. Build storehouses and gather the food in them with its stalks and ears, for that will preserve it longer, and the stalks will serve as fodder for the animals. When the lean years come, sell that, and great wealth will accrue to you." The king said: "Who will do this for me? Who will gather it and sell it for me, and take the work of it off my hands?" So he said: ﴿Appoint me over the treasuries of the land﴾... and so on. The apparent meaning is that the king agreed to his request when he asked, and the reason he did not mention the king's agreement was to indicate that this was a matter that could not be refused, so there was no need to state it explicitly, especially after mentioning what all the rulings of sovereignty encompass.

Al-Tha'labi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said: ﴿Appoint me over the treasuries of the land﴾, he would have been appointed immediately. But he delayed that for a year."

Then, as is narrated from Ibn Abbas and others, [the king] crowned him, placed his ring on him, clothed him with his sword, and set up for him a throne of gold inlaid with pearls and rubies, thirty cubits long and ten cubits wide.

Page 6
