He spread cushions on it and draped over it a robe of brocade (*istabraq*). He (peace be upon him) said: "As for the throne, I will strengthen your kingdom with it. As for the ring, I will manage your affairs with it. As for the crown, it is not of my clothing nor the clothing of my forefathers." The king said: "I have placed it upon you out of reverence for you and acknowledgment of your merit." So he sat upon the throne, the kings submitted to him, the king entrusted his affairs to him, he established justice in Egypt, and both men and women loved him.

During the years of famine, he sold food to the people of Egypt: in the first year for dirhams and dinars, until none of them remained; in the second year for jewelry and gems; in the third year for riding animals and livestock; in the fourth year for slaves and maidservants; in the fifth year for estates and property; in the sixth year for children; and in the seventh year for their persons, until he had enslaved all of them. This was among the things permitted in their law. They said: "We have never seen a king more majestic and greater than him today." Then he said to the king: "How did you see the work of Allah the Exalted in what He has granted me? What do you think of these people?" The king said: "The decision is yours, and we are your followers." He said: "I call Allah the Exalted to witness, and I call you to witness, that I have freed them and returned their property to them."

Perhaps the wisdom in that was to demonstrate his power and generosity, and that they would afterwards submit to his command, so that their faith would be sincere and they would follow him in what he commanded them. Thus no one could say: "What is the benefit of acquiring that great wealth only to squander it?"

It is also reported that during that period he (peace be upon him) would not eat to the point of satiety. It was said to him: "Do you go hungry while the treasuries of the land are in your hand?" He said: "I fear that if I become full, I will forget the hungry." He (peace be upon him) commanded the king's cooks to make his meal at midday, and by this he intended to taste the flavor of hunger so that he would not forget the hungry. It was said: "For this reason, kings made their meal at midday."

Allah, glorified and exalted, has indicated the great kingdom He gave him in His words, may He be exalted:

And thus (i.e., like this wondrous establishment) ﴿We established Joseph﴾, meaning We made for him a place ﴿in the land﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt. It has been reported that it was forty farsakhs (a farsakh is a unit of distance, roughly three miles) by forty. Expressing the aforementioned making as "establishment in the land," attributed to His own pronoun (exalted is He), contains an honouring of him (peace be upon him) and an emphasis on the completeness of his authority, and an indication that this was achieved from the outset, not that it came about after asking, which is evident. The lam in (*li-Yūsuf*) — according to what Abu al-Baqa' claimed — may be additional, meaning "We established Yusuf," and it may be as it is, with the object omitted, meaning "We established for him the affairs." What clarifies the truth has already passed for you.

﴿He settles in it﴾, i.e., he descends from its regions and lands, ﴿wherever he wills﴾. The phrase "wherever he wills" is an adverbial complement of *yatabawwa'* (he settles). It has also been permitted that it be an object, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾. The phrase "from it" (*minhā*) is connected to what comes after it. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "wherever" (*ḥaythu*), and this has been objected to on the grounds that *ḥaythu* is not complete without its genitive complement, and placing the circumstantial clause before the genitive complement is not permitted. The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause of Yusuf, and the pronoun in *yashā'* (wills) refers to him. It has also been permitted that it refer to God, exalted is He, in which case there is a shift (iltifāt) in the discourse. This is supported by the fact that Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, and, according to a variant from them, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' read *nashā'* (We will) with the nūn, for then the pronoun unquestionably refers to God, exalted is He.

﴿We bestow Our mercy﴾, i.e., Our favour and Our bounty in this world, such as dominion, wealth, and other blessings, ﴿on whom We will﴾, in accordance with the wisdom that calls for the will. It has been said that by "mercy" is meant prophethood, but this is not the case. ﴿And We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾. (56) Rather, We pay them their rewards in this world for their goodness. By this is meant, as has been said, faith and steadfastness in piety, for His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 57:

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾ (57)

In this, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) has been placed in the position of the pronoun referring to ﴿the good-doers﴾, and the past and future verb forms have been combined to draw attention to this. The meaning is: "and their reward in the Hereafter is better." The construction of the genitive (al-idafah) here expresses association (al-mulabasah).

Placing a negated sentence after an affirmed sentence indicates that the basis of the aforementioned will (mashi'ah) is the good-doing of the one who is struck by the aforementioned mercy. Mentioning the third sentence, which is emphasized, comes after removing the suspicion that the fruits of good-doing are restricted to the immediate reward mentioned. From this it is understood that what is meant by ﴿whomever We will﴾ is whomever We will to strike with mercy from among Our servants who believed and remained steadfast in mindfulness. It has been objected that this is contrary to the apparent meaning; the apparent meaning is rather to take "man" (man) in a more general sense than what has been mentioned. In that case, it is not far-fetched that by mercy is meant the blessing that is not given in exchange for any deeds, and by reward is meant what is given in exchange for some of those deeds. The matter of placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun remains as it is, as if it were said: We bestow favour upon whomever We will of Our servants, however they may be, and We bless them with dominion, wealth and other things, not in exchange for anything. And We fully pay the rewards of the believers who remain steadfast in mindfulness among them, and We give them in this world what We give them in exchange for their faith and their steadfastness in mindfulness; and what We give them in exchange for that in the Hereafter, of the great and lasting bliss, is better for them than what We give them in this world, because of its greatness and its permanence.

It has been objected that this involves applying the term mercy to what befalls the disbeliever, such as dominion and wealth, although it is not mercy, as many verses indicate and as the statement "God Most High has no blessing upon a disbeliever" implies. It was answered that the statement concerning "the Merciful" (al-Rahman), that He is the One who shows mercy to both believer and disbeliever in this world, is clear in validating the application of the term mercy to what befalls the disbeliever of such things. Likewise the verse ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ is clear in validating the view that the disbeliever is in some respect shown mercy. The matter of indication is easy. As for the statement "God Most High has no blessing upon a disbeliever," it was said only by some, based on a reading whose outcome is praised in its definition. Even if you refuse, I do not think so; so why should it not be said that he expressed what was mentioned by the term mercy, out of regard for those among the believers who are included in the general sense of "man"?

Yes, it is objected to the interpretation of mercy here as the blessing that is not given in exchange for any deeds, and of reward as what is given in exchange for them, that there is the report narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, who said: "The believer is rewarded for his good deeds in this world and the Hereafter, while the wicked person is hastened good in this world, and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter," and he recited the verse. This clearly indicates that what befalls the disbeliever of what was mentioned earlier is in exchange for a deed of his, and that the verse contains what points to this, and it is none other than ﴿We bestow with Our mercy whom We will﴾. It may be answered that perhaps he understood ﴿the good-doers﴾ as including disbelievers who perform what is good, such as maintaining kinship ties, supporting the oppressed, feeding the poor and the like; so restricting the indication to what has been mentioned is not admitted. Yes, this report clearly disturbs the earlier interpretation, since according to it the verse has no reference to the disbeliever at all, so there is no sense in reciting it immediately after that statement.

Some have generalized the times in ﴿We bestow﴾ and ﴿We do not waste﴾, saying: "We bestow in this world and the Hereafter, and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers, but We pay their rewards both in the immediate and the deferred." This was supported by the argument that there is no reason for restriction, and that the report of Sufyan indicates generality. It was objected that whoever restricted this to this world did so in order that what follows would be a new foundation (ta'sis), and that the report does not indicate this, since it is derived from the whole of the verse; and in this there is what there is.

From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that ﴿the good-doers﴾ was interpreted as ﴿the patient﴾; perhaps he, may God be pleased with him, if the report is authentic, judged that this suited the context better. Whatever the case, the verse contains an indication that what God Most High has prepared for Yusuf, peace be upon him, of reward and recompense in the Hereafter is better than what He gave him in this world of dominion.

﴿The brothers of Joseph came﴾, seeking provisions because the affliction that had struck the land of Canaan and the lands of Syria had struck Egypt as well. The affliction had befallen the family of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and its people had been struck by it. So he summoned his sons, all except Benjamin, and said to them: "O my sons, I have heard that in Egypt there is a righteous king who sells food. So equip yourselves, set out for him, and you will buy from him what you need." So they set out until they arrived in Egypt and entered upon him (peace be upon him) while he was in the session of his governorship. He recognized them, owing to the strength of his understanding and because their previous condition had not greatly changed from their condition on the day of separation, since they were men and their appearance and attire were similar in both states. Also, his resolve was tied to them and to knowing their circumstances, especially in a time of famine. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) had been expecting their arrival, because of what he knew of the interpretation of his dream. It is narrated that they gave their lineage when asking permission to enter upon him, so he recognized them and ordered that they be lodged. For this reason al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "He did not recognize them until they made themselves known to him." This was criticized in al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir), on the ground that the placement of the particle "fa" (then, immediately) between their entry upon him and his recognition of them rejects the statement of al-Hasan, and indicates that their mere entry upon him was immediately followed by recognition without delay. Concerning this there is room for reflection.

﴿And they did not recognize him﴾. (58) That is, while they were in the state of not recognizing him, because they had forgotten him owing to the long lapse of time and the difference between his condition in himself, his station, and his attire, and because they believed he had perished. It was also said: they did not recognize him because he (peace be upon him) had made them stand in the position of people in need, at a distance from him, and spoke to them through an intermediary. It was also said: this was purely because He, glory be to Him, did not create recognition in their hearts, in fulfilment of what He had reported, that He would inform them of their affair while they did not perceive. Thus this was a miracle for him (peace be upon him). He set recognition (ma'rifah) against denial (inkar), in accordance with the common usage. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: "Ma'rifah and 'irfan are knowing a thing through reflection following its traces, so it is more specific than 'ilm (knowledge). Its origin is from 'araftu, meaning I attained its 'arf, that is, its scent." Denial (inkar), knowledge ('ilm) and ignorance (jahl) are the opposites of recognition (ma'rifah). Since their denial of him (peace be upon him) was a continuous matter in both the state of presence and the state of absence, it was expressed by a nominal sentence, unlike his (peace be upon him) recognition of them.

[Page 9]

﴿When he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: he equipped them with their supplies and loaded their camels with what they had come for. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) sold each of them only one camel-load, because it is reported that he would not sell any of those who came for provisions more than that, distributing it fairly among the people. What will come later, God willing, in their words, ﴿and we will gain an extra camel-load﴾, supports this. The root meaning of jihaz (provisions) is what the traveller needs of food and goods. The jihaz of a bride is what she is escorted to her husband with, and the jihaz of the dead is what is needed for his burial. It is also read with a kasra on the jim (ji-haz). He said, ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, and did not say "a brother of yours" (akhikum), in order to emphasise his not knowing them, as if he did not know who he was. Had he attached the possessive, it would have implied that he knew him, since the possessive suggests this. For this reason they say: in "send a boy of yours" (arsil ghulaman laka), "a boy" is unspecified; in "send your boy" (arsil ghulamaka), the boy is known between you and the addressee by an existing agreement. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) said this because it has been said that they asked him for an extra load beyond the usual for Binyamin, and he gave them that, on the condition that they bring him, showing them that he wanted to verify their truthfulness. It is also said: when they saw him and spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them, "Who are you? For I do not recognise you." They said, "We are a people from the land of Syria, herdsmen, afflicted by hardship, so we have come to seek provisions." He said, "Perhaps you have come as spies, to look for the weak points of my land." They said, "God forbid! We are brothers, sons of one father, who is an elderly, truthful prophet among the prophets, named Ya'qub." He said, "How many are you?" They said, "We were twelve, and one of us perished." He said, "How many are you here?" They said, "Ten." He said, "Where is the eleventh?" They said, "He is with his father, who is consoled by him for the one who perished." He said, "Who will bear witness for you that you are not spies, and that what you say is true?" They said, "We are in a land where no one knows us, so no one can bear witness for us." He said, "Leave one of you with me as a pledge, and bring me your brother from your father, who carries a message from your father, until I believe you." They cast lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un. It is also said that he (peace be upon him) himself chose him, because he was the best of them in judgement concerning him; but the well-known view is that the best of them was Yahudha. So they left him with him. From this the reason for this statement is known. It has been criticised, saying that it is not supported by the command to bring him being mentioned at the time of equipping them, nor by the urging to give full measure, nor by the kindness in lodging them, nor by restricting oneself to withholding the measure without mentioning the message. Moreover, if Shim'un were detained, that would be a calamity in which every saying would be forgotten. Some have said that the report is weakened by its including the slander against his brothers, making them spies, unless it is said that this was by revelation.

Ibn al-Munir said: this is not correct, because if he thought they were spies, how would he ask one of their brothers from them? And what the noble text contains contradicts it. He elaborated on this. It has been criticised as being of no substance, because when they told him that they were the sons of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), he asked for their brother, and with this the situation becomes clear. Ibn Jarir and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when they entered upon him (peace be upon him), he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's cup from which he drank, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and make it hum, tapping and humming. Then he said, "Indeed this cup tells me a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Yusuf, whom his father loved more than you? You took him away and threw him into the well, and you told your father that the wolf had eaten him, and you came with a false blood-stained shirt." He said: some of them began to look at one another and marvel that the cup informs of this. There is a contradiction here with the earlier report. There are other reports on this matter, and all of them are unsound, so let us confine ourselves to what God, exalted, has related of what they said to Yusuf (peace be upon him).

And he said: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it for you. The choice of the present-future form, although this statement comes after the equipping, indicates that this is a continuous custom. ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾. (59)

This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), meaning: "Do you not see that I give you full measure continuously, while I am in the utmost kindness in lodging you and hosting you?" And so it was. The words of some of them imply generality in both clauses, so that the addressees are included in that. The seeing is restricted to the giving of full measure because the address occurs in its course. As for the kindness in lodging, it was continuous both before and after this, and for this reason it is reported with a nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah). He (peace be upon him) did not say this as a favour, but to urge them to carry out what he had commanded them. The restriction in the measure to the mention of giving full measure is because his dealing with them in this is like his dealing with others in observing the duties of justice. As for hospitality, people have no right to it, so he gives them of it what he wills. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam.

﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (of grain) for you with me﴾: a warning to them for not bringing him. What is meant is that there will be no measure for you the next time, let alone its full delivery. ﴿And do not come near me﴾: that is, do not come near me by entering my land, let alone (receiving) kindness in lodging and hospitality. This is either a prohibition (nahy) or a negation (nafy), conjoined to the conditional clause (jaza') under both readings. It was said that according to the first reading it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), so that an imperative (insha') is not conjoined to a declarative (khabar). It was answered that conjoining is tolerated here, because the prohibition falls as a consequence (jaza'). In this there is evidence that they were intending to obtain grain again and again, and that this was known to him, peace be upon him. The apparent view is that what he did with them was by revelation; otherwise righteousness would require him to hasten to his father and summon him. But God, glorified is He, willed to complete the reward of Ya'qub (Jacob) in his trial, and He is the doer of what He wills, with regard to His vicegerent.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 61:**

﴿They said, "We will seek to entice him away from his father."﴾ That is, we will deceive him, win him over gently, and strive hard in this matter. This indicates the value of the request and the difficulty of obtaining it. ﴿And indeed, we will surely do it.﴾ (61) That is, we are certainly capable of doing this; we will not be unable to accomplish it, we will most certainly do it, and we will neither neglect nor be lax about it. According to the first interpretation, the clause is a *tadhyil* (a concluding, emphatic clause) that confirms the meaning of the first clause and establishes the fulfillment of the promised outcome by attributing the *musabbab* (the effect), namely the act, to the *sabab* (the cause), namely the capability. According to the second interpretation, it is a confirmation of fulfilling the promise, and there is nothing in it indicating that the promised outcome is achieved first.

[Page 10]

﴿And he said﴾: Yusuf, peace be upon him, said ﴿to his servants (fityan)﴾, meaning his servant-boys who measured out the grain, as Qatadah and others said. Or it means his attendants who were assigned to his service, as has been said. Fityan is the plural of fata (young man), or a collective noun (ism jam') for it according to one view, but that is not correct. Most of the seven readers recited ﴿li-fityatihi﴾ (to his servant-boys), which is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah, a plural form used for small numbers). The first reading was preferred because it better matches His words: ﴿Put their merchandise in their saddlebags﴾, since rihal (saddlebags) is a plural of abundance (jam' kathrah), and matching a plural with a plural requires that the individual items be distributed one-to-one, so the plural of abundance should correspond to the plural of abundance. On the second reading, one of the two plurals is used metaphorically for the other. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, appointed a man for every saddlebag to put in it their merchandise (bidaʿah) with which they had bought the food. The goods were sandals and leather. The original meaning of bidaʿah (merchandise) is a substantial portion of wealth kept for trade, and what is meant here is the price of what they had bought.

Rahl (saddlebag) is what is placed on the back of a mount of the rider's baggage and other things, as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). Al-Ragheb (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: it is what is placed on a camel for riding; then it is used figuratively sometimes for the camel itself and other times for what one sits on at a dwelling. Its plural of paucity is arhilah.

Apparently this command was after they had been equipped, but it has been said that it was before that, so there is a transposition in the order, and there is no need for that. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them and out of fear that his father would not have anything with which they could return a second time. All of this was to secure their return with their brother, as indicated by His words: ﴿so that they might recognise it﴾, meaning, that they might recognise the obligation to return it and the generosity in it. So la'alla (so that / perhaps) is to be taken in its literal sense, and there is an implied omitted element in the speech. It is also possible that the meaning is "in order that they might recognise it", and then no supposition is needed. This is clearly connected to His words: ﴿when they return﴾, meaning, return ﴿to their family﴾, since their recognition of it is conditioned upon returning and emptying the sacks, definitively. As for recognising the obligation of generosity in returning it, even though in itself it is not conditioned on that, nevertheless, since its beginning was then, it was conditioned by it: ﴿so that they might return﴾. (62) As much as I requested from them, since the favour of giving both payments, especially when the merchandise is scarce, is among the strongest motives to return.

It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, did it because he did not consider it generous to take a price from his father and brothers, and he is "the generous son of a generous man". This is a true statement in itself, but the stated reason rejects it. Similar to this in this regard is what Ibn Atiyyah claimed, that it was obligatory for him, peace be upon him, to give them gifts and to console them in that hardship, since he is a just king and they are people of faith and prophethood. More strange than this is what has been said: that he, peace be upon him, did that as a preliminary to placing the drinking cup (siqayah) in his brother's saddlebag afterwards, so that it would be clear that he had not stolen, for one who reflects on the story. Some have explained the placing of the mentioned item for their return by saying that their religion would compel them to return the merchandise, given the possibility that it had not happened intentionally, or intentionally as a test. So they would return, according to this, either intransitively or transitively, and the meaning would be "they would return it", i.e., they would give it back. But in this there is that the manner of placing it indicates that it was by way of favour, so the possibility of anything else is extremely remote. Do you not see how they were certain of this when they saw it, and made it evidence of the earlier favours, as you will be informed, God willing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 63:

﴿When they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us, and we shall receive measure."﴾ That is: it has been decreed that it be withheld from us after today, if we do not take our brother Binyamin, since the king said to us: ("If you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me"). The expression of this by "withheld" is a metaphor (majaz) for what was mentioned, and the reason for employing it is that no actual past withholding had occurred. In it there is evidence that the exchange of grain (imtiyar) had been a repeated, customary practice between them and him, peace be upon him. It has also been said: the verb is in its literal sense, and the meaning is that it was withheld from them to measure out another load for their absent brother, and their camel was returned unloaded, according to a report that he, peace be upon him, did not give him a wasq (load).

﴿So send with us our brother﴾, Binyamin, to Egypt. In it is an indication that the basis of the prohibition is his not being with them.

﴿Nakhtal﴾ (we shall receive measure): that is, of the food what we need. It is the answer to the demand. It has been said: the original would be "yarfa'u al-mani'" (he will remove the obstacle) and "naktal," so the answer would be "yarfa'u," but it was elided and "yaktal" was placed in its position, because when the withholding of measure was made conditional on the non-arrival of their brother, sending him was the removal of that obstacle, and that was put in its place because it is the intended goal. It has also been said: the last of the two clauses was brought in a sequential arrangement (tartib) indicating the first of them, for emphasis. The original form of this verb is *naktil* on the pattern *nafʿil*; the yā' was changed to alif because it was vowelled and the preceding letter was open, then it was deleted to avoid the meeting of two unvowelled letters. Among the strange things is that al-Sajawandi reported that al-Mazini asked Ibn al-Sikkit in the presence of al-Wathiq about the pattern of *nakhtal*, and he said: "tafʿal." Al-Mazini said: "Then its past tense would be *kutal*," and he rebuked him in the strongest terms.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yaktal* with the yā' of the third person, by ascribing it to the brother metaphorically, since he is the cause of the measuring out, or (the sense is): "our brother will measure out, so his measuring will be added to our measuring." Abu Hayyan strengthened, by this reading, the view that *muni'a* remains in its literal sense. The Imam likewise (said).

﴿And indeed we are its guardians﴾ (63): from anything harmful befalling him. This is a closing of the door to excuses, and they exaggerated in this, as is not hidden. In some reports: "and his condition is not hidden": when they entered upon their father, peace be upon him, they greeted him with a weak greeting. He said to them: "O my sons, why do you greet me with a weak greeting, and why do I not hear among you the voice of Shim'un?" They said: "O our father, we came to you from the presence of the greatest of people in kingship, the like of whom has not been seen in knowledge, judgment, humility, tranquility and dignity. And if there is a resemblance to you in him, he resembles you. But we are a household created for trial. He accused us and claimed that he would not believe us until you send Binyamin with us with a message from you, informing him of your sorrow, what it is that has saddened you, and of the swift onset of white hair upon you and the loss of your sight. Measure has been withheld from us regarding the future if we do not bring him our brother, so send him with us, that we may receive measure, and indeed we are his guardians until we bring him back to you."

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 12, verse 64:

He said, ﴿Shall I entrust him to you⁠—﴾ is a rhetorical question of denial (istifham inkari). ﴿Amanukum⁠﴾ is read with a long alif, a fatha on the meem and a damma on the noon. It is a present-tense verb from the pattern *‘alima*, and *amanahu* and *ta'manahu* have the same meaning. The sense is: "I will not entrust him to you except in the way I entrusted you before," that is, "except with a trust like my trust in you concerning his brother Yusuf (Joseph) ﴿before﴾. You also said about him what you said, and then you did to him what you did. So I do not trust you, nor your guarding." ﴿But I entrust my affair to Allah, the Exalted.﴾

﴿So Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ (64)

So I hope that He will show mercy to me by guarding him, and that He will not join two calamities upon me. As you can see, this is an inclination on his part, peace be upon him, toward permitting and sending him, because he saw the benefit in it. It also contains, as is not hidden, a great deal of reliance upon Allah, the Exalted. For this reason it is narrated that Allah, the Exalted, said: "By My might and My majesty, I will return both of them to you, since you relied upon Me."

﴿Guardian⁠﴾ (*hafizan*) is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*), like the expression *lillahi darruhu fari san* ("how excellent he is as a horseman"). More than one scholar permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) objected to this, saying it is not a good reading, because it restricts the superiority to this state. It was answered that it is a necessary, emphasizing circumstance (*hal lazimah mu'akkidah*), not a specifying one (*mubayyinah*), and that such usage is common. Moreover, this view depends on an implied meaning (*mafhum*), which is not considered authoritative. Even if it were considered, the reading would still be reduced to specification, though this is open to question.

Most of the seven canonical readers (*al-sab'ah*) read ﴿*hifzan*⁠﴾ with a kasra on the ha. Its accusative form, according to Abu al-Baqa', is specification only, and nothing else. Al-A'mash read ﴿*khayru hafizin*⁠﴾ in the construct form (*idafah*) with the singular *hafiz*. Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿*khayru al-hafizin*⁠﴾ in the construct form and the plural. Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that he read: ﴿So Allah is the best guardian, and He is the best of guardians⁠﴾. Abu Hayyan said: "It is appropriate that the clause ﴿and He is the best of⁠﴾ ... etc. be taken as an explanation of the clause before it, not as Qur'an itself. The reason for this has already passed."

[p. 12]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 65:**

﴿When they opened their belongings﴾. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: *mata'* (goods, belongings) is everything from which one benefits in some way. In the verse it means food, though it has also been said to mean the container. Both are *mata'*, and the two are interdependent, since the food was in the container. The meaning is that when they opened the containers of their food, ﴿they found their merchandise﴾ that they had given as payment for the food, ﴿returned to them﴾, that is, as a favour. They knew this from the situation, as was explained earlier. ʿAlqamah, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Aʿmash read (رِدَّتْ) *ridat* with a kasra on the *ra'*. This happened because the vowel of the assimilated *dal* was transferred to the *ra'* after they imagined that the *dal* was free of a damma. This is a dialect of Banu Dabba, just as the Arabs transferred the vowel in (قِيلَ) *qila* and (بِيعَ) *biʿa*. Qutrub reported this transfer in a sound letter that is not assimilated, as in (ضِرِبَ زَيْدٌ) *dhiriba Zaydun*.

﴿They said﴾ is a explanatory resumption (*istiʾnaf bayani*), as if it were asked: "What did they say then?" So it was said: "They said to their father." Perhaps he was present at the opening. ﴿O our father, what more could we want?﴾ If *al-baghy* is interpreted in the sense of seeking, as a group of scholars held, then (ما) *ma* may be interrogative, in an accusative position as a fronted object of (نَبْغِي) *nabghi*. The meaning would then be: "What do we seek beyond what we have described to you of the king's kindness to us and his generosity, which calls us to obey his command and to return to him for our needs?" They had told him this, as it is reported that they said to him (peace be upon him): "We came to the best of men. He lodged and honoured us with a honour such that, had a man from the family of Yaʿqub been in his place, he would not have honoured us as he did." His words, may He be exalted, ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ form a resumed sentence that clarifies what the denial implies about the extent of the kindness reaching its limit. It is as if they said: "How could it not be so, when this is our merchandise, which he returned to us as a favour we did not know of, after bestowing upon us great bounties that weigh heavily on the shoulders? Is there any increase beyond this that we should seek?" They meant by this that such (kindness) is sufficient to make obedience to his command obligatory and to make it right to turn to him for drawing more. They did not mean that it is sufficient absolutely, so that one should refrain from seeking its like. This is clear.

The clause ﴿returned﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to ﴿our merchandise﴾, with (قَدْ) *qad* implied according to those who hold that it is obligatory in such cases. The operative element is the sense of pointing (*al-ishara*). To make it the predicate of ﴿this﴾, with ﴿our merchandise﴾ as its explanation, is not valid. The choice of the passive form has been said to indicate the perfection of the kindness, which arises from the perfection of concealment, as is understood from the perfection of their unawareness of it, to the extent that they did not perceive it or its doer. It has also been said that it indicates the determination of the doer, and there is something in this too of praising him.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿and we will bring provision for our family﴾, that is, we will bring back provisions for them. (المِيرَةُ) *al-mira* is with a kasra on the *mim* and a sukun on the *ya'*. It is food that a person (يَمْتارُهُ) *yamtaruhu* procures, that is, brings from one land to another. Its essence is: we will bring them food from the king. It is conjoined with an implied element that the return of the merchandise applies to, that is, "so we will be supported by it, and we will bring provision for our family". ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾ from harm, as we have promised. Its being built on what preceded is by consideration of its indication of the king's kindness, for this helps in protection. ﴿And we will gain more﴾, that is, through it. For this reason he placed the report about it between the root and the increase. ﴿A camel's measure﴾, that is, one camel's load beyond the loads of our camels, according to the known apportionment from the king. In common usage (البَعِيرُ) *al-baʿir* is the counterpart of the she-camel, though it may be applied to her as well. In one dialect its *ba'* is pronounced with a kasra. Its plurals are (أبعِرَة) *abʿira*, (بِعِران) *biʿran* and (أباعِر) *abaʾir*. It is reported from Mujahid that he interpreted it here as a donkey, and it is mentioned that some Arabs call a donkey (بَعِيرٌ) *baʿir*, but this is anomalous.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿That is an easy measure﴾, that is, a measure (مَكِيلٌ) *makil* that is ﴿easy﴾, meaning small, not burdensome to our effort. (65) It may be a reference to what was measured for them at first. The sentence is a resumption brought to answer what might be said to them: "You have spoken truly in what you said, but what is the need to commit to this, when you have brought the food?" So it is as if they said: "What we have brought is not sufficient for us, so we must return once more and take the same amount with an addition, and this cannot happen without taking our brother with us." It may also refer to what our camels carry. The sentence is a resumption that serves as a reason for what preceded concerning the increase, as if it were said: "What need is there for the increase?" So it was said: "What our camels carry is small and does not suffice us." It has also been said that the meaning is: that additional measure is small and does not trouble the king, or is easy for him and not a burden to him. On this view the sentence is a resumption brought to repel what might be said: "Perhaps the king will not give you more than ten (camel-loads) of anything, or will consider that much or difficult for him." This is as you see. It is also permitted that this refers to the measure they are about to receive, and what their speech contains and what is joined to it, which is the measure of a camel obtained through their brother, who is entrusted with guarding him. It is as if, when they had said what they said and openly stated what is understood from it, they were exaggerating in order to bring their father round. So they said: "That for which we are preparing is an easy measure, with no hardship in it and no trial to follow." The measure may remain in its verbal-noun sense, though speech in this style rarely (follows that).

Some have permitted that this is from the words of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him), with the reference being to the measure of one camel. He said that one camel's load is not a thing for which one should risk a son. On this view it would have been apparent that it is mentioned together with his earlier or later words. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿what we seek﴾ is "what goal do we pursue among our affairs?" The clauses that follow are an elaboration and explanation of what the denial implies, namely that they were obtaining some of their aims or were able to achieve them. So it is as if they said: "This merchandise is present, so we are supported by it, we bring provision for our family, we guard our brother from what is disliked, and we gain through it beyond what we measure for ourselves, a camel's measure. So what thing do we seek beyond these aims?" What we have mentioned about conjunction with the implied element is the well-known view. In the *Kashshaf* it is said that you may hold that (نَمِيرُ) *numir* and what follows it is conjoined to the whole of ﴿what we seek﴾, and the meaning is the coming together of these two statements from them in existence. No further connective is needed, since both are reported as statements of theirs, and the purpose of all of them is to draw Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) away from his opinion, and that if the king is kind, guarding (their brother) is the easiest thing. The interrogative form does not prevent conjunction, since it returns to a negation. Some scholars agreed with him on this.

Ibn Masʿud and Abu Haywa read (ما تَبْغِي) *ma tabghi* with the *ta'* of address. ʿAʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) related this from the Prophet (ﷺ). The address is to Yaʿqub (peace be upon him), and the meaning is: "What thing is there beyond these aims, which include the safety of our brother and the abundance of our means?" Or: "beyond what the king has done of kindness that calls us to turn to him?" The resumed sentence also clarifies this. Or: "What thing do you seek as a witness to the truth of what we have described to you of his kindness?" The sentence mentioned is an expression of the witness implied by the force of the denial. It is possible that (ما) *ma* is negative, with the object of (نَبْغِي) *nabghi* omitted, so that the meaning is: "We seek nothing other than what we have seen of the king's kindness in making it obligatory to return to him", or: "We seek nothing other than these aims." The view that the meaning is "we seek from you no other merchandise with which to buy" is weak. The resumed sentence in every case is a reason for the negation. As for when *al-baghy* is interpreted as going beyond the limit, then (ما) *ma* is merely negative. The meaning is: "We do not transgress in speech, and we do not lie about what we have described to you of the king's kindness to us and his generosity, which requires what has been mentioned." The resumed sentence explains what they claimed of not transgressing. His words, ﴿and we will bring provision﴾ and so on, are conjoined to ﴿what we seek﴾, meaning: "We do not transgress in what we say, and we bring provision, and we do such and such." Thus the causes for permission to send him came together. The first is like a preparation and introduction to the rest, and the connection in this respect is that all share in the sense that the goal depends on them in some way. Moreover, if there were no connection except being spoken of together, that would suffice, as was stated a moment ago from the *Kashshaf*.

It has also been permitted that (ما) *ma* is a subject-initial word, that is, a parenthetical concluding sentence (*jumla tadhyiliyya iʿtiradiyya*), as in your saying: "So-and-so speaks the truth, and truth is clear." It is as if it were said: "And it is fitting that we bring provision." The emphasis that the concluding sentence requires is that the meaning is: the king is kind and we are in need, so why hesitate about sending him, when its two grounds are confirmed? Al-ʿAllama al-Tibi said: the emphasis and conclusion are valid only because the discussion concerns the procuring of provisions, and each of the sentences has the same meaning, or the meaning is: "We seek nothing (beyond) in our opinion, and we do not turn aside from what is right in what we advise you of, namely sending our brother with us." All the sentences are for explanation as well, except that there is an omitted element to which the discourse leads, namely: "Our merchandise is present, so we are supported by it, and we bring provision for our family, and we act thus and so." He said this is, as it has been said, a clear and good way that suits their situation with their father, so consider this.

ʿAʾishah and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami read (ونَمِيرُ) *wa-numir* with a damma on the *nun*. It has come as (مارَ عِيالَهُ) *mara ʿiyalahu* and (أمارَهُم) *amarahum* with the same meaning, as in the *Qamus*.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 12, Verse 66:**

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you"﴾ after I had seen from you what made the tears flow, ﴿until you give me a solemn covenant (mawthiq) from God﴾, that is, until you give me something by which I can secure a binding pledge from Him. So *al-mawthiq* is a *masdar mimi* (a noun of place or instrument formed with the prefix *mim*) in the sense of the object, i.e. *al-mawthaq* (the instrument of binding). He, peace be upon him, wanted them to swear to him by God, exalted is He. The reason the oath by Him, glorified is He, is called a covenant from Him is that it is by this that agreements are confirmed and strengthened. God, exalted is His standing, has permitted this, so it is a permission from Him, exalted is He. ﴿That you will surely bring him to me﴾ is the answer to an implied oath (*qasam mudmar*), since the meaning is: "until you swear by God and say, 'By God, we will surely bring him to you.'"

In *Majma' al-Bayan*, quoting Ibn 'Abbas, it is reported that he, peace be upon him, asked them to swear by Muhammad (ﷺ), the seal of the prophets and the master of the messengers. The apparent reading is that this report is not sound. Al-'Imadi mentions that he, peace be upon him, said to them: "Say: By God, Lord of Muhammad (ﷺ), we will surely bring him to you."

﴿Unless you are encompassed (yuhat bikum)﴾, that is, unless you are overpowered and are unable to do that, or unless you are all destroyed. Both of these are reported from Mujahid. The root is from the encompassing of an enemy, and its use for destruction is because the one encompassed by an enemy usually perishes. The exception has been said to be *mufarragh* (an exception with no stated object, where the exception operates on the general circumstances), from the most general of states, and the implied meaning is: "you will surely bring him to me in every state, except the state of being encompassed by you." This was refuted on the basis that a *masdar* formed from *an* and a verb does not stand in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier, a term describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), as a plain *masdar* does. Thus one may say *ji'tuka rakdan* (I came to you running), meaning *rakidan* (running), but not *ji'tuka an tarkuda* (I came to you that you run), even though it is equivalent in meaning, because in their view the *hal* is indefinite, whereas *an* with what follows it is definite, on the level of a pronoun. It was answered that what is meant by *hal* is not the technical *hal* but the *hal* in the linguistic sense, and this comes back to the accusative of the *masdar* (the verbal noun with *an*) functioning as an adverbial of time. There is a question about this.

In *al-Bahr* it is said that if it is assumed that *an* with the verb stands in the position of a *masdar* functioning as an adverb of time, meaning "you will surely bring him to me at every time, except a time of being encompassed by you," then according to Ibn al-Anbari it is not permitted, because he prohibits the *masdar* with *an* from functioning as an adverb, and requires the plain *masdar*. So one may say *kharajna sihayta al-dik* (we went out at the crowing of the rooster), but not *kharajna an yasih al-dik* (we went out that the rooster crows). Ibn Jinni, who permits this, allowed it, as in the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

*"By God, the mother of one son (Shahla) is not more grieved than I am that her little one should be humiliated."*

It has also been said that the exception is *mufarragh* from the most general of causes, on an interpretation of the statement in terms of negation, which is what it suggests, meaning: "you will surely bring him, and you will not refrain from bringing him, except by being encompassed by you." This is like their saying: "I have sworn you to do it, unless you do it," meaning: "I do not ask anything but your doing it." The apparent reading is that the interpretation should also be considered on the first view, since the exception there is *mufarragh*, as you know. It is only permissible in an affirmative statement when the generality is sound and evident, as in "I read except on Friday," because it is possible to read on every day other than Friday. Here, however, it is not sound, because it is not possible for the brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, to bring their brother at every time and in every state except the time of their being encompassed, since it is clear that they would not bring him to him while he was on the road or in Egypt. Unless it is said that this is of that kind, and that the generality and comprehensiveness in it are customary, meaning: in every state in which bringing him is conceivable.

Abu al-Su'ud, may God have mercy on him, objected to the permission of the first view without interpretation, saying: "You know that since bringing him is not one of the actions that extend over states in a concomitant manner, as in your saying, 'I will surely hold you to account, unless you repay me my debt,' and it was not his intention, peace be upon him, that it be concomitant, by way of substitution, with what is other than the excepted state, as when you say, 'Pray, unless you are in a state of ritual impurity (muhdith),'" but rather merely the actual realization and occurrence of it without any hindrance to it, as in your saying, "I will surely perform the pilgrimage this year, unless I am prevented (uhsar)." Your intention is only to inform that nothing other than the state of being prevented stops one from the pilgrimage, not to inform that it is concomitant with those states by way of substitution, as is your intention in the example of prayer. The consideration of the states together with it is from the perspective of their not preventing it, so the meaning reverts to the interpretation mentioned. End of quotation.

One of the scholars has examined this with three objections. The first: if what is meant by "you will surely bring him" is only information about the mere realization and occurrence of bringing him, without any hindrance to it, then there would be no need for the mentioned interpretation, namely the interpretation by negation, as is clear to the one who reflects, so his statement conveys the opposite of what he means. The second: we grant that the intention of the speaker in "I will surely perform the pilgrimage..." is not information about concomitance with the states other than the state of being prevented by way of substitution, but we do not grant that his intention is only information about the non-prevention of what is other than the state of being prevented; rather there is a mutual necessary connection between them, and that does not entail the need for the interpretation by negation. The third: if he meant by "the consideration of the states..." that the bringing of him was not accompanied by the consideration of the states, as is the apparent reading, then that is disputed. If he meant that the consideration of the states with it entails the aspect of their not preventing it, then that is granted, but it does not entail the need for the mentioned interpretation either, and the claim is nothing but that. End of quotation. This is as you see, so reflect.

Then they agreed to what he, peace be upon him, wanted. ﴿So when they gave him their covenant﴾, that is, their pledge from God, exalted is He, as he, peace be upon him, wanted. ﴿He said﴾, by way of presenting it, out of his trust in God, exalted is He, and as an urging on them to honour their oath by Him, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿God is witness over what we say﴾, during the request for the covenant and its being given from both sides. The use of the present-tense form (*istiqbal*) is to bring the scene to mind, which leads them to firmness and to guarding their memory of Him and their being mindful of Him. ﴿Guardian (wakil)﴾ (66). That is, an observer and a watcher, for the one entrusted with a matter watches over it and protects it. It has been said: the meaning is that He, glorified is He, will requite them for that.

﴿And he said﴾, advising them when he had resolved to send them all off: ﴿O my sons, do not enter﴾ Egypt ﴿by one gate﴾. He, peace be upon him, forbade them this out of caution against the evil eye (al-'ayn), because they were people of beauty and fine bearing, and they were well known among the people of Egypt for the favour and honour with the king that no one else had. So they were liable to be struck by the evil eye if they entered as one group. Since they had been unknown and unnoticed among the people, he had not instructed them to scatter on the first visit. It is also possible that his fear for them from the evil eye on this second occasion was because Benjamin, his beloved, whom he consoled himself with in place of his brother Joseph, peace be upon him, was among them, and he had not been among them on the first occasion. So he had neglected their matter and had not been concerned for them, because of their evil conduct regarding Joseph. The view that he, peace be upon him, forbade this so that they would not be suspected, given the earlier statement ﴿You are spies﴾, is not based on anything at all. Similar to this is what has been said: that it was in hope that they would overhear news of Joseph, peace be upon him. ﴿The evil eye is real﴾, as is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. It is also authentically related with the addition: "Had anything been able to outrun the decree, the evil eye would have outrun it. And when you are asked to wash, then wash." It is also reported: "The evil eye can bring a man into the grave and a camel into the cooking pot." The Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, used to seek protection for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the words: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and venomous creature, and from every envious, harmful eye." And he would say: "Your father used to seek refuge with them for Isma'il and Ishaq, peace be upon them."

Some scholars have a detailed and extended discussion on this point, which you may read without harm, and it is as follows: The influence of one thing on another is either psychic (nafsani) or physical (jismani), and each of these is either psychic or physical in its effect. Thus there are four types, under which fall the forms of revelation, miracles,

[p. 16]

marvels (karamat), inspirations, dreams, the kinds of magic, the evil eye, the nayranjat (natural magic and talismanic sciences), and the like. As for the first type, namely the psychic influence on a similar thing, it is like the influence of the exalted principles (al-mabadi' al-'aliyah) on human souls through the outpouring of knowledge and insights. Two categories fall under this:

The first concerns true knowledge, in that it is cast into a soul prepared for it, such as knowledge without the intermediary of teaching and learning, until one comprehends the realities of things as they are, to the extent of human capacity. Thus the knowledge of the first and the last was cast into our Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, although he, peace and blessings be upon him, had not recited a book before, nor written it with his right hand.

The second concerns strong imagination, in that there is cast into one who is prepared for it that which strengthens him to imagine past matters, to be informed of unseen future matters, and dreams and inspirations also fall under this type. Some kinds of magic may also fall under it, namely the influence of strong human souls, in which the two powers of imagination and estimation (wahm) are strong, upon other weak human souls in which these two powers are weak, such as the souls of the simple-minded, children and the common people, whose rational faculty is not strong, so that they imagine what does not exist outside as existing, and what exists as the opposite of its actual state. In this category of magic, use may be made of actions and movements which produce bewilderment in the senses and astonishment in the imagination, and among these is hasty and confused speech.

As for the second type, namely the psychic influence on the physical, it is like the influence of human souls on bodies, in their nourishment, growth, standing, sitting, and so on. Of this kind is one category of miracles, which concerns the motive power of the soul, such that its power reaches the point where it can act upon the world as it acts upon its own body, such as the destruction of a people by a violent wind, a thunderbolt, an earthquake or a flood. Often one seeks this by humble supplication and entreaty to the exalted principles, as when one asks for water for the people and they are watered, or prays against them and they perish, or prays for them and they are saved. This category also includes a kind of magic, as in some evil souls in which the estimative power grows strong for some reason, such as spiritual exercise and striving, so the owner directs it to affect whomever he wishes, with complete attention and sincere resolve, until the desired result is achieved, which is that the person is affected with illness and wasting of the body, and this may reach death.

As for the third type, namely the physical influence on the physical, it is like the influence of medicines and poisons on bodies. This includes the kinds of nayranjat and talismans, for they act through the influence of some natural compounds on others, by virtue of properties in them, like the attraction of the magnet to iron and the snatching of straw by amber. It may also be sought in this by fortifying suitable matters with the heavenly bodies which act upon the world of generation and corruption, as is observed in the forms of figures placed at specific times in known configurations, in opposition to certain directions and in alignment with certain stars, by which much harm from animals is warded off.

As for the fourth type, namely the physical influence on the psychic, it is like the influence of beautiful or ugly forms on human souls, in attracting them or repelling them. Counted among this is the influence of various kinds of songs, dancing and entertainments on some souls, and the influence of eloquent speech on one who has taste for it, as his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying indicates: "Indeed, some eloquence is magic."

Having established this, know that they differed concerning the causing of the evil eye. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i denied it vehemently and did not mention for this any argument, let alone proof. Others among the Ahl al-Sunnah, the Mu'tazilah and others affirmed it, but they differed about its mode. Al-Jahiz said: "Parts emanate from the eye and reach the admired person, and affect him as poison affects bodies." So the influence, in his view, is from the physical upon the physical.

The Qadi refuted this, saying: "If the matter were as he said, the eye would have to affect the person who is not admired just as it affects the one who is admired." The Imam responded to this, saying: "This is the refutation of a weak man, for when the one who casts the eye admires something, he either loves its continuance, as when he admires his child for example, or he dislikes it, as when he perceives that the admired thing is in the possession of his enemy and envier. If it is the first, then at that admiration there arises a strong fear of its loss, and this necessitates the confinement of the spirit within the heart, so the heart and the spirit become very hot, and there arises in the visual spirit a strong, heating quality. If it is the second, then at that admiration there arises a severe concern and great grief because the admired thing has come into the possession of his enemy, and this also necessitates the confinement of the spirit and the arising of the strong heating quality. In both cases the ray of the eye becomes heated and so it affects. This is not so when there is no admiration, and thus the difference is clear. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the one who casts the eye to perform ablution, and the one who was afflicted to bathe." End of quotation. As for what he indicated, that the one who casts the eye may afflict his child, for example, this is something experience has borne witness to. But the Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad, from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Haythami said: "Its men are the men of the Sahih," that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The evil eye is real; the devil and the envy of the son of Adam harm with it." Its apparent meaning requires something other than that.

As for what he mentioned about the command to perform ablution and bathing, it has come in some narrations. The manner of it is that the one who casts the eye washes his face, his two hands, his two elbows, his two knees, the extremities of his two feet, and the inside of his waist-wrapper, that is, the part of the wrap adjoining his body; it has also been said his hips, and it has been said his genitals. He pours the water used for washing over the head of the one who was afflicted. It has already been mentioned: "When you are asked to wash, then wash." This is addressed to those who cast the eye, meaning: when what is customarily required of washing is requested from you, then do it. The command is recommended (nadb) according to some, but al-Mawardi said, following the majority: it is obligatory. So it is obligatory for the one who casts the eye to wash, then give the water to the one who was affected, because this is what the apparent command requires, and because it has been tested and the cure by it is known, so in it there is deliverance from destruction, like feeding one in extreme need. It has been mentioned that this is a matter of worship (ta'abbudi), but this contradicts what the Imam indicated, that the wisdom in it is to cool that heat. This is taken from the words of Ibn al-Qayyim, when he said in explaining this: "Just as the antidote for the venom of a snake is taken from its flesh, so the remedy for this matter is taken from the trace of the person who casts the eye, and the trace of that eye is like a fire-blaze that has struck the body, so in bathing there is the extinguishing of that blaze." And this, with its defects, is more complete than the words of the Imam.

What he established in defence of al-Jahiz is refuted in that it does not close the door of objection to what he mentioned about the mode of the causing of the evil eye, for it is refuted by what is established: that some who cast the eye may afflict the one who is described to them and imagined, even if between them there are farsakhs (long distances). And the assumption that those parts extend to where the afflicted person is, is something hardly acceptable, as is not hidden from anyone with insight.

The philosophers (al-hukama') said, and some of the verifying scholars of the Ahl al-Sunnah chose this: this is from the psychic influence upon the physical. They based this on the principle that it is not a condition of the agent that its influence be according to these sensible qualities, namely heat, cold, moisture and dryness. Rather, the influence may be purely psychic, as is indicated by the fact that a plank of little width, when placed on the ground, can be walked upon by anyone, but if it is placed between two high walls, not everyone can walk upon it, and this is only because the fear of falling from it causes the fall. Also, when a person imagines that someone is harming him, anger arises in his heart and his temperament grows hot; the source of that is nothing but the psychic imagining. Indeed, the source of bodily movements in general is nothing but psychic imaginings. And when it is established that the soul's imagining causes a change in its own particular body, it is not far-fetched that some souls are such that their influences extend to the bodies of others. Also, the essences of souls differ, so it is not impossible that some souls are such that they affect the change in the body of another animal on condition that they see it, or see its image, as has been reported, and marvel at it. And when it is established that this is not impossible, and experiences bear witness to its occurrence, it must be affirmed without hesitation. Also, since the occurrence of this is most frequent when the eye is used and one looks with it at a thing, the influence is attributed to the eye; otherwise the actual agent is the soul, and attributing the influence to it is like attributing burning to fire and quenching to water and the like.

The true agent of effects is Allah, exalted is His authority, by consensus. But His custom has been that He creates them through causes, without any rational dependence of them upon these causes, as the ignorant philosophers suppose, as has been reported from the early generation (salaf); or [that He creates them] at the occasion of the causes without any real influence of the causes in any way, as has become widespread from al-Ash'ari.

The meaning of his words, peace be upon him, "The evil eye is true" (al-ʿayn ḥaqq), is that its harm reaching a person through it is something that occurs and is decreed in the divine order. There is no doubt about its occurrence, and it is like other observed effects, such as those of fire, water, and medicines, for example. You know that everything depends on the divine will: whatever God wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. The wisdom behind God's creating influence in the matter of the evil eye is unknown to us. Abu Hashim and Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi claimed that this belongs to the interest of moral obligation (taklif). They said: "It is not impossible that the evil eye is true in the sense that when its owner sees a thing and admires it with approval, it is in the interest of that person's obligation that God change that thing so that the heart of that responsible person no longer remains attached to it. Then it is also not unlikely that if he remembers his Lord at that moment, turns away from admiration, and asks his Lord, may He be glorified, to preserve that thing, the interest changes, and God preserves it and does not destroy it." This, as you see, is [weak]. Furthermore, what he pointed to regarding the benefit of remembering God the Exalted and seeking refuge in Him, may He be glorified, is true. Scholars have stated that supplications and incantations (ruqā, sing. ruqyah, a recitation or invocation for healing) are among the means for warding off the harm of the evil eye. Indeed, some of them can even be a cause for returning the evil eye's arrow to the one who casts it. Ibn ʿAsakir reported that Saʿid al-Sahi was told: "Guard your she-camel from so-and-so, the one who casts the evil eye." He said: "He has no way to reach it." So he cast his eye on it, and it fell, convulsing. The Sahi was informed, so he came to it and said: "The restraint of the restrainer and the flame of the one who kindles, you have returned the eye of the one who cast it upon himself, upon the dearest of people to him, upon his liver and his two kidneys. Rashiq and what is fitting for his wealth. Then return the gaze; do you see any flaw?" (the verse), and the two eyeballs of the one who cast it came out, and the she-camel was saved.

The legitimacy of ruqyah for the evil eye, which benefits from it, is indicated by what the reports indicate. In some of them it is related that he, peace be upon him, said: "There is no ruqyah except for the evil eye or the sting (ḥummah)." What is meant is that there is no ruqyah more excellent and beneficial than the ruqyah for the evil eye and the sting. Otherwise, he, peace be upon him, did perform ruqyah for some of his companions for other ailments. Whoever knows of himself that he has the evil eye should not look at anything with an admiring gaze, and should mention God the Exalted when he sees what is pleasing. Many experienced people have stated that if he does this, it does not have an effect. Al-Ajhuri reported that it is recommended for the one who casts the evil eye to invoke blessing upon the one he has affected, saying: "O God, bless him, and do not let him be harmed. Whatever God wills; there is no power except with God." In Tuhfat al-Muhtaj, it is stated that among the remedies for it, that is, for the evil eye, which is tested and which the Prophet, peace be upon him, commanded, is that the one who casts the evil eye performs ablution, up to the end of what we have mentioned just now, and that he supplicates for the one he has affected, and that the one affected says: "Whatever God wills; there is no power except with God. I have protected myself with the Living, the Self-Subsisting, who never dies, and I have warded off evil from myself with a thousand: there is no might and no power except with God." It is also recommended for the judge (qāḍī) to say this for someone who sees himself healthy and his conditions balanced. In the commentary on Muslim, it is reported from the scholars that it is incumbent upon the ruler to prevent the one known for this from mixing with people, and to provide for him from the public treasury (bayt al-māl) if he is poor, for his harm is greater than the harm of the leper whom ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, prevented from mixing with people. I have also seen that some of our companions held the view that it is recommended [to do so]. And there is no expiation (kaffārah) upon the one who casts the evil eye. It is said: because the evil eye is not usually considered a killing agent, and the effect occurs at it, not by it, at least according to outward appearance. This is unlike the sorcerer, for they have stated that he is killed if he confesses that his sorcery usually kills. It is reported from the Malikis that there is no difference between the sorcerer and the one who casts the evil eye, so both are killed if they kill. Furthermore, the evil eye, according to what is reported from al-Razi, does not affect one who has a noble soul, because of the exaltation of the thing that is involved. What Imam Ahmad reported in his Musnad supports the claim. It has been objected to with what al-Qadi reported: that a prophet found his people to be numerous, and a hundred thousand of them died in one night. He complained of that to God the Exalted, and He, may He be glorified and exalted, said to him: "You admired them, so they were harmed. Why did you not protect them when you admired them?" He said: "My Lord, how should I protect them?" He said: "Say: 'I have protected you with the Living, the Self-Subsisting,'" up to the end of what has preceded. It may be answered that what al-Razi mentioned is the more usual case. Indeed, if this report is sound, it must be interpreted as meaning that when that prophet, peace be upon him, neglected remembrance at the time of admiring them, he was rebuked concerning them so that he would ask and thus know. So it is like being struck by the evil eye, not that he was literally one who casts the evil eye. This is it, and God knows best.

Then, peace be upon him, did not suffice with prohibiting entry through one gate, but added to it his words: ﴿And enter from different gates﴾, as an explanation of what was meant by it. This is because not entering through one gate does not necessarily entail entering through different gates. In entering through two or three gates there is some kind of gathering, like that in entering through one gate, which would make the danger possible. He did not suffice with this command, even though it entails the earlier prohibition, only to show the utmost care for it, and to make clear that it is what is meant by the aforementioned command, and not to establish something else. ﴿And I cannot avail you﴾, that is, I cannot benefit you nor can I avert from you by my planning ﴿anything from God﴾, that is, anything of His decree upon you. For caution does not avail against destiny. He, peace be upon him, did not intend by this, as some have said, to nullify caution entirely, for how could that be when He, may He be glorified, said: ﴿Take your precaution﴾, and said, mighty is He and exalted: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾. Rather, he intended to show that what he enjoined upon them was not something that necessarily brings about what is feared. It is rather planning and clinging to ordinary means, which have no effect except by God's permission, and that this is not a resistance against destiny, but rather seeking help from God the Exalted and fleeing from Him to Him. ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, that is, there is no judgment at all except for God. None shares with Him, and nothing prevents Him. ﴿Upon Him﴾, may He be glorified, and none other, ﴿I have relied﴾ in everything I do and leave undone. In this there is evidence that arranging the means does not contradict trust in God (tawakkul). And in the report: "Tie it and trust [God]."

﴿And upon Him﴾, mighty is His authority and none other, ﴿let those who rely (tawakkul) rely﴾ (67). That is, those who wish to rely upon God. It has been said: He combined the conjunction wāw and the particle fāʾ in coordinating a clause with a clause, with the foregrounding of the prepositional phrase for exclusivity. The wāw is to convey the coordination of the act of others with the restriction of trust to God, may His affair be exalted, over his own act. The fāʾ is to convey the causality of his act, being a prophet, for the act of others among those who follow him. It is, as some have stated, superfluous, where he said: "There must be a statement that the fāʾ is superfluous and conveys causality, and it is necessary to hold that a superfluous element may indicate a meaning other than emphasis." It has been mentioned that if he had suffices with fāʾ alone and said: "So upon Him let those who rely rely," it would convey the causation of exclusivity, not the basic fact of trust, which is the intended meaning. All of this is not free from scrutiny. Some have chosen that the fāʾ was used only for emphasis, as is the common practice with superfluous particles. So reflect. Whatever the case, his sons, peace be upon him, enter into the general scope of the command with priority. In this style there is what is not hidden of the excellence of his guidance and direction of them to rely upon God, may His affair be exalted, in what they are about to do, not depending upon the planning he enjoined upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 68 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ from the separate gates of the city. It was said: he had four gates, and they entered through them. He suffices with mentioning it, since it implies refraining from what they had been forbidden.

[p. 20]

Its summary: when they entered dispersed, ﴿that entering would not avail them anything against Allah﴾, from His side, may He be glorified, ﴿anything﴾, i.e., nothing of what He had decreed for them, may His majesty be exalted. The clause was said to be the response (jawab) of ﴿lamma﴾ (when, as soon as). The combining of the past and the future forms is to establish the required correspondence between the response of ﴿lamma﴾ and what follows it, for the non-avail in actuality is realized only when the feared harm descends, not at the time of entering. What is actually realized at that time is what the aforementioned combination conveys: that entering would not avail them in what would come later. The intent is not to explain that entering was the cause of non-avail, as in His saying: ﴿Then when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ (35:42), for the coming of the warner there is a cause of the increase of their aversion. Rather, it is an explanation that it was not a cause of benefit, even though benefit was expected at first glance, since it happened in accordance with what he (peace be upon him) had enjoined upon them. This is similar to your saying: "He swore that he would give me my right at the arrival of the term, but when it arrived he gave me nothing." The intent is to explain that the arrival of the term was not a cause of giving, even though giving was hoped for by the requirement of the oath, not to explain that its arrival was a cause of non-giving. So the outcome is an explanation that the intended purpose did not follow from the known plan, even though its occurrence was hoped for, not an explanation that its non-occurrence followed from it. It is also permissible that this is intended, based on what he (peace be upon him) mentioned within his counsel, that his plan would not avail them anything against Allah, the Exalted. It is as if it were said: "When they did what he had enjoined upon them, that did not benefit them anything, and the matter happened as he (peace be upon him) had said, so they met what they met." Thus it is of the type of the occurrence of the expected.

End quote. To the view that the response is what has been mentioned went Abu Hayyan, and he said: in it is proof for whoever claims that ﴿lamma﴾ is a particle of necessity for necessity, not a temporal adverb meaning "when", for if it were so, it would not be permissible for it to be governed by what follows the negative particle ﴿ma﴾. Perhaps whoever holds that it is an adverb permits that, on the basis that the adverb is given latitude which is not given to other things. Abu al-Baqa' said: regarding the response of ﴿lamma﴾ there are two views. The first is that it is ﴿āwā﴾ (he drew his brother close), which is the response of the first and second ﴿lamma﴾, as in your saying: "When I came to you and spoke to you, you answered me." What made this good is that their entry upon Yusuf (peace be upon him) followed their entry through the gates. The second is that it is elided, meaning: they complied, or they fulfilled their father's need. Ibn Atiyya also went to the latter view. It is not hidden that on this view and on what preceded it, the difficulty of explaining the matter of the sequence is removed. What the author of the Qil (the view cited) indicated in the second of his two views is what the apparent words of many exegetes require, where they mention that this is from Him, may He be exalted, a confirmation of what Ya'qub (peace be upon him) indicated in his saying: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾ (12:67).

The view that the purpose of the plan is not achieved has been objected to: the aim was nothing but averting the evil eye from them, and that was realized by their entering dispersed. This objection also applies to the last view, as is not hidden. It was answered: the intent of averting the evil eye is that no harm should touch them at all, and the evil eye was singled out because it is evident. It was said: the evil eye also struck them, so the aim did not follow from the plan; rather, what he (peace be upon him) intended was defeated by his plan. This was criticized as far-fetched. It was deemed more plausible that the meaning is that he (peace be upon him) feared for them the evil of the eye, but another harm befell them that had not occurred to his mind, so the averting of what he feared did not benefit anything.
