In that case, it can be claimed that their entering through the gate their father had commanded them was beneficial to them in that it averted the eye from them. However, when there befell them what befell them, namely the attribution of theft to them and their disgrace in this, together with their brother, by the finding of the drinking cup in his baggage, and the doubling of the calamity upon their father, that no longer counted as a benefit. So it is as though their entering did not benefit them anything. The statement made regarding the combining of the past and future forms has also been objected to: the well-known view is that its purpose is to convey continuity, as the indication of this has passed more than once, and the apparent meaning does not indicate that. It was said: if the purpose here is that, the statement may carry two meanings: the negation of continuing benefit, or the continuation of its negation. In this there is

[p. 21]

room for reflection, so reflect deeply on this. As for what we have indicated about the extra ﴿min﴾ in the accusative, this is one of two views mentioned by al-Razi regarding the verse. The second is the permissibility of its being extra in the nominative, in which case there is no pronoun of entering in the statement, as is not hidden. It was said: if on this view the nominative is considered to be a pronoun of the matter, it would not be far-fetched, meaning: the matter would not avail them anything from Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Except a need﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but rather a need ﴿in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾, i.e., he made it manifest and enjoined it upon them, to dispel the passing thought, not believing that planning had any effect in changing the decree. By "the need" is meant his (peace be upon him) compassion and his protectiveness, lest they be harmed.

Al-Raghib mentioned that the need for a thing is the poverty towards it together with love for it, its plural being ḥājj, ḥājāt and ḥawā'ij, and the verb ḥāja yaḥūju, iḥtāja. Then he cited the verse. Some denied that ḥawā'ij (the plural) is used for it at all, but this is refuted by its occurrence in eloquent speech. In the explicit naming of him (peace be upon him) there is an indication of tenderness, compassion and mercy, for he (peace be upon him) was well known for sorrow and tenderness. It is also permissible that the pronoun in ﴿fulfilled it﴾ refers to the entering, in the sense that that entering fulfilled a need in the soul of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), namely his wish that their entering be through separate gates. The meaning then is: that entering did not avail them anything from the side of Allah, the Exalted, but it fulfilled a need present in the soul of Ya'qub, since it happened according to his wish. The exception is also disjunctive. The clause ﴿fulfilled it﴾ is an attribute of ﴿need﴾. It is also permissible that it be the predicate of ﴿illā﴾, since it has the meaning of ﴿lākin﴾ (but), and this is a particle which has a subject and predicate, so when it is interpreted with it, its predicate may be elided or stated explicitly, as al-Qutb and others transmitted from Ibn al-Hajib. In this there is the point that the function of ﴿illā﴾ in the sense of ﴿lākin﴾ is something no grammarian of Arabic has held. Al-Tibi permitted the exception to be connected (istithna' muttasil), on the basis of the line of poetry:

"There is no fault in them, save that their swords..."

Then the meaning is: what his sons' bequest did not avail them anything except his compassion which was in his soul. It is a necessity that a father's compassion, alongside the decree of Allah, the Exalted, is like dust scattered in the air. Thus it availed them nothing at all. ﴿And indeed he was possessed of knowledge﴾ great ﴿because of what We had taught him﴾, i.e., because of Our teaching him through revelation and the establishment of proofs, since he did not believe that caution averts destiny, until the flaw in his opinion would be shown when the effect did not follow, or since he firmly stated that it would not avail them anything from Allah, the Exalted, and so the situation was as he said. Thus the ﴿lām﴾ is causal, and ﴿mā﴾ is verbal-masdarial (infinitival), and the object pronoun refers to Ya'qub (peace be upon him). It was permitted that ﴿mā﴾ be a relative noun, with the pronoun referring to it, and the ﴿lām﴾ is the complement of ﴿ʿilm﴾ (knowledge). By knowledge is meant preservation, i.e., he is possessed of preservation and vigilance regarding what We taught him. It was said: the meaning is that he is possessed of knowledge of the benefits of what We taught him, and of the good use of it, and this is a reference to his (peace be upon him) acting according to what he knew. What was indicated first is the better view. The reading of al-A'mash ﴿mimmā ʿallamnāhu﴾ supports the causal sense. In the emphasis of the sentence by ﴿inna﴾ and the ﴿lām﴾, in the indefiniteness of ﴿ʿilm﴾, and in its causation by the teaching attributed to the pronoun of majesty, there is an indication, which is not hidden, of the greatness of Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) station, the elevation of his rank of knowledge, and its grandeur. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ (68).

[The remaining text, "the secret of destiny," is the subject of the continuation.]

Note: the passage given contains the sentence "... ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ سِرَّ القَدَرِ" which begins the next discussion; I have translated it below as it stands in the passage:

They do not know the secret of destiny (qadar), and they suppose that caution averts it. It was said: the meaning of ﴿they do not know﴾ is that the obligation of caution, although it does not avail anything against destiny. This was refuted on the grounds that the context of explaining the non-achievement of the sought aim from the initial principles rules it out. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿they do not know﴾ is that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) had this degree of knowledge, and by "most people" is meant then the polytheists, for they do not know how Allah guided His friends to the knowledge which benefits them in this world and the next. This is far removed from what we are concerned with.

[p. 22]

The one who made the object "the secret of destiny" is the view taken by more than one of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), and some of the later eminent scholars who cling to the skirts of the Sufis, may Allah sanctify their secrets, have striven to explain its meaning and to verify the nullity of caution. He said: "Indeed for us there is qada' (divine decree) and qadar (divine measure), and a secret of qadar, and a secret of its secret." Its explanation is that the existent possibilities, although they are created with respect to their external existence, are eternal with respect to their knowledge-existence, and they are called by this consideration "the dispositions of things," "the lofty letters," and "the fixed entities" (al-a'yan al-thabita). Then these fixed entities are relational forms and shadows of the essential modes of the Necessary Existence, may He be exalted. Just as the Necessary Existence, may He be exalted, and His essential modes, may He be glorified, are sanctified from accepting change, eternally and everlastingly, so too the fixed entities, which are their shadows and forms, cannot change from the judgments which they have in their own essence. Thus qada' is the universal judgment upon the essences of existent things, with circumstances that flow and judgments that occur to them from eternity to eternity. Qadar is the detailing of this universal judgment by specifying the bringing into being and manifestation of the entities at times and periods, which their readiness requires, and by linking each of their states to a determined time and a particular cause. The secret of qadar is that it is impossible for any entity to appear except in accordance with what its readiness requires. The secret of the secret of qadar is that those readinesses are eternal and not made by the making of a maker, since those entities are shadows of essential modes sanctified from making and being affected. There is no doubt that the universal judgment upon existent things follows His knowledge, may He be exalted, of their fixed entities, and His knowledge, may He be glorified, of those entities follows the very essence of those entities, since eternal knowledge has no effect upon the known, by affirming for it a matter that is not established, or by negating from it a matter that is established. Rather, His knowledge, may He be exalted, of any matter occurs only in the way in which that matter is in its own essence. As for the entities, you have known that they are shadows of eternal matters sanctified from the blemishes of change, so they were eternal, and Allah, the Exalted, knew them as they were, and decreed and judged as He knew, and measured and brought into being as He decreed and judged. Thus qadar follows qada', which follows knowledge, which follows the known, which follows what is a shadow of Him. To Him, may He be glorified, the whole affair returns. It is therefore impossible that there should appear the opposite of what He knew. For this reason caution is vain. Nevertheless, it was commanded, in observance of the causes, for suspending them would undermine the ordering of this world. For this reason it is reported that one of the prophets (peace be upon them) abandoned pursuing the means of obtaining food and said: "I will not strive to seek anything, since Allah, the Exalted, is the one who has undertaken my provision. I will neither eat nor drink unless He, may He be glorified, is the one who feeds me and gives me drink." He remained for days in this state, until his soul nearly rebelled against what he endured. So Allah, may He be glorified, revealed to him: "O so-and-so, if you remained so until the Day of Resurrection and did not pursue any cause, I would not provide for you. Do you want to nullify My causes?"

Some verifiers said: the reason for the obligation of caution is that many matters have been decreed as conditional, and their attainment has been tied to the voluntary acts of humans, through arranging their causes and removing their impediments. So it is possible that guarding against what is disliked is among what is tied to a voluntary act, namely caution. This does not contradict what we have said, as is not hidden.

The Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn al-'Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, mentioned that the divine decree (al-qadar) is a station between the Essence (al-dhat) and the manifestations (al-maẓahir). Whoever God teaches, knows it, and whoever God makes ignorant of it, remains ignorant of it. God, exalted is His station, is not known, and so the decree is also not known. He has concealed its knowledge so that the Truth (al-Haqq) is not shared with the servant in knowing the realities of things by way of encompassing them. For if the servant knew any known thing by way of encompassing it in all its aspects, as the Truth knows it, the Truth's knowledge would not be distinguished from the servant's knowledge of that thing. This equality does not apply to what is known of Him, for the discussion concerns what is known in this manner. The servant is ignorant of the mode of the attachment of knowledge in general to its object, so it is not valid that sharing with the Truth in knowledge of some object should occur. Among the objects of knowledge is knowledge itself, and there is no aspect of the objects of knowledge except that the decree has a judgment in it, which none knows but Him, glory be to Him.

[p. 23]

If the decree were known, then it would be known; and if its judgments were known, the servant would be self-sufficient in knowledge of everything and would not need Him, glory be to Him, in anything, and He would have absolute self-sufficiency. The secret of the decree is the very essence of His governance over the creatures, and this secret is not disclosed to them until the Truth makes them see it.

The prohibition against seeking knowledge of the decree has been reported. In some reports it is related that 'Uzayr, peace be upon him, used to ask a great deal about it, until the Truth, glory be to Him, said to him: "O 'Uzayr, if you ask about it, I will surely erase your name from the register of prophethood." Close to this kind of question is asking about the causes of things in their hidden depths, for the acts of the Truth should not be sought to be explained by causes. For there is no cause that necessitates the bringing into existence of a thing, except the very reality of the Essence, and the receptivity of the very reality of the contingent for the manifestation of existence. Eternity does not admit questions about causes, and asking about that proceeds only from one who is ignorant of God, exalted is He. So understand this, and may God, glory be to Him, take charge of your guidance.

﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself﴾, meaning he drew him close, that is, Benjamin. The exegetes say: When they entered upon him, peace be upon him, they said, "O King, this is our brother whom you ordered us to bring to you. We have brought him to you." He said to them, "You have done well and you have been right, and you will find that with me." They also conveyed to him his father's message, for when they bade him farewell, he, peace be upon him, had said to them, "Convey my greetings to the King of Egypt and say to him: Our father sends blessings upon you, prays for you, and thanks you for your kindness to us." Abu Mansur al-Muhrani said: He, peace be upon him, addressed him with this in a letter, and when Joseph, peace be upon him, read it, he wept. Then he honored them, lodged them, and treated them generously as guests. He had them sit two by two at a table, but Benjamin remained alone, so he wept and said, "If my brother Joseph were alive, he would have seated me with him." Joseph, peace be upon him, said, "Your brother has remained alone." They said to him, "He had a brother, but he perished." He said, "Then I will seat him with me." He took him and seated him with himself at a table, and began eating with him. When night came, he ordered them to do the same, saying, "Each two of you shall sleep on a bed." Benjamin remained alone, so he said, "This one will sleep with me on my bed." So he slept with Joseph, peace be upon him, on his bed. Joseph, peace be upon him, kept embracing him and smelling his scent until morning. He asked him about his children, and he said, "I have ten sons, whose names I derived from the name of a brother of mine who perished." Joseph said to him, "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said, "Who would find a brother like you, O King? But Jacob and Rachel did not bear you." Then Joseph, peace be upon him, wept, rose to him, embraced him, and at that point made himself known to him. ﴿He said, "Indeed I am your brother"﴾, namely Joseph, ﴿so do not be distressed﴾, that is, do not grieve, ﴿over what they used to do﴾. (69)

It means: concerning what passed between us. Indeed God, exalted is He, has been good to us and gathered us together in goodness. And do not inform them of what I have informed you of. The view that he, peace be upon him, made himself known to him and informed him that he was truly his brother is the apparent one, and it is related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Ishaq and others. However, Ibn Ishaq said that he, peace be upon him, said to him after making himself known: "Do not mind anything you see of hardship in my scheming to take you from them." Ibn Atiyyah said: On this interpretation, ﴿what they used to do﴾ may refer to what his attendants, peace be upon him, did concerning the drinking cup and similar matters. By my life, this is something that one with even little knowledge of the methods of speech would hardly say. Wahb said: He, peace be upon him, only informed him that he was standing in for his brother who had gone, in affection, and did not reveal the matter to him. The meaning of "do not be distressed" etc. is: do not grieve over what you encountered from them of envy and harm, for you are safe from them. It is related that he said to Joseph, peace be upon him: "I will not leave you." He said: "You know my father's distress; if I detain you, his grief will increase, and there is no way to that except that I attribute to you what is not becoming." He said: "I do not mind; do what you wish." He said: "I will put my cup into your baggage, then I will call out against you that you have stolen it, so that I may have a pretext to bring you back after I release you with them." He said: "Do it."

[Page 24]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 70:

﴿When he had equipped them with their provisions﴾ and given them full measure, and had added to each of them, as is reported, a camel's load, ﴿he placed the drinking-cup﴾ (al-siqayah). It is a vessel from which the king drinks, and with it food used to be measured out for the people. It is also said that with it animals were watered and grain was measured, and that it was of silver inlaid with jewels, as is reported from Ikrimah; or it was without such adornment, as is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. And from Ibn Zayd it is reported that it was of gold. It is also said that it was of silver plated with gold. It is also said that it was an elongated vessel resembling the Persian makkuk (a measure of capacity shaped like a double cone with its two ends meeting), which non-Arabs use. It is reported that al-Abbas had one like it, which he drank from in the Jahiliyyah. And because food was scarce in those years, he limited its measuring to that vessel. The apparent view is that the one who placed it was Yusuf himself, peace be upon him. And it appears, from his being a king, that he, peace be upon him, did not place it with his own hand, but commanded someone, who placed it ﴿in the baggage of his brother﴾ Benjamin, knowingly or unknowingly.

It is read (wa-ja'ala) with a waw, and in that there are two possibilities. The first is that the waw is superfluous, according to the school of the Kufans, and what follows it is the response of (lamma). The second is that it is conjunctive, coordinating with an omitted element, which is the response, meaning: when he had equipped them, he delayed them until they set off, and he placed (the cup). ﴿Then a caller called out﴾: a announcer proclaimed, as in Majma' al-Bayan; and in al-Kashshaf and others: a caller proclaimed.

It was objected to this that the grammarians said: one does not say "a standing man stood," because it conveys no benefit. It was answered that they meant that such a caller's role is to inform of what he proclaims, in the sense that he is described by an implied attribute that completes the benefit, i.e. a specific man was appointed to the call. ﴿O caravan! Indeed you are thieves﴾. (70) It may be said: the analogy of what is in the noble text to the example mentioned is not in its proper place, and the benefit is often completed by something that is not among the parts of the sentence. From this is the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: "The fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer, and does not drink wine while he is a believer."

The ir (caravan) is the camels bearing loads, so named because they go to and fro (ta'iru), and it is a collective noun with no singular. What is meant here is the people of the caravan, as in his, may God bless him and grant him peace, saying: "O horses of God, mount!" This is either by way of metonymy or by ellipsis, except that the meaning is considered in the verse and not in the hadith. It is also said: the ir is a caravan of donkeys, and then the term was extended to every caravan, as though it were the plural of ayr with a fatha on the ayn and sukun on the ya', meaning a donkey; its original form was uyur with a damma on the ayn and the ya', the damma was deemed heavy on the ya', so it was dropped, then the ayn was kasra because of the heaviness of the ya' after the damma, as was done in bid, the plural of abyad, and ghid, the plural of aghyad. The ir here is taken to mean a caravan of camels; this is what is related from most scholars, while from Mujahid it is reported that it was a caravan of donkeys. As for the address ﴿Indeed you are thieves﴾: if it was by the command of Yusuf, peace be upon him, then perhaps by theft was meant their taking him from his father by way of betrayal, like thieves, and Benjamin's inclusion in it is by way of subordination. Or what is meant is the theft of the drinking-cup, and the necessary consequence of a lie is no objection, since when it contains a benefit it is permitted. As for its being with the consent of his brother, that does not remove the commission of a lie; it only removes the harm to the brother from it. Or the meaning may be interrogative, i.e. "Are you indeed thieves?", and the distance in this is not hidden. Otherwise it comes from the caller, on the basis of his claim. It was said: the first is the more apparent and better suited to the context. In al-Bahr: what appears is that this stratagem, the accusing of the innocent of theft, and the bringing of grief upon Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was by revelation from God Most High, for what He, glory be to Him, knew of the good in it, and for what He willed of their trial thereby. This is confirmed by His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿Thus did We plan for Yusuf﴾. And al-Yamani read ﴿Indeed you are thieves﴾ without the lam.

They (the brothers) said, ﴿and turned toward them﴾, meaning toward the seekers of the drinking-cup (siqayah) that is implied by the speech, or toward the caller (mu'adhdhin), if he was intended as a plural, as though he (peace be upon him) had appointed callers to proclaim this over what was in the sea. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun (damir) in ﴿they said﴾. It was brought in to indicate their alarm at what they had heard, because it contrasted with their own condition. That is, they said while turning toward them: ﴿What is it that you are missing?﴾ (71).

That is, "what thing is it that you are missing?" or "what is it that you are missing?" Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said that loss (al-faqd) is the absence of a thing after its existence, so it is more specific than non-existence (al-'adam), since the latter is also said of what never existed at all. It has also been said that loss is the absence of a thing by its having strayed from you, not by your own action. The essential meaning is: "What has gone missing from you?" The form of the imperfect (mustaqbal) tense is used to bring the scene vividly before the mind (istihdar al-surah).

Al-Sulami recited ﴿you are missing﴾ (tufqidun) with a dammah on the letter ta', from afqadtuhu, meaning "I found it lost," in the same way as ahmadtuhu means "I found it praised" (mahmud). Abu Hatim considered this recitation (qira'ah) weak, and its wording is as mentioned. On both recitations, the deviation from what the apparent wording would require, namely their saying "what has been stolen from you?", is, as has been said, to demonstrate their complete innocence by showing that nothing had been stolen from them at all, let alone that they themselves were the thieves. What is possible is that something might be lost from them, so they ask them, "what (is it)?" In this there is guidance for them to observe good manners and to avoid rashness and attributing innocence to something in which there is no good, especially by way of emphasis. For this reason they changed their speech, when they said in their reply:

**Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, commentary on Surah 12, verse 72:**

﴿They said: "We miss the king's measuring cup"﴾. He did not say "you stole it" or "it was stolen." It has been said: the apparent course would have been for them to hasten to deny that they were thieves. But they said this seeking to complete the claim, since it is possible that within it there is something that would invalidate it, so it would not need dispute. They shifted from "what was stolen from you" to what is in the glorious composition, because of what was mentioned just before. The *suwa'* (measuring cup), on the pattern of *ghurab* (crow), is the measure, and it is the *siqayah* (drinking vessel). It was not referred to by that name, for the sake of emphasis in conveying the meaning and clarity. For this reason the verb and the future form were repeated, for what preceded, or for *mushakalah* (correspondence of wording).

Al-Hasan, Abu Hayawah and Ibn Jubayr read it, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah, as the majority read it, except that they pronounced the *sad* with a kasra. Abu Hurayrah and Mujahid read *sa'* (*ṣāʿ*) without a waw, on the pattern of *fa'l*, so the alif in it is a substitute for an open waw. Abu Raja' read *sawʿ* (*ṣawʿ*) on the pattern of *qaws* (bow).

Abdullah ibn 'Awn ibn Abi Arṭaban read *ṣuwʿ* (*ṣuwʿ*) with a damma on the *sad*. All of these are dialectal forms for *al-sa'* (the measure), which is among the words that may be masculine or feminine. Abu 'Ubaydah did not know the feminine usage. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr, as transmitted from them by the author of *al-Lawami'*, read *ṣuwāgh* (*ṣuwāgh*) with the *ghayn* pointed, on the pattern of *ghurab* as well. Yahya ibn Ya'mar read it the same way, except that he dropped the alif and made the waw sukun. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *ṣawgh* (*ṣawgh*) as a verbal noun from *sāgha, yaṣūgh*, used with the sense of the passive participle. The same is intended by *ṣuwāgh* and *ṣawgh* in the two readings, that is: "We miss the king's crafted vessel."

﴿And for whoever brings it﴾, that is, whoever brings it at all, even if he does so on his own initiative. It has been said: whoever points out its thief and exposes him. ﴿A camel's load﴾, that is, of food, as a reward for him. Regarding *al-himl* (the load), according to *Majma' al-Bayan*, it is with a kasra for what is detached and with a fatha for what is attached. It seems that he (al-Alusi) was pointing to what al-Raghib mentioned: that *al-hamal* with a fatha is used for burdens carried internally, like the child in the womb, water in the cloud, and fruit on the tree. ﴿And I am its guarantor﴾. (72) That is, I am a *kafil* (surety) who will deliver it to him, and this is the statement of the *mu'adhdhin* (announcer).

By this, as in *al-Hidayah* and its commentaries, it has been used as evidence for the permissibility of making *kafalah* (suretyship) conditional upon conditions, because its announcer tied the obligation to the suretyship because of the obligation of property, which is the bringing of the king's measuring cup, and his proclamation by the command of Yusuf, peace be upon him. And the law of those before us is law for us if it passes without denial. Two matters were raised against this. The first is what some of the Shafi'is said: this verse is to be understood as a *ju'alah* (reward contract) for what one brings, not as an explanation of *kafalah*. So it is like the statement of one whose slave ran away: "Whoever brings him, he has ten dirhams." This is not *kafalah*, because *kafalah* is only when one takes on an obligation on behalf of another, whereas here he has taken on the obligation on his own behalf. The second is that the apparent meaning of the verse is abandoned, because in it there is ignorance of the party to whom the guarantee is owed, and this invalidates the *kafalah*.

The first was answered: *al-za'm* (guarantee) is a true term for *kafalah*, and acting upon it wherever possible is obligatory. So its meaning is like the announcer's saying to others: "The king said: for whoever brings it, a camel's load, and I am its guarantor." Thus he is a guarantor on behalf of the king, not on his own behalf, and the true reality of *kafalah* is realized.

The second was answered: the verse mentions two matters, *kafalah* together with *hamalah* (carrying of the reward) for the party to whom the guarantee is owed, and its attribution to the cause of the obligation. The impermissibility of one of them by a proof does not entail the impermissibility of the other.

In *Kitab al-Ahkam* it is reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that *za'im* means *kafil*, so some people thought that this is a *kafalah* of a person. This is not so, because the speaker made a camel's load a wage for whoever brings the measuring cup, and confirmed it with his words "and I am its guarantor," meaning a *damin* (one who is liable). So he bound himself to guarantee the wage in return for returning the cup. This is a basis for the permissibility of someone's saying: "Whoever carries this goods to such and such a place, for him is a dirham," and that this is a permissible *ijarah* (hire contract) if he does not stipulate with a specific man. Likewise Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said in *al-Siyar al-Kabir*: "Perhaps the camel's load was a known measure, so it is not said that *ijarah* is not valid except with a known wage." This was mentioned by some of the researchers.

The Imam said: the verse indicates that *kafalah* was valid in their law, and the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) ruled by it in his saying: "The guarantor is liable." It is not a *kafalah* of something unknown, because a camel's load of food was known to them, so the *kafalah* of it was valid. However, this is a *kafalah* of property for returning the stolen goods, and it is a *kafalah* of what is not yet obligatory, because it is not lawful for the thief to take anything in exchange for returning the theft.

Perhaps such a *kafalah* was valid among them. It has been objected: there is no evidence that the one who returns it is the one who is known to have stolen it, so as to require adopting the view that this was valid in their religion. The full discussion is in its proper place.

[p. 27]

﴿They said, "By Allah!"﴾ Most of the grammarians (al-nahwiyyun, the scholars of Arabic grammar) hold that the *ta'* (ت) is a substitute for the *waw* (و), as it is substituted in *turath* and *tawrah* according to the Basran school (al-Basriyyun). It is also said that it is a substitute for the *ba'* (ب). Al-Suhayli said that it is an original letter in its own right. Al-Zajjaj said that it is not used for swearing except with Allah specifically. This was challenged by the claim that it is used with "the Lord" (al-Rabb) without qualification, or qualified by the Ka'bah, and with "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman). They also say *tahiyyatika* ("By your greetings") as well. Whichever view is correct, there is in swearing by it a sense of wonder, as if they were amazed that they were accused of what was mentioned, given what they had witnessed of their own conduct. It is narrated that they used to tie the mouths of their camels so that they would not eat any of the people's crops or food. Their affair was well known in Egypt for chastity, righteousness, and perseverance in the various forms of obedience. For this reason they said, ﴿You certainly know﴾ with a firm knowledge that corresponds to reality, ﴿that we did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾, that is, to steal, since theft is among the greatest kinds of corruption. Or [it means] that we did not come to cause any kind of corruption in it at all, let alone what you have attributed to us of theft. The negation of coming *for* corruption, even though it does not necessarily entail what the context requires, namely the negation of corruption absolutely, nevertheless they treated the coming that results in that, even by way of coincidence, as a coming for the purpose of corruption, taken as an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), as a claim, to make manifest the extent of its ugliness in their eyes and to heighten the impossibility of its issuing from them. So it is as though they said: if corruption were to issue from us, our coming would be for that, intending by it to disparage its condition and to display the complete purity of our innocence from it. Thus it has been said.

It is also said: they intended to negate the necessary implication of coming for corruption in general, which is the conception of corruption, emphasizing their distance from it. So it is as though they said: corruption has never crossed our minds, nor has it been connected to our imagination, let alone that it should occur from us. Its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿and we were not thieves﴾ (73). That is, we were never described as thieves at any time. It is apparent that this falls within the domain of knowledge, like the first, and its reasoning is that knowledge of their witnessed conditions entails knowledge of their unseen conditions. The oath, in reality, is upon the two matters that fall within the domain of knowledge, not upon the knowledge of the addressees regarding that, except that they mentioned it for the sake of testimony and emphasis of the speech. For this reason the Arabs treated knowledge in the manner of an oath, as in his saying:

"And indeed I know that my death will come; indeed, its arrows never miss their aim."

In this there is the imposition of the proof upon them, and the confirmation of the matter of wonder understood from the *ta'* of the oath in their speech, as it is in it.

Some of them mentioned that it is permissible that ﴿what we came for...﴾ (*ma ji'na*) be the object of the knowledge, and that it be the answer of the oath, or the answer of the knowledge, since it includes its meaning. And this does not contradict what preceded.

"They said" — that is, the people of Joseph, peace be upon him. "What then is its recompense" — that is, the drinking-bowl and the speech are with an omitted modifier, meaning: what is the recompense of its theft? The pronoun (in "its") refers either to the act of theft (saraqa) or to the thief (al-sariq). The "recompense" is attributed to the crime literally and to its perpetrator metaphorically. It may also be said that there is an omitted modifier here; so understand this. The intended meaning is: what is the recompense for that in your view and in your law? "If you are liars" — that is, in claiming innocence, as is the apparent meaning; and the use of "in" (in) in the conditional is out of consideration for their side.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 75:

﴿They said﴾, that is, the brothers, ﴿"The penalty for it is: whoever is found in his saddlebag﴾, that is, the taking of whoever is found to have the goblet in his saddlebag, ﴿"and its penalty is that he himself be held in bondage."﴾ The mudaf (the omitted noun, "taking" or "the penalty of") is understood, because the verbal noun (masdar) cannot be a predicate describing the essence (dhat), and because the very essence of whoever is found in the saddlebag is not, in reality, the penalty. They chose the expression "being found in the saddlebag" rather than "stealing," although stealing is what is meant, because the taking and enslavement being the custom among them and part of the law of their father (peace be upon him) applies only to the thief, not to whoever has another's property in his possession, whatever the case. This indicates the complete integrity of their character, as though their souls would not submit to them and their tongues would not help them to utter it, affirming it of any one of them in any way. And as an emphasis on this indication, they turned away from "whoever is found with him" to "whoever is found in his saddlebag." ﴿"So he himself is its penalty."﴾ That is, his taking is his penalty, and this is a restatement of the preceding ruling, as in your saying: "The guest's right is that he be honoured, so it is his right." It is not merely emphasis: the purpose of the first is to convey the ruling, and the purpose of the second is to convey its being a right and to safeguard its importance, as if it were said: "This is what has been made clear and verified for the one who considers the question; there is no doubt about it." It has been said: the particle "fa" (then) was used here to mark that it follows from what came before, by way of claim; otherwise the apparent thing would have been to omit it, given the emphatic position. From this it is known that an emphatic clause may be conjoined for a rhetorical purpose, even though the scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) have not mentioned it. It has also been allowed that ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun serving as subject, with this clause as its predicate, and the "fa" is for the subject being implicitly conditional; the subject-predicate clause is the predicate of ﴿its penalty﴾. And that ﴿man﴾ be a conditional subject, with ﴿was found in his saddlebag﴾ as the conditional verb, and ("its penalty, so he himself is its penalty") with the "fa" as the linking particle, the condition and its consequent being also a predicate, as in the possibility of the relative. This has been objected to: it entails that the clause occurring as predicate of the subject is devoid of a returning pronoun to it, since the pronoun mentioned refers to the one who, not to the subject. It was answered that the apparent noun, namely the second penalty, was put in place of the pronoun, and linking may be effected by the apparent noun as it is by the pronoun. The original is: "its penalty is whoever is found in his saddlebag, so he is he," that is, "so he is the penalty." In the shift, there is what has been understood from the earlier statement, the removal of ambiguity, and magnification, especially in such a position; it is almost like a necessity. Al-Zajjaj explicitly stated that the explicit noun is better here than the pronoun, and he justified this by some of what has been mentioned, and he recited:

"I do not see death preceding death; a thing has troubled death, the rich man and the poor man alike."

With this, the objection raised in al-Bahr against this construction is dispelled, namely that placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for linking is only eloquent when the context is one of exaltation, as Sibawayh said; so the noble wording should not be read that way. It is also possible that ﴿its penalty﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "the matter asked about, its penalty," so that it is a quotation of the questioner's words, and ﴿whoever is found﴾ ... and so on is an explanation and the beginning of the legal verdict. This, as has been said, is like one who asks about the penalty for hunting by a muhrim (one in ihram) and then says: "The penalty for hunting in the sacred state..." And then: ﴿"And whoever of you kills it intentionally, the penalty is the like of what he has killed of livestock"﴾. The mufti's saying "the penalty for game of the sacred precinct" is by estimate "the matter about which you asked is that," and what follows is an explanation of the ruling and an elaboration of the answer; the estimate is not "what I am mentioning is the penalty for game of the sacred precinct," because the position of question and answer stands in for that. Yes, when the scholar begins by raising a question, then this estimate is suitable there.

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that there is no great benefit in predicating the penalty of the matter asked about, since it is already known that the matter asked about is that, from their saying: ﴿"Then what is its penalty?"﴾ and the same applies to the example. It was answered that the benefit of this may be that the mufti informs the questioner that he has grasped his question, so that he accepts the verdict and does not hesitate about it, supposing inattention in it to the verification of the matter asked; and this is a noble benefit.

Some have claimed that the clause made of the predicate and the omitted subject has the sense of a denying interrogative, as if the questioner denies that the matter asked about is that, since its answer is evident, and then he returns and answers; and this, as you see, is weak.

﴿"Thus﴾, that is, like that exact penalty, ﴿"do We recompense the wrongdoers"﴾, by theft. The apparent reading is that this is part of the brothers' speech, so it is an emphasis of the ruling mentioned after an emphasis, and an explanation of the ugliness of theft; they did this in confidence of their complete innocence of it, and they were unaware of what was done to them. It has also been said that it is from the speech of Yusuf's companions (peace be upon him). And it has been said that it is his own speech, that is: like the penalty you have mentioned, We recompense the thieves.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 76 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So he began﴾. It has been said that this refers to the caller (al-mu'adhdhin), and this was preferred because his mention came closer before. It has also been said that it refers to Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is narrated that when his brothers said what they said, his companions told him: "We must search your baggage." So they brought them back after they had traveled a stage, or after they had left the settlement heading toward him, peace be upon him. ﴿Then he began with their bags﴾, that is, with searching the bags of the ten brothers. This was preferred because of the conversation of Yusuf, peace be upon him, which apparently requires that what is mentioned happened after they were returned to him. It is not hidden that the apparent meaning is that the attribution of the searching to him, peace be upon him, is metaphorical, and that the one who actually searched was his companions, by his command. ﴿Before﴾ the search of ﴿the bag of his brother﴾ Binyamin, in order to clear the accusation.

It is narrated that when the turn came to his bag, he said: "I do not think this one has taken anything." They said: "By God, do not leave him until you have searched his baggage, for that will be more soothing to your soul and ours." So he did, and then ﴿he brought it out﴾, that is, the drinking cup or the measuring vessel (al-suwa'), because, as you know, it is one of the words that are used both as feminine and masculine among the scholars of language. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the theft understood from the speech, meaning: then he brought out the theft from his brother's bag. He did not say "from it," referring back to the bag, or "from his bag," referring back to his brother, intending greater disclosure and clarification. The "wi'a" (bag) is the container in which a thing is kept. It seems that what is meant by it here includes the baggage and other things, because this is more suited to the situation of a search, and for this reason the word "rihal" (baggage) was not used, as has been said. Accordingly, he, peace be upon him, searched everything in which the cup could possibly be kept among what was with them,
[p. 29]
of baggage and other things.

As for their saying: "The pairing of a plural with a plural requires the distribution of individuals over individuals," as the meticulous scholar Abu al-Qasim al-Samarqandi said, it does not require that every pairing entail the one-to-one correspondence of each individual, because the distribution of individuals over individuals may be equal, as in "the people mounted their animals" (rakiba al-qawmu dawabbahum), and may also be unequal, as in "the people sold their animals" (ba'a al-qawmu dawabbahum), for it is understood from it that each of them sold what he owned of an animal. This point was already drawn attention to earlier. In that case, it is possible that what is meant by "the bag of his brother" is one bag or many.

Al-Hasan read "wu'a" with a damma on the waw, and it is reported similarly from Nafi'. Ibn Jubayr read "i'a," replacing the kasra-ed waw with a hamza, as they said "ishah" for "wishah" (a sash) and "isadah" for "wisadah" (a cushion). The change of a kasra-ed waw at the beginning of a word into a hamza is regular in the dialect of Hudhayl.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this wondrous scheme, namely guiding the brothers to the aforementioned legal opinion by putting it on their tongues and leading them to it through those who asked for the ruling, without their realizing it. ﴿We devised for Yusuf﴾, that is, we contrived and arranged, for the sake of achieving his purpose, through the preliminaries he had arranged, such as placing the cup and what follows it. Thus "kayd" (devising) is a linguistic metaphor in this sense. Otherwise its literal meaning, which is to make another believe something contrary to what you conceal and intend, as they said, is impossible for Him, exalted is He. It has been said that this is to be understood as a figurative representation (tamthil). It has also been said that in the word "kayd" there are two attributions: implicitly to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and explicitly to Him, glorified is He. The first is literal and the second is metaphorical, and the meaning is "We devised the scheme of Yusuf." But this is not right. In Durar al-Murtada it is said that "kidna" means "aradna" (We willed), and he recited:

"She plotted and I plotted, and that is the best of wills, Had it returned from the amusements of passion what has passed."

The preposition "li" (for) here indicates benefit, not like the "li" in His saying: ﴿so that they may plot against you a plot﴾, where it indicates harm, according to the common usage.

﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾, that is, in his authority, as is narrated from Ibn Abbas, or in his judgment and ruling, as is narrated from Qatadah. The sentence is a resumption and an explanation for that scheme, as if it were said: "Why did he do that?" And it is answered: "Because he could not have taken his brother, as the penalty for the presence of the cup with him, under the king's law concerning the thief, except by that scheme. For the penalty for the thief in their religion, as is narrated from al-Kalbi and others, is that the fine be multiplied against him, and in another narration that he be beaten, instead of being seized and enslaved, as is the law of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. So he could not, by what he did, take his brother on the charge of theft attributed to him in any way whatsoever."

﴿Unless God wills﴾, that is, except in the state of His will, which is an expression for that scheme, or except in the state of His will to seize him in that manner. It has been permitted that what is meant by that scheme is the aforementioned guidance and all its preliminaries leading to it, all together, from the guidance of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and his people, to what proceeded from them of actions and sayings, as explained in order. The matter of the causation is as it is, except that the meaning on this possibility is: "Like this scheme, reaching to this degree, We devised for Yusuf, peace be upon him, and We did not limit ourselves to some of it, because he could not have taken his brother under the king's law by it, except in the state of Our will to bring about what happens." So it functions as a formal condition in the place of an efficient cause, namely the guidance of his brothers to the aforementioned legal opinion. The restriction derived from placing the prepositional phrase first is taken relative to some. The same applies to the interpretation of those who explained "kidna li-Yusuf" as "We taught him" and "We revealed to him," meaning: like that teaching which entails what has been explained, "We taught him," without some of it alone. The exception is in every case from the most general of states. It has been permitted that it be from the most general of causes and reasons, meaning: he could not have taken his brother under the king's law for any cause or reason
[p. 30]
and for any means, except for the cause of His will, exalted is He. In either case it is a continuous exception, because taking a thief, when he is from those who hold that and believe it a religion, especially with his consent and legal opinion about it, is not contrary to the religion of the owner. Therefore the king and his companions did not dispute with him over the contradiction of their religion, rather they did not count it as a contradiction.

It has also been said that the clause ﴿He could not have﴾ and so on is in the position of explanation and interpretation of the scheme, and that the meaning of the exception "unless God wills" is that God wills to make that ruling the ruling of the king. This is open to discussion. It has been permitted that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: but his taking him, by God's will and His permission, was under a religion other than the king's religion.

﴿We raise by degrees﴾, that is, many lofty ranks of knowledge. Its accusative status, as transmitted from Abu al-Baqa', is adverbial of place, or by removal of the preposition, meaning "to degrees." Many have permitted the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). In any case the object is His saying: ﴿whom We will﴾, meaning: We will raise him as wisdom requires and as the benefit demands, just as We raised Yusuf, peace be upon him. The choice of the imperfect form is to indicate that this is a continuous custom, not restricted to this matter. The sentence is resumptive and has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge﴾, of those raised, ﴿is one who knows﴾. (76) — none of them can attain his level.

Our master, the learned scholar, Shaykh al-Islam, may his secret be sanctified, said in explaining the connection of the verse with what precedes: If "kayd" is taken as an expression for guiding the brothers to the legal opinion and inciting them to it, or as an expression for that together with its preliminaries leading to it, then the raising of Yusuf, peace be upon him, means what is taken into account, by conditional or partial sense, of his guidance, peace be upon him, to what is completed on his part of the preliminaries leading to the retention of his brother. The meaning is: We guided his brothers to the legal opinion, because he was not able to attain his purpose without it, or: We guided each of them, and Yusuf and his companions, to what proceeded from them, and We did not limit ourselves to what was completed on the part of Yusuf, because he was not able to attain his purpose by that alone.

In that case, His saying, ﴿We raise﴾ up to ﴿knows﴾, is an clarification of that, meaning that the aforementioned raising does not bring about the full attainment of his aim, since that is not such that nothing escapes his knowledge. Rather, We raise each one We raise according to his preparedness, and above each one of them is a Knower beyond measure, who raises each of them to what suits him of the ladders of knowledge. He raised Yusuf to that, and knew that what the circle of his knowledge contains does not suffice for his aim, so he guided his brothers to the aforementioned legal opinion, and what happened happened. It seems that he, peace be upon him, was not certain that this would proceed from them, though he was hopeful of it, for that is up to God, exalted is His majesty, in existence and non-existence. The mention of the attribute of knowledge serves to specify the aspect of superiority, and the intensive form together with indefiniteness and the shift to the third person indicate the greatness of His status above his status and the majesty of the measure of His all-encompassing knowledge, glorified is His majesty, as is not hidden.

If it is taken as an expression for the teaching that entails the legal opinion, then the raising is an expression for that teaching and the legal opinion, and although it was not within his power, peace be upon him, it was within his knowledge through revelation and teaching. The meaning is: like that teaching, reaching this degree, We taught him, and We did not limit Ourselves to teaching what lies beyond the legal opinion that would proceed from his brothers, since he was not able to attain his purpose regarding his brother except by that. In that case, His saying, ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, is an clarification of His saying, ﴿We devised﴾, and an explanation that this is of the kind of raising to the lofty degrees of knowledge, and a praise of Yusuf, peace be upon him, for being raised to them. ﴿And above﴾, and so on, is a consolation for him, meaning: We raise lofty degrees to whom We will raise, and above each of them is a Knower who is higher in degree. Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "Above every scholar is a scholar, until knowledge ends with God, exalted is He." The meaning is that the brothers of Yusuf were scholars, but Yusuf was more excellent than them. End.

What Zamakhshari chose, as has been said, is the discourse of the appendix (tadhyil), but he was brief in his speech to the point that its import became obscure, and he counted this among the weak points, where he said: "And above every possessor of knowledge is a Knower: above him is one higher in degree than him in knowledge, or above all the scholars is a Knower
[p. 31]
who is beyond them in knowledge, and He is God, mighty and exalted." The explanation of this, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is that his purpose was to clarify the way of the appendix with this sentence. So it indicates that it is either by way of emphasis for the elevation of Yusuf's degree over his brothers in knowledge, meaning he surpassed them in knowledge, because above every possessor of knowledge is a Knower of higher degree than him. In this there is also praise for him, that those he surpassed are scholars too. Or it is by way of establishing that God, exalted is He, raised him in degrees, and that is to Him, with no one contesting it with Him. So he said: "And above all the scholars is a Knower who is beyond them. He raises whom He wills, bringing him near to Himself through knowledge, as He raised Yusuf, peace be upon him." He mentioned that what is said, that the "all" in the second case is collective and in the first case means "each one," is an unclear statement, because what enters upon an indefinite noun is not collective. The root of the point regarding the distributive is that if one looks at knowledge and its endlessness, the first case would apply, and it would ascend without end, since his knowledge is infinite, rather exalted above limit in every respect. And there must be a restriction in the word "all," and the meaning is: above each one of the scholars is a scholar, and so on, until it ends. If one looks at the knower and his conferring of knowledge upon the other, the second case would apply, and the meaning is: above each one is one Knower, and it is then more fitting that He be above all of them, since the second is caused by the first, and because the meaning is evident from it, consider it as "above all the scholars." Both aspects suit the context. End.

It may be that the consideration that the first sentence praises Joseph (peace be upon him) and magnifies the status of scheming, and that the second sentence is a humbling, is the most apparent, so reflect. Some who held that He, exalted is His majesty, is Knowing by His essence and not by an additional attribute of knowledge have argued from this verse. The gist of their argument is that if He, glorified is He, had an attribute of knowledge additional to His essence, He would be one possessing knowledge by virtue of being characterized by it, and every possessor of knowledge has above him one who is knowing (ʿalīm), by the verse, so it would follow that above Him, and more knowing than Him, exalted and high is He, there would be another knower, and that is utterly false. It has been answered that what is meant by "every possessor of knowledge" is the created beings who possess knowledge, because the discourse concerns creation; and because ʿalīm is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah), its meaning being "more knowing than every possessor of knowledge," so it is necessarily God, exalted is He, who is meant by it, and whatever is opposite to Him must be among the creatures, lest it be included in what is opposite to Him. That the intended sense of ʿalīm is this is one of two reports from the Rabbi (al-Ḥabr, i.e. Ibn ʿAbbās). ʿAbd al-Razzāq and a group related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: We were with Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and he narrated a hadith, whereupon a man present said: "And above every possessor of knowledge is one who is knowing." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Evil is what you have said! Allah is the Knowing (al-ʿAlīm), and He is above every knower." To this view also went al-Ḍaḥḥāk, for Abū al-Shaykh related from him that after reciting the verse he said: "He means by that Himself, exalted is He."

Furthermore, if what the one adducing this proof stated were correct, Allah, exalted is He, would not be knowing; this is based on the apparent agreement of the opponent with us in the soundness of our statement "above all scholars is one who is knowing." For it follows, upon accepting his proof, that if Allah, exalted is He, is knowing, there would be above Him one who is more knowing than Him. If he answers by specifying the example, then the verse is like it.

Some seven readers, not one alone, read "darajāti man nashāʾu" (دَرَجاتِ مَن نَشاءُ) with the genitive construction. It has been said: the first reading is more suited to the concluding phrase, since in it the elevation is attributed to the one to whom superiority (al-fawqiyyah) is attributed, not to his degree; but the matter in that is easy. Yaʿqūb read with yā' in "yarfaʿu" (يَرْفَعُ) and "yashāʾu" (يَشاءُ). ʿĪsā al-Baṣrah read "narfaʿu" (نَرْفَعُ) with nūn, "darajātin" (دَرَجاتٍ) nunated, and "man yashāʾu" (مَن يَشاءُ) with yā'. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: this is a reading that is disliked, yet its denial is not possible. ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥabr read "wa-fawqa kulli dhī ʿālimin ʿalīm" (وفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عالِمٍ عَلِيمٌ), and it is construed, as in al-Baḥr, either as an addition of dhī, or on the basis that "ʿālimin" is a verbal noun with the meaning of "ʿilm," like "al-bāṭil," or on the basis that the implied sense is "every person who is knowing." What is in al-Durr al-Manthūr is that he, may Allah be pleased with him, read "wa-fawqa kulli ʿālimin ʿalīm" (وفَوْقَ كُلِّ عالِمٍ عَلِيمٌ) without "dhī," and perhaps this is the more firmly transmitted. And Allah, exalted is He, is the All-Knowing.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 77]

﴿They said﴾, that is, the brothers, ﴿"If he steals"﴾, meaning Benjamin, ﴿"then a brother of his has stolen before"﴾, meaning by this Yusuf, peace be upon him, and what befell him from the side of his paternal aunt. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related on the authority of Mujahid (chain of narration), who said: "The first hardship that came upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, as far as I have been informed, was that his aunt was raising him. She was the eldest child of Ishaq, peace be upon him, and she had the belt of her father, and they used to inherit it by seniority. So she loved no one as she loved him. When he grew up, Ya'qub's heart was drawn to him, so he came to her and said: 'O sister, hand Yusuf over to me, for by God I cannot bear to be without him for an hour.' She said: 'By God, I will not leave him. Leave him with me for some days, so that I may look at him; perhaps that will comfort me.' When Ya'qub, peace be upon him, left her, she set about that belt and tied it on Yusuf, peace be upon him, under his garments. Then she said: 'The belt of my father Ishaq is missing. Look for whoever took it.' They searched, and then she said: 'Search the people of the house.' They searched them, and they found it with Yusuf, peace be upon him. She said: 'By God, he is a slave to me; I may do with him whatever I wish.' Ya'qub came to her, and she told him the matter. He said to her: 'It is up to you, if he did it.' So she kept him, and he could not get him back until she died."

Ibn Mardawayh related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, on the authority of the Prophet ﷺ, that he said concerning the verse: "Yusuf, peace be upon him, stole an idol of his grandfather, his mother's father, made of gold and silver; he broke it and threw it on the road, so his brothers reproached him for that." Other than one narrator related on the authority of Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "Yusuf, peace be upon him, was a small boy with his mother at the house of a maternal uncle of his, and he was playing with al-Nu'man. He entered a church of theirs and found a small golden statue, so he took it. That is the theft they meant." Mujahid said: "A beggar came to him one day, and he took an egg and gave it to him." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "He took a hen and gave it to the beggar." Wahb said: "He, peace be upon him, used to hide food from the table for the poor." It was also said, and said, and it is related from Ibn al-Munir that this is an affectation (taṣallufun) that does not allow such a thing to be attributed to the household of prophethood, nor indeed to any of the noble people; therefore it must be abandoned, and Makki went to this view. Some of them said: the meaning is, "If he steals, then a like one of the children of Adam has stolen before," and he mentioned for it parallels in hadith. It was said: "This is a statement worthy of acceptance."

You know that counting everything said about the meaning of the brother's theft as affectation is itself an affectation, for in it there is what is not objectionable to attribute to the household of prophethood. Even if one claims that their attribution of theft to Yusuf, peace be upon him, is something whose like is not fitting to attribute to them, because that is a lie, since there is no theft in reality, and they are the people of the household of prophethood who do not lie, the narration of his being eaten by the wolf has come, and they are not infallible, neither at the beginning nor at the end. As for what the one said, and it was said: "It is a statement worthy of acceptance," it is refused by what follows, as is not hidden from one who has taste. Moreover, that in itself is far-fetched in taste.

They used the word ﴿"if"﴾ (in) because they were not certain of his theft merely from the emergence of the drinking-cup from his baggage, for they had found their merchandise in their own baggage and they had not been thieves. In some of the reports, when they saw the drinking-cup brought out from his baggage, they were ashamed and said: "O son of Rahil, how did you steal this cup?" He raised his hand to the sky and said: "By God, I did not do it." They said: "Then who placed it in your baggage?" He said: "The one who placed the merchandise in your baggage." So if their saying ﴿"if he steals"﴾ and so on was after this resistance, then the apparent meaning is that it was this that prompted them (because). As for their saying ﴿"Indeed your son has stolen"﴾, it is based on the apparent evidence and the claim of the people, and their knowledge is likewise based on that. It was also said: they were certain of that, and the ﴿"if"﴾ is merely for the conditional. This is perhaps preferable, given the apparent sense of what will come, if God the Exalted wills to verify it. And ﴿"he steals"﴾ is for narrating a past situation. The meaning is: "If he has stolen, it is no novelty, since a like one has preceded from his brother." It seems they intended by this to ward off disgrace from themselves and to confine it to the two full brothers. The indefinite ﴿"a brother"﴾ is because those present had no knowledge of him.

Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, Ibn Abi Surayj on the authority of al-Kisa'i, al-Walid ibn Hassan and others read ﴿"then has been stolen (fa-qad suriqa)"﴾ with the doubled letter and in the passive voice, meaning he was attributed to theft.

﴿So Yusuf concealed it﴾: the pronoun refers to what is understood from the speech and the context, that is, he hid the resentment that came over him, peace be upon him, because of what they said. It was also said: he hid their statement or the attribution of theft to him, so he did not answer them concerning it. ﴿"In himself"﴾, not that he disclosed it to some of his companions, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And I spoke to them a secret speech"﴾.

[Page 33]

﴿And he did not reveal it﴾, that is, he did not make it manifest to them, neither by word nor by deed, forgiving them and showing forbearance. This is an emphasis of what preceded. ﴿He said﴾, that is, in himself, and this is a resumption (istinaf) based on a question arising from the report of the concealing mentioned, as if it were said: "What did he say to himself in the midst of that?" So it was said: ﴿"He said: You are worse in place"﴾, that is, in standing in theft. Its sum is that you are more firmly established in the attribute of this description and more powerful in it, since you stole your brother from your father, then you began to slander the innocent. Al-Zajjaj said: the concealment here is according to the condition of tafsir (exegesis of a pronoun), because ﴿"He said: You..."﴾ and so on is a substitute for the pronoun, and the meaning is: Yusuf concealed in himself his saying: ﴿"You are worse in place"﴾. The feminine form is in regard to its being a sentence or a word. Abu 'Ali criticised this, saying that concealment according to the condition of tafsir is of two kinds: one is that it is explained by a single word, as in "How excellent a man" and "his lord, a man"; the second is that it is explained by a sentence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Say: He is God, One"﴾. The origin of this is that it occurs at the beginning, then the abrogating particles enter upon it, as in ﴿"Indeed whoever comes to his Lord as a sinner"﴾.

﴿"For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded"﴾. What is not included in them is the healing of the soul, which is bestowed, and other things. The explanation of the pronoun in both places is connected with the sentence preceding it, which contains that pronoun, and is related to it, and is not cut off from it. What al-Zajjaj mentioned is cut off, so it is not from the concealment according to the condition of tafsir. In the Anwar al-Tanzil (of al-Baydawi) it is said that what is explained by a sentence is only the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). This was objected to by denial. In the Kashf (of al-Tibi) it is said: this is not at all from explanation by sentences, so as to be objected to on the ground that it is among the special features of the pronoun of the matter, which must be placed at the beginning. Rather, it is like ﴿"And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and Ya'qub: O my sons"﴾ and so on.

It was objected that in that verse there is the explanation of a sentence by a sentence, whereas here there is the explanation of a pronoun by a sentence. In the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) he made ﴿"You are worse in place"﴾ the explained element, and in this there is obscurity, because that is the content of the saying. Some used this verse to establish the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi) by making ﴿"He said"﴾ and so on a substitute for "concealed". Perhaps the matter does not depend on that, for what we have indicated is that the meaning is "he said in himself". Yes, Abu Hayyan said: the apparent meaning is that he, peace be upon him, addressed them and confronted them with it after he had concealed, out of dislike of their saying, in himself, and his purpose was rebuke and denunciation of them. This is strengthened by their having refrained from interceding for themselves and turning instead to intercede for him through his father. But this is open to examination. ʿAbd Allah and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿"So he concealed it"﴾ with the pronoun in the masculine.

﴿And God knows best what you describe﴾. (77). That is, He knows to the utmost degree of knowledge that the matter is not as you describe, namely the issuing of theft from us. So the form ʾafʿal is merely for intensification, not for preferring His knowledge over theirs; how could it be otherwise, when they have no knowledge of that at all? This was said by more than one. Abu Hayyan said: the meaning is "He knows best what you describe yourselves with, of yourselves, since He, glory be to Him, knows the realities of matters and how the theft of his brother occurred, whose theft you have attributed to him." Then ʾafʿal is on its apparent meaning. It was objected that there was no knowledge among them, and preference requires sharing. It was answered that sharing according to their own supposition suffices, for they claimed knowledge for themselves. Do you not see their saying: ﴿"Then a brother of his has stolen before"﴾, stated categorically?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 78:

﴿They said﴾ when they saw the signs of his (Yusuf's) intention to take Benjamin, pleading: ﴿O Chief (al-'Aziz), indeed he has a father, an elderly old man﴾, one advanced in years, who could hardly bear to be parted from him, and he is but a remnant of life, by him he consoles himself for his lost full brother. It was also said: they meant "a great elder in standing," and the description, according to both views, is the locus of the benefit; otherwise, the information that he has a father is already known from what preceded. ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, instead of him, for we are not in his (father's) position in love and tenderness. ﴿Indeed we see you to be among the good-doers﴾. (78)

Meaning: "Bestow upon us, then complete your kindness, for bestowing a favour is only by completing it." Or: "It is your custom to be generous in general, so continue in your custom and do not change it with us, for we are the most deserving of people of that." Thus, on the first reading, "good-doing" is specific, and on the second, it is general. The sentence, on both readings, is a concluding parenthetical remark (i'tiradh tadhyili) upon what some of the meticulous scholars have held. Another group held that if "good-doing" is meant toward them, the sentence is resumptive (mustanafa), explaining what came before, since taking the substitute is itself a kindness toward them; and if what is meant is that the generality of this is part of your practice and custom, the sentence is emphatic of what came before, and the mention of a general matter as a concluding remark is more fitting for that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 79:

﴿He said: "God forbid!"﴾ That is: we seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, a seeking of refuge (mu'adhan) from taking [him]. The verb was omitted and the verbal noun (maṣdar) was put in its place, annexed to the direct object, and the preposition was omitted, as in similar cases. ﴿Except him in whose possession we found our property﴾ because our taking him is only in accordance with your ruling, so it is not for us to violate what it requires. ﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾. That is: if we took other than the one in whose possession we found our property, even with his consent. (79). In your school of law and your sharia. And it is not for us to do that. The use of the first-person plural form, while the address comes from his brothers in the singular, is from the manner of addressing kings with their customs (sunan al-muluk). It also signals that taking and giving is not something one decides alone, but depends on the opinions of the people who loosen and bind (ahl al-ḥall wa al-'aqd, the notables who have authority to decide).

The choice of ﴿the one in whose possession we found our property﴾ over "the one who stole our property" is the more concise, because it fits better with what occurred in the consultation and the ruling (fatwa). Or it is for establishing the truth and avoiding a lie in speech while achieving the purpose, for they do not take the finding of the cup in his possession as anything other than theft. The word mata' (property) is a term for what is benefited from, and by it is meant the cup (ṣuwā'). How elegant its use is alongside "taking," by which is meant enslavement and servitude. Perhaps for this reason it was chosen over "the cup." The apparent meaning is that "taking" in their speech is also to be understood in this sense, literally.

Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that this may be figurative (majāz), because they know that it is not permissible to enslave a free person who is not a thief, [the word] "substitute" (badal) being from "the Sunnah has decreed his bondage." So their saying that is like when you say to one whose action you dislike: "Kill me, and do not do such-and-such," while you do not want him to kill you, but you are exaggerating in seeking to make him relent. Then he said: On this basis the statement of Yusuf (peace be upon him), ﴿God forbid!﴾, is appropriate, for it is seeking refuge from what is not permissible. It is possible that they did not intend this meaning, and it would be far-fetched for them, who are prophets, to intend the enslavement of a free man. So nothing remains except that they intended by that a guarantee (ḥamāla), that is: take one of us and keep him with you until your companion returns to you, and their purpose by that is that Binyamin would reach his father and [the father] would know the clear state of affairs. End of quote. This is a statement that is not to be relied upon at all, as is not hidden.

For the response of Yusuf (peace be upon him) there is a hidden meaning, which is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only commanded me by revelation to take Binyamin, for purposes known to Him, glorified is He, in that. So if I took someone other than him, I would be wronging myself and acting contrary to the revelation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 80:

﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, i.e., they despaired of Joseph, peace be upon him, that he would respond to them and grant their request. The form is istaf'ala used in the sense of fa'ala, like sakhira and istaskhara, and 'ajiba and ista'jaba, as in al-Bahr. Some others said: the sin and ta' are added for emphasis, meaning they despaired with complete despair, because what they sought was something whose attainment is highly desired. Perhaps the attainment of this degree of despair for them was due to what they witnessed of his seeking refuge in God Most High from what they had asked, which indicates that this matter was, in his view, in the highest degree of disliking, something to be avoided and to seek God's protection from, and from calling it wrongdoing in his saying: ﴿Surely then we would be wrongdoers﴾.

In some reports, when they saw the cup come out of his baggage, and they had already given the verdict they had given, they remembered their covenant with their father. Ruby (Rubil) was seized with anger among them, and nothing could stand before his anger; his hair stood on end until it burst out of his garments. He said: "O King, you must release our brother, or I will cry out a cry such that no pregnant woman in Egypt will remain without giving birth." Joseph, peace be upon him, said to a small child of his: "Get up to this one and touch him, or take his hand." Whenever one of the sons of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, touched him, his anger would subside. When the child did so, his anger subsided. Then he said to his brothers: "Who among you touched me?" They said: "None of us touched you." He said: "Indeed a boy of the family of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, touched me." Then he said to his brothers: "How many markets are there in Egypt?" They said: "Ten." He said: "You take care of the markets, and I will take care of the king; or you take care of the king, and I will take care of the markets." When Joseph, peace be upon him, sensed this, he rose toward him, seized him by the collar, threw him down, and said: "You, O company of Hebrews, claim that no one is stronger than you in strength." At that point they submitted and said: ﴿O Chief of the Realm﴾ ... etc. It is possible on this basis that their complete despair resulted from the combination of both matters.

Some allowed that the pronoun in ﴿from him﴾ refers to Benjamin, and this was objected to on the grounds that they did not despair of him, as evidenced by their eldest brother remaining behind on his account. Abu Rabi'ah reported from al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir that he read (istā'yasū) from ayisa, a metathesis of ya'isa. The evidence for the metathesis, as in al-Bahr, is that the ya' of ayisa was not changed into an alif, despite its being vowelled and the letter before it being open. The sense is: when their hope was completely cut off, they ﴿withdrew﴾ (khalaṣū), meaning they separated themselves from others and kept apart from people.

The statement of al-Zajjaj: "some of them separated from others" is open to scrutiny. ﴿Confidentially⁠ (najiyyan)﴾, i.e., conferring together, consulting one another about what they would say to their father, peace be upon him. He used the singular, though the apparent form would be the plural, because it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the plural pronoun; because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), like tanājī, it was applied to those conferring, as an intensive; or because it is taken as a derived noun; or, even if originally a verbal noun, it covers the few and the many; or because it is of the pattern of the verbal noun, since faʿīl is among the patterns of verbal nouns and means mufāʿil, like jalīs meaning mujālis and ʿashīr meaning muʿāshir, i.e., each one conferring with another, so they are conferring with one another. Its plural is anjiyah. Labid said:

*And the confidants of the caliphate witnessed, high up, Ka'b and the ranks of kings, witnessing.*

And al-Jawhari recited:

*Indeed, when the people were confidants, and stirred like the stirring of the well-rope there, advise me, and do not advise against me.*

This is contrary to analogy, since its analogical plural as an adjective would be af'il' like ghaniy and aghniya'.

﴿The eldest of them said﴾, i.e., their leader, who is Simeon, as said by Mujahid; or their eldest in age, who is Reuben, as said by Qatadah; or their eldest in intellect, who is Judah, as said by Wahb and al-Kalbi. From Muhammad ibn Ishaq it is reported that he is Levi. ﴿Did you not know﴾, as if they had unanimously agreed during their private conference to return without him, and he did not approve of it, so he said, rebuking them: ﴿Did you not know that your father has taken a solemn pledge from you before God﴾, a covenant by which one is bound, namely their oath by God Most High; and its being "from Him" is because it was by His permission, so it was as if it proceeded from Him Most High, or it is from His direction, glorified be He, so "from" is ibtidā'iyyah (indicating origin). ﴿And before this﴾, i.e., before this, and the prepositional phrase is connected to the saying of God Most High: ﴿You neglected concerning Joseph﴾, i.e., you fell short regarding his matter, and you did not keep your father's covenant concerning him, though you had said what you said. Here "mā" is superfluous (zā'idah), and the clause is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah). This, it is said, is the best and safest interpretation of the verse. It is also permitted that mā be a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, its position being in the accusative as a conjunction with the object of ﴿you know﴾, meaning: did you not know your father's taking a pledge from you and your prior neglect concerning Joseph, peace be upon him? Two matters were raised against this: the separation between the conjunction and the conjoined by an adverbial phrase, and the fronting of the complement of the relative particle upon it.
