Grammarians differ on the permissibility of both, and the correct view is permissibility, especially with the expanded adverbial phrase. It was also said:
<page 36>
that conjunction is permitted upon the noun of "inna", and then it requires a predicate, because the first predicate cannot validly be its predicate; so it is ﴿in Joseph﴾ or "from before", meaning: did you not know that your prior neglect occurred concerning Joseph, peace be upon him, or that your neglect which exists or existed concerning Joseph, peace be upon him, occurred before?

It was objected that the context requires only the information that this neglect occurred; the prior neglect should not be described as occurring concerning Joseph, as the first reading implies, nor should the neglect existing concerning him be described as occurring before, as the second reading implies.

In it also is what Abu al-Baqa' mentioned, which Abu Hayyan followed: that the adverbs of time and place (ghayat) do not occur as predicates, complements, qualifiers, or circumstantial clauses. Sibawayh explicitly stated this, whether they are used with a genitive or not. So we say: "Saturday is a blessed day, and the journey is after it," but we do not say "and the journey is after" (without a noun). Al-Samin answered this in ad-Durr al-Masun: this prohibition is because there is no benefit, due to the omitted genitive not being known; so it should be permitted when the genitive is known and indicated, as in the noble verse. It was countered that permissibility of omitting the genitive in adverbs of time and place is conditional on the presence of an indication that determines the omitted item, as al-Radi explicitly stated; this shows that the prohibition is not grounded in what was mentioned.

Al-Shihab said: what they mentioned is not agreed upon. Imam al-Marzuqi said in the commentary on al-Hamasah that they occur as qualifiers, predicates, complements, and circumstantial clauses, and this parsing mentioned here was reported from al-Rummani and others, and it was supported by Arab usage that establishes it. Furthermore, regarding their definiteness through addition, given consideration of an omitted genitive identified by the preceding speech, there is disagreement; the well-known view is that they are definite, and some said they are indefinite, the assumed phrase being "from before something," as in the commentary on al-Tashil. The eminent author of ad-Durr followed a fine path: that when the genitive is known and indicated, specifically and determinately, the predication is valid because a benefit results; but if it is not determined, when the indication is of generality rather than specificity, and the phrase is assumed as "from before something," predication is not valid, since there is no thing except that it is before some thing, so there is no benefit in the predication; then it is both definite and indefinite. There is no contradiction between his statement and al-Radi's, though al-Radi's statement is not agreed upon. He ended. It is, as he said, a precious verification.

It was also said: the place of the verbal noun in the nominative case is as the subject, and the predicate is "from before," and the discussion above applies to it. It was also said: ﴿mā﴾ is a relative pronoun, and its position in the case is what preceded, nominative or accusative, and the clause ﴿you neglected﴾ is its relative clause, the returning pronoun being omitted, and "neglect" here means "precedence" from "forerunner," not "shortcoming," i.e., what you had previously committed of wrongdoing. It was objected to this that the saying of God Most High "from before" would be a repetition; if it is made a predicate, the statement would not be beneficial; and if it is connected to the relative clause, then together with the repetition it requires fronting the complement of the relative clause before the relative pronoun, which is impermissible. It was also said: ﴿mā﴾ is an indefinite qualifying noun, and its position is what preceded, and there is much to say about it.

﴿So I will not leave the land﴾ is a consequence of what he mentioned and what was mentioned with it. ﴿Left⁠ (barih)⁠﴾ is complete when used thus, in the sense of "went" and in the sense of "became manifest," as in their saying: "the concealment became manifest (barih al-khafa')." Here it has been construed with the meaning of "parted from," so ﴿the land﴾ is in the accusative as an object. It cannot be incomplete, because "the land" cannot validly be a predicate about the speaker here; nor is it in the accusative as an adverbial of place, nor by removal of the preposition. By it he meant the land of Egypt, i.e., "I will not part from the land of Egypt," following the requirement of the covenant. ﴿Until my father permits me﴾
<page 37>
to depart, by returning to him; ﴿or God decides for me﴾ regarding leaving it in a way that does not lead to breaking the covenant, or regarding the release of my brother by some means. In al-Bahr it is said: he made this conditional on two ends: a specific one, which is his father's permission, and a general one, which is God Most High's judgment for him. It seems that after he conditioned it on the first, he returned and entrusted the matter to the One whose is the judgment, exalted be His majesty, and intended His judgment, glorified be He, in a way that would be an excuse for him, even if it were death. The apparent view is that the more beloved of the two ends to him was the first; therefore he placed ﴿for me﴾ first in it and postponed it in the second; so let this be understood. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾. (80) Because He, glorified be He, judges only with truth and justice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 81:

﴿Return to your father and say﴾ to him, ﴿"O our father, indeed your son has stolen."﴾ The apparent meaning is that this statement is part of the speech of their eldest, though it has been said that it is from the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and this is far-fetched. Just as the apparent meaning is that they intended that he had actually stolen.

﴿And we did not testify﴾ concerning him ﴿except to what we knew﴾ of his theft, and we observed it, when the king's bowl was taken out from his baggage.

﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen.﴾ (81) And we did not know that he would steal when we gave you the covenant, or we did not know that you would be afflicted by him as you were afflicted by Yusuf. Al-Dahhak read (sāriq, "a thief") as an active participle.

Ibn Abbas, Abu Ruzayn and al-Kisa'i, in one narration, read (suriqa) with a doubled ra, in the passive voice, meaning he was attributed with theft. So the meaning of "And we did not testify..." etc. is: "And we did not testify except to the extent of what we knew of the attribution of theft, and we were not guardians of the hidden matter, whether he stole in truth or the bowl was planted in his baggage without his awareness." This reading has been praised for the purity (of Benjamin) it contains, so they said. The apparent view is that the claim that certainty was derived from the taking out of the bowl from his baggage is not sound, for how could it produce certainty when the possibility that it was planted in it without his awareness remains? The fact that the mere existence of an item in the hand of the accused after his denial was, in their law at first, grounds for theft... It has been said: the apparent position is that a clear preponderant assumption stands in the place of knowledge. Do you not see that testimony is permitted on the basis of presumption (istishab), and it is called knowledge, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿If you know them to be believers﴾? They were only firm about this because the opposing possibilities were remote in their view, and since the judgment of theft, and likewise their knowledge, was based on what they witnessed of the outward matter, the two readings agree, and ﴿And we were not﴾ and so on is interpreted in the manner it was interpreted on the last reading. It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿we did not testify﴾ and so on is that our testimony in our lifetime was never about anything except what we knew, and this is not a testimony from us; rather it is a report about the conduct of your son according to their assertion. ﴿And we were not﴾ and so on as it is. This is also the view that they were not firm. In al-Kashf, which taste bears witness to, they were firm, and their saying: ﴿If he steals, then indeed a brother of his stole before﴾ is a clear preparation. The claim of knowledge does not necessitate knowledge. If it was due to the remoteness of the opposing possibilities, it is not a forbidden lie; otherwise its extent is a lie in claiming knowledge, and this was not their first lie, and it occurred before they repented. For this reason their father also accused them of treachery in this matter as well. Moreover, their saying: ﴿Its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage﴾ emphasized with that emphasis indicates that they regarded finding it in the baggage as conclusive; otherwise they would have had to say: "Its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage, [as] a transgressor or a thief" and the like. For firmness can be attributed to them there, so why not here? End of quotation. In it there is a conflict with some of what we hold, and likewise with what we mentioned in the interpretation of (its recompense) and so on. Perhaps the matter here is easy. From the strange interpretations: the meaning of their saying ﴿for the unseen﴾ is "for the night," and this meaning is found in the dialect of Himyar, and it is as if they said: "And we did not testify except to what we knew from the outward state of his, and we were not guardians of the night, that is, we did not know what happens in it, so perhaps he stole in it, or it was tampered with against him." I do not know what motivated this obscure interpretation when the dawn of the well-known meaning is clear. Whatever the case,
Page 38
the lam in ﴿lil-ghayb﴾ is for emphasis, and the intended meaning is "guardians of the unseen."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 82:

﴿Ask the town in which we were﴾: they mean, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan, Egypt. It was also said: a town near it, where the caller (al-mu'adhdhin) caught up with them. The first view is evident on the basis that the one searching for them was Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the second is evident on the basis that he was the caller (al-mu'adhdhin). Asking the town is an expression for asking its people, either as a figurative usage (majaz, a non-literal use of words) in the word "town," by its application to them through the relation of locality and place (al-halliyyah wa al-mahalliyyah), or in the attribution (al-nisbah). Or a genitive-annexed noun (mudaf) is understood in it, which is also a majaz according to Sibawayh and a group. In al-Mahsul and elsewhere it is stated that ellipsis (idmar) and majaz are mutually exclusive, neither being a division of the other, and most scholars hold them to be opposites. Whichever is the case, the thing asked about is omitted because it is known. The sense of the meaning is: send someone you trust to the people of the town and ask them about the story. ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾: that is, its companions, with whom we set out and whom we were with, for the story is well known among them. They were a people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. It was also said they were from San'a. The discussion here concerns figurative usage and ellipsis, just like the discussion above.

It was also said: there is neither figurative usage nor ellipsis in either place, and the intended meaning is to refer the verification of the matter and the knowledge of the essence of the story to asking the inanimate objects and the animals themselves, on the basis that he, peace be upon them, was a prophet, so it is not far-fetched that they could speak and inform him of this by way of a departure from the customary order. It was objected that this is something that should not be intended and that the context does not require it, because it is not the place to display a miracle. Some eminent scholars said: it is better to leave the town and the caravan on their apparent meaning, without supposing any genitive-annexed noun added to them, and the speech is then based on the claim that the matter is so manifest that the inanimate objects and animals have come to know of it. Similar usage has been common in speech, old and new. Among it is the saying of Ibn al-Dumaynah:

Ask the level, sandy plain, from the sand-hill where the ben-trees grow, whether the remains of your abode have come to life.

And his saying:

Ask my resting place about me and about her, for we are content with what the resting places tell of us.

And his saying:

Ask the stars of the night whether sleep has visited my eyelid, and how could one visit who does not know?

It is not hidden that such a usage does not avoid resorting to a figurative usage. Indeed, it is a subtle meaning, but the majority hold otherwise, and most of them accept the figurative usage of omission. ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ (82). In what we have told you. The intention is not to establish their truthfulness by what was mentioned, so that it would be a petitio principii (musadarah). Rather, it is the emphasis of their truthfulness by what conveys that through the nominal sentence, inna, and the lam, and this is what is meant by the one who said: it is an emphasis in the place of an oath. It may be understood, as has been said, that he intends that there is an implied oath here. It was also said: the intention is affirmation, and there is no petitio principii, in the sense that we are a people whose custom is truthfulness, so what we have told you is not a lie, and we do not suppose that you are in doubt about its non-acceptance.

﴿Qala﴾ (He said). That is, their father, peace be upon him. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) answering a question that arises from what came before, as if it were said: "What happened when that speaker said to the brothers what he said?" It is answered: their father said, when they returned to him and told him what they told him: ﴿Bal sawwalat lakum anfusukum amran﴾ (Nay, your own souls have made a matter seem fair to you). The part about their return is omitted to indicate that their hastening to accept that speaker's words and returning with them to their father is a settled matter, clear without explanation. What needs explaining is his response. It is reported that when they resolved to return to their father, Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to them: "When you come to your father, greet him and say to him: 'The king of Egypt prays for you that you will not die until you see your son Yusuf, so that he may know that in the land of Egypt there are righteous people like him.'" So they set out until they reached him, informed him of everything that had happened, and he wept and said what he said.

﴿Bal﴾ (Nay) is a particle of retraction (idrab). According to what has been said, it is a retraction not from the explicit content of their words, for they were truthful in them, but from what those words imply: the claim of innocence from having caused what befell him, and that nothing had come from them that led to that, in word or deed. It is as if he said: "The matter is not as you say; rather, your souls made a matter among the matters seem fair and easy to you, and you came to him, intending by that the ruling that the thief be seized for his theft, and that is not the religion of the king."

Abu Hayyan said: here there is an omitted statement from which the retraction occurs, and the implied meaning is: "It is not true as you reported; rather, your souls made seem fair..." and so on. This is the view of Ibn 'Atiyyah, who claimed that it is the apparent meaning, in the manner of what was said in the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him: "He thought ill of them" (12:83 cf. 12:58), except that his thought there was correct, while here it was not verified. Ibn al-Munir, explaining this view here, mentioned that although they did not rely on any accusation against Benjamin, and did not tell their father anything except the actual fact in its clear form, and they left him in Egypt only because they were overpowered and could not take him along, nevertheless, when they were with their father, peace be upon him, at that time, they were under suspicion, and they were worthy of being suspected because of what they had previously done to Yusuf, peace be upon him. A clue that confirmed and strengthened the suspicion was present for him: the king's taking him for the theft. That would not have happened except according to his own religion, not according to theirs, nor according to the religion of any other people. So he thought that they were the ones who had given that ruling after the theft they mentioned had become apparent, deliberately, so that he would be left behind alongside them. Accusing one who is in a position where suspicion can reach him is not a defamation, especially in matters concerning a father with a son. Then he said: It is possible that the reason which justified this view regarding them is that they made the mere presence of the goblet in the baggage of the one in whose baggage it is found a theft, without referring the ruling to the establishment of his being a thief by a known means. This, in our law, does not establish theft against the one accused of it. If it was also so in their law, then the failure to specify the ruling indicates that they were eager to seize him, and that is part of "taswil" (making something seem fair), even if that required it in their law. But the principal reliance is on the first answer.

The tanwin in ﴿amran﴾ (a matter) is for magnification, meaning: a great matter. ﴿Fa-sabrun jamil﴾ (So patience is beautiful), that is: so my affair is that, or: so patience is beautiful and more beautiful. The full discussion of this has already been presented, so recall it.

﴿'Asa Allahu an ya'tiyani bihim jami'an﴾ (Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me), meaning Yusuf, his brother Benjamin, and the one detained in Egypt. ﴿Innahu huwa al-'Alimu﴾ (Indeed He is the All-Knowing) of my condition and theirs, ﴿al-Hakim﴾ (the All-Wise). (83) He is the One who tries, and removes the trial according to perfect wisdom. It has been said: he hoped only because of the vision Yusuf, peace be upon him, had seen, so he was awaiting it and had good expectation of Allah, the Exalted, especially after the peg had reached the hips and the belt had passed the flanks. For Allah's custom is that when hardship reaches its extreme, He places after it a great relief. To this is added what was reported about the king of Egypt, that he prayed that he would not die until he saw his son.

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, i.e., he turned away from them out of dislike for what they had brought. ﴿And said, "Oh my grief over Joseph!"﴾ Al-asaf (grief) is the most intense sorrow over what has been lost. The apparent meaning is that he, peace be upon him, attributed it to himself, and the alif is a substitute for the ya' of the first person, for lightness. The meaning is: "O my grief, come, for this is your time." It has also been said that the alif is the alif of nudba (lamentation), with the ha' omitted, but the first view is the one relied upon. He grieved over Joseph, even though the immediate calamity was the loss of his two sons, because the loss of Joseph was, for him, the foundation of all calamities. Even though much time had passed, his heart had seized him completely, so he could never forget him, and he never departed from his thoughts. As one poet said: "The greatest of calamities did not make me forget its distance, but the scratching of a wound with another wound is more painful."

It is not objected that this contradicts the rank of prophethood, since that grief would imply knowledge of God, and whoever knows Him loves Him, and whoever loves Him does not have his heart free to love other than Him. This is because it has been said that this is a natural love, which does not preclude coexisting with love of God the Exalted. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: such intense love removes thoughts from the heart, and its possessor is often returning to God the Exalted, often supplicating and humbling himself before Him, and this becomes a cause for complete absorption. What the Sufis (may God sanctify their secrets) have said on this station will come, if God the Exalted wills, in the chapter on allusion (al-ishara). It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, was confident of the life of his two sons, knowing their location, and hopeful of their return; but as for Joseph, there was nothing in his case that stirred the chain of his hope except the mercy and grace of God the Exalted. There is a discussion on this point.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "No nation among the nations has been given [the words] 'Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return' except the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ)", i.e., they were not taught them and were not granted success in them at the descent of a calamity upon them. Do you not see that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, when what befell him befell him, did not say them and said what he said? And regarding ﴿Asafa﴾ [there is a remark].

﴿Yusuf﴾ is an excellent paronomasia (tajnis), without affectation, and it is of the kind that adds splendor to noble speech. ﴿And his eyes turned white from the sorrow﴾, i.e., because of it. In reality, grief is the cause of weeping, and weeping is the cause of the whitening of his eye, for when tears flow abundantly they erase the blackness of the eye and turn it into a murky whiteness. So the cause of the cause was placed in the position of the cause, because it is more apparent. As for the "whitening," it has been said that it is a metonymy (kinaya) for blindness, so that his sight was entirely lost, peace be upon him. Abu Hayyan preferred this, based on God's words ﴿so he regained his sight﴾, and sight is contrasted with blindness. It has also been said that it is not a metonymy for that, and the meaning of the verse is that a film came over his eyes, whitening them, and he, peace be upon him, perceived only weakly. The discussion of the ruling on blindness with respect to the prophets, peace be upon them, has already passed, and al-Hasan was among those who held it permissible.

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in his Zawa'id, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him that he said: "From the time Joseph left Ya'qub, peace be upon him, until the day he returned, eighty years passed, during which grief did not depart from his heart, and his tears flowed upon his cheeks. He did not cease weeping until his sight was lost, and on the earth that day there was no one more honored by God the Exalted than him."

The apparent meaning is that this condition did not arise for him at the last calamity. This is shown by what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym: that Jibril, peace be upon him, entered upon Joseph, peace be upon him, in the prison and recognized him, and said to him: "O noble king, honored by his Lord, do you have any knowledge of Ya'qub?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What has he done?" He said: "His eyes have turned white from grief over you." He said: "How far has the grief reached?" He said: "He has grieved seventy times [as much as a woman bereaved of her child]." He said: "Does he have a reward for that?" He said: "Yes, the reward of a hundred martyrs."

Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read ﴿min al-hazan﴾ with a fatha on the ha' and the zay, and Qatadah read them with a damma, and the verse is used as evidence for the permissibility of lamenting and weeping at times of calamity. Perhaps restraint from such things does not fall under obligation, for few are those who can control themselves in severe trials.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) transmitted from the hadith of Anas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) wept over his son Ibrahim and said: 'The eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we do not say except what pleases our Lord, and indeed we are saddened by your separation, O Ibrahim.'" What is forbidden is only what the ignorant do of wailing, striking the cheeks and chests, rending garments, and tearing clothes. They also transmitted from the hadith of Usama that "the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, was brought a child of one of his daughters who was dying, so he seated him in his lap while his soul rattled like water in a waterskin, and his eyes overflowed, upon him be the prayer and peace. Sa'd said: 'O Messenger of God, what is this?' He said: 'This is a mercy which God the Exalted has placed in whomever He wills of His servants, and God only shows mercy to those of His servants who are merciful.'"

In al-Kashshaf: "It was said to him, peace be upon him: 'You weep, though you have forbidden us from weeping?' He said: 'I did not forbid you from weeping; I forbade you from two foolish sounds: a sound at joy and a sound at sorrow.'" And from al-Hasan that he wept over a child or someone else, and he was asked about that, and he said: "I did not see that God the Exalted made grief a shame for Ya'qub, peace be upon him, ﴿so he was a suppressor of grief﴾. (84)

[Page 41]

That is, filled with anger at his sons, holding it within his heart and not showing it. It has also been said: filled with grief, holding it in and not revealing it. It is from kazm al-siqa' (the closing of a waterskin) when one ties it after filling it, so fa'il here is in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., maksum (closed), as in the case of Yunus, peace be upon him: ﴿when he called out while he was suppressing [his grief]﴾. It may also be in the sense of fa'il, as in God's words ﴿and those who suppress [their anger]﴾, from kazm al-ghayz when one swallows it, i.e., intensely swallowing anger or grief, because he never complained of it to anyone. Its origin is from the camel's kazm, when it returns its cud into its belly, so it is as if he, peace be upon him, returns that into his belly again and again without letting anyone know of it. In the expression there is metaphor on both readings, which is not hidden. The latter of the two is preferred, because fa'il in the sense of fa'il is common, whereas fa'il in the sense of

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 85:**

﴿They said﴾, that is, the brothers. It was also said that they were others among his followers, peace be upon him. ﴿By God, you will not cease﴾, meaning you will not cease and will not stop, ﴿remembering Joseph﴾ in grief over him. The negative particle has been elided, as in the line of poetry:

*"So I said, 'By God's oath, I will not cease sitting here, even if they cut off my head and my limbs before you.'"*

This is because when an oath is not accompanied by a sign of affirmation, it is understood as negative. The sign of affirmation is the lam (lam al-ta'kid, emphatic lam) and the nun of emphasis (nun al-ta'kid), and both are obligatory in the answer to an affirmative oath. When they are not mentioned, this indicates that the statement is negative, because a negated statement does not take them. Had the intended meaning here been affirmation, it would have said *latafta'anna* (you will surely cease). The obligation of the lam and the nun is the view of the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun). The Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun) and al-Farisi said that it is permissible to use only one of them. Elision also occurs when the verb is in the present sense, as in the reading of Ibn Kathir, ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ (75:1), and in the line of poetry:

*"Indeed I hate every man who embellishes speech and does not act."*

From this arises a legal question: if someone says, "By God, I will stand," he breaks the oath if he stands, and if he does not stand, he does not break it. There is no difference whether the speaker knows Arabic or not, according to what Khayr al-Din al-Ramli ruled. He also mentioned that the oath of divorce is the same. So if someone says, "Divorce is incumbent upon me, with three, you will stand now," she is divorced if she stands, and is not divorced if she does not stand. This question is important, and there is no harm in establishing the truth regarding it, even if it leads to departing from what we are concerned with. So we say: many scholars have said that if the common people drop the lam and the nun in the answer to an affirmative future oath, and one of them says, for example, "By God, I will stand," he does not break the oath by not standing, and so there is no expiation (kaffarah) for him. Al-Maqdisi objected to this, saying that expiation should be obligatory for them, because it is customary among them to swear in this way. He supported this with what is in al-Zahiriyya: that if one makes the letter ha' (in *billah*) quiescent or puts it in the accusative, it is an oath, even though the Arabs never spoke with anything other than the genitive. He also said that it should be an oath even if it lacks the lam and the nun. This is shown by the statement in al-Walwaliyya: "Glory be to God, I will do it; there is no god but God, I will do it" is not an oath unless one intends it. Al-Khayr al-Ramli objected to this, saying that what was reported does not support his claim. As for the first point, it is a change of inflection that does not prevent the word's established meaning, so making it quiescent, raised or accusative does no harm, because a grammatical error (lahn, a mistake in Arabic) does not prevent the contract from being valid. As for the second point, it is not part of the disputed matter, since the disputed matter is affirmation and negation, not whether it is an oath. What we have mentioned has been transmitted from the school (al-madhhab), and transmission must be followed. He examined this.

First: the lahn, as in al-Misbah and elsewhere, is an error in Arabic. Second: what is in al-Walwaliyya is in dispute, because he used the imperfect verb without the lam and the nun and made it an oath with the intention. If it were a negation, it would have to be said that with intention it is an oath on the non-performance of the action, as is clear. He only required the intention for this because it is not customary.

Al-Fadil al-Halabi said: al-Maqdisi's research is sound. The objection that it contradicts the transmitted ruling is answered by saying that the transmitted ruling was according to the custom of the early Islamic period, before the language changed. But now they never bring the lam and the nun into an affirmative oath at all, and they distinguish between affirmation and negation by the presence or absence of *la* and *la*. Their convention in this is nothing but the convention of the Persians and others in their oaths and other matters. End quote. This is supported by what al-Allama Qasim and others mentioned: that the speech of every contracting, swearing and stipulating person is understood according to his custom and habit, whether it agrees with the speech of the Arabs or not. The same is in al-Fath. The grammarians distinguished between *bala* and *na'am* in answers: *bala* is used to affirm what follows a negation, and *na'am* is used for confirmation. So if it is said, "Zayd did not stand," and you say *bala*, the meaning is "he did stand," and if you say *na'am*, the meaning is "he did not stand." It is reported in the commentary on al-Manar from al-Tahqiq that what is considered in the rulings of the Law is custom, so that each of the two is put in the place of the other. The same is in al-Talwih. The statement of al-Muhit, "An oath in Arabic is to say in the affirmative, 'By God, I will surely do it,'" and so on to the end of what he said, is an explanation of the ruling according to the rules of Arabic, the custom of the Arabs, and their established habits free from grammatical error. The speech of people today, except for rare exceptions, departs from those rules. So it is a conventional language of their own, like all foreign languages whose speakers have modified them. They are not to be dealt with according to other than their own languages and their intention, except for those among them who commit to the inflection or intend the meaning. So he should be held to his intention. For this reason al-Saihani said: our oaths today do not depend on emphasis, for we have established them in a new form, agreed upon them by a recent convention, and made them common by widespread usage, so our treatment must be according to this. What they said is that if the linking *fa'* for the answer of a conditional is dropped, it is an immediate (tanjiz) not a suspended (ta'liq) statement, so that if he says, "If I enter the house, you are divorced," she is divorced at once. This is also based on the rules of Arabic, and it is contrary to current usage. So it should be based on custom, making it a suspended statement, and this is what is reported from Abu Yusuf.

In al-Bahr: the disagreement is based on whether it is permissible to omit the *fa'* by choice or not. The people of Kufa permitted it, and Abu Yusuf made rulings on this basis. The people of Basra forbade it, and the school (al-madhhab) follows this. In the commentary on al-Maqdisi's versified Kanz: it is appropriate to prefer the view of Abu Yusuf, because the *fa'* is often omitted in eloquent speech, and because they said: "Common people are not held to lahn in their speech," as in their saying "anti wahidatun" with the accusative, which no one has held. End quote.

This is what was mentioned, but it concerns the oath, not the conditional statement. Although the conditional statement is called an oath (halif) and a yamin (oath) by the jurists, it is not called a qasam (oath by God), for a qasam is specific to oaths by God Most High, as al-Qahistani declared. So the requirement of the lam and the nun in the affirmative does not apply to it, neither according to the jurists nor according to the philologists. Among such expressions is "It is incumbent upon me to forbid (haram) what I do not do," and "Divorce is incumbent upon me, I will not do such and such," for by this is meant, by custom, "If I do such and such, then she is divorced." So it must be enforced against them, as declared in al-Fath and elsewhere. Al-Halabi said: with this is refuted what some of the eminent scholars imagined, that in the statement of the speaker, "Divorce is incumbent upon me, I will come today," if he comes today the divorce falls, and otherwise not, because of the absence of the lam and the nun. You know that the grammarians only required that in the answer to an affirmative oath, not in the answer to a conditional. How can it be right for any intelligent person, let alone a learned one, to say, "If Zayd stands, I will stand," meaning "If Zayd stands, I will not stand"? And "I will come" is not the answer to the condition, but the verb of the condition, because the meaning is "If I do not come today, then you are divorced." This error has befallen many of the jurisprudents (muftis), such as Khayr al-Din al-Ramli and others.

Sayyid Ahmad al-Hamawi said in his great Tadhkira: a question was put to me in this form. A man became angry at his wife's son and said, "Divorce with three is incumbent upon me, I will complain about you to the naqib tomorrow morning." When morning came, he left him and did not complain, and some time passed. Does divorce fall upon him in this situation or not? The answer: when he abandons his complaint and some time passes after his oath, divorce does not fall upon him, because the verb mentioned came in the answer to the oath, and it is affirmative, so the negation is to be assumed where it was not emphasised.

[Page 43]

Then he said: I answered, after praising God Most High, that the ruling of this respondent that divorce does not fall, justified by what was mentioned, shows the extent of his ignorance and foolishness, and the frequency of his recklessness in religion and his lack of restraint. For that applies to the verb when it comes as the answer to an oath by God Most High, such as *tafta'*, not to an oath in the sense of a suspended statement with what is burdensome, such as divorce, emancipation and the like. In that case, if the swearer rises in the morning and does not complain, the three divorces fall upon him, and his wife is separated from him with irrevocable separation. End quote. How well he spoke, and how good is the saying of the poet:

*"Part of religion is removing the veil from every liar, and from every innovator who brings wonders."*

*"Were it not for believing men, the cloisters of God's religion would be demolished on every side."*

[Note in the original:] *Fata'a* is one of the sisters of the defective *kana* (kana al-naqisa), as we pointed out. It is also said *fata'a* like *daraba*, and *afta'a* like *akrama*. Ibn Malik claimed that it means to calm down and to slacken, so it is then complete (tamma), and on that basis came Mujahid's interpretation of *la taftu* as "la tafturu" (you will not slacken) from his love. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as meaning that he, may God's mercy be upon him, made *futu'* and *futur* brothers, that is, mutually concomitant, not that they share a meaning. The word that means to slacken and calm down is *fath'a* with a thāʾ, as in al-Sihah: from *fathi'at al-qidr*, when its boiling calms, and of a man when his anger calms. From this Abu Hayyan censured Ibn Malik in what he claimed and asserted that it is a case of scribal confusion (tasif). It was objected that the matter is not as he said, for Ibn Malik transmitted it from al-Farra', and al-Sarqusti explicitly stated it. It is not impossible for two roots to agree in meaning, and this is common. Ibn Malik compiled this in a book he named *What Differs in Dots and Agrees in Meaning*, and the author of al-Qamus transmitted it from him. He used the verse as evidence for the permissibility of swearing on the basis of strong probability (ghalabat al-zann). It was also said that they knew this from him, but they treated it as a denial, and so they emphasised it with an oath, meaning: we swear by God Most High that you will not cease remembering Joseph, grieving over him.

﴿until you become consumed﴾, meaning ill, close to death. It was said: *haraḍ* is one whom grief or sickness has melted, and made emaciated and thin. In origin it is a verbal noun of *haraḍa*, so one is *ḥariḍ* with a kasra on the ra'. It is also said *aḥraḍanī*, as in the line:

*"I am a man whom love has seized, and it has worn me down, until I am worn out and sickness has wasted me."*

Because it is so in origin, it is not made feminine, dual or plural, since the verbal noun applies to the few and the many. Ibn Ishaq said: *ḥaraḍ* is a corrupt person who has no reason. It was read *ḥariḍan* with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and kasra on the rā'. Al-Hasan al-Basri read *ḥuruḍan* with two ḍammas, and similar to it among adjectives are *rajulun junubun* and *ghurubun*.

﴿or you become among the perishing﴾ (85). That is, among the dead. As for *aw* (or), it was said it may mean *bal* (rather) or *ila* (until), so there is no objection that the order should be the reverse of *ḥattā takūna ḥaraḍan*. If it is for alternation, it prevents the absence of both, and the ordering follows the order of occurrence, as was said regarding God's words: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him﴾ (2:255); or because it is more frequent.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** (Commentary of al-Alusi) on Surah 12, verse 86:

﴿He said: "I only complain of my anguish (*bathth*) and my grief to God."﴾ *Al-bathth* originally means stirring up a thing and scattering it, as when the wind scatters the dust (*baththa al-rih al-turab*). It is used for a distress that its bearer cannot bear, as if it has become so heavy upon him that he cannot carry it alone, so he disperses it among those who will help him bear it. Thus *bathth* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used in the sense of the passive participle (*bi-ma'na al-maf'ul*), and in it there is an explicit metaphor (*isti'ara tasrihiyya*, a metaphor in which the comparison is stated through the word itself). It is also permissible for it to mean the active participle, i.e., the distress that has stirred up and scattered the thought. In either case, the apparent meaning is that the people (his companions) said what they said as a means of consolation and of drawing out his complaint. He therefore replied to them: "I do not complain to you, or to anyone else, of what I have, so that you may take trouble to console me. Rather, I complain of my distress ﴿and my grief to God﴾, exalted is He, seeking refuge at His threshold, pleading before His door for its removal, for He is the One able to do that." In a report from Ibn ʿUmar, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among the treasures of righteousness is concealing charity, and keeping secret one's calamities and illnesses, and whoever spreads (his grief, *batha*) does not remain patient." Al-Hasan and ʿIsa read *ḥazanī* with two fatḥas (*ḥazanī*), and Qatadah read it with two ḍammas (*ḥuznī*).

**Page 44**

﴿And I know from God what you do not know.﴾ That is, from His kindness and mercy. ﴿What you do not know.﴾ (86)

So I hope that He will have mercy on me, be kind to me, and not disappoint my hope. The sentence is according to an elision (*hadhf mudaf*, an omitted word, with the sense being "from the kindness of God"), and *min* is explanatory (*bayaniyya*), placed before what it explains, which the grammarians have permitted. It is also permissible for it to be inceptive (*ibtida'iyya*, indicating origin or source), meaning: "I know through revelation, inspiration, or some cause of knowledge from Him, exalted is He, what you know of the life of Yusuf, peace be upon him."

It is said that he, peace be upon him, knew this from the dream, as was mentioned above. It is also said that he saw the Angel of Death (*malak al-mawt*) in a dream, and the Angel informed him that Yusuf was alive. Many have mentioned this, but they did not cite any chain of transmission (*sanad*) for it. What is reported from Ibn Abi Hatim, from al-Nadr, is that he said: "It reached me that Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, remained for twenty-four years not knowing whether Yusuf, peace be upon him, was alive or dead, until the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, appeared to him in the form of a man. He said to him: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am the Angel of Death.' He said: 'I beseech you by the God of Yaʿqub: have you taken the soul of Yusuf?' He said: 'No.' At that, he, peace be upon him, said:"

﴿O my sons, go and seek out information about Joseph and his brother﴾: that is, learn about them. It is from the form *tafa''ala* (a verbal form that often indicates effort or seeking), derived from *al-hiss* (sense perception), which originally means perceiving through a sense organ. Likewise, the root sense of *al-tahassus* is seeking perception, and its use for "learning" is a use of the word for something that follows from its meaning. Close to it is *al-tajassus* with a *jim*. It has been said that *tahassus* with a *ha'* is used for good and *tajassus* with a *jim* for bad, but this was refuted by the fact that the reading here is also *fa-tajassasu* with a *jim*. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: The root of *al-jass* is touching the pulse and perceiving its beat in order to judge health or sickness. It is more specific than *al-hiss*, since *al-hiss* is perceiving what the senses perceive, while *al-jass* is perceiving a state of something from that. "From Joseph and his brother" means from their news. The third (Benjamin) is not mentioned, because his absence was by choice and its removal is not difficult. Even if that is assumed, the motive among them to seek news of him, since he was their brother, was strong, so there was no need to command them to do so. The preposition *min* is connected to what precedes it, and it has the sense of *'an* (about), based on what is reported from Ibn al-Anbari (Ibn al-Anbari), that one does not say *tahassastu min fulan* but *tahassastu 'anhu*. It is also permissible that *min* is partitive, meaning: seek some of the news of Joseph and his brother.

﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾: that is, do not lose hope in His relief and His easing, glory be to Him. The original meaning of *al-rawh* with a *fatha* is, as al-Raghib said, breathing; it is said: a person "found relief" (*arah*) when he breathed. Then it was used metaphorically for relief, as it is said: he has *tanfis* (relief), from *nafas* (breath).

Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Hasan and Qatadah read *rawh* with a *damma*, and it was explained as mercy, as a metaphor from its well-known meaning, because mercy is the cause of life just as the spirit is. Its attribution to Allah, exalted is He, is because it comes from Him, glory be to Him. Ibn Atiyyah said: It seems that the meaning of this reading is: do not despair of a living being who has the spirit of Allah that He gave him, for whoever still has his spirit is hoped for. From this is his (the poet's) saying:

*"And in the one whom the earth has covered, hope [for the one who is gone]."*

And the saying of Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

*"Every absent one returns, but the absent one of death does not return."*

Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) read *min rahmati Allah* (from the mercy of Allah), and Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read *min fadli Allah* (from the bounty of Allah). According to Abu Hayyan, both are an explanation, not a reading. It was also read *ta'yasu* (with a different vowel pattern), and al-A'raj read *tay'asu* with a *kasra* on the *ta'*. The imperative and prohibition, according to what has been said, are guidance for them toward some of what was left vague in His saying: *"And I know from Allah what you do not know"* (12:86). Then he, peace be upon him, warned them against neglecting to act on the requirement of his prohibition by saying: *"Indeed, [the matter is that] no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people"* (12:87), because they do not know Allah, exalted is He, and His attributes, for the one who truly knows does not despair in any state. Or it is an emphasis on what they already know of this. Ibn Abbas said: The believer has good expectations from Allah, exalted is He, in affliction, and praises Him in ease.

[Page 45]

Al-Imam (i.e., Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned that despair does not occur unless a person believes that God is not able to do everything, or is not knowing of all that is known, or is not generous. Believing in any one of these three entails disbelief. Since despair occurs only when one of them occurs, and each of them is disbelief, it is established that despair occurs only for one who is a disbeliever. Some of our companions used the verse as evidence that despairing of the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, is disbelief, and claimed that it clearly indicates this.

Al-Shihab (al-Alusi himself) said: There is no evidence in it for that; rather, that is established by another proof. The majority of jurists hold that despair is a major sin. The implication of the verse is that it is one of the attributes of disbelievers, not that whoever commits it becomes a disbeliever by committing it. That it occurs only when one of the disbelief-causing beliefs mentioned by al-Imam occurs is itself open to objection, because it is possible that a person despairs of Allah's mercy toward him while believing in His all-encompassing power, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and the greatness of His generosity, merely from magnifying his sin, for example, and believing that he is not worthy of Allah's mercy, without any slightest particle of those evil beliefs that cause disbelief occurring to him. This requires no more than that it entails prior disbelief, not that committing it itself is disbelief. So it has been said. It has also been said: It is better to hold that despair may coexist with faith, and that the claim that it occurs only through one of the mentioned beliefs is neither clear nor clarifying.

Yes, that it is a major sin is beyond doubt. Indeed, it was reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is among the greatest of major sins. Likewise, *qunut* (utter hopelessness) and bad opinion of Allah. They distinguished between them: despair is the absence of hope that any kind of mercy will befall him; *qunut* is that, with the addition of a state that is stronger in determination that it will not happen; and bad opinion is that, with the addition that, since He does not show him mercy, he will be punished more severely, like the disbelievers. Ibn Nujaym mentioned in some of his treatises what makes the disagreement between those who say despair is disbelief and those who say it is a major sin verbal. He said: The jurists have listed among the major sins feeling secure from the plotting of Allah and despair of His mercy, and in the books of creed it is said that despair of the mercy of Allah is disbelief, so this requires reconciliation. The answer is that by despair is meant denying the breadth of mercy for sins, and by security is meant believing there is no plotting; the jurists' meaning of despair is despair due to magnifying one's sins and considering forgiveness of them unlikely, and by security is security due to overwhelming hope, to the point that it has entered the category of security. He then said: The approach of the jurists is more in accordance with the Sunnah, because of the hadith of al-Daraqutni from Ibn Abbas traced to the Prophet, in which he counted it among the major sins and linked it with associating partners with Allah. End. This is a precious verification, so let it be understood.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 88:**

﴿Then when they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, after they had returned to Egypt in compliance with their father's command. It was not mentioned explicitly to signal their haste in doing what they had been ordered, and to indicate that this was a certain matter that did not need to be mentioned or explained. The Jews deny that they returned after taking Benjamin to their father and then came back to Egypt. They claim that when they came the first time for provisions, he accused them of being spies, so they made their excuses and mentioned that they were the sons of God's Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob), and that they were twelve sons, one of whom had perished, while his brother remained with their father, consoling himself with him for the one who had perished, since he loved him greatly. He said: "Bring him to me so that I may verify your truthfulness," and Shim'un was held with him until they should come. When they brought him, and what happened regarding the matter of the theft occurred, they showed submission and humility, and he, peace be upon him, could no longer control himself until he made himself known to them. Then he ordered them to return to their father to tell him the news and to bring him. This is what their Torah contains today. ﴿And what is after the truth but error?﴾

﴿They said: O Chief of the Treasury (al-'Aziz)﴾. They addressed him thus to glorify him, in accordance with their earlier address to him, as is evident. Did they know his name or not? I have not seen anyone raise this question. If they did know it, then the matter of their ignorance becomes more striking. What is meant, according to al-Imam (al-Razi) and others, is: O King, the Mighty, the Invincible. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾: the emaciation resulting from severe hunger. The word "family" is meant to include the wife and others. ﴿We have brought goods of little value (muzjah)﴾, that is, goods that are pushed away, which every merchant pushes aside out of indifference and contempt. It derives from azjaytuhu, meaning "I pushed him and drove him away," and the wind "drives" (tuzji) the clouds. They recited for Hatim:

*"Let a guest who is turned away weep for Mulhan, and a widow who is driven off with the night, a widow."*

It is used metaphorically for the little or the poor in quality, because out of lack of care it is pushed away and discarded. It was said: their goods were among the wares of the Bedouins, namely wool and ghee. It was said: pine nuts and green seed (habbat al-khadra'), narrated from Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam. It was said: flour of moql (a kind of resin) and aqt (dried curd). It was said: dried meat and grass. It was said: ropes, saddlebags, and sacks. It was said: they were counterfeit dirhams that were not accepted except at a loss, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. What is narrated from al-Hasan explains it as merely "little" and nothing more. In any case, muzjah is a true attribute of the goods. Al-Zajjaj said: it derives from their saying "So-and-so makes his life pass (yuzjii al-'aysh)," meaning he gets through his time with little. The sense is: "We have come with goods by which time is passed, which are not of the kind that is benefited from," and the estimation on this view is "goods by which the days are passed," meaning they are got through with them and one endures upon them until they end, as it has been said:

*"Pass through the days and you will pass through them, and the houses of sorrow you will not enter."*

What was mentioned first is preferable. From al-Kalbi it is narrated that muzjah is from the language of non-Arabs, and it was said that it is from the Coptic language. Ibn al-Anbari criticized this, saying: it is not appropriate to attribute to a non-Arabic language a word whose derivation and inflection are well known; therefore the attribution to that language is rejected, and the word is muzjah.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "muzjiyah" with imalah (vowel inclination toward ya') because its original form has a ya'. Apparently, they put this speech first so that it would serve as a means to achieve their aim, by arousing compassion, stirring kindness and mercy, and moving the chain of tenderness. Then they said: ﴿So give us full measure﴾, that is, complete it for us and do not reduce it, due to the scarcity or poor quality of our goods. This has been cited as evidence that measuring is the duty of the seller, but there is no evidence in it. ﴿And be charitable to us (wa-tasaddaq 'alayna)﴾: the apparent meaning is by completing the measure, or by overlooking the matter and accepting the inferior goods, or by adding more than their equivalent.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij said that they meant: "Be charitable to us by returning our brother Benjamin to his father." It was said: this is the most fitting interpretation given their situation with regard to their father's command. It seems they meant: "Favor us with that," since returning a brother is not literally charity; and the word sadaqah has come in the sense of favor, as one says: "Allah the Exalted gave charity (tasaddaqa) to so-and-so with such-and-such." As for al-Hasan's words to someone who heard him say: "O Allah, give charity to me (tasaddaq 'alayya)": "Indeed Allah the Exalted does not give charity; only one who seeks reward gives charity. Say: O Allah, give me, or favor me, or have mercy on me." This was refuted by the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "A charity with which Allah the Exalted has given charity to you, so accept His charity." It has been answered by taking the expression figuratively and by mushakala (a stylistic parallelism). Al-Hasan rebuked the speaker only because he was not eloquent, as in the story of the deceased. Some claimed that carrying the word on its figurative sense is also necessary if the intent is to seek an increase over what is given for the price, based on the view that the prohibition of accepting charity is not specific to our Prophet ﷺ, as Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah held. Rather, it is general to him, peace be upon him, and to those before him among the prophets, peace be upon them, and their families, as others held. And the askers are, without doubt, of one of the two groups. It was objected: even if we grant the generality, we do not grant that what is forbidden is taking charity absolutely; rather, what is forbidden is taking obligatory charity (zakah), and what is in question here is not that.

The apparent meaning, as al-Zamakhshari said, is that they humbled themselves before him, peace be upon him, with their saying ﴿adversity has touched us﴾ and so on, and they asked him to give them charity with their saying "be charitable to us." So if the verse is not taken in its apparent sense, that introduction would not correspond to it, nor would this confirmation: ﴿Indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾ (88). By mentioning Allah the Exalted, His reward, and the things that move people to do that, and that the one who does it is in a high position with Him, the Exalted.

Al-Naqqash said: deviating from "Indeed Allah will reward you for your charity" to the wording found in the noble verse is a way out of lying, so it is of the type of ma'arid (indirect speech). For they believed him to be a disbelieving king, and something similar was narrated from al-Dahhak. As for the reason they did not begin with what they had been commanded, on the view that is contrary to the apparent meaning regarding the object of the charity: what they chose contained an attraction of compassion and mercy. It is as if they wanted to fill the basins of his heart with its flowing water, so as to water with it the trees of their search, so that they might bear for them the fruit of their father's aim. Some scholars explained it along similar lines. Then he said: "Moreover, their saying ﴿and be charitable﴾ and so on is a speech with two faces, for it admits being carried to both senses. So perhaps he, peace be upon him, took it as a request for the return, and for that..."

He said, responding to what they had hinted at and woven into their speech of that kind: ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ The apparent sense, on this reading, would be to limit the reproach to what he had done with the brother. However, he (peace be upon him) also alluded to what had been done to himself, since both had been subjected to the same act. What is meant is their isolating them from their father and humiliating them, to the point that he could speak to them only in helplessness and abasement. The question is not about knowledge of the act itself, since a deliberate act is necessarily preceded by awareness. Rather, it concerns its ugliness, as shown by His words: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾ (89). That is, "Have you come to know the ugliness of what you did, now that your ignorance at the time has gone, or not?" It also contains an excuse for them and a prompting of them to it, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ On this basis, the apparent meaning is that this was not an expression of gloating, but an exhortation to desist and counsel to them, in view of his seeing their weakness and submissiveness, together with a subtle rebuke for their having had ignorance, and that such ignorance is ill-suited to people like them. So, to Allah belongs this noble character: how he gave up his share of revenge for the sake of the right of Allah, Exalted is He, in a manner that also includes the right of both brotherhoods, and gentleness in making them hear it, together with a warning that this harm is more deserving of being uncovered.

It has been said: it is also possible that this statement from him (peace be upon him) was separate from their words, and a reminder to them of what their duty and obligation were, namely to turn away from all demands and devote themselves entirely to seeking Binyamin. Indeed, it is possible that he (peace be upon him) came to know, by way of revelation (waḥy, divine inspiration) or inspiration (ilhām), of his father's instruction and his sending them to spy on him and his brother. Then, when he saw them occupied with other matters, he said what he said. The apparent meaning is that when he (peace be upon him) saw what he saw from them, and he was among the most tender-hearted of Allah's creatures, and the Book had reached its appointed term, he began to uncover his affair, and so he said what he said.

It is related from Ibn Ishaq that when they appealed to him for compassion, he was moved for them and had mercy on them, to the point that his tears flowed as he wept and he could not control himself. So he began to make himself known to them. By what they had done to him, he meant everything that had happened, and by what they had done to his brother, he meant the harm they had done to him, their harshness toward him, their bad treatment of him, and their isolating him, as you have heard. He did not mention to them what they had inflicted upon their father, according to what has been said, out of exalting his station and magnifying his rank, by not mentioning him alongside himself and his brother, even though that is among the branches of what was mentioned.

It has also been said: they delivered to him a letter from their father, and its text, as in al-Kashshaf, was: "From Ya'qub, Isra'il of Allah, son of Ishaq, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah, to the Ruler of Egypt. To proceed: we are a household upon which affliction has been decreed. As for my grandfather, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire to be burned, but Allah, Exalted is He, saved him, and the fire was made cool and safe for him. As for my father, a knife was placed on his nape to be slaughtered, but Allah, Exalted is He, ransomed him. As for me, I had a son, and he was the dearest of my children to me. His brothers took him away to the wilderness, then they brought me his shirt stained with blood and said, 'The wolf has eaten him.' My eyes were lost from weeping for him. Then I had another son, who was his full brother, and I used to be consoled by him. They took him away, then they returned and said, 'He has stolen, and you have detained him for that. We are a household that does not steal, and we do not give birth to a thief. So if you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will invoke upon you a supplication that will overtake the seventh of your offspring.' And peace."

Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar account from Abu Rawq. When Joseph (peace be upon him) read the letter, he could not restrain himself, and his patience gave way, so he said that to them. It is also reported that when he read the letter, he wept, and he wrote the reply: "Be patient as they were patient, and you will prevail as they prevailed."

What I have indicated, that the intended meaning is affirming ignorance for them in reality, is the apparent meaning. It has also been said that no negation of knowledge from them was intended, since they were learned men, but because they did not do what knowledge requires, and abandoning what knowledge requires is the conduct of the ignorant, he called them ignorant. It has also been said that what is meant is that they were ignorant of the outcome to which the matter would lead. It is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan that ﴿ignorant﴾ means children, before you reached the age of maturity and sound judgment. But this has been criticised: it is not the correct interpretation, because it does not agree with the reality, and it contradicts ﴿while we are a company﴾. So the apparent meaning is that this attribution is not sound. Al-Tahrir claimed that the view of the majority, that the interrogative is for affirmation and reproach, and that his intention (peace be upon him) was to magnify the event, namely: how great is what you committed against Joseph and his brother. It is like saying, "Do you know whom you disobeyed?" It has also been said that hal here means qad, as in ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was nothing worth mentioning?﴾, and the purpose is also reproach. Both of these opinions are not to be relied upon, and the correct view is what has preceded. Among the strange views that cannot be sustained at all is what al-Tha'labi relates: that when they said to him what they said, he became angry with them and ordered their execution, so they wept and became distressed, and he was moved for them and said: ﴿Do you know...﴾, and so on.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 90:

﴿They said: "Are you truly Joseph?"﴾ This is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqrir), and for this reason it is emphasised with ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) and the lam, because emphasis requires certainty, which is incompatible with a genuine interrogative. It is possible that they said it out of astonishment and amazement. Ibn Kathir, Qatadah and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿innaka﴾ without the interrogative hamzah. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "The apparent meaning is that the interrogative is intended, and it is far-fetched to take it as a pure declarative statement, although some have said so, because of the contradiction between interrogative and declarative if the speakers are one group. If it is assumed that some of them asked and others declared, and each is attributed to the whole group, it becomes possible, but even so it is distant." In both readings, ﴿anta﴾ (you) is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿Yusuf﴾ is its predicate, and the clause is in the nominative position as the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. ﴿Anta﴾ cannot be an emphatic restatement of the pronoun which is the subject of ﴿inna﴾, because of the intervening lam. Ubayy read ﴿a-innaka aw anta Yusuf﴾, and Ibn Jinni in al-Muhtasab explained this as an ellipsis of the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, estimating it as ﴿a-innaka la-ghayru Yusuf aw anta Yusuf﴾ (Are you not Joseph, or are you Joseph?). Al-Zamakhshari likewise, except that he estimated it as ﴿a-innaka Yusuf aw anta Yusuf﴾, then said: "This is a speech of astonishment and wonder at what is being heard, so he repeats the verification." In al-Kashf he said: "What he estimated is better, because of the fewness of the ellipsis and the strength of the indication of what is omitted, although the first estimate follows the rule of interrogation more closely. Perhaps the most suitable is to estimate ﴿a-innaka anta aw anta Yusuf﴾, as a way of making himself unknown, so that the address to Joseph means: 'Are you the well-known Aziz of Egypt, or are you Joseph?' They found it improbable that the Aziz should be Joseph, or that Joseph should be an Aziz. This also has the fewness of the ellipsis, together with the difference between the conjunct and the conjoined, the strength of the indication of what is omitted, the adherence to the rule of interrogation, and the added benefit of suggesting the distance between the two states."

If it is said: "The former is more in accordance with the well-known reading, because of the strength of the indication that he is himself," it is answered: "It is sufficient for the indication of all these aspects that the interrogative is not applied in its literal sense. Moreover, the non-contradiction between his being their addressee, the well-known one, and his being Joseph is also a strong indication, together with the added benefit of mentioning the cause of their astonishment. This is a statement which bears the marks of verification."

They differed concerning the means by which they recognised him, peace be upon him. It was said: they recognised him by his appearance and his features, and he had brought them close to himself, though he had not brought them near before. It was said: he used to speak to them from behind a screen, and when he wanted to make himself known to them he lifted it, and they recognised him. It was said: he smiled, and they recognised him by his front teeth, which were like strung pearls, and the light of his smile illuminated what was around him. It was said: he, peace be upon him, removed the crown from his head, and they looked at a mark on his forehead which Ya'qub, Ishaq and Sarah had possessed, similar to it, resembling a white birthmark, and so they recognised him by that. To all of this is added their knowledge that what he addressed them with could not issue in such a form except from an upright Muslim of the lineage of Ibrahim, not from some dignitary of Egypt. Some have claimed that they only said this by way of supposition, and did not recognise him until he informed them about himself: ﴿He said: "I am Joseph"﴾. But what is relied upon is what has preceded.

﴿I am Joseph, and this is my brother﴾ is an answer to their question, and he added to it his saying ﴿and this is my brother﴾, meaning from both my parents, in exaggeration in making himself known. One of the careful scholars said: They asked him in astonishment about his being Joseph, seeking to verify it while imagining, because of the intensity of their amazement, that he was not him. So he answered them with what confirms it, emphatically. For this reason, peace be upon him, he did not say: "Yes," or "I am he," but repeated the explicit name: ﴿and this is my brother﴾, which stands in the position of ﴿I am Joseph﴾, without doubt. Moreover, in it there is what supports it, in his saying: ﴿God has indeed favoured us﴾. Al-Tibi allowed that this may be in the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), as if, when they asked him in astonishment, "Are you Joseph?", he replied: "Do not ask about that, for it is evident. But ask what God the Exalted has done for you of bounty and honour, and likewise for my brother," and this has nothing to do with that, as is not hidden. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that in the addition to the answer there is exaggeration and magnification of the status of the brother, and a completion of what his saying ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ conveyed, as indicated by ﴿has favoured﴾, and so on. It is as if he said: "Do you know what you did to us of separation and humiliation? I am Joseph, and this is my brother, whom God the Exalted has favoured with deliverance from what we were tested with, with reunion after separation, honour after abasement, and intimacy after estrangement." It is not far-fetched that there is in it an allusion to the answer to their request for the return of Benjamin: that he is my brother, not your brother, so there is no basis for your demand. End of quotation. Yet there is in it what there is. The clause ﴿has favoured﴾ and so on, according to Abu al-Baqa', is a new independent sentence. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from Joseph and ﴿brother﴾, but this was criticised as far-fetched, since there is then no governing element for the circumstantial clause, and it cannot be so because ﴿this﴾ is a reference to one person, while ﴿upon us﴾ refers to both of them together. ﴿Indeed he﴾, that is, the matter, ﴿whoever fears God﴾, that is, performs piety in all his states, or guards himself against what brings on the wrath of God the Exalted and His punishment, ﴿and is patient﴾ under trials and tribulations, or under the hardship of acts of obedience, or from disobedience which the soul does not find pleasant, ﴿then indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ (90). That is, their reward. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to draw attention to the fact that those described with piety and patience are also described with goodness. The clause is in the position of the reason for the favour. Abu Hayyan preferred that there be no restriction in piety and patience. Mujahid said: the meaning is whoever fears God by abstaining from sin and is patient in prison. Al-Nakha'i said: whoever guards against fornication and is patient in celibacy. It was also said: whoever guards against sins and is patient under the harm of people. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is whoever fears God the Exalted and is patient, refraining from sins and persevering in acts of obedience. Sahib al-Fara'id criticised him, saying that this involves taking ﴿whoever fears﴾ in a metaphorical sense, while there is no obstacle to taking it literally, and departing from that to metaphor without necessity is not permissible. Rather, the correct view is to say: whoever fears, that is, whoever refrains from abandoning what he has been commanded and committing what he has been forbidden, and is patient in adversities. That is by his choice, and this is not by his choice, so he is a good-doer. The mention of patience after piety is of the mention of the particular after the general. It is also possible that this was intended to mean persistence in piety, as if it were said: whoever fears and perseveres in piety. End of quotation.

The first view inclines towards what Abu Hayyan mentioned. Al-Tibi criticised this, saying that this clause is a reason for what precedes and an indirect allusion to his brothers, that they did not fear His punishment, the Exalted, and did not persevere in His obedience and in the obedience of their father, nor in refraining from disobedience, when they did what they did. Thus the meaning of piety would be fear, and the meaning of patience would be patience in obedience and in refraining from disobedience. This was rejected on the ground that the allusion is already present in the other interpretation, so that he interpreted it in that way to avoid repetition with patience. There is room to examine this. Qunbul read ﴿man yattaqi﴾ with the ya' affirmed. It was said: it is jussive, with the ya' which is the final radical of the word dropped, and this ya' is a vowel-lengthening ya' (ya' al-ishba'). It was also said: its jussive form is by dropping the estimated vowel, and the grammarians have judged this to be a valid usage. It was also said: it is nominative, and ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, and the jussive word is conjoined to it by a kind of assumption, as if he assumed that ﴿man﴾ was conditional and ﴿yattaqi﴾ jussive. It was also said: ﴿yasbir﴾ is nominative like ﴿yattaqi﴾, except that the ra' was made quiescent to avoid a succession of vowels, even though this occurs across two words, as it was made quiescent in ﴿ya'murukum﴾, ﴿yush'irkum﴾ and similar forms; or it is for pausal reasons, and continuous speech is treated as pause. The best of these views, as stated in al-Bahr, is that ﴿yattaqi﴾ is jussive according to a dialect, even though it is rare. As for the statement of Abu 'Ali that it should not be understood in this way because it occurs only in poetry, it is not to be heeded, since other leading grammarians have related it as a dialect, in verse and in prose.

They said, ﴿By God, God has certainly preferred you over us﴾. That is, He chose you and favoured you over us, through piety and patience. It was also said: through kingship. It was also said: through patience and knowledge, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: through forbearance and forgiveness, as mentioned by Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The author of al-Ghaniyyan said: through beauty of form and character, knowledge, forbearance, benevolence, kingship and authority, and patience over our harm to him. The first view is the more apt.

(And indeed) that is, the matter being such that ﴿we were certainly sinners﴾. That is, we were deliberately committing sin when we did what we did, and for that reason He honoured you and humiliated us. Thus the waw is a waw of circumstance (ḥāliyya), and in (inna) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa), its noun being the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the lam found in the predicate of kāna is the displaced lam (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa). Khāṭi'īn is from khaṭi'a when one intends (it), whereas akhṭa'a means one aims at what is right but is not granted success in it. In their statement, "This is from seeking to lower him (istinzāl) by his benevolence, peace be upon him, and acknowledging what they did against him, together with an indication of repentance," there is no concealment of what is intended. For this reason...

[Page 50]

He said: ﴿No reproach﴾, meaning no rebuke or blame upon you. Its root is from *al-tharb* (the thin fat inside the abdomen and over the paunch). The *tafʿīl* form here indicates removal: the removal of the *tharb*, as in *tajlīd* (flogging) and *taqrīʿ* (chastising), which mean removing the skin and striking. It was borrowed for blame that tears at reputations and removes the brightness of the face, because when fat is removed, emaciation and what is displeasing appear, just as when blame is given, faults become visible. The common element between them is the appearance of deficiency after completeness and the removal of what gives perfection and beauty. ﴿Upon you﴾ is connected to an omitted predicate that occupies the position of the predicate of *lā* (the particle of negation). ﴿Today﴾ is connected either to that omitted predicate or to the adverb, meaning: no reproach is established upon you today. The restriction to "today" is not meant to indicate that reproach occurs at other times, for he, peace be upon him, did not reproach them at the first meeting and the kindling of his anger, so afterwards is even more so.

Al-Murtaḍā said: "Today" is used in place of the whole of time, as in his saying:

*Today, whoever used to envy us shows us mercy, and today we follow those who were once followers of us.*

It is as if the meaning is "after today." Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that it be connected to *tathrīb* (reproach), but Abū Ḥayyān objected, saying: That is not permitted, because *tathrīb* is a verbal noun, and its complement has been separated from it by *ʿalaykum*, which is either a predicate or a qualifier, and separation between them with something of this kind is not allowed, because the complement of a verbal noun is part of it. Also, if it were connected to it, its being built (indeclinable) would not be permitted, because in that case it would be of the type of the one resembling the annexed noun (*shabīh bil-muḍāf*), which is called the extended and the prolonged, and so it must be inflected and nunated. If it is said that the predicate is omitted and ﴿upon you﴾ is connected to an omitted element indicated by ﴿reproach﴾, and that omitted element is what governs *al-yawm* (today), with the sense: no reproach upon you today, as they parsed ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah﴾, meaning: no protector protects today, that would be a strong opinion, because when the predicate of *lā* is known it is often omitted according to the people of the Ḥijāz, while the Banū Tamīm do not pronounce it. Likewise Abū al-Baqāʾ prohibited this and gave as his reason the necessity of the inflection and the nunation. It was objected that what is stated in the grammar texts is that the one resembling the annexed noun is reported to be used without nunation, as in *lā ṭāliʿ jabalan* (there is no one climbing a mountain). And in the hadith: *lā māniʿa li-mā aʿṭayta wa lā muʿṭiya li-mā manaʿta* (there is no preventer of what You have given, and no giver of what You have withheld), which is agreed upon by the narrators. The disagreement is only whether it is indeclinable or inflected with its nunation dropped. In *al-Taṣrīḥ*, quoting *al-Mughnī*, it is stated that the accusative of the one resembling the annexed noun with its nunation is the view of the Basrans, while the Baghdadis permitted *lā ṭāliʿ jabalan* without nunation, treating it as the annexed noun in this respect just as they treated it like the annexed noun in inflection. On this the hadith is explained: *lā māniʿa* ... etc.
