It is possible, then, that the basis of what Abū Ḥayyān and others said is the view of the Basrans. The hadith mentioned does not necessarily have to be understood as Dunūshirī said, following the statement of *al-Mughnī* in the second aspect of the fifth chapter, namely that it may be interpreted as the noun of *lā* being singular, with the *lām* connected to the predicate, and the sense being: *lā māniʿa li-mā aʿṭayta*, and likewise what follows it. Al-Raḍī mentioned that an adverbial phrase after negation is not connected to the negated element but to an omitted element which is the predicate, and that ﴿today﴾ in the verse is the object of ﴿upon you﴾, though the reverse is also permissible. The objection regarding the separation between the verbal noun and its complement with what has been said about it was also raised. It was said: ﴿upon you﴾ is an explanation of the *lām* in *suqyā laka* (watering for you), so it is connected to an omitted element, and ﴿today﴾ is the predicate.

It is also permitted that the predicate is that (i.e., "no reproach") and that ﴿today﴾ is connected to his saying: ﴿May Allah forgive you﴾. It is reported from al-Murtaḍā that he said in *al-Durar*: Some people have weakened this view on the ground that supplication does not govern what precedes it, and this is not well known. Ibn al-Munīr said: If it were connected to it, they would have been certain of forgiveness by the report of the Truthful (Ṣiddīq), and it would not be as they said: ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins﴾. This was answered by saying that there is no benefit in this, because forgiveness, which is the covering of the sin on the Day of Resurrection so that they will not be held to account for it and not be rebuked, occurs only at that time. As for before it, the matter is the announcement of it, and the knowledge of its certain occurrence through the report of the Truthful, and this does not prevent requesting it, because what is impossible is requesting what is already obtained, not requesting what is known to be obtained. Moreover, it is permissible that it be a means of humbling oneself, and the case of the forgiveness sought by the prophets, peace be upon them, is taken as an example. There is no difference between supplication and report here. End.

It may also be said: What they requested from their father was forgiveness for what concerned him and what returned to his right, and they did not have knowledge that this had been realized. Moreover, it is permissible to say that they did not at that time believe in his prophethood, and they thought him to be like themselves, not a prophet, for not much time had passed after the recognition that he was Joseph, and this period is not enough for the recognition that he is also a prophet. What took place in the conversation does not indicate that. Understand this. Many have gone to interpreting the statement as a supplication, while a group also went to its being a report, and this judgment, although it concerns the unseen, was made. It was said: Because he, peace be upon him, pardoned their offence at that time, and they had confessed it too, so there is no doubt that Allah, glorified is He, will forgive them what concerns Him and what concerns Joseph, peace be upon him, by the requirement of His promise, exalted is His majesty, to accept the repentance of His servants. It was also said: Because he, peace be upon him, had been informed of this by revelation. You know that most readers stop at ﴿today﴾, which clearly indicates that it is not connected to ﴿May Allah forgive﴾. This is the choice of al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Isḥāq and others, and they chose that the following sentence is a supplication, which is what inclines the taste. And Allah knows best. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾ For everyone who shows mercy other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, shows mercy only through His mercy, glorified is He, and this is based on bringing benefit or repelling harm; at least it is the repelling of the spiritual pain he feels in himself from what he finds in the one shown mercy. It was also said: Because He, exalted is He, forgives minor and major sins which no one other than Him, glorified is He, forgives, and He bestows His favour on the penitent by accepting them. The sentence is either an explanation of confidence in the answering of the supplication, or a confirmation of the obtaining of forgiveness, because He pardoned them, so Allah, exalted is He, is more worthy of pardon and mercy towards them. This is it.

[Page 51]

Among the generosity of Joseph, peace be upon him, is what is reported: his brothers sent to him saying: "You invite us to your food morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you because of what we did to you." He, peace be upon him, said: "The people of Egypt, even though I have become their ruler, used to look at me with the first eye and say: Glory be to Him who raised a slave who was sold for twenty dirhams to what he has reached. And I have now become honoured by you and exalted in the eyes, since people know that you are my brothers and that I am a descendant of Abraham, peace be upon him." The apparent meaning is that by this there came to people knowledge that had not come before, for he, peace be upon him, as indicated by some of the preceding verses, and the reports had already informed them that he was the son of so-and-so and of such-and-such.

Likewise what Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The king once said to Joseph, peace be upon him: "I love that you mix with me in everything except my family, and I am too proud that you should eat with me." Joseph, peace be upon him, became angry and said: "I have more right to be proud. I am the son of Abraham, the friend of Allah; I am the son of Isaac, the sacrifice of Allah; and I am the son of Jacob, the prophet of Allah." But that did not spread widely, or did not give people knowledge. And in the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews today: when he, peace be upon him, saw his brothers' great embarrassment, he brought the nearest of them to him and said: "Do not let it grieve you that you sold me and brought me to this place, for Allah, exalted is He, knew what would befall you of drought and famine and what would strike you from that. So He did what brought me to this place and this position, to remove from you through me what would fall upon you, and for that to be a cause of your remaining in the land and the spreading of your offspring in it. Two years of the years of drought have passed, and five years remain. Today Allah, exalted is He, has made me a counsellor to Pharaoh, a lord of his household, and a ruler over all the people of Egypt, so let your affair not trouble you."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 93:

﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾ It is the shirt he was wearing at that time, as is the apparent meaning. However, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others that it was the shirt which Allah, exalted is He, clothed Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with when he was thrown into the fire, and it was one of the shirts of Paradise. Ya'qub (peace be upon him), when it reached him, placed it in a silver tube and hung it around the neck of Yusuf. It would not come upon any of the afflictions of this world except that it cured it, by the permission of Allah, exalted is He. This view is weakened by the fact that His saying, ﴿Indeed I smell the scent of Yusuf﴾, indicates that he (peace be upon him) was wearing it as an amulet, as the reference to it with the pronoun suggests. But this weakening is weak, as is not hidden. It has also been said that it is the shirt that was torn from behind, and that he sent it so that he would know that he had been protected from immorality. Its remoteness is not hidden. Whichever it is, the "ba'" (in "bi-qamisi") is either for accompaniment or for attendance, meaning: go taking it with you or carrying it, or it is for transitivity, as has been said, meaning: take away my shirt, this one. ﴿Then cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight﴾, meaning: he will become one who sees. This is supported by ﴿and he regained his sight﴾, or: he will come to me while he is seeing. And His saying supports this: ﴿and bring me all your family﴾. (93) Among the women and descendants and others not covered by the word "family", so they said.

The summary of the two views, as some of the careful scholars have said, is that the "coming" in the first view is metaphorical for "becoming", and the father's coming to him is not mentioned because he is too exalted to be a follower, rather to avoid the command to the brothers to bring him, since that is a kind of compulsion upon the one who is brought, and so it is left to his own choice. In the second view it is literal, and in it is the aforementioned avoidance. And the certainty that he will be among those who come without doubt, out of trust in his affection, and that the purpose of casting it is his coming, in the state he loves, of being healthy and with sound sight. In it is also that his becoming seeing is a settled matter, decided; the discussion is only about whether the casting causes his coming in that condition. So this view is more preferable, although the first, regarding acceptance, holds a place. In it is an indication that he (peace be upon him) had lost his sight. Yusuf's knowledge of that may be by their informing him, and may be by revelation. Likewise his knowledge of what follows from the casting may be from revelation too, or from prior acquaintance with the special properties of that shirt through experience or the like, if by the shirt is meant the one that was in the amulet. The first possibility is certain if by it is meant another, as is apparent.

Al-Imam said: It is possible to say: perhaps Yusuf (peace be upon him) knew that what afflicted his father's sight was only from much weeping and constriction of the heart. So when his shirt is cast upon him, his chest must expand and intense joy must arise in his heart, and that strengthens the spirit and removes weakness from the faculties. Then his sight is strengthened and that deficiency leaves him. This much can be known by reason, for the medical laws indicate its soundness, but I do not see it.

Al-Kalbi said: Those family members were about seventy persons. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that they were seventy-two of his offspring and his offspring's offspring. It was also said: eighty, and it was said: ninety. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Ibn Mas'ud that they were ninety-three, and it was said: ninety-six. They multiplied in Egypt, and then they left it with Musa (peace be upon him), and they were six hundred thousand and five hundred and some seventy men, apart from the descendants and the elderly. The descendants were one million and two hundred thousand, according to what has been said.

﴿And when the caravan departed﴾ it set out from the outskirts of Egypt, heading for the place of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), which was near Bayt al-Maqdis. The claim that it was in al-Jazira is not to be relied upon. It is said: "fasala min al-balad, yafsilu fusulan," when one departs from a town and passes its walls, and it is intransitive. "Fasala al-shay'," meaning "he separated it," is transitive. Ibn 'Abbas read it as ﴿wa-lamma infasala al-'ir﴾ (And when the caravan separated).

﴿Their father said﴾, Ya'qub (peace be upon him), to those who were with him: ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾, that is, "I smell it." This is the existence of the sense of smell. Allah caused him to smell the fragrance of Yusuf (peace be upon him) that clung to the shirt, from a distance of eight days, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said it was from eighty farsakh (a farsakh being a unit of distance, roughly three miles). In another report from al-Hasan, it was from a distance of thirty days, and in yet another from him, from a distance of ten nights. It is also narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Harawi that the wind asked permission to convey the fragrance of Yusuf (peace be upon him), and Allah permitted it. Mujahid said: the wind struck the shirt, and the fragrances of Paradise were carried into this world and reached Ya'qub (peace be upon him), so he found the scent of Paradise, and he knew that there was nothing in this world except that which came from that shirt, and so he said what he said. The idafa (construct phrase) makes this less likely, for it then indicates the slightest connection, whereas before it, although it was also like that, it was far stronger than this, as is clear.

﴿Were it not that you would think me senile﴾ (94). That is, that you would attribute to me ﴿al-fanad﴾ (with two fathas). It is used in the sense of corruption, as in the verse:

"Except Sulayman, when God said to him: Stand in the wilderness and keep it away from al-fanad."

It also means weakness of opinion and intellect due to decrepitude and old age. It is said: "fanada al-rajul" when one attributes al-fanad to him. It is said that it is derived from al-fanad, which is a stone, as if he were made a stone because of his lack of understanding, as it is said:

[Page 54]
"If you have not loved and do not know what passion is, then be a stone, of dry, hard rock."

Then it was extended, so it is said: "fannadahu" when one weakens his opinion and blames him for what he did. The poet said:

"O my blamers, leave off reproach and censure of me, for what I have said of the matter is not to be rejected."

It is also said: "ajfanda al-dahr fulanan," meaning that time corrupted him. Ibn Maqtal said:

"Leave time to do what it wills, for when it is charged with corrupting people, it corrupts."

It is said: "shaykh mufannad" when his opinion has become corrupt. One does not say "'ajuz mufannada," because she has no opinion in her youth to be weakened, as stated by al-Jawhari and other lexicographers. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it in al-Kashshaf and others, and al-Samin found it strange. Perhaps its basis is that she has intellect, though deficient, which is further diminished by old age, so consider this.

The response to ﴿lawla﴾ is omitted, meaning: were it not for your censure of me, you would have believed me, or I would have said: "Indeed, Yusuf is nearby," or "his meeting is near," or something similar. As for the addressees, it is said they were those of his children who remained, apart from those who had gone to obtain provisions, and they were many. It is also said they were his grandchildren and those of his close kin who were present with him, and this is the well-known view.

*"They said"*: i.e., those addressed. *"By God, you are surely in your old error."* That is, you are still astray from the right course, persistently, through excessive love for Joseph, frequent mention of him, expecting to meet him, and making it (that love) firmly established and lasting in you.

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that *al-dalal* (error) here means love. Muqatil said it means misery and hardship. It was also said that it means perdition and loss, from the expression "the water went astray in the milk," meaning it went into it and was lost. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it was interpreted as madness, which is unfitting. It seems that he gave this interpretation for the sake of an explanation of this kind. Qatada said: They spoke a harsh word, one that such people should not say to such a person, peace be upon him. Perhaps they only said this because they thought he had died.

﴿So when the bearer of good news arrived﴾. Mujahid said: he was Yahudha. It is related that he said to his brothers: "You know that I once went to my father with the shirt of grief, so let me go to him with the shirt of joy." Then they left him alone. In another report from Ibn Abbas, he was Malik ibn Dhu'r. The well-known report from him is the one already mentioned. The "an" (أنْ) is a *sila* (a superfluous particle), and its addition after *lamma* (لَمّا) is regular. Ibn Mas'ud read: "and the bearer of good news came from in front of the caravan" (وجاءَ البَشِيرُ مِن بَيْنِ يَدَيِ العِيرِ). This is counted as a reading of interpretation (*qira'at tafsir*, a reading that explains rather than replaces the text).

﴿He cast it﴾, that is, the bearer of good news cast the shirt ﴿over his face﴾, that is, the face of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). It was also said that the subject of "cast" is the pronoun referring to Ya'qub (peace be upon him) as well. The first view is more consistent with his saying: "Cast it over my father's face" (فَألْقَوْهُ عَلى وجْهِ أبِي), and the second view makes it unlikely that the bearer was Malik, as is not hidden. It was said that the second view is more fitting to good manners (*adab*). This is attributed to Farqad, who said: he (peace be upon him) took it, smelled it, then placed it over his eyesight ﴿and he regained his sight﴾. The apparent meaning is that the whole face is intended by "face," and it is the custom that when a person finds an object he believes to carry blessing, he wipes his face with it. It was also said that "face" is used to mean the two eyes, since they are in it. It was also said that the whole is used to mean a part. According to some, *irtadda* (ارْتَدَّ) is among the sisters of *kana* (كانَ), meaning "became," so *basiran* (بَصِيرًا) is its predicate. Abu Hayyan held that it is not among its sisters, so *basiran* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). The meaning is that he returned to his former state of soundness of sight.

Some claimed that the statement implies his sight became stronger than it had been, because *fa'il* (فَعِيلًا) is one of the forms of intensive (hyperbolic) nouns, and it is only changed from *yuf'il* to this form for that meaning. This was refuted on the grounds that *fa'il* here is not intensive, since the intensive form is that which is derived from *fa'il* (فاعِلٍ) by adjustment, whereas *basir* here is an active participle from *basura bi-al-shay'* (بَصُرَ بِالشَّيْءِ), and it follows the pattern of *fa'ula* (فَعُلَ), like *zarufa*, so one says *fa'a zarif*. Even if it meant *mubsir* (مُبْصِرٍ, one who sees), as claimed, it would still not be intensive, because *fa'il* in the sense of *mufil* is not intensive, as in *alim* and *sami'*. In any case, the apparent meaning is that his regaining sight (peace be upon him) by casting the shirt over his face is nothing but a breach of customary practice (*kharq al-'ada*, a miracle), and the miraculous is not novel in this story. It was also said that this happened because he (peace be upon him) was revived until his heart grew strong and his natural warmth increased, so his light reached the brain and passed on to the sight. From this same principle comes the healing of lovers by what blows upon them from the land of the beloved, as one said:

"Indeed I seek healing by every cloud
That blows toward me from the direction of your land, a breeze."

Another said:

"O breeze of the morning, what is it with you? Whenever
You draw near to us, your fragrance spreads sweet.

As if Sulayma had been told of our sickness,
So she gave you her scent, and you came as a physician."

And other things beyond counting, which is close to what I heard a moment ago from the Imam.

Moreover, it is reported in some traditions that he (peace be upon him) asked the bearer: "How is Yusuf?" He said: "He is the ruler of Egypt." He said: "What do I do with rule? On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete." Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan who said: When the bearer came to him (peace be upon him), he said: "You have found nothing with us, and we have not baked bread for seven days, but may Allah make the agonies of death easy for you." It is also reported in another narration that he said to him: "I do not know what reward to give you today," and then he supplicated for him with that.

﴿He said: Did I not tell you﴾. It may be that this is addressed to those who were with him before, meaning: "Did I not tell you that I surely find the scent of Yusuf?" It may also be that it is addressed to his sons who had arrived, meaning: "Did I not tell you not to despair of the mercy of Allah?" This second reading is more fitting with His words: ﴿Indeed I know from Allah what you do not know﴾. (96). The basis of the prohibition is the knowledge that he (peace be upon him) was given from Allah, glorified is He. The sentence, under both possibilities, is a new (independent) clause; under the latter it may be the content of the saying, meaning: "Did I not tell you when I sent you to Egypt and ordered you to search, and forbade you from despairing of the solace of Allah, the Exalted: Indeed I know from Allah what you do not know, concerning the life of Yusuf (peace be upon him)." Al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan) preferred that it is the content of the saying, and that is so.

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins."﴾ They asked him, peace be upon him, to seek forgiveness for them, and they addressed him with the title of fatherhood to stir his compassion and tenderness. They gave the reason for this in their words: ﴿Indeed, we were sinners.﴾ (97) That is, it is among the due right of one who acknowledges his sin that he be pardoned and that forgiveness be sought for him. It seems they were confident of his pardon, and for this reason they limited themselves to asking for forgiveness and included the seeking of pardon within that request. It was also said that when they addressed him in this way, they meant: "And by the right of your compassion for us, ask forgiveness for us, for were it not for that, we would be ruined, having deliberately committed sin. So who will have mercy on us if you do not have mercy on us?" But this is not the case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 98:

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ (98)

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Prophet (marfu'an, meaning the report is attributed directly to the Prophet), that he (peace be upon him) deferred asking forgiveness for them until the pre-dawn (al-sahar), because supplication is answered at that time. It is also narrated from him, in the same manner, that he deferred it until the night of Friday. This is related in a long hadith which al-Tirmidhi transmitted and graded as hasan (sound). It was also said that he deferred it until the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). Ibn Jubayr and a group said: until the white nights (al-layali al-bidh), for supplication is answered during them. Al-Sha'bi said: he deferred it until he asked Yusuf (peace be upon him); if Yusuf pardoned them, he would ask forgiveness for them. It was also said that he deferred it in order to know their state regarding sincere repentance.

Some scholars objected to some of these views, arguing that sawfa (سوف) rules this out, because it is more emphatic than the letter sin (س) in expressing deferment (tanfis), so its proper usage would have been sin. This was answered with what is in al-Mughni (Ibn Hisham's grammar work) that the view mentioned is the position of the Basran grammarians and others, who treat the two as equivalent. Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: this objection is not valid so as to need a reply, because tanfis means deferment in general, even if it is less than an hour. So deferring it until the pre-dawn, for example, and that day passing, is a place for deferment with sawfa.

It was also said: he (peace be upon him) intended continuous asking of forgiveness for them, and this is based on the view that sin and sawfa indicate continuity in the future. There is a discussion on this by the grammarians. Indeed, some reports indicate that he (peace be upon him) continued for a period of time asking forgiveness for them. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Anas ibn Malik who said: When God Most High gathered his family with his sons and comforted his eye, his sons withdrew to speak privately (najiyyan). Some of them said to others: "Do you not know what you did, and what the Shaykh suffered from you, and what Yusuf suffered from you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then their pardon of you may deceive you. So how will you face your Lord?" Their affair settled on going to the Shaykh and sitting before him, with Yusuf beside him. They said: "O our father, we have come to you with a matter we have never come to you with before, and a calamity has befallen us the like of which has never befallen us," until they stirred him, and the prophets (peace be upon them) are the most merciful of creation. He said: "What is wrong with you, my sons?" They said: "Do you not know what we did to you, and what we did to our brother Yusuf?" They said: "Yes." They said: "Have you not pardoned us?" They said: "Yes." They said: "Then your pardon will not avail us anything if God Most High has not pardoned us." He said: "What do you want, my sons?" They said: "We want you to supplicate God, glorified is He. When the revelation comes to you from God Most High that He has pardoned what we did, our eyes will be comforted and our hearts will be at peace; otherwise there will be no comfort of the eye for us in this world, ever." He said: So the Shaykh stood, faced the qiblah, and Yusuf (peace be upon him) stood behind him, and they stood behind both of them, humble and submissive. He supplicated, and Yusuf said "Amin," but He did not answer concerning them for twenty years. When the twentieth year came to an end, Gabriel descended upon Ya'qub, peace be upon them both, and said: "God Most High has sent me to give you glad tidings that He has answered your supplication concerning your son, that He has pardoned what they did, and that He has ratified their covenants after you concerning prophethood."

It was said: this, if authentic, is evidence of their prophethood, and that what came from them occurred before they were made prophets. But the truth is that it is not authentic, and a verification has passed on this which is sufficient, so recall it.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'A'isha who said: The sons of Ya'qub were not forgiven except after twenty years, and their father was before them. They were not forgiven until Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and taught him this supplication: "O Hope of the believers, do not cut off our hope. O Helper of the believers, help us. O Aider of the believers, assist us. O Lover of those who repent, accept our repentance." So he deferred it until the pre-dawn, supplicated with it, and they were forgiven.

Abu 'Ubayd and others transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that what will come, if God wills, is connected to this, and it is among the transposition and displacement of the Qur'an, and the original is: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if God wills." You know that this is something one should not pay attention to, for that is undoubtedly the speech of Yusuf (peace be upon him). I do not know what called for committing it, and perhaps it is pure ignorance.

Know that some later scholars, in discussing this verse, mentioned that the correct view is that "Astaghfiru" (أستغفر) is transitive to two objects, as one says: "I asked God forgiveness for the sin" (استغفرت الله الذنب), and Ibn Hisham explicitly stated this. In "Astaghfir lana" (اسْتَغْفِرْ لَنا), the first of the two objects has been omitted and the second mentioned, while in "Sawfa astaghfiru" (سَوْفَ أسْتَغْفِرُ) the matter is reversed. Perhaps the secret, and God knows best, is that the omission of the first object in the first case is for generality, meaning: ask forgiveness for us for everyone we wronged, so that it includes Him, glorified and exalted, and includes Yusuf, Benjamin and others. The second object was not omitted either, to record upon themselves their committing sins, because the context is one of acknowledging error and seeking compassion for what has passed. So the fitting thing is explicit mention. As for its affirmation in the second case, it is because it is the original, together with an alert that the more important matter to which concern should be directed and the face sincerely turned is asking forgiveness of the Lord and seeking His pleasure, for when He is pleased, He is content. Moreover, Yusuf and his brother had shown signs of pardon, and the tenderness of brotherhood had reached them. As for the omission of the second object in that case, it is for brevity, since it is known from the first, together with the nearness of mention. End quote. Perhaps the deferment according to this is so that their turning to God Most High increases, and that would be more hopeful for achieving the intended aim.

[p. 56]

[p. 57]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 99:**

﴿So when they entered upon Yusuf﴾. It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) sent to his father an provision and two hundred riding animals, so that his father and those with him could prepare to come to him. In the Torah, he (peace be upon him) gave each of his brothers a robe of honor, gave Binyamin three hundred dirhams and five robes of honor, and sent to his father ten donkeys loaded with choice gifts and ten others loaded with wheat and food.

It is also reported in some traditions that he (peace be upon him) went out, together with the king, with four thousand soldiers, nobles and all the people of Egypt to receive them. They met him (peace be upon him) while he was walking, leaning on Yahudha (Judah). He looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, my father, but this is your son Yusuf." It was said to him: "You are coming, and he has made this welcome for you, as you see." When he met him, Yusuf (peace be upon him) went to greet him with the salam first, but this was prevented, so that it would be known that Ya'qub is more honored by Allah the Exalted than he is. So he embraced him, kissed him, and said: "Peace be upon you, O you who have removed sorrows from me."

It is also reported that he (peace be upon him) said to his father: "O my father, you wept for me until your sight went away. Did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and then I would be separated from you."

In the speech there is concision (ijaz), and the implied sense is: "So Ya'qub (peace be upon him) set out with his family, and they traveled until they came to Yusuf. When they entered upon him, and that was, it is said, the day of 'Ashura' (the tenth of Muharram), ﴿he took his two parents to himself﴾, that is, he drew them to himself and embraced them. By "his two parents" are meant his father and his maternal aunt Layya. It was also said: Rahil (Rachel), but this is not the case. The maternal aunt is treated as the mother because of her compassion, just as the paternal uncle is treated as the father. From this is His saying: ﴿and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ (2:133). It was also said that when he (Ya'qub) married her after his mother, she became a stepmother (rabbah) to Yusuf (peace be upon him), so she took the position of a mother because she was like her in being the wife of the father and in standing in her place. A stepmother is called 'mother' even if she is not an aunt. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Some have said: the meant ones are his father and his grandmother, the mother of his mother; this was related by al-Zahrawi. Al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq said that his mother (peace be upon him) was alive, so there is no need for interpretation. But what is well known is that she died at the birth of Binyamin. It is also reported from al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq that this view is held as well, except that they both said: Allah the Exalted restored her to life for him so that his dream would come true. The apparent meaning is that this has not been established, and had such a thing been established, it would have become well known."

In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads: "He took his two parents and his brothers to himself."

﴿And he said: Enter Egypt﴾. It seems that he (peace be upon him) pitched a tent outside the city at the place of meeting, and stayed in it, so they entered upon him there, and he took his parents to himself there. Then he asked them to enter the city. Thus there are two entries: one is their entry upon him outside the city, and the second is their entry into the city. It was also said: they only entered upon him (peace be upon him) in Egypt, and by his saying ﴿Enter Egypt﴾ he meant: settle there and remain in it, ﴿if Allah wills, secure﴾ (99). That is, safe from famine and all other hardships. The exception (istithna'), according to al-Taysir, falls within the security and not within the command to enter, because it only applies to a promise and not to a command. In al-Kashshaf it is said that the will (of Allah) is connected with entering in a state qualified by security, because the intention is to their being characterized by security in their entering. So it is as if it was said: "Submit and be secure in your entering, if Allah wills." The meaning is: "Enter Egypt secure, if Allah wills; you will enter secure." So the apodosis is omitted because the speech indicates it. Then the apodosis clause was inserted between the circumstantial phrase (hal) and the one it qualifies (dhu al-hal). End of quotation. It seems that by his saying "it is as if it was said..." he indicated that the construction carries the meaning of supplication (du'a'). Al-'Allama al-Tibi went this way, and in al-Kashf he said: this contains an indication that the manner is intended by the command, as when you say: "Enter prostrating," you command both. There is no indication in it that the construction carries the meaning of supplication, so the meaning is not according to that. The truth is with al-'Allama, as is not hidden. Sahib al-Fara'id (the author of al-Fara'id) claimed that the sense is: "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills; you will enter secure," so that "secure" is connected to the omitted apodosis, and then there is no need for transposition or for making the apodosis an interposed clause. It was objected to this that there is no doubt that this exception in the middle of the speech is like the basmalah at the start of an action, for blessing and seeking baraka; and using it with the apodosis is like an abrogated law, so it is good for it to be placed in the speech as an interposed element. Understand.

[Page 58]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 100 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And he raised his parents﴾ upon the throne when they came to Egypt, ﴿upon the throne﴾, meaning upon the couch (*sarir*), as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said, honouring them more than he had done with his brothers. ﴿And they fell down before him﴾, that is, his parents and his brothers. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the brothers only, but this is not right, for the dream requires that the two parents and the brothers all fell down before him. ﴿Prostrating﴾, that is, upon their foreheads, as is apparent, and it is, as Abu al-Baqa' said, a *hal muqaddarah* (a circumstantial clause that is anticipated), because prostration comes after falling down. Such a practice was permissible among them, and it functions as a form of greeting and honour, like standing, shaking hands, kissing the hand and similar customs of people that are common in showing reverence and respect. Qatadah said: "Prostration was the greeting of kings among them. Allah the Exalted gave this community (*ummah*) the greeting of the people of Paradise, *al-salam*, as an honour from Him, the Exalted, which He hastened for them." It was also said: it was nothing but a bowing of the head. It was also said: it was like a deep bowing (*ruku'*) without placing the forehead on the ground. It was also said: what is meant is humility, and by falling down is meant passing by, as in His saying: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down upon them deaf and blind﴾. It has been said that what is meant is that they did not pass by them in that manner, but you know that the wording is apparent in the sense of falling down.

It was also said, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, that the meaning is: they fell down on account of Yusuf, prostrating to Allah in thanks for the blessing He had granted them. This was criticised on the grounds that his saying ﴿O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream﴾ refutes it, since in it is ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾. It was answered that the one who holds this view makes the *lam* in both places a *lam* of causation (*ta'lil*). It was also said that the *lam* in both places carries the meaning of *ila* (to), as in *salla li-l-Ka'bah* (he prayed toward the Ka'bah). Hassan said:

I did not know that time would turn away from Hashim, and then from him who is Abu Hasan,
Was he not the first to pray toward your qiblah, and the most knowing of people in matters and the sunan?

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned that the view that the prostration was to Allah the Exalted and not to Yusuf, peace be upon him, is good. The evidence for this is that His saying ﴿and he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him prostrating﴾ indicates that they ascended and then prostrated. Had the prostration been to Yusuf, peace be upon him, it would have occurred before the ascent and the sitting, since that is more emphatic in humility. This is unlike the prostration of thanks to Allah the Exalted. Opposing the apparent order is clearly opposing the apparent meaning. He then addressed what is raised against it, from what you know, with what you know. Then he said: "It is decisive in my view, for it is far from the intellect and religion of Yusuf, peace be upon him, that he would be content for his father to prostrate to him, given his precedence in the rights of parenthood, old age, knowledge, religion and the perfection of prophethood."

It was answered that the delay of the falling down after the raising is not explicit regarding the intended meaning, because the order of mention need not necessarily follow the order of occurrence. Perhaps it was delayed so that there might be joined to it the mention of its being the interpretation of his dream and what is connected to it. It is also possible that Allah the Exalted had commanded Ya'qub to do this for a wisdom known only to Him, and Yusuf, peace be upon him, knew of the matter, so he had no choice but silence and submission. It seems that in His saying ﴿O my father﴾ ... and so on, there is an allusion to this, as if he were saying: "O my father, it is not fitting for one like you, with your eminence in knowledge, religion and prophethood, that you should prostrate to your son. But this is a matter I was commanded to do, and an obligation I was charged with, for the dreams of prophets are true, just as the dream of Ibrahim concerning the slaughter of his son became a cause for the obligation of slaughter in waking life." For this reason it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when he, peace be upon him, saw the prostration of his parents and brothers to him, it alarmed him and his skin shuddered at it. It is not far-fetched that this was part of Allah the Exalted's intensifying the trial for Ya'qub, peace be upon him, as if it were said to him: "You were always longing for his union and grieving at his separation, so when you find him, prostrate to him." It is also possible that he, peace be upon him, did this despite his great rank so that the brothers would follow him in it, since pride may lead them to be proud of it, which would drive to the stirring up of old grudges and the non-forgiveness of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is not hidden that the answer to the first objection does not avail, since you know that its basis is conformity with the apparent meaning. The possibilities mentioned in the answer to the second objection were also mentioned by al-Imam, and they are as you see. The best of them is the possibility that Allah the Exalted commanded him to do so for a wisdom known only to Him.

Some people held that the prostration was only by the brothers, fleeing from attributing it to Ya'qub, peace be upon him, for the reason you know. But this has been refuted by what we indicated earlier, that the dream requires generality. Al-Imam answered this by saying that the interpretation of a dream need not correspond to the dream in every respect of form and attribute. Thus the prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon is interpreted as the greatness of the eminent among people toward him, peace be upon him. There is no doubt that the going of Ya'qub and his sons from Canaan to Egypt because of him is in the utmost degree of honouring him, so this degree is sufficient for the validity of the dream. As for the interpretation being like the original, step by step and exactly, no one of the intelligent has required this. End of quotation. The truth is that the prostration, in whatever sense it was, occurred from both parents and the brothers together. The heart inclines to the view that it was a bowing, like the greeting of non-Arabs and of many people today. It is not far-fetched that it was by falling down, and there is no objection to its being from the two parents while they were on the couch of his kingdom, and his dream does not refuse this, peace be upon him.

﴿From before﴾, that is, from before your prostration, or from before these events. The adverbial phrase is connected to *ru'yaya* (my dream). It was also permitted that it be connected to an interpretation, since the dream was interpreted with this before it occurred. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it be connected to a deleted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from *ru'yaya*, and the validity of ends of phrases (*al-ghayat*) functioning as circumstantial clauses has been discussed earlier.

﴿My Lord has made it true﴾, that is, sincere, and a dream may be described as such, even if metaphorically. A group parsed it as a second object of *ja'ala*, which here means *sayyara* (to make). It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause, meaning He established it correct; that it be an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning a making that is true; and that it be a verbal noun not from the verb's wording but from its meaning, because *ja'alaha* means *haqqaqaha* (made it real), and *haqqan* means realisation. The clause, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is a *hal muqaddarah* or *muqarinah* (a circumstantial clause either anticipated or simultaneous).

﴿And He has been good to me﴾. The original usage, as in al-Bahr, is that *al-ihsan* is followed by *ila* or the *lam*, as in His saying: ﴿And be good as Allah has been good to you﴾. It may also be followed by the *ba'*, as in His saying: ﴿And to the parents, kindness﴾, and as in the words of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

Treat us ill or treat us well, without blame from us,
Nor being disliked, if she turns away.

Some interpreted *ahsana* as including the meaning of *latafa* (to be gentle), and the grace in this is not hidden. However, some objected to the construction of *lataf* with the *ba'*, claiming that it is only followed by the *lam*, so one says *latafa Allahu lahu* (Allah was gentle to him), meaning He conveyed to him his aim by gentleness. This is what is in the *Qamus*, but the known usage is its construction with the *ba'*, and this is explicitly stated in the *Asas*, and this is what is relied upon. It was also said that the *ba'* means *ila*. It was also said that the object is deleted, meaning: be good in His dealing with me, so the *ba'* is connected to the deleted object. In this there is deletion of the verbal noun while its complement remains, which the Basrans forbid. His saying ﴿when He brought me out of the prison﴾ is governed by *ahsin* or by the deleted verbal noun, according to those who permit that. If it is causal (*ta'liliyyah*), then the goodness is the bringing out of prison after he had been tested with it

*[p. 60]*

and what was joined to it. If it is temporal (*zarfiyyah*), then it is other than these two. He, peace be upon him, did not explicitly mention the story of the well, out of fear of reproaching his brothers and out of forgetting what had passed from them, since the apparent sense is that they were present, the speech following directly upon their falling down prostrate. Also, the goodness was only complete after his coming out of prison, with his reaching the king and his freedom from slavery and accusation. He was content with what is implied by his saying ﴿and He brought you from the desert﴾, that is, the *badw* (desert). Its original meaning is the open land, and it was called so because what is in it appears to the viewer, there being nothing to conceal it. Then it was applied to the wilderness in general. Their dwelling was, as it is said, on the borders of Syria, in the desert of Palestine. They were owners of camels and sheep. Al-Zamakhshari said: they were people of tents and owners of herds, moving among the waters and the pastures. Some people claimed that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, moved to the desert only after prophethood, because Allah the Exalted did not send a prophet from the desert. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Ya'qub, peace be upon him, had moved to Bada and settled there, and from there he came to Yusuf, and there is a mosque for him at the foot of its mountain." Ibn al-Anbari said: Bada is the name of a known place; it is said to be between Shi'b and Bada, and these are two places mentioned by Jamil in his saying:

You are the one who made Shi'b beloved to me, toward Bada,
And my homelands are other lands than these two.

So *al-badw* on this view means the going to this place, and it is said *badā al-qawm badwan* when they came to Bada, as one says *aghāru ghawran* when they came to Ghawr. The meaning is: he brought you from the direction of Bada, so they were then town dwellers. This is what al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*, and al-Qushayri mentioned it, but it is very contrary to the apparent sense.

﴿After Satan had stirred up discord between me and my brothers﴾, that is, he corrupted and incited. Its origin is from *nazagha al-rabid al-dabbah* when he goaded the animal and drove it to run. This was attributed to Satan metaphorically, because it was through his whispering and his casting. In it is also an evasion from reproaching them. He mentioned it to magnify the matter of goodness, because blessing after trial has a more beautiful effect. Al-Jubba'i, al-Ka'bi and al-Qadi cited the verse as evidence against compulsion (*jabr*), but there is room for dispute.

﴿Indeed my Lord is gentle with what He wills﴾, that is, gentle in arranging it, since there is no difficulty but that His will takes effect in it, and it becomes easy without it. This is what many said, and its summary is that *al-latif* here means the one who knows hidden matters, who arranges them, and who makes their difficulties easy, and that His will takes effect. Whenever He wills something, He makes its causes easy. He, glorified be His majesty, is called *al-Latif* because what is gentle passes through easily. To this points the speech of al-Raghib, where he said: "*Al-latif* is the opposite of the dense, and by the gentle is expressed light movement and handling of subtle matters. So Allah the Exalted is described by it for His knowledge of subtleties and His kindness to the servants." So the *lam* is connected to *latif*, because the meaning is that He arranges what He wills, according to what many said. Some said: the meaning is "for the sake of what He wills." On the first reading it is transitive with the *lam*, and on the second it is not transitive with it. What is in this has already been mentioned.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of the aspects of the interests, ﴿the All-Wise﴾. (100) Who does everything in accordance with wisdom, and none other than Him.

It is related that Yusuf took his father, peace be upon them both, around his treasuries, and when he brought him into the treasury of the papers (*qirtas*), he said: "O my son, how disobedient you are to me! These papers, and what you wrote to me from eight stages (of travel)!" He said: "Gabriel commanded me." He said: "Did you not ask him?" He said: "You are more open with him than I am." So he asked him. Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "Allah the Exalted commanded me to do that because of your saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him﴾." He said: "Then why did you not fear me?"

*[p. 61]*

This is a good objection-and-answer passage; I'll translate it faithfully.

This is a clear excuse for Yusuf, peace be upon him, for not informing his father of his safety. Several scholars have stated explicitly that he, peace be upon him, was inspired (awhā ilayhi) to keep the matter hidden from his father until the decreed term (al-Kitāb ajalahu) is reached. But the question remains: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was among the greatest of the prophets in person, as a father and as a grandfather, and was famous throughout the corners of the earth. Yet one who was such, then suffered a tremendous calamity concerning the dearest of his sons to him, that calamity could not have remained hidden; rather, it must have become so widely known that everyone would have known of it, especially since a long period passed while he was in that grief, which became proverbial. And Yusuf, peace be upon him, was not in a place far from his place, nor did he settle in hidden corners, nor was he obscure in reputation; rather, he was the place of return for the common and the elite, and a caller to Allah the Exalted in private and in public, in times of joy and in times of trial. So how could his affair have been obscured, and his news not reach his father?

It is answered that this is nothing but a matter of breaking the customary course (min bāb kharq al-'ādah), and scholars differed about the length of the period between the dream and the manifestation of its interpretation. It was said: eighteen years. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, in his Zawa'id al-Zuhd, transmitted from al-Hasan that the period was eighty years. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that it was ninety-seven years, and from Hudhayfah that it was seventy years. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah that it was thirty-five years. A group transmitted from Salman al-Farisi that it was forty years, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn Shaddad said: at this point the interpretation of the dream concludes, and Allah the Exalted knows best the realities of matters.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 101:

﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me of the kingdom﴾, meaning a great portion of it. The *min* here is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*). The view that it is redundant (*ziyada*) or that it specifies the genus (*li-bayan al-jins*) is far-fetched, and magnifying the matter is part of what the context requires. Some scholars supplied *'azīman* (great) in the noble text as its object, as Abu al-Baqa' transmitted, but this is nothing. The apparent meaning is that he intended by that portion the kingdom of Egypt, while ﴿the kingdom﴾ encompasses Egypt and other lands. From the words of some scholars it may be understood that ﴿the kingdom﴾ could mean Egypt and the portion could mean some part of it. One of them claimed that this does not contradict the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Thus did We establish Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, because he was not independent in it, though he was empowered. But this requires reflection. It was also said that he meant the kingdom of his own self, in carrying out his desires. 'Ata' said: he possessed his enviers through obedience and the attainment of hopes, but this is not the meaning.

﴿And You have taught me of the interpretation of events﴾, meaning some of that as well. The intended meaning of *ta'wil al-ahadith* (the interpretation of events) is either the teaching of the interpretation of dreams, which is the apparent meaning, or the making understood of the hidden secrets of the divine books and the subtle details of the ways of the prophets. On both interpretations, peace be upon him, was not given all of that. The ordering according to the non-apparent meaning is clear. As for the apparent meaning, the placing of the bestowal of kingship before that in mention is perhaps because the context is one of enumerating the blessings flowing upon him from Allah, the Glorified, and kingship is more deeply rooted in being such than the teaching mentioned, although that too is a great blessing in itself. So reflect and ponder.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Dhar read (*ataytani* and *'allamtani*) with the *ya'* omitted in both, relying on the kasra. Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from the latter (*ataytani*) without *qad*.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning their Creator and Inventor. It is in the accusative either as an adjective of *Rabb*, or as an apposition, or as an explanation, or as governed by *a'ni* (I mean), or as a second vocative. Describing Him, exalted is He, with this after describing Him with lordship is an exaggeration in arranging the beginnings of what follows from His saying: ﴿You are my Guardian﴾, the one who manages my affairs and undertakes them, or the one who is loyal to me and a helper in this world and the Hereafter. So *wali* is either in the sense of guardianship or of loyal support. It is also permitted that it means *mawla* (master), like *mu'ti* (giver) in form and meaning, i.e., the One who gives me the blessings of this world
[Page 62]
and the Hereafter. ﴿Take me [in death]﴾, i.e., seize me, ﴿as a Muslim and join me with the righteous﴾. (101)

From my forefathers, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, or with the righteous in general, in rank and honor, as has been said. It was objected that Joseph, peace be upon him, is among the great prophets, and righteousness is the first of the degrees of believers, so how is it fitting for him to ask to be joined to one who is at the beginning? It was answered that he, peace be upon him, asked for it out of humbling himself, so his way is the way of the prophets' seeking forgiveness. There is no question and no answer if what is meant by the righteous is his noble forefathers: Ya'qub, Ishaq and Ibrahim, peace be upon them.

The Imam said: Here and there is another station in the verse, according to the people of unveilings (*ahl al-mukashafat*, mystics who receive divine disclosures). It is that when the separated souls (*al-nufus al-mufaraqa*) are illuminated with divine lights and the sanctified radiance, and they are mutually compatible and alike, the light that is in each of them is reflected to the other because of that harmony and kinship, so those lights become greater and those lustres grow stronger. An example of this is polished, pure mirrors: when they face one another and the sun shines upon them, the light is reflected from each of them to the other, and there the light grows, the radiance becomes complete, and the brilliance and gleam reach a degree that weak eyes can bear. Thus it is here. The Imam ended. And it is, as you see, [far-fetched].

The truth is that righteousness is predicated by gradation (*maqul bi-l-tashkik*), varying in strength and weakness, and the context requires that he, peace be upon him, meant by the righteous those characterized by the rank that is given attention among the ranks of righteousness. We have already mentioned what the people of unveilings say about righteousness, so refer back to it.

There remains the question of whether the scholars of tafsir differed over whether this (the request) is from him, peace be upon him, a wish for death and a request for it, or not. Most of them held that he asked and wished for it. The Imam said: It is not far-fetched for a rational man, when his intellect is complete, to wish for death and to have a great desire for it, because then he perceives his deficiency, together with his eagerness for its removal, and his knowledge that absolute perfection belongs only to Allah, the Exalted. So he remains in an unrest that only death removes, and therefore he wishes for it. Also, he sees that worldly happiness is quickly gone, on the brink of annihilation, and the pain that arises when it departs is greater than the pleasure that arises when it is attained. Moreover, there is no pleasure except that it is mixed with what spoils it. Indeed, if it were examined closely, you would not find any real pleasure in these bodily delights; what they amount to is the repelling of pains. The pleasure of eating is nothing but the repelling of the pain of hunger. The pleasure of intercourse is nothing but the repelling of the pain arising from the tickling caused by the arrival of semen in its vessels. Likewise, leadership and rule repel the pain arising from the desire for vengeance and the like. All of these are base in that respect. Through death one is freed from need for them. Moreover, the core of worldly pleasures is eating, intercourse and leadership, and each of these in itself is base and blameworthy. Eating is the moistening of food with the saliva gathered in the mouth, and there is no doubt that this is repugnant in itself. Then when it reaches the stomach, transformation and putrefaction appear in it. Despite that, man shares it with base animals: the dung beetle delights in dung as a man delights in sweets. The wise have said: whoever's aspiration is what enters his belly, his worth is what leaves his belly. Intercourse is at its utmost described as the expulsion of a residue produced from food, by means of a skin tanned with urine and menstrual and postpartum blood, with movements that, if you saw them from another, would make you laugh; and in it too is that shared quality. The most that is hoped from it is the attaining of a child, which brings preoccupation of the mind and scheming to gather wealth and the like. As for leadership, when there is nothing in it but that it is always on the verge of vanishing, because of the many who contend for it and whose gaze covets it, its possessor is ever fearful and anxious about that, and that alone would suffice as its defect. It may also be said: the soul was created disposed to seek pleasures and to have a fierce passion for them, and a complete desire to reach them. So as long as it is in this bodily life, it seeks them, and as long as it is so, it is in the very midst of calamities and the depths of regrets. This consequence is disliked, and what necessitates it is likewise. Therefore the wise man wishes for the end of this bodily life so that he may rest from that toil. And to Allah, the Exalted, belongs the saying of one who said:

*The bed of death is a sleep in which the body rests,*
*while life is like sleeplessness.*

And he said:

*All of life is toil, so I wonder at none but one who desires increase.*
*Surely grief at the hour of loss*
*is multiples of joy at the hour of birth.*

Many have mentioned that wishing for death out of love for meeting Allah, the Exalted, is nothing to be faulted. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him," and the hadith continues. Yes, wishing for death when a calamity has come down is forbidden. In the report: "None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him."

Others said: He, peace be upon him, did not wish for death; he only enumerated Allah's blessings upon him, then prayed that those blessings would endure for the rest of his life, so that when his appointed time came, He would take him in Islam and join him with the righteous.

The conclusion is that he, peace be upon him, sought only to be found (at death) upon Islam, not merely to die. Nothing contradicts the two views in that it is known that prophets, peace be upon them, do not die except as Muslims: either because Islam here means submission to all that Allah has decreed, or because this is an explanation, since, though it does not fail, it is only by the will and decree of Allah, the Exalted. Those who adopt the first view say that a week had not passed before Allah took him. Al-Hasan adopted the second view and said: he, peace be upon him, lived for many years after this request.

The historians related that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, remained with Yusuf for twenty-four years, then died, and he bequeathed that he be buried in al-Sham beside his father. So Yusuf took him and buried him there, and he (Yusuf) lived after him for twenty-three years, or it was said more. Then his soul yearned for an everlasting kingdom, so he wished for death, and Allah took him in a good and pure state. The people of Egypt then disputed over his burial place until they nearly came to fighting. So they decided to place him in a chest of marble and bury him in the Nile, so that the water would pass over him and then reach Egypt, so that they would have a share in him. They did so. Then Musa, peace be upon him, wished to move him to the burial place of his forefathers. So he brought him out, after four hundred years, according to what is said, from the marble chest because of its weight, and placed him in a wooden coffin, and transported him there. His age was a hundred and twenty years. It was said: a hundred and seven years. From the wife of the Aziz he had Ifrathim, who was the grandfather of Yusha' (Joshua), peace be upon him, and Mishā, and Rahma, the wife of Ayyub (Job), peace be upon him. After him, the Pharaohs inherited Egypt from the Amalekites, and the Children of Israel remained under their hands on the remnants of the religion of Yusuf and his forefathers, peace be upon them, until Allah, the Exalted, sent Musa, peace be upon him, and what happened, happened.

In the Torah it is said that Yusuf, peace be upon him, settled his father and brothers in a place called Ain Shams in the land of al-Sadir, and he remained there seventeen years. His age when he entered Egypt was a hundred and thirty years. When his death drew near, he summoned Yusuf, peace be upon him, who came with his two sons, Mishā, who was his firstborn, and Ifrathim. He brought them to him, prayed for them, placed his right hand on the head of the younger and his left on the head of the elder. Yusuf wished the opposite of that, so he spoke to his father about it. He said: "My son, I know that what descends from this younger will be more numerous than what descends from this elder." And he prayed for Yusuf, and blessed him, and said: "My son, I am dying. May Allah, the Exalted, be with you and return you to the land of your father. My son, when I die, do not bury me in Egypt, but bury me in the burial place of my forefathers." Yusuf said: "Yes, my father," and he swore to him. Then he called all his sons and informed them of what would befall them in their days. Then he charged them to bury him beside his forefathers in the land that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had bought from Ephron the Hittite in the land of al-Sham, and made it a burial ground. When he had finished his testament, peace be upon him, he died. Yusuf, peace be upon him, threw himself upon him, kissing him and weeping, and grieved greatly. The people of Egypt also grieved for him greatly. Then Yusuf went with him, along with his brothers and all his family except the children, accompanied by the king's commanders and the elders of the people of Egypt, and they buried him in the place he had wished. Then they returned. Yusuf's brothers feared that he, peace be upon him, would treat them badly after their father's death. When he learned of this from them, he said to them: "Do not fear; I fear Allah, the Exalted." Then he consoled them and comforted their hearts. Then he and his father's family settled in Egypt, and he lived a hundred and ten years, until he saw grandchildren of Ifrathim, three generations. The sons of Makir son of Manasseh were also raised in his lap. Then, when he sensed the nearness of his end, he said to his brothers: "I am dying, and Allah, the Glorified, will remember you and return you to the land which He swore to give to Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub. When He, the Glorified, remembers you and returns you to that land, carry my bones with you." Then he, peace be upon him, died, and they embalmed him and placed him in a coffin in Egypt. He remained until the time of Musa, peace be upon him. When Musa departed, he carried him, as he had instructed, peace be upon him.

﴿Dhalika﴾ (That) refers to what has been mentioned of the news of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the sense of distance it carries, as has been explained many times before. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). It is the subject (mubtada'), and His statement, exalted is He, ﴿from the news of the unseen﴾, which no one hovers around, is the predicate (khabar). His statement, glorified is He, ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ is a second predicate after the first, or a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in the predicate. It is also permitted that ﴿dhalika﴾ be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) serving as the subject, with ﴿from the news of the unseen﴾ as its relative clause and ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ as its predicate. This is based on a less preferred view, which treats the other demonstrative nouns as relative pronouns too.

﴿And you were not with them﴾, meaning the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿when they agreed upon their plan﴾, which was their placing him in the depths of the well, ﴿while they were scheming﴾ (102). Against him, and plotting harm for him. The clause is said to serve as evidence that this is from the news of the unseen and is revealed to him, peace and blessings be upon him. The meaning is that this report is unseen, and you knew it only through revelation, because you were not present with the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when they resolved on what they intended, namely to place him in the depths of the well while scheming against him. It is well known, and not hidden from your deniers, that you never met anyone who heard that and then you learned it from him. This is from the theological (kalami) method, as several scholars have stated. The final part was omitted, although what indicates the matter mentioned is both of the two things together, because it is known from another verse, such as His statement: ﴿You did not know it, neither you nor your people, before this﴾.

Some verifiers said: this is a mockery of those who denied him. This is because He, exalted is He, made the doubtful matter his, peace be upon him, being present before the sons of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, as schemers, and then He negated it by His statement: ﴿And you were not with them﴾. What a doubter could doubt before acquiring knowledge is his receiving it from the people of this story, and the apparent sense of the speech was that this should be negated. So He did not make the doubtful matter something beyond doubt, because his, peace and blessings be upon him, not meeting anyone or hearing from anyone was, to them, as clear as the break of dawn. The thorough mockery came, and the resulting meaning became: "You have known, O obstinate ones, that he was not a witness to the past generations, and your denial of what he reported leads you to be obstinate by claiming that he witnessed those among them who passed away." This is like His statement: ﴿Or were you witnesses when God enjoined this upon you?﴾ From this appears the benefit of shifting from the style of ﴿You did not know it, neither you nor your people﴾ to this style, which is more eloquent than what was mentioned first. Another subtle point is also mentioned for leaving that out: the thing mentioned is their scheming and what they plotted, and it is among what they concealed so that no one else would know it, so it is not possible to learn it from others. This is not free of beauty. Whichever of these is the case, the verse contains a declaration that the report mentioned is the truth that corresponds to reality, and that what the People of the Book transmit is not as it really is.

Page 65

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 103:

﴿And most of the people﴾. The apparent meaning is generality. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the people of Makkah. ﴿Even if you were eager﴾, i.e., for their faith, and you exerted yourself in displaying the decisive signs that indicate your truthfulness to them, ﴿they would not be believers﴾. (103)

This is because of their determination upon disbelief and their persistence in obstinacy, a decisive judgment required by their state of readiness. The verb (haraṣa) (to be eager, to covet) is of the pattern (ḍaraba) and (ʿalima), and both are eloquent usages in the language. The answer to (law) (if) is omitted, because it is known, and the clause is a parenthetical insertion between the subject and the predicate.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him), and it was revealed explained in full detail. The Prophet (ﷺ) hoped that this would be the cause of their Islam. It was also said: they promised him that they would embrace Islam, and when they did not do so, Allah consoled him with this. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. It was said: concerning the Christians. It was said: concerning the polytheists only. It was said: concerning the People of the Book only. It was said: concerning the Zoroastrians (al-Thanawiyya).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 104:

﴿And you do not ask them for it﴾, i.e., for this news, or for its kind, or for the Qur'an; whichever it is, the pronoun refers to what is understood from what precedes it. The meaning is: you do not seek from them, in return for conveying it, ﴿any reward﴾, i.e., any wage whatsoever, as the carriers of reports (ḥamalat al-akhbar) do. ﴿It is nothing but a reminder﴾, i.e., it is nothing but admonition and exhortation from God, Exalted is He, ﴿to the worlds﴾, entirely. The sentence serves as a justification for what precedes it, because general admonition is incompatible with taking payment from some of them, since it is not restricted to them. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that it is nothing but an admonition from God, glorified is He, which I have been commanded to convey, so it has become obligatory upon me; how then would I ask a reward for performing an obligation? This is contrary to the apparent sense, and on this reading the verse becomes evidence for the prohibition of taking payment for the performance of obligatory duties. And Mubashshir ibn Ubayd read it as (وما نَسْألُهم), with the nun.

[p. 66]

﴿And how many a sign﴾, i.e., and how many a sign. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: *ka'ayyin* is a noun, in meaning like *kam* (how many) which expresses multiplicity and is in the informative mode. It is composed of the particle of comparison *ka-* and *ayyin*, the interrogative *ayyin* with tanwin. It has been reported (in its composed form), and for this reason it is permissible to pause on it with the nun, because the tanwin, once it entered the composition, resembled an original nun. For this reason it is written with a nun in the Mushaf. Whoever pauses on it by dropping the nun considers its original ruling. It has also been said that the *kaf* in it is the extra (*za'ida*) one. Ibn 'Usfur said: "Do you not see that you do not intend by it the meaning of comparison, and yet it is obligatory and not connected to anything, and *ayyin* is its genitive complement?" It has also been said that it is a simple noun, and Abu Hayyan preferred this. He said: "What indicates this is the Arabs' playing with it in their dialects. Its use for interrogation is rare, to the point that the majority denied it." From this is the statement of Ubayy to Ibn Mas'ud: "*Ka'ayyin* do you recite a verse of Surat al-Ahzab?" He said: "Seventy-three." The usual use of it is informative, and it requires to be at the head of its clause, so it does not take a genitive preposition, contrary to Ibn Qutayba and Ibn 'Usfur. It does not need a transmitted authority, and analogy with *kam* requires that it be followed by a noun in the genitive (*mudaf*). It is not memorized (as such), and it is not predicated of except by a verbal clause beginning with a past or present verb, as here. Abu Hayyan said: "By analogy it should be in an accusative position, as an absolute object, an adverb of time or place, or the predicate of *kana*, just as that is the case with *kam*." In the *Basit* it is said that it may be a subject and predicate, and also an object. It is also pronounced *ka'in*, with a long vowel, in the pattern of the active participle of *kana*, with a quiescent nun, and Ibn Kathir recited it thus. (It is also read) *ka* with a short vowel, in the pattern of *'ama*. (*Ka'ayy*) in the pattern of *rama*, and Ibn Muhaysin recited it thus. (*Ka'iy*) with the *ya'* placed before the hamza. Sahib al-Lawami' mentioned that al-Hasan recited *kai* with a kasra on the ya', without hamza, alif or shadda.

﴿sign﴾ is in the position of a specification (*tamyiz*). The *min* is extra, and the genitive of the specification of *ka'ayyin* with it is the usual rule, or the more frequent one. It has also been said that *min* is explaining the implied specification. By "sign" is meant the proof of the existence of the Creator, His oneness, the perfection of His knowledge and power. Although it is singular in form, it is plural in meaning, i.e., signs, because of the place where it occurs. The meaning is: and however many of the signs that prove the truth of what you have brought you wish, other than this sign, ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., existing in them, from the celestial bodies, the stars and the changes of their states, and from the mountains, the seas, and all the other wonders in the earth that are beyond counting, for limitation:

*And in every thing there is a sign that indicates that He is One.*

﴿they pass by them﴾, they see them. ﴿and they turn away from them﴾, not reflecting upon them, nor taking heed from them. In this there is an emphasis of the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and a censure of the people for what is in them. The apparent view is that ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ is in the position of an adjective to *aya* (sign), and the clause ﴿they pass by﴾ is the predicate of *ka'ayyin*, as we have indicated earlier. The reverse has also been permitted. 'Ikrima and 'Amr ibn Qa'id recited *wal-ardu* (and the earth) with a nominative ending, so that *fi as-samawat* is the predicate of *ka'ayyin*, and *al-ard* is a subject whose predicate is the clause after it. The pronoun in *'alayha* then refers to the earth, not to the signs, as in the well-known recitation. Al-Suddi recited *wal-arda* with an accusative ending, as an object of a verb omitted that is explained by ﴿they pass by﴾. This is the construction called *al-ishtighal al-mufassar* (the verb-occupied construction, where the omitted verb is explained by a verb of similar meaning). The pronoun in *'alayha* is as it was before, i.e., "and they tread the earth; they pass by upon it." It has also been permitted to posit *yatauna* (they tread) as governing *al-ard*, and the clause ﴿they pass by﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it or from the pronoun of its governing word.

'Abdullah recited *wal-ardu* with a nominative ending and *yamshuna* (they walk) instead of *yamurruna* (they pass by). The meaning according to the three recitations is that they come and go on the earth, and see the traces of the destroyed nations and the signs and lessons in them, and yet do not reflect upon that.

﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾ in their affirmation of His existence and His being the Creator, ﴿except that they are associators [of others with Him]﴾. (106) With Him, glorified is He. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to "most of them," meaning: most of them do not believe except while they are associating others with Him. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, and Qatādah said: they are the people of Mecca. They believed and associated others [with God]. In their talbiyah (the pilgrim's chant), they used to say: "Here I am, O God, here I am; here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." Hence, "When the Prophet (ﷺ) heard one of them say, 'Here I am, You have no partner,' he would say to him: 'Qatt, qatt,' meaning: that is enough for you, and do not add anything except a partner..." etc.

It was also said: they are those who believed when the smoke overtook them in the years of drought, and then returned to association after it was lifted. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah, and Mujāhid that these are the disbelievers of the Arabs in general: they affirmed the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of death, but associated others by worshipping idols and images. It was also said: they associated others by their saying, "The angels are the daughters of God," glorified is He. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that they are the People of the Book: they affirmed God, the Exalted, but associated others with Him by disbelieving in His Prophet (ﷺ), or by worshipping ʿUzayr and al-Masīh, peace be upon them both.

It was also said: they associated others by adopting [sons] and by taking their rabbis and monks as lords. It was said: they are the disbelievers who sincerely call upon God in times of distress but associate others with Him once they are saved from it; this is related from ʿAṭāʾ. It was said: they are the Thanawiyyah (dualists), who believed in Light and Darkness. It was said: they are the hypocrites who displayed faith and concealed disbelief; this is attributed to al-Balkhī. It is reported from al-Habr (the learned one, i.e., Ibn ʿAbbās) that they are the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) who believed in general terms and disbelieved in detail. It is reported from al-Ḥasan that they are those who show off in their deeds, and showing off is hidden association. It was said: they are those who look to means and rely upon them. It was said: they are those who obey creatures in disobedience to the Creator. It may also be said, considering the implication of the verse, that they include everyone who affirms God, the Exalted, and His Creatorship, for example, but who commits what counts as association in whatever form it takes. Among them are the worshippers of graves, who vow to them and believe that benefit and harm come from those whose state God, the Exalted, knows best. Today they are more numerous than worms. The Karramiyah (a sect) cited the verse as evidence that faith is merely verbal affirmation, but there is room for scrutiny in this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 12, verses 107–108:**

﴿Are they then secure from the overwhelming punishment of Allah?﴾ That is, a punishment that will cover them and encompass them. The interrogative is one of denial, carrying the sense of reproach and threat, as in al-Bahr (the exegesis *al-Bahr al-Muhit*). The discussion of the conjunction and the grammatical position of the interrogative is well known in its essentials and has been mentioned more than once before.
