By this punishment is meant what includes both the worldly and the otherworldly, according to what has been said. In al-Bahr there is something explicit about the worldly, by way of contrast with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Or the Hour will come upon them suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, without any prior sign, and this is the apparent meaning, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ its coming, not prepared for it.

﴿Say: This is my way﴾, that is, this is the way, which is the calling to faith and monotheism, my way. So they have said, though the apparent meaning is that they took the calling to faith from His words, exalted is He: ﴿And most of mankind will not believe, however eager you are﴾, to convey that he calls them to faith with earnestness and zeal, even if it does not benefit them. And the calling to monotheism is from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except that they associate others with Him﴾, because it indicates that its being a reminder for them, by its including monotheism, is so, but they do not raise their heads to it, like all the signs of the horizons and of the souls that point to His unity, exalted is He, in essence and attributes. This was explained by His words, exalted is He: ﴿I call to Allah﴾, that is, I call people to knowing Him, glorified is He, through the attributes of His perfection and the descriptions of His majesty, and monotheism is among them. So the clause has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical parsing).

It has also been said that the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*, circumstantial accusative) relating to the *ya'* (the pronoun of "I"), and the governing element in it is the sense of pointing. This has been criticised on the ground that a circumstantial clause coming from a genitive-attached noun in such a construction contradicts the rules apparently, and that it is not like ﴿Follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (hanifan)﴾. It was also objected that this involves restricting a thing by itself, and that is not the case.

﴿On clear insight﴾, that is, with clear proof and evident evidence, not blind. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿I call﴾. Abu Hayyan claimed that the apparent connection is that it attaches to "I call." The words, exalted is He: ﴿I am﴾ are an emphasis for that pronoun or for the pronoun in the circumstantial phrase. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and whoever follows me﴾ are conjoined to the one who has the circumstance, and the attribution of "I call" to him is by way of prominence (*taghlib*), as was established in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾. Some have posited in such cases a verb governing the conjoined noun, but the verifying scholars did not rely on it. Its conjunction to "I am" was prohibited on the ground that it is an emphasis, and it is not valid for the conjoined element to be an emphasis just as the element it is conjoined to is. It was objected that this is not necessary, as the words of the verifying scholars imply. It was also permitted that "whoever" (*man*) be a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "and whoever follows me is likewise," that is, a caller. And it is permitted that ﴿on clear insight﴾ be a fronted predicate, with "I am" as the subject and what is conjoined to it as well.

﴿And glory be to Allah﴾, that is, I declare Him far above, glorified and exalted is He, with an absolute declaration of His freedom from partners. This is included under the "saying." Likewise ﴿and I am not of those who associate others with Allah﴾. (108) At any time whatsoever. The statement confirms what preceded concerning the calling to Allah, exalted is He.

And 'Abd Allah recited ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ with the masculine form. The word "way" (*sabil*) is feminine, and it may also be masculine.

[Page 68]

Verse 109 is a rebuttal of their saying, "If your Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels" (*law shaa'a rabbuka la-anzala malaa'ikatan*), and a denial of it. It is also said that the intended meaning is the denial that women can be prophets, and this is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both. Some claimed that the verse was revealed concerning Sajah bint al-Mundhir, the self-proclaimed prophetess, about whom the poet says:

"Our prophetess has become a woman, circled around;
yet the prophets of Allah have always been men.

So the curse of Allah and of all the peoples
be upon Sajah and upon whoever led her astray with falsehood,

I mean Musaylima the liar, may he never be watered,
his echoes, with rain-cloud water wherever they may be."

This claim has no soundness, because her claim to prophethood came after the Prophet ﷺ, and the fact that it is a report of the unseen has no indication supporting it.

*﴿Nuhi ilayhim﴾* means "We reveal to them, as We revealed to you." Most of the Seven Readers read *yuha* with a *ya'* and a fatha on the *ha'*, in the passive voice. The reading with *nun*, which is the reading of Hafs, Talha and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, is consistent with *arsalna* (We sent).

*﴿Min ahl al-qura﴾* (from the people of the towns): because their people, as Ibn Zayd and others said, are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the desert. There is no doubt about this. That is why it is said: "The people of the desert are the people of harshness." They mention that living in the desert (*al-tabaddi*) is disliked, except during times of strife. A hadith says: "Whoever dwells in the desert becomes harsh." Qatada said: "We do not know that Allah ever sent a messenger except from the people of the towns." It is reported from al-Hasan that he said: "No messenger was sent from the people of the desert, nor from women, nor from the jinn." As for His saying, *﴿Wa jaa'a bikum min al-badw﴾* (and He brought you from the desert), its discussion has already passed a moment ago.

*﴿Afa-lam yasiru fi al-ard fa-yandhuru kayfa kana 'aqibatu alladhina min qablihim﴾* (Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the end of those before them?): of those who denied the messengers and the signs, from the people of Noah, the people of Lot, the people of Salih and all others whom Allah punished, so that they would beware of denying you. This was narrated from al-Hasan. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the end of those before them who were infatuated with the world and consumed by it, so that they would give it up and refrain from loving it. It seems that the one who permitted this interpretation had in mind what will be mentioned. The interrogative here, in the view of the grammarians, is for reproach and rebuke.

*﴿Wa-la-dar al-akhirati﴾* (and surely the abode of the Hereafter): according to the Kufans, this is an attributive construction (*idafat al-sifa ila al-mawsuf*), meaning *wa-la al-dar al-akhira* (and the Hereafter abode). The Basrans supposed a noun modified by it, meaning *wa-la-dar al-hal* (the abode of the state), or *al-sa'a* (the Hour), or *al-hayat al-akhira* (the Hereafter life). This is the preferred view of most scholars in such cases. *﴿Khayrun lilladhina ittaqaw﴾* (is better for those who are God-conscious), i.e., those who avoid shirk and sins. *﴿Afa-la ta'qilun﴾* (Will you not then use your reason?). (109). That is, will you not use your intellects so that you know the superiority of the abode of the Hereafter and thus seek to reach it through God-consciousness?

It has been said that this is part of what is said after *qul* (say), meaning: "Say to them, addressing them: *afa-la ta'qilun*." In that case the address is on its apparent level. The Exalted's saying *﴿Wa ma arsalna min qablika﴾* up to *﴿min qablihim﴾* or up to *﴿ittaqaw﴾* is a parenthetical clause between the speech of the saying and what is said. Some scholars inferred that this is an iltifat (a shift in address). A group read *ya'qilun* with a *ya'*, in consideration of His saying *﴿Afa-lam yasiru﴾*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 110 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾ is a terminal clause (ghayah) for an omitted element indicated by the context. According to some, the implied meaning is: "Let not their prolonged ease and comfort in what they enjoy deceive them, for those before them were given respite until the messengers despaired of victory over them in this world, or of their faith, because they were immersed in disbelief and persisted in rebellion without any restraint." Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: The implied meaning is: "We did not send before you except men, who called their peoples and were denied, and they endured. Their call and their peoples' denial were prolonged, ﴿until, when they despaired﴾ ... etc." Al-Qurtubi said: The implied meaning is: "We did not send before you except men, then We did not punish their nations, until, when they despaired ... etc." Al-Zamakhshari said: The implied meaning is: "We did not send before you except men, so the victory was delayed, until, when ... etc." Perhaps the first view is preferable, although it involves much omission, and the form istif'al (ist-f'ala) carries the meaning of the basic form (mujarrad), as we have indicated
[p. 69]
earlier, and the discussion of this has already passed.

﴿And they thought that they had been denied﴾ is read with the lightened form and the passive voice (kudhibu). This is the reading of Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Talha, al-A'mash, and the Kufans. Scholars differ on how the verse is to be understood with this reading. It is said: the three pronouns refer to the messengers, and "thought" (zann) means "supposed" (tawahhum), neither in its original meaning nor in its figurative meaning, which is certainty. The implied subject of "they were denied" is either their own souls (anfusuhum) or their hope (raja'uhum), since hope may be described as true or false. That is, their souls deceived them when they told them that they would be victorious, or their hope of victory deceived them. The meaning is that the period of denial and enmity from the disbelievers, and the waiting for victory from Allah the Exalted, had been prolonged and extended, until they sensed despair and supposed that there would be no victory for them in this world. ﴿Our victory came to them﴾ suddenly. It is also said: all the pronouns refer to the messengers, "thought" carries its ordinary meaning, and the implied subject of "they were denied" is whoever informed them about Allah the Exalted. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Al-Tabarani and others related from Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulayka, who said: Ibn Abbas recited "qad kudhibu" with the lightened form, then said: "It means they were broken faith with, and they were human beings." He recited: ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: When is the victory of Allah?﴾ Ibn Abi Mulayka said: Ibn Abbas held that they despaired or weakened, so they supposed that they had been broken faith with. Al-Bukhari narrated this from him in the Sahih. This has been objected to on the ground that it contains what is not fitting to attribute to the prophets, peace be upon them, but rather to the righteous of the community. For this reason it has been transmitted from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and others related through Urwa that he asked Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about this verse. He said: I said: "Were they lied to, or were they denied?" Aisha said: "Rather, they were denied," meaning [that the reading is the heavier form]. I said: "Perhaps it is: 'and they thought that they had been lied to' (lightened)?" She said: "God forbid! The messengers would never think that about their Lord." I said: "Then what is this verse?" She said: "They are the followers of the messengers who believed in their Lord and affirmed them. The trial lasted long upon them, and the victory was delayed from them, until, when the messengers despaired of those among their people who denied them, and the messengers thought that their followers had denied them, the victory of Allah the Exalted came at that moment."

Some have answered that he, may Allah be pleased with him, may have meant by "thought" what occurs to the mind and passes through the heart of the whispers of doubt and inner speech, which is part of human nature. Majd ibn Taymiyya went to the view that all the pronouns also refer to the messengers, inclining to what was narrated from Ibn Abbas, claiming that this is the apparent meaning, and that the verse is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿When he wished, Satan cast into his wish; then Allah abrogates what Satan casts, then Allah establishes His verses﴾. For the casting into the heart, into the tongue, and into the deed is of one category, and Allah the Exalted abrogates what Satan casts. Then he said: "Zann is not used in the Book and the Sunnah to mean firm belief (i'tiqad rajih), as it is in the terminology of some scholars, who call a weak belief (i'tiqad marjuh) wahm (illusion)." The Prophet ﷺ said: «Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most untruthful of speech». And the Glorified said: ﴿Indeed, suspicion avails nothing against the truth﴾. So a weak belief is zann, and it is wahm, and this may be a sin that weakens faith without removing it, and it may be inner speech for which one is pardoned, as the Prince of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Allah the Exalted has overlooked for my community what their souls speak of, so long as they do not speak it or act upon it». And it may be of the kind of whispering which is the pure form of faith, as is established in the Sahih, that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "O Messenger of Allah, one of us finds in himself something that he would rather be burned to cinders or fall from the sky to the earth than speak of." He ﷺ said: «Have you indeed found it?» They said: "Yes." He said: «That is the pure form of faith». And in another hadith: «One of us finds something so great that he is ashamed to speak of it.» He said: «Praise be to Allah who has turned his scheming into whispering».
[p. 70]
A parallel to this is what is authentically reported from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «We have more right to doubt than Abraham, peace be upon him, when his Lord said to him: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾». So the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, called the difference between faith and tranquility of heart "doubt" concerning the reviving of the dead. On this basis it is said: the promise of victory in this world to a person may be something in which he believes in its fulfillment, but his heart may waver about it, so it is not at rest. The failure of tranquility then becomes a supposition that it is a lie. Doubt and the supposition that it is a lie are of one category. These matters do not impair obligatory faith, even if some of them are sins. The prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from being left to persist in such things, as in their actions, as is known from the principles of the Sunnah and the hadith. In the narration of such matters there is a lesson for the believers, peace be upon them, for they will inevitably be tested with something greater than that. So they should not despair when they are tested, and they should know that one greater than them was tested, and the outcome was good. Thus the doubter becomes certain, the sinner repents, and the believer's faith is strengthened. On this basis the emulation (ittisa') of the prophets is valid. For this reason the Glorified said: ﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson﴾. If the one who is followed were absolutely infallible, emulation would not be possible, for the follower would say: "I am not of his kind, for he is not to be reproached for a sin." So when he sins, the follower despairs of following and imitating him, because of the sin that he committed, which spoils the following on the view of infallibility. This is different from when it is known that something has occurred and has been made up for by repentance, for then the command to follow becomes valid, as it is said: "The first to sin, transgress and then repent and regret was Abu al-Bashar, Adam."
"And whoever resembles his father has not wronged."
And following them is not obligatory in what they were forbidden and committed and then repented of, because of the certainty of the command to follow them in what they affirmed, was not forbidden, and committed without repenting of it. What has been mentioned is no less than the abrogated actions of theirs: if what they were commanded to do, and were permitted, was afterward abrogated, the following is cut off in it. So what they were not commanded to do and did, and repented of, is more fitting and more appropriate for the cutting off of following in it. End.

It is not hidden that what he mentioned entails the possibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, committing major sins, and Allah forbid it, without persisting in them. To say this is great ignorance, and no one of sound heart would venture it. Moreover, his speech carries a distance of its own. Would that he had been content with making the pronouns refer to the messengers and interpreting "thought" as "supposition," as others have done, for that is harmless. Likewise there is no harm in understanding Ibn Abbas's words to mean that he intended by "thought" what occurs as whispering, and an example of it is inner speech, for that is other than the whispering from which the prophets, peace be upon them, are exempt. Or [it may be understood] that he intended by this the exaggeration of delay and the length of the period, by way of metaphorical allegory (isti'ara tamthiliyya, a metaphor built on an image), in that the resemblance of exaggerated delay to the supposition of a lie, by consideration that each of them entails the non-occurrence of the desired result, so the expression for one of them is used for the other. It is also said: the three pronouns refer to the people addressed, because the mention of the messengers demands that [reference]. A parallel to this is his saying:

"Did you see the lightning, which I watch, when it flashed, and I spent the night thinking it a dark, rushing cloud?"

Here the pronoun in "akhaluhu" refers to the thunder, which was not mentioned explicitly, but was dispensed with by the flash of lightning. Or, if you wish, you may say: their mention has already occurred in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen what was the end of those before them?﴾ So the pronoun refers to "those before them," from among those who denied the messengers, peace be upon them. The meaning is: the addressees supposed that the messengers had lied to them about what they claimed of prophethood, and about what they promised to those who did not believe, of punishment. This is also narrated from Ibn Abbas. Abu Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and others related through various chains from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to read "kudhibu" with the lightened form and say: "until, when the messengers despaired of their people that they would respond to them, and their people supposed that the messengers had..."
[p. 71]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 110 (part 2 of 2):

They denied them regarding what they had brought, when the messengers (the prophets) received Our help. This is also related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Rabi'ah ibn Kulthum, who said: My father told me that Muslim ibn Yasar asked Sa'id ibn Jubayr, saying: "O Abu 'Abd Allah, there is a verse that has troubled me greatly: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied﴾. Is it that the thought (zann) is that the messengers thought they had been lied to, or that they thought they had been denied (with the verb read in the passive, with a light or heavy consonant)?" Sa'id said: "Until, when the messengers despaired of their people responding to them, and their people thought that the messengers had lied to them, Our help came to them." Muslim then rose to him, embraced him, and said: "May Allah relieve you of your distress as you have relieved mine." It is also related that he said this in the presence of al-Dahhak, who said to him: "If you had travelled to Yemen for this, it would have been little."

It was also said: the pronoun in (ẓannū, "they thought") refers to those to whom the messengers were sent, and the pronoun in (annahum, "that they") and (kudhdhibū, "they were denied") refers to the messengers, peace be upon them. That is: they thought that the messengers, peace be upon them, had been let down regarding what they had been promised of help, and the matter became confused for them.

More than one of the Seven readers, along with al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', Ibn Abi Mulaykah, al-A'raj, and, according to the well-known report, 'Aishah, read (kudhdhibū, "they were denied") with the doubled letter and in the passive voice. On this reading the pronouns refer to the messengers, peace be upon them. That is: the messengers thought that their nations had denied them regarding what they had brought, because of the long duration of the trial upon them, and then the help of Allah the Exalted came to them at that moment. This is the explanation of 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, which al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, related. The "thought" (ẓann) here is taken in its own sense, or in the sense of certainty (yaqin), or of supposition (tawahhum).

From Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak it is related that they read (kudhdhibū) lightly and in the active voice. Then the pronoun in (ẓannū) refers to the nations, and the pronoun in ﴿annahum qad kudhdhibū, "that they had been denied"﴾ refers to the messengers. That is: those to whom the messengers were sent thought that the messengers had lied regarding the help or the punishment they had promised them.

It is also permissible that the pronoun in ﴿ẓannū﴾ refers to the messengers, and the pronoun in ﴿annahum qad kudhdhibū﴾ refers to those to whom they were sent. That is: the messengers, peace be upon them, thought that the nations had denied them regarding what they had promised them, namely that they would believe. The apparent meaning of the thought is, as has been said, that it is in the sense of certainty.

It has also been read, as Abu al-Baqa' said, (kadhdhabū) with the doubled letter and the active voice, and this was interpreted as meaning that the messengers, peace be upon them, thought that the nations had denied them in this promise of theirs.

The well-known objection concerning the verse is that, on the first reading, it apparently attributes an unfitting kind of thought to the noble prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. Some have also objected to attributing despair (istiya's) to them, peace be upon them, on the basis that the apparent meaning is that they despaired of what they had been promised and told would happen, and that this too is not fitting to attribute to them. It has been answered that this is not intended; rather, what is intended is that they despaired of the faith of their people.

It has been objected that the clause ﴿wa-ẓannū annahum qad kudhdhibū﴾, which apparently means that they thought they had been denied regarding what they had been promised, is far from this answer.

Al-Majd (al-Fayruzabadi) mentioned in this context something other than what he had mentioned first, namely that both the despair and the thought that they had been denied are connected to something added to what was promised, by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning). That is, the report of their despair is unrestricted, and there is nothing in the verse that indicates that it is limited to what they had been promised and told would happen. If that is so, it is known that when Allah the Exalted promises the messengers an unrestricted help, as is the general pattern of His announcements, its time, place, and manner are not specified. People often believe in the promised matter certain attributes that the speech of the Truth, exalted is He, did not indicate, but rather they believed them on the basis of other causes. Likewise, a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, believed that the Prophet's ﷺ announcement to them that they would enter the Sacred Mosque and circumambulate it would occur in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, because the Prophet ﷺ went out performing 'umrah and hoped to enter Makkah that year, circumambulate, and perform the sa'y (running between al-Safa and al-Marwah). When they despaired of that in that year, after the polytheists prevented them, until he, peace be upon him, agreed with them to the well-known treaty, something remained in the hearts of some of them. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, although he was among the muhaddithun (scholars of hadith), said: "Did you not tell us, O Messenger of Allah, that we would enter the House and circumambulate it?" He said: "Yes. Did I tell you that you would enter it this year?" He said: "No." He said: "You will enter it and circumambulate it." Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said the same to him. So he made clear that the promise from him, peace be upon him, was unrestricted and not bound to a time. That the Prophet ﷺ went toward Makkah in that year and intended it does not necessitate restricting the promise of Allah the Exalted to entering in that year. Perhaps he, peace and blessings be upon him, only set out on the basis of the supposition that the matter would be so, and it was not, and there is no harm in that. It is not a condition for the Prophet ﷺ that everything he intends must happen. Rather, it is among the completions of Allah's blessing upon him that He turns him from what he intends to another matter that is more beneficial than what he intended, as was the case in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. Nor does it harm that the matter came out contrary to what he, peace be upon him, supposed. Muslim related in his Sahih that he, peace be upon him, said regarding the pollination of palm trees (ta'bir al-nakhl): "I only supposed a supposition, so do not hold me to account for supposition; but when I tell you something from Allah the Exalted, take it, for I will never lie about Allah the Exalted." From the same category is his ﷺ saying in the hadith of Dhu al-Yadayn: "The prayer was not shortened, nor have I forgotten," then it became clear that he had forgotten. In the story of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah, concerning whom the verse was revealed: ﴿If a degenerate comes to you with news, verify it﴾, and in the story of the Banu Ubayriq, concerning whom it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾, there is sufficient evidence that he ﷺ may suppose something and then Allah the Exalted makes it clear in another way. If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who is what he is, is like this, then what do you think of the other noble messengers, peace and blessings be upon them?

What strengthens this is that the majority of muhaddithun and fuqaha' hold that it is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to exercise ijtihad in the legal rulings of the Sharia, and that error in this is permissible for them, but they are not left to persist in it. There is no doubt that this is less serious than error in supposing what is not among the legal rulings of the Sharia at all. Once this is established, it is not far-fetched to say that those messengers, peace be upon them, were informed of the punishment of their people but no specific time was given for it to them. So they exercised ijtihad and fixed a time for it according to what appeared to them, just as the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fixed the year of al-Hudaybiyah for entering Makkah. When the period lengthened, they despaired and supposed that their own selves had lied (to them), and their ijtihad had erred. There is in this no supposition that the promise of Allah the Exalted is false, nor does it imply that at all, so there is no harm. You know that what is more in keeping with the glorification of the messengers, peace be upon them, and further from hovering around the sacred boundary of what is not fitting for them, is to refrain from attributing supposition to anyone other than them, may Allah the Exalted bless and grant peace to them. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿jā'ahum﴾ (came to them), in all the readings and aspects, refers to the messengers. It has also been said that it refers to them and to the believers: ﴿jā'a al-rusula wa-man āmana bihim naṣruna﴾ (the help of Us came to the messengers and to those who believed in them). ﴿fa-nujjiya man nashā'﴾ (so whomever We willed was delivered): He delivered them, and they are the messengers and the believers who followed them. They were not specified by name, to indicate that they are the ones who deserve that Allah wills their deliverance, and no one else shares in that with them.

ʿāṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Yaʿqūb read (fa-nujjiya) with a single nūn, a doubled jīm, and an open yā', as a past-tense verb in the passive voice, with (man) as its deputy subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil). Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Talhah, and Ibn Hurmuz read it likewise, except that they made the yā' quiescent. It is interpreted as a past-tense verb as well, as in the previous reading, except that the yā' was made quiescent according to the dialect of those who find vowel-movement on the yā' burdensome in all cases. An example of this is the reading of one who read (mā tuṭʿimūna ahlīkum, "what you feed your families") with a quiescent yā'.

It has been said that the original form was nunjī with two nūns, and the first nūn was assimilated (idgham) into the jīm. Abu Hayyan rejected this on the grounds that the nūn is not assimilated into it. It was answered that some have held that its assimilation is permissible. This reading is related from al-Kisa'i and Nafi'.

A group read, as the rest of the Seven read, with two nūns, as the present-tense form of unjiya, except that they opened the yā'. Hubayrah related it from Hafs from ʿāṣim. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah claimed that this was an error on Hubayrah's part, since there is no justification for the fatha. Abu Hayyan replied that the justification is apparent, for they have mentioned that after a conditional particle and its response, the present tense may come in the subjunctive, with an implied (an) after the fa', as in the reading of one who read (wa-in tubdū mā fī anfusikum aw tukhfūhu yuḥāsibkum bihi Allāh fa-yaghfira, "and if you reveal what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it, so He forgives") with the subjunctive on yaghfira. There is no difference in this between the conditional particle being a jussive-governing particle or not.

Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Abu Ḥaywah, Ibn al-Samayqaʿ, ʿĪsā al-Baṣrah, Ibn Muḥaysin, and likewise al-Hasan and Mujahid in one narration, read (fa-najā) as a past-tense verb with a light consonant, with (man) as its subject. It is related from Ibn Muhaysin that he read it likewise, except that he doubled the jīm, and in that case the subject is the pronoun of the help, and (man) is its object.

The reading of ʿĀṣim and those with him has been preferred, because the copies of the mushaf agree on writing it with a single nūn. Makki said: "Most copies of the mushaf have it so," and I am thus aware of a difference regarding the orthography. The claim of consensus was related from al-Ja'bari, Ibn al-Jazari, and others. From al-Ja'bari it is also said that the reading of one who read with two nūns agrees with the orthography in terms of its implied form, because the second nūn is quiescent and hidden (ikhfā') before the jīm, just as it is hidden before the ṣād and the ẓā' in (lanansuru, "we will surely help"). Ikhfā' (concealment), since it is a kind of covering, resembles idgham, since it is a kind of disappearance. Just as it is elided in idgham, it is elided in ikhfā'; indeed, according to him it is more fitting in this case because of the closeness of the connection.

It is related from Abu Ḥaywah that he read (fa-nujjiya man yashā'), with the third-person yā' (ghaybah), meaning: whomever Allah the Exalted wills to deliver.

﴿And the punishment of Us is not turned back from the criminal people﴾ (110): when it descends upon them. In it is a clarification of who is the object of the will, for it is understood from the contrast that those who are not criminals are the ones intended. Al-Hasan read (ba'suhu, "His punishment") with a third-person pronoun, meaning: the punishment of Allah the Exalted. What the sentence contains of threat and warning for the contemporaries of the Prophet, may Allah bless him, is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 12, verse 111 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Certainly there was in their stories﴾, that is, the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their nations. It has also been said: the story of Yusuf, his father, and his brothers, peace be upon them. This was narrated from Mujahid. It has also been said: the stories of those and these. The word *qasas* (stories) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle. Al-Zamakhshari preferred the first view on the basis of the recitation of Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, reported from al-Kisa'i and from Abd al-Warith, from Abu Amr, *qişaşihim* (with a kasra on the *qaf*), the plural of *qişşa* (a story). This was refuted on the grounds that the story of Yusuf, his father, and his brothers contains various stories and reports, and also that the plural may be used for the singular. It was answered that this is as has been said, but it is contrary to what is ordinarily understood, since in such a case one says *qişşa* for *qişaş*. Ibn Atiyya confined himself to the third view, and his preference for it is clear. ﴿A lesson for people of understanding﴾, that is, for those whose intellects are free from the illusions arising from habit and the senses. The root *lubb* means the pure essence of a thing; then it was applied to the purified part of the intellect. Thus every *lubb* is an intellect, but not every intellect is a *lubb*. Many have said that *lubb* is the intellect in general, and it was so named because it is the purest of a human being's faculties. It occurs in the Qur'an only in the plural. The *ibra* (lesson), as al-Raghib said, is the state through which one arrives from knowledge of what is observed to what is not observed. In al-Bahr it is said to be the indication by which one passes over to knowledge. ﴿It was not﴾, that is, the Qur'an, indicated by what has preceded, a clear indication. Abu Hayyan favoured the pronoun referring to the stories mentioned before. Some preferred the first view, because it works with both recitations, unlike referring it to the preceding noun, which does not work with the recitation *qişaş* with a kasra on the *qaf*, since the pronoun would then have to be feminine. Some permitted its reference to *qaşaş* in the recitation with the fatha, and to the kasra-reading in that recitation as well, and likewise to the kasra-reading itself. The masculine form is due to the predicate. This, as you see, is [weak]. ﴿A narrative that is invented﴾, that is, fabricated. ﴿But it is a confirmation of what was before it﴾ of the heavenly scriptures, ﴿and a detailed explanation﴾, that is, a clarification ﴿of all things﴾. It has been said: that is, of what is needed in religion, since there is no religious matter that does not rest upon the Qur'an, either directly or through an intermediary. Ibn al-Kamal said: *kull* (all) here is for emphasis and magnification, not for comprehensiveness and generality, as in His saying: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾. Whoever has not noticed this has needed to restrict the word "thing" to what relates to religion, and then labored to explain it, saying: "since there is no religious matter..." etc., and did not realize that the expression "detailed explanation" cannot bear this interpretation. It was answered that whenever the word *kull* can be taken in its true general sense, it is not to be taken in another sense, and that restriction is not objectionable. Moreover, he himself committed this in his explanation of His saying: ﴿and a detailed explanation of all things﴾. That the expression "detailed explanation" cannot bear that interpretation is open to dispute. Some people took *kull* in the general sense without restriction, holding that the Qur'an contains an explanation of everything of the affairs of religion and of the world and other matters that God wills. But the degrees of explanation vary according to the variation among people of knowledge, and this is not far-fetched for one who has a heart or gives ear while being a witness. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the detailed explanation of every event that befell Yusuf, his father, and his brothers, peace be upon them, which is of concern. This is based on the view that the pronoun in *kana* (was) refers to "their stories". ﴿And guidance﴾ from error, ﴿and mercy﴾ by which one attains the good of both abodes, ﴿for a people who believe﴾. (111) They affirm with a true affirmation. They are singled out for mention because they are the ones who benefit from it. *Tasdiq* (confirmation) is in the accusative as the predicate of the omitted *kana*, meaning: "but it was a confirmation". The use of a verbal noun as a predicate is not obscure.

Hamran ibn A'yan and Isa al-Kufi, as mentioned by the author of al-Lawami', and Isa al-Thaqafi, as mentioned by Ibn Atiyya, read *tasdiqu* in the nominative, and likewise the nominative for what is coordinated with it, on the assumption: "but it is a confirmation..." etc. The Arabs have used both the nominative and the accusative in such cases. Among them is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

*And my wealth was not an inheritance I had received, nor was it blood-money, nor gain from a sin.*
*But the gift of God from every journey, to every one veiled in curtains, bearing the burden.*

It is narrated with *ata'* in the accusative and in the nominative. And God, the Exalted, is the guide to the right path.

* * *

(From the allusive meanings in this surah) He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. It is the narration of what happened to Yusuf, his father, and his brothers, peace be upon them. This was the best of stories because it includes mention of the lover and the beloved, which souls find delightful, or because it shows the realities of the love of lovers and the purity of the secret of the knowers, and alerts to the good ends of the truthful, and urges following the path of those who rely upon God, and emulating the asceticism of the ascetics, and indicates severance to God and dependence upon Him when calamities descend, and reveals the states of traitors and the ugliness of the ways of liars, and tests the elect with various kinds of trials and changes them into various kinds of favours and bounties, along with mention of what indicates the governance of kings and their conduct toward their subjects, and so on. It has also been said: because it is free of commands and prohibitions, the hearing of which occupies the heart. ﴿When Yusuf said to his father: "O my father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾ This is the first beginning of unveilings, for they mention that the states of those who receive unveilings begin with dreams, and when the state grows strong, the vision becomes unveiling. It has been said: he, peace be upon him, was led in a manner similar to that in which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was led, for he began with true dreams, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began with them, so that he saw no dream except that it was like the break of dawn. Then solitude was made beloved to him, as indicated by his saying: ﴿My Lord, the prison is dearer to me﴾, just as solitude was made beloved to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so that he would seclude himself in the cave of Hira for many nights. But it may be objected that the story of the prison came after he was given prophethood. So reflect.

One of the great scholars mentioned that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was the second Adam, because of the garment of lordship that he wore, the same as that which Adam, peace be upon him, wore, and he was the locus of the manifestation of the Truth to creation, *if only they knew*. When the angels saw what they saw of Adam, they prostrated to him. Here, those who prostrated to Yusuf were the sun, the moon, and the stars counted, indicated by his parents and brothers, who, according to the view of their prophethood, are better than the angels, peace be upon them. And it is no wonder that they prostrated to one from whose face holy lights and spiritual rays shine.

*If they could hear as I heard her talk, they would fall before Azza in bowing and prostration.*

It may also be said: when Abraham, peace be upon him, saw in the cheek of the star, the spot of the moon, and the brow of the sun the signs of having come into being, he turned his face from them toward the court of eternity, exalted above change and guarded from whatever entails deficiency, saying: ﴿Indeed I am free of what you associate﴾. God, the Exalted, made the sun and the moon prostrate, and made stars of some of his sons prostrate in place of the stars, in magnification of his affair and as an emphasis on exalting the majesty of greatness. Since disavowal was delayed until the third, the prostration was delayed until the third of the sons. The intention of this is only to explain some of the secrets of singling out the one mentioned for the vision, though it is possible that there was something that could be his dream of prostration, interpreted through the prostration of his parents and brothers to him, peace be upon them, in the world of beauty. So reflect.

﴿He said: "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers."﴾ In this there is an allusion to some of the etiquette of the disciples, for they have said: they should not disclose the secret of unveiling except to their shaykhs, and should not fall into peril, and should not be subject to the eyes of jealousy.

*If they divulge the secret, their blood is made lawful, and likewise the blood of those who divulge is made lawful.*

﴿Lest they plot a plot against you﴾. This is one of the general inspirations, which are warnings and good tidings. It is possible that he, peace be upon him, knew this from the dream. Some have said: Jacob arranged for Yusuf, peace be upon them both, at that time out of fear for him, and so he was left to his own arrangement, and what befell him befell. Had he left the arrangement and returned to submission, he would have been protected. ﴿Certainly there were in Yusuf and his brothers signs for those who ask﴾. These include the shining rays of the Truth from his face, the appearance of knowledge of the unseen from him, the abundance of generosity in his deeds, the good outcome of patience in its end, the evil state of the envious, and the fact that what God has decreed cannot be annulled, and other things. Some have said: among the signs in Yusuf, peace be upon him, is that he is a proof against everyone whom God has made beautiful in form, that he should not disfigure it by disobedience. Whoever does not observe God's blessing and disobeys is most like a whitewashed privy or dung adorned with silver.

Ibn Ata' said: among the signs is that no sorrowful believer hears this story and believes in it without finding relief and consolation from what it contains.

﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.﴾ It has been said: this weeping was that of joy at their success in attaining their aim, but they made it appear as weeping of grief over the loss of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It has also been said: it was not real weeping, but feigned weeping without tears. They came in the evening so that they would be bolder in offering excuses in the darkness, or in order to deceive their father and make him think that it was real weeping and not feigned, for had they come in the morning they would have been exposed.

*When tears mingle upon the cheeks, it becomes clear who wept from among those who feigned.*

﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. It is tranquillity before the decrees of destiny, in secret and openly. Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: beautiful patience is to meet trial with a broad heart and a joyful face. Al-Tirmidhi said: it is that the servant surrenders his reins to his Master and gives himself over to Him, along with true knowledge. When one of His judgments comes, he remains steadfast, submitting, and does not show distress at its arrival, nor appear troubled by it. Al-Shibli recited on the reality of patience:

*Tears have traced a line upon the cheek, and whoever has never read will read it clearly.*
*The patient one of patience sought help from patience, so the lover cried out to patience: "Patience!"*
